# GEMS Research · iGEM 2026 Report

A review of the iGEM 2026 Top 10 teams across all three sections, every special prize winner and nominee, and the academic and industry currents around them. Live site: https://timmy97-tw.github.io/2026GEMSReport/


# Results
- **Undergrad** — Stanford University (Therapeutics, United States) · 1st Runner-up UCAS-China; 2nd Runner-up Princeton
- **Overgrad** — TU Delft (Biomanufacturing, Netherlands) · 1st Runner-up WageningenUR
- **High School** — Lambert-GA (Conservation, United States) · 1st Runner-up HongKong-JSS
- **Top 10 Undergrad** — Cornell, Heidelberg, LYON, NUS-Singapore, Princeton, Stanford University, UAlberta, UCAS-China, UCNZ, UOttawa
- **Top 10 Overgrad** — Athens, ETH-Zurich, GU Frankfurt, KAUST-KSA, Marburg, Muenster-University, Toronto, TU Delft, UZurich, WageningenUR
- **Top 10 High School** — Eton-College-UK, GCGS, GEMS-Taiwan, GHCIS, HangzhouFourteenAP, HFI, HKSSC, HongKong-HS, HongKong-JSS, Lambert-GA


# Overview

## 18 findings, and where to read each one

_The 2026 Best Wiki winners all build a layer like this — each claim in two sentences, with a link straight to the evidence. It works, so this report does it too._

### Closing the model–data loop is the single best predictor of a Top 10
Teams that both fit a model to their own measured data and validate it against something held back reached a Top 10 at **53%**; teams that did not, at **23%** — less than half the rate. All nine who closed the loop without a Top 10 won or were nominated for a major special prize anyway. It needs no GPU and no licence.

### At high-school level the gap is evaluation discipline, not tools
Eton-College-UK used logistic regression and a PSSM but ran cluster-aware cross-validation, a label-shuffle control and an ablation. Lambert-GA won Best Model for benchmarking the confidence metrics themselves and publishing that its own hit was not top-scoring. GCGS reached the Top 10 with no model page at all.

### 8 of 21 award-winning tools are still usable, and the reason is hosting
Every live tool was hosted on wiki-freeze day; every source-only tool's wiki lists localhost as its only address. Not a coding or budget decision — a hosting decision made months early. Two high-school teams out-shipped most of the universities. Stars and forks across every repo checked: zero.

### The best figures build the reader's doubt into the picture
GEMS-Taiwan's provenance rail turns amber exactly where measurement stops and modelling begins. DKU gives "not assessed" its own verdict so an unmeasured gate cannot read as a passed one. Mingdao's captions carry the instrument, the buffer, the replicate count and a link to the raw CSV. DTU shows which stakeholders never replied.

### The deadline, not the people, is what limits Science for Good
8 of 21 award-winning software tools still run, every repository checked has zero stars and zero forks, no team in 106 ran an inter-lab measurement ring, and only nine or ten of 71 closed loops were closed by a non-expert. These are deadline artefacts. GEMS's answer is a **club-form programme with no deadline**, carrying a few problems across years — its definition, criteria and current pipeline are on this tab.

### The loops that closed were closed by experts, not by publics
Of all 106 decorated teams, **71** can point at a stakeholder who visibly changed the design. But almost every one of those stakeholders was a credentialled technical expert. The publics, patients and communities the criterion is rhetorically about changed the vocabulary and not the vector, with **nine or ten exceptions in 106**. (The first pass scored 93 files and found 64 and six-to-seven; the figures here are the recount on the closed set.)

### The best education work was designed from data and measured like an experiment
UCAS-China made compliance the target after a 461-person questionnaire, not awareness. GU Frankfurt sent nineteen members to a professional science-communication course first. Oxford built a podcast that deliberately pairs stakeholders who disagree. And the sharpest teams publish the lesson that failed.

### The credible commercial sections published a model showing their own product losing
Worldshaper-Shanghai reports a negative NPV for its own enzyme. DTU-Denmark's LCA finds cement co-processing beats its route on almost every indicator, then converts each loss into an engineering target. Stockholm dismantled its venture when the safety board killed open-water release — and won the Safety and Security Award.

### Best Wiki winners ship an executive layer, not better graphics
Three of the four serve text that is readable before any script runs; the fourth mirrors every page as Markdown. All four build a layer that answers each medal criterion in two or three sentences and deep-links the evidence, failures included. Dark mode, late alt-text sweeps and mascot systems correlate with nothing.

### Taiwan won well, but only in the high-school tier
Thirteen competing teams returned six award wins — more than any East Asian territory except China, and more than Hong Kong on fewer teams. But every technical award came from the high-school tier, there were zero nominations in any parts award and zero in Best Software, and Hong Kong tripled Taiwan's Top 10 count.

### The divide is not medical versus agricultural — it is platform versus applied
Therapeutics teams close loops with non-experts about as often as bioremediation teams do. What actually separates the field is whether anyone outside a lab ever operates the thing: across the platform villages — Foundational Advance, Space, Software & AI, Biomanufacturing — **2 of 26** decorated teams closed a design loop at all, against **14 of 45** in the applied villages.

### Nobody ran an inter-lab measurement ring — in a competition about measurement
69 of 106 decorated teams record working with another team, but almost all of it is meet-ups. **Not one** ran an inter-lab measurement ring, and collaboration does not predict placing: substantive collaborators reached a Top 10 at 29%, attendance-only teams at 48%. The one team that offered to do real shared work publicly got **zero replies** — and won Best Software and Best Wiki anyway.

### Nobody measured an escape rate
19 of 106 decorated teams describe a genetic containment device. **Zero** report a measured escape frequency, and only two name a DNA-synthesis screening regime. The sharpest result in the category is a negative one: the Safety winner found that a published Addgene kill switch failed first, weeks before its own circuits.

### Winning parts are won on documentation, not on novelty
Winners' headline parts carry **10,388 to 83,030 characters** of registry documentation across three to six typed documents; sampled nominee parts carry 440 to 2,500, usually Design only. The high-school basic-part winner is a 247 bp native promoter copied from GenBank. Both improved-part awards had **zero nominees** — the cheapest category in iGEM to enter.

### Measurement discipline does not win anything — do it anyway
Across 39 wikis read directly: 97% show a blank control, 72% calibrate into an absolute unit, but only **15%** compute a limit of detection for their own assay and **5%** ever measure one sample twice. And it does not predict placing: over all 106 files, teams mentioning calibration reached a Top 10 at 27% against 29%. **No effect.** The Best Measurement winner's nine pages contain the words *error bar* and *standard deviation* zero times.

### Six of twenty instruments could be rebuilt by a stranger
Across the 2026 Best Hardware, Best Measurement and Best Alternative Platform cohorts, 20 instruments were built and **6** publish enough — bill of materials, geometry files, firmware, assembly guide — for someone in another country to rebuild them. **Nine publish no geometry file at all.** Exactly one has ever been used by anyone outside the team that built it.

### Everyone disclosed their AI use — the argument is over what counts as AI
The expected finding was that almost nobody disclosed. The actual finding is **106 of 106**, because iGEM 2026 made AI Tool Use a required block of a Bronze medal deliverable — a requirement produced total compliance overnight. But only **4 of 106** state what AI did *not* do, and of the 40 teams using a foundation model, only 15 file it as AI at all. AlphaFold is filed as biology.

### One team in 106 shines light on B. subtilis, and it is this one
Both trend reviews independently named optogenetic control in *Bacillus subtilis* as the white space this roadmap should aim at — a twelve-paper literature in all of PubMed. The census tested that against the competition itself. **5 of 106** used light as a control input in any organism; **5 of 106** worked with *B. subtilis*; the two sets overlap in exactly **one** team, which is GEMS-Taiwan. Outside GEMS the intersection is **0 of 105**. The gap in the literature is mirrored precisely in iGEM, and nobody in this cohort is competing for it.

_Method and limits. Each card summarises an analysis published in full on the tab it links to, where the evidence, the named teams and the limits of the method are set out. Where a finding rests on a number, the analysis says how the number was computed and what it cannot see._

## Two questions, thirty teams

_This report asks the same two questions of every team it looks at._

The first question is computational. Where does a project stop being wet biology and start being a model, a pipeline, a dataset, a piece of software? What did that layer actually decide — did it change an experiment, or was it decoration added after the fact? The teams that win are increasingly the ones where the answer is "it changed the experiment".

The second question is social. Who outside the team touched this project, and what did they change about it? A list of meetings is not integrated human practices. A design that is visibly different because somebody outside the lab said something is.

That second question is asked here in iGEM's terms because that is what the evidence is made of — but it is not what **Science for Good** means at GEMS. At GEMS it names a club-form programme with no competition deadline, carrying a few well-chosen problems across years rather than seasons: problems that matter to someone outside GEMS, that can actually be deployed, whose effect can be counted, and that get cheaper as they spread. The Science for Good tab sets out that definition, what is currently in the pipeline, and what the 2026 cohort's record says about which work survives a deadline and which does not.

Everything else here — the trend tabs, the roadmap — exists to answer a third question that only GEMS Research can answer: given what 2026 looked like, what should a growing research institution in Taiwan be building in 2027 and beyond?


# Dry lab

## What 2026's best teams actually reached for

_A census of the computational tools named across all 106 team files in this report — and the one habit that separates the podium from everybody else._

Across the 106 team files gathered here, **AlphaFold is still the default**: it is named by 32 teams, more than any other modelling tool and four times as often as Boltz. ProteinMPNN appears in 14 files, Rosetta in 12, ESMFold and RFdiffusion in 8 each. The academic literature has already moved past this — open models now match or beat the gated flagship — but iGEM has not caught up. That lag is an opportunity: a team that works fluently with the current open stack is doing something most of the competition is not.

The second pattern is that **the dedicated systems-biology tools have quietly lost**. COPASI, once the standard way an iGEM team built a kinetic model, appears in **one** file out of 106. Tellurium appears in one. MATLAB holds on in five. Everything else is Python — named by 44 teams, more than any other single item in the census, usually SciPy integrating an ODE system written by hand, with scikit-learn behind it in 12 files for anything statistical. Teaching COPASI as the entry point to modelling now teaches a tool the field has left behind.

The third pattern is the surprise. **Techno-economic analysis — costing the thing, modelling unit economics — is done by more high-school teams than undergraduate ones**: 11 against 8, and a far higher share of a smaller tier. High-school teams are being pushed hard on implementation and business thinking, and they are delivering it. Meanwhile GROMACS, full molecular dynamics, appears in 7 undergraduate files, 1 overgraduate file and **never once** in a high-school one. The two tiers are not weaker and stronger versions of each other; they are differently shaped.

**Then the finding that matters.** We checked which teams do both halves of modelling properly: fit the model to their own measured data (parameter estimation, regression, R², RMSE, confidence intervals, error bars) *and* validate it against something held back (held-out data, cross-validation, a separate experimental test). Only **19 of 106** teams do both.

Of those 19, **10 are Top 10 teams — 53%**. Of the 87 that do not close the loop, 20 are Top 10 — **23%**. A team that closes the model–data loop is more than twice as likely to place. And of the nine who closed it without reaching a Top 10, every one still won or was nominated for a major special prize: XJTLU-China and Jilin-China in Best Model, NJU-China took Best Software & AI Project, UBC-Vancouver took Best Diagnostics, CAU-China took Best Food & Nutrition.

This is the single most actionable number in the report. Not which model you use — whether you close the loop between the model and your own data. It is also, conveniently, the cheapest capability to build: it needs no GPU, no licence and no collaboration. It needs a student who knows what a residual is.

### 53% versus 23%
Teams that both fit their model to their own data and validated it against something held back reached a Top 10 at 53%. Teams that did not reached it at 23% — less than half the rate. Note the sample is already decorated: every team here is a Top 10 or special-prize winner or nominee, so this is loop-closure separating winners from other winners, not from the general field.

### AlphaFold has not been displaced inside iGEM
32 of 106 teams name AlphaFold, four times the rate of Boltz. The research literature moved to the open stack over the past year; the competition has not. The teams already working in Boltz and the MPNN family — Lambert-GA, Heidelberg, GU Frankfurt, DTU-Denmark, Princeton — are visibly ahead of the curve rather than merely current.

### Python ate the modelling stack
COPASI appears once in 106 files. Tellurium once. MATLAB five times. Python appears in 44 team files, more than any other item in the census, usually SciPy integrating a hand-written ODE system, with scikit-learn behind it for anything statistical. For a programme deciding what to teach, this settles the question: teach Python and the numerical stack, and treat SBML-based tools as an interchange format rather than a starting point.

### High-school teams cost their projects; undergraduates often don't
Techno-economic analysis appears in 11 high-school files against 8 undergraduate ones, and in a far higher share of the smaller tier. Full molecular dynamics runs the other way: 7 undergraduate files, 1 overgraduate, and never once in a high-school file. The tiers are differently shaped rather than simply further apart, and a high-school programme that assumes it must catch up on everything is aiming at the wrong gap.

### Publishing your failures: an effect that shrank when we added data
Several analysts noticed the same thing independently — Toronto, WageningenUR and UZurich each put a prominent negative result on the wiki, and two won the award in that exact category. On the first 54 files the pattern looked real: 54% against 41%. Re-run across all 106 it collapses to **33% against 27%**, and the measurement was always partly circular — it detects how candid *our own summary* of a team was, not reliably how candid the team was. We are leaving it in because reporting the finding that weakened is the same discipline the rest of this page is about. Publish the negative result because it is honest, not because it wins prizes.

### The cheapest capability is the one that correlates with winning
Closing the model-data loop needs no GPU, no licence, no partner lab and no new chassis. It needs a student who can fit a curve, report an uncertainty and hold data back for a test. That is a term's teaching, and on this evidence it moves the result more than any tool choice. It is Phase 2 of the roadmap for exactly this reason.

_Method and limits. Counts come from pattern-matching the dry-lab and science-for-good fields of all 106 team files in this report, not from reading the wikis a second time, so a technique a team used but did not write up is invisible here. The sample is decorated teams only — every file is a Top 10 or special-prize winner or nominee — so the baselines are not the whole competition. The loop-closure test looks for explicit language about fitting, uncertainty and validation; a team that did the work but described it loosely will be undercounted. An earlier version of this page reported 71% against 40% from a 54-file snapshot taken while research was still landing; the figures above supersede it. Read the numbers as a ranking, not a measurement._

## The high-school ceiling, measured honestly

_What a high-school dry lab can actually reach in one season — and the finding that the gap is not about tools._

Read the ten High School Top 10 dry labs side by side and the first surprise is how ordinary the software is. **Eton-College-UK** built its protease substrate predictor out of L2-regularised logistic regression and a BLOSUM62-smoothed position-specific scoring matrix — techniques older than the students using them. **HFI** used NetLogo, which is free and was designed for schools. **GHCIS** used a local install of NUPACK. **HangzhouFourteenAP** used PyMOL and FoldX. **HKSSC** used AlphaFold, UCSF Chimera and HotSpot Wizard. **HongKong-HS** reused another team's tool outright — miRADAR, released by Wageningen's 2024 team — rather than rebuilding it. Almost none of this costs money, and none of it requires a cluster.

Only **Lambert-GA**, the Grand Prize winner, works at the frontier of the toolchain: BindCraft, Boltz-2, Protenix, Mosaic. And even there the thing that earned Best Model was not the tools. It was that they **benchmarked the confidence metrics themselves** — ipSAE, ipTM and a 38-metric ensemble, against 5,721 labelled experimental designs — found the ensemble barely beat chance at ROC-AUC 0.541, noticed that their own eventual hit did not have the best score, and published all of that rather than quietly reporting the hit.

That is the pattern, and it holds across the whole tier. **The differentiator at high-school level is evaluation discipline, not tool sophistication.**

The evidence is specific. Eton clustered near-duplicate sequences by Hamming distance and split whole clusters across folds, then ran a label-shuffle control and a composition-only ablation — three cheap steps that separate a real classifier from a leaky one. **HongKong-JSS** split runs into calibration and validation *before* fitting anything, subtracted a matched control from the same run and timepoint, and reported RMSE on held-out runs with the failures left in. HKSSC could not measure molar enzyme concentration, so rather than report an invalid *k*cat/*K*m they defined and justified a mass-normalised metric valid only below *K*m, then ran a two-way ANOVA, found unequal variances, and moved to a median-based test. GHCIS specified its colour-classification algorithm down to the equation and the threshold, including an explicit **"unresolved, and must not be read as Negative"** state, and shipped it with one-command Docker deployment. HangzhouFourteenAP reported the prediction that lost: FoldX ranked Y166Q first, the bench preferred Q172P, and the wiki revises its own ranking while using BCA normalisation to rule out protein load as the explanation.

**GEMS-Taiwan** belongs on that list and is worth reading closely, because the wiki is unusually candid about its own weaknesses. The strengths are real: a genuinely pre-registered growth-rate forecast, registered on 1 October and scored on run 6, which landed inside its stated interval; an autoencoder that flagged a failing photometer 26.7 hours before it died; and a crop-stress index fitted to 25 years of county rice yields rather than to expert judgement. The weaknesses are stated by the team itself: secreted activity at n=1 and below the limit of quantitation; two induction runs that disagree on the *sign* of the change; a Hill curve assumed to hold at 20 L when every induction ran at a single light intensity; a 2.44× rice canopy correction that is modelled, not measured; an efficacy coefficient of 0.58 explicitly withdrawn; and a payback period of 68 years on the team's own loss figure against a partner's 4.9 years, with the disagreement named rather than resolved. Naming the disagreement instead of picking the flattering number is the practice worth keeping.

**And the control case.** **GCGS** reached the High School Top 10 with no model page and no software page at all — both routes return 404. Its one modelling claim is an undocumented circuit-level simulation with no parameters, equations or tooling named. A team can still place in the top ten of its section with essentially no dry lab. What GCGS could not do is win a modelling, measurement or software prize, and that is the precise shape of the opportunity.

### Lambert-GA, and what the frontier costs
Four linked models: protein-design metric benchmarking on 5,721 labelled designs, a Sobol-analysed oral pharmacokinetic model, a 13-ODE SimBiology RNAi network, and an individual-based six-year, 800-run colony epidemiology. They produced the first reported DWV VP3 minibinder for under $400 of compute, released the open-source PRINCE site ranker (45.8% top-3 hit rate against 23.8% random on a no-homolog subset), and an $80 dryer externally validated at two universities. This is the ceiling, and it is reachable.

### GCGS: Top 10 with no dry lab at all
Both /model and /software return 404. The single modelling claim is an undocumented circuit-level simulation with no parameters, equations or tooling named. GCGS still reached the High School Top 10 on the strength of a clean two-cycle DBTL and its Best New Improved Part. Read it as the honest floor: the dry lab is not what gets you into the top ten — it is what gets you a prize.

### Three cheap controls that separate real from leaky
From Eton-College-UK, and transferable to any student machine-learning project: cluster near-duplicate sequences by Hamming distance and split whole clusters across folds, so the model cannot memorise a near-copy; run a label-shuffle control, which must collapse to chance; run an ablation that strips the information you claim to be using. None of these needs a GPU. Together they turn a high-school classifier into something a reviewer can believe.

### Split before you fit
HongKong-JSS divided its runs into calibration and validation before fitting anything, subtracted a matched control from the same run and timepoint, inverted the fit to predict unknowns, and reported RMSE on the held-out runs with the failures left in — then published a list of the statistics they had not yet done. That last habit is rarer and more valuable than the first.

### Publish the prediction that lost
HangzhouFourteenAP's FoldX pipeline ranked Y166Q first; the bench preferred Q172P. Rather than bury it, the wiki revises its own ranking, demotes the failed candidate to a mechanistic probe, and uses BCA normalisation to rule out protein load as the confound. Lambert-GA did the same at a larger scale by showing its own hit was not the top-scoring design. A dry lab earns more credibility from one well-controlled loss than from three unexamined wins.

### The gap is one term of teaching, not a budget line
Every practice above — cluster-aware splits, label-shuffle controls, calibration/validation separation, provenance tagging, publishing the loss — costs nothing but attention and can be taught in a term. The tools the 2026 high-school field actually used are free: NetLogo, NUPACK, PyMOL, FoldX, scikit-learn, ImageJ, Chimera, the AlphaFold server. GEMS does not need to buy its way to the ceiling. It needs to make evaluation discipline the house style.

_Method and limits. Drawn from the ten High School Top 10 team files in this report, each researched from the team's own 2026 wiki. Tool lists are what each team names; a team may have used more than it wrote down. The judgement about what 'stands out' is ours, and a reader who disagrees should open the team file and the wiki behind it — both are linked. GEMS-Taiwan is the report author's own team and has been assessed on the same terms as the rest._

## Does award-winning iGEM software survive the Jamboree?

_Of 21 software tools released by award-winning iGEM 2026 teams, 8 are live and usable by a stranger today, 11 are source-only, and 2 have already gone dark._

**Eight of twenty-one.** That is the honest base rate for award-winning iGEM 2026 software that a stranger can open and use today, four weeks after the Jamboree. Eleven more are source-only: the code is public, populated and often genuinely good, but using it means cloning a repository and running Docker. Two are already dead — Vilnius-Lithuania's Ladder Detector now answers "This service has been suspended by its owner" at ladder-detector.onrender.com, and TAU-Israel's CERNAL fails to resolve at both cernal.app and cernal.duckdns.org, the two addresses its own wiki advertises.

The striking thing is that nothing is a stub. Every repository checked was populated with real code, a README and a licence. iGEM's mandatory GitLab deposit has solved the empty-repo problem completely. What it has not solved, and cannot, is hosting: the competition requires you to publish source, and publishing source is where most teams stop.

The live ones have one habit in common, and it is not budget. **They bought a domain and pointed it at a running backend before the wiki freeze, then wrote the wiki around a URL rather than around an install command.** NJU-China's Atlas sits on starase-atlas.org, XJTLU-Software's AMPilot on ampilotlab.com, Toronto's PETadex on petadex.net, Stanford's RADAR-Scout on Vercel. Two of the eight are high-school teams running real inference in public: GHCIS's ARGUS answers `{"status":"ready"}` at argus.ucuv.dpdns.org, and HK-Joint-School's PyroForge reports `models_ready: true, esm_ready: true` — an ESM protein model loaded and serving, from a school team.

The source-only group is not lazy; it is mostly careful. ETH-Zurich's deCISion ships 28 CI-tested checks, a Docker build and an MIT licence. UMA Malaga's Diana has a 10 GB reproducible Docker stack and a BIOLOGICAL_REPORT.md mapping each biological step to code. Uni-Padua-IT's ReTIsigner is a thoughtful fork of a published tool, Apache 2.0, one `docker run` from working. These teams decided, often explicitly and for defensible reasons — cost, patient data, a 4 GB index — that local execution was the right call. The cost is simply that nobody will ever casually try them.

Two teams published a live URL that is not the tool, and both said so honestly. UMA Malaga's diana-grna-designer-7723f5.igem.wiki opens with "Saved results, not the live tool... The pages cannot analyse a variant you type." GU Frankfurt's HUSH page says "This page shows its web app in action" and then presents a clickable mockup of screenshots. Judges reward the appearance of a deployed tool, so the gap between a demo and a deployment is exactly where a link check gets fooled.

Outside use is the bleakest column. Across every GitLab repository examined the star count is zero, the fork count is zero, and the last commit falls in the October freeze window — with one exception, DKU's pepticraft-2, touched on 5 November. Uni-Padua-IT published an open call on 9 August offering to codon-optimise any team's sequence, received no replies, and reported that on their wiki. The only genuine external-adoption signal found anywhere was on Stanford's SynBase, which displays "837 learners" — and that is a teaching platform, not a research tool.

One more caution for anyone citing datasets as deliverables. Toronto's PETadex front end is live and excellent, but the 23.8 GB Zenodo deposit its wiki cites, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23457986, returns 404, and a Zenodo search for "petadex" returns zero records. The web app survived; the archival half of the release did not.

For GEMS the lesson is narrow and cheap. Shipping a tool outsiders use is achievable — eight teams did it, including two high schools — but it is a hosting decision, not a coding decision, and it has to be made months before the wiki freeze. The teams that got there treated the public URL as the deliverable and the repository as the backup. The ones that did not now own excellent code that nobody will run.

### AMPilot — the only tool with a working public API
XJTLU-Software's antimicrobial-peptide workbench at ampilotlab.com opens in guest mode with no account, and its /api/v1 routes are documented in a published OpenAPI 3.1 spec. A live call to /api/v1/corpus/search returned real literature evidence with provenance, licence and retrieval date attached — no key, no sign-up. The spec states the API is deterministic, stateless and calls no language model, which is what makes it safe for someone else to build on. It is the clearest example this year of a team designing for a second user rather than a judge.

### Two high-school teams out-shipped most universities
GHCIS's ARGUS runs a real backend at argus.ucuv.dpdns.org — its /api/ready endpoint answers with JSON, not a static shell — alongside a Docker and a native Node deploy path, role-based access and SQLite persistence. HK-Joint-School's PyroForge serves protein thermostability prediction at pyroforge.26650078.xyz with /health reporting ESM models loaded and ready. Both URLs are reachable right now. Neither team had a university budget; they had a cheap domain and a decision to host.

### Vilnius deployed, then switched it off
Ladder Detector automates gel-image annotation, a genuinely unglamorous and genuinely useful job, and Vilnius-Lithuania did the right thing by deploying it publicly. The URL on their wiki, ladder-detector.onrender.com, now returns HTTP 503 and the text "This service has been suspended by its owner." The Apache-2.0 source is intact on GitLab and still runs via docker compose, so the work is not lost — but every citation of that wiki link now points at a dead page. A free hosting tier is a deadline, not a deployment.

### Diana and HUSH publish a URL that is not the tool
UMA Malaga's live site opens with a disclaimer: "Saved results, not the live tool... The pages cannot analyse a variant you type." It publishes unedited CLI output with the commit hash, Docker image digest and tool versions recorded — excellent reproducibility practice, but not a service. GU Frankfurt's HUSH page likewise says it "shows its web app in action" and then walks through a mockup of screenshots. Both are more honest than most, and both are exactly why a 200 response proves nothing until you read the page.

### ETH-Zurich's deCISion is the best source-only release
The Best Software winner for Overgrad ships MIT-licensed with a web interface, a JSON API, a CLI, 28 automated tests on every push through GitLab CI, a Docker build, a CITATION.cff and a demo video. It exports FASTA, GenBank and SBOL3 and takes any .pdb or .cif structure, so it would work on someone else's data without modification. The only address on the wiki is localhost:4173. Everything needed to deploy it exists in the repository; nobody deployed it.

### Toronto's app is live; its dataset DOI is not
PETadex at petadex.net is one of the strongest tools of the year: a sharded DIAMOND search over a 298.7M-sequence corpus, with worked examples loaded and ready to run, nothing to install. But the wiki cites a 23.8 GB Zenodo deposit at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23457986, and that DOI returns 404 — a Zenodo API search for "petadex" finds zero records. The interactive half survived and the archival half did not, which is the opposite of what long-term preservation is supposed to deliver.

**Checklist**

- Buy a domain and deploy the tool publicly before the wiki freeze, not after it — every tool that is alive today was hosted on freeze day.
- Put a clickable URL at the top of the software page; if the only address on the page is localhost, assume nobody outside the team will ever run it.
- Let strangers in without an account — guest mode or a no-key API. CERNAL gated behind a lab login is dead; AMPilot's keyless API still answers.
- Pay for hosting that outlives the free tier, and check the URL again a month after the Jamboree. Vilnius's deployment lasted weeks.
- Expose a documented HTTP API with an OpenAPI spec alongside the UI, so the tool can be a step in someone else's pipeline rather than a destination.
- Ship a health endpoint that returns real JSON, so anyone — including a judge or a reviewer — can prove the backend is running and not a static shell.
- Accept standard inputs (FASTA, GenBank, SBML, .pdb/.cif) and export standard outputs (SBOL, GenBank, CSV); hard-wiring the tool to your own chassis caps its audience at your team.
- Never present a mockup or saved output as the running tool — and if you do publish saved results, label them as plainly as UMA Malaga did.
- Verify every archival DOI resolves before you cite it; Toronto's 23.8 GB Zenodo deposit 404s while the web app it supports stays up.
- Recruit one outside user and record what they did. Across all 21 tools the only external-adoption number found anywhere was SynBase's 837 learners; stars and forks were zero everywhere.

_Method and limits. Starting from the 2026 Best Software winners and nominees, the Best Software & AI winners and nominees, and the Best Model and Best Hardware winners, every tool's wiki software page was read (via curl where server-rendered, via the browser pane for client-rendered SPAs), every GitLab and GitHub repository was queried through the GitLab API for file tree, licence, stars, forks and last-commit date, and every candidate deployment was first checked with curl and then opened in a browser and read, because a 200 from an SPA catch-all route proves nothing — starase-atlas.org returns its index page for any /api path, so apparent API endpoints had to be inspected by content. Where a backend health endpoint existed it was called directly (ARGUS /api/ready, PyroForge /health, AMPilot /api/v1/corpus/search, which returned real data). A link check cannot tell you whether the science is correct, whether the tool gives sensible answers on data it has not seen, whether the maintainers intend to keep paying for hosting, or whether anyone is actually using it — zero stars and zero forks mean no public signal, not necessarily no users. Cornell and KAUST-KSA released no standalone software and are listed but excluded from the base rate; TAU-Israel, HK-Joint-School, DKU and XJTLU-Software had no local research file, so their tools were identified from their wikis directly._

## How the best teams made complex data honest, not just pretty

_The visualisation work that stood out in 2026 was not the most beautiful. It was the work that made it impossible to misread the data._

Almost every 2026 wiki has charts. The ones worth studying share a single instinct: **they build the reader's doubt into the picture**.

The clearest example is **GEMS-Taiwan**'s provenance colour-coding. Its dose ledger is drawn as one top-to-bottom chain, from 1.67 mL on a 10 cm plate down to US$3,800 of capital per hectare, with a rail running down the left that is green while every row still rests on a measurement and **turns amber at the rice canopy correction** — so a reader sees exactly where measurement stops and modelling begins. Every model input is tabulated with a provenance column. **TU Delft** does the same thing in a different register, labelling every cell of its decision matrix Factual, Inferred, Estimated or Speculative, with a legend stating that the tag records the evidence and not the judgement. **BOKU-Vienna** attaches a parameter-provenance table to its interactive widget. **XJTLU-China** runs an evidence-coverage track underneath its priority profiles, so a high score sitting on thin evidence cannot be mistaken for a finding.

The second instinct is **a state that refuses to be misread**. **DKU**'s safety panel resolves to four verdicts rather than three — clear, exceeded, borderline, and *not assessed* — precisely so an unmeasured gate can never be read as a passed one; 198 of its 496 constructs carry no immunogenicity measurement, and the interface says so rather than showing a zero. It goes further: because the MHC class I predictor accepts only 5-15 residue peptides and returns zero outside that window, a stored zero is explicitly not presented as evidence of low immunogenicity. **GHCIS** ships the same idea in its colour classifier, with an explicit "unresolved, and must not be treated as Negative" state. **UMA Malaga** conveys status by shape and text rather than colour alone.

The third is **telling the reader how to read it**. BOKU-Vienna puts an explicit "How to read this graph" panel beside each one. XJTLU-China numbers eighteen model figures so they read as a single argument rather than a gallery, aligning six normalised feature tracks above a composite score so you can see which feature drove a peak.

The fourth is **captions that carry the whole experiment**. **Mingdao**'s figures are plain, and that is the point — each names the instrument (a BioTek Synergy H1 plate reader; a FORA G31 glucose meter, range 20-600 mg/dL), the buffer, the temperature, the replicate count and the error measure, links its own raw CSV by filename, and where error bars are too small to see, *the caption says so* and points at the table of values.

The fifth is **showing the absences**. **DTU-Denmark**'s interactive stakeholder map colour-codes each pin by engagement status so that non-responses stay visible, and the team names the organisations that never replied. **BNDS-China** prints a caveat directly on its influence map stating that appearing on it does not mean an interview took place.

And a note on accessibility, because the wiki analysis found that late alt-text compliance sweeps correlate with nothing. **BAID-China** shows what doing it properly looks like instead: every chart on the wiki redrawn in the eight-colour Okabe-Ito colour-blind-safe palette, chosen for luminance separation so the figures survive greyscale, with a published colour-blindness simulation verifying that elements stay distinguishable under red-green, blue-yellow and total colour-blindness. That is a design decision taken at the start, not a checkbox at the end.

Interactivity, finally, earns its place only when it lets the reader change something. **UPF-Barcelona**'s RK4 solver gives every parameter a live slider that takes effect *during* the running simulation. BOKU-Vienna's trade-off widget moves a vitamin flux against growth rate with the team's own measured points overlaid. DTU-Denmark's process-flow diagram zooms from a five-route overview into the enzymatic routes with every parameter printed on the box - acid molarity, temperature, residence time, enzyme loading, number of reuses. An animation that only plays is decoration; a control that changes the answer is an argument.

### Colour the rail where measurement stops
GEMS-Taiwan draws its dose ledger as one chain from 1.67 mL on a plate to US$3,800 per hectare, with a rail down the left that is green while each row rests on a measurement and turns amber at the rice canopy correction. Anyone can see where the evidence ends. TU Delft does the same with Factual / Inferred / Estimated / Speculative tags on every cell of its decision matrix.

### Give "not assessed" its own state
DKU's safety panel resolves to clear, exceeded, borderline and not assessed — four verdicts, so an unmeasured gate can never read as a passed one. 198 of its 496 constructs have no immunogenicity measurement and the interface says so instead of showing a zero. GHCIS ships the same idea as "unresolved, and must not be treated as Negative".

### Put the whole experiment in the caption
Mingdao's figures are plain and rigorous. Each names the instrument, the buffer, the temperature, the replicate count and the error measure, and links its own raw CSV by filename. Where the error bars are too small to see, the caption says so and points at the table of values. A figure a reader can audit beats a figure a reader can admire.

### Show who did not reply
DTU-Denmark colour-codes every pin on its stakeholder map by engagement status, so non-responses stay visible, and names the organisations that never answered. BNDS-China prints the caveat on its influence map that appearing there does not mean an interview happened. A map with no gaps is a map that has been tidied.

### BAID-China redrew every chart in a colour-blind-safe palette
The eight-colour Okabe-Ito palette, chosen for luminance separation so the figures survive greyscale, with a published colour-blindness simulation verifying that elements stay distinguishable under red-green, blue-yellow and total colour-blindness. The wiki analysis found late alt-text sweeps correlate with nothing; this is the alternative — a decision taken at the start.

### Interactivity only counts if the reader can change the answer
UPF-Barcelona gives every parameter a live slider that takes effect during the running simulation. BOKU-Vienna moves vitamin flux against growth rate with the team's own measured points overlaid and a "How to read this graph" panel beside it. DTU prints every parameter on the box of a zoomable process diagram. An animation that only plays is decoration.

_Method and limits. Drawn from the dataviz field of every team file in this report, each researched from the team's own 2026 wiki. Interactive behaviour is as the analysts described it after opening the pages; we have not re-tested every widget here. The examples are chosen because they illustrate a transferable device, not because they are the only teams doing good work. GEMS-Taiwan is the report author's own team and appears on the same terms as the rest._

## Can anyone rebuild the hardware?

_Of 20 instruments built by the 2026 Best Hardware, Best Measurement and Best Alternative Platform cohorts, 6 publish enough for a stranger in another country to rebuild them. Nine publish no geometry file at all. One has ever been used by someone outside the team that built it._

**Six of twenty.** That is how many award-winning iGEM 2026 instruments a stranger could actually rebuild: NCKU-Tainan's CAPTURE-Screen fluorescence reader, Lambert-GA's Vapor-X vacuum dryer, UNILausanne's C.L.A.W. LAMP incubator, Hongwen School's BrewXOS Fermenter Mini, TU Darmstadt's anaerobic chamber trio, and GEMS-Taiwan's four ReLEAF devices. Two more — Princeton's gyroid biofilter and CalPolySLO's emulsification washboard — are single printed parts where an STL plus print settings is the whole deliverable, which takes the generous count to eight. Everything else is missing at least one thing a second builder cannot do without.

The sister analysis of software found that every repository was populated, because iGEM mandates a GitLab deposit, and that the thing separating live tools from dead ones was a hosting decision. Hardware has no such floor. **There is no `2026/hardware` group on gitlab.igem.org at all** — the API returns 404 for it while `2026/software` returns a group called Software. Every hardware release in this cohort is improvised: a sub-project filed under `/software/`, a personal GitHub account, an Onshape link, a Google Drive folder, or loose files on the wiki's asset store. Nothing in the competition ever asks a hardware team to press Export.

And pressing Export is exactly the separating habit. The teams you cannot rebuild from are not lazy and their CAD is not missing — it is visibly, beautifully *rendered*. Cornell's Best Hardware winner has an exploded view of the Arachne electrospinner and a bill of materials so good it names Analog Technologies' AHV24V30KVR5MAW at $419.00 across 40 priced line items totalling $1,213.35 — and then says, in the present tense of a page that will not change again, "we plan to provide a bill of materials, CAD files, circuit diagrams, assembly documentation, and an operation manual." Two PDFs went up; no CAD file, no schematic file and no firmware ever did. CAU-China's OptiX phone spectrometer has an interactive exploded CAD view with numbered, clickable components and the most careful calibration chain in the whole cohort — and not one downloadable file, not one priced part, on a $12–30 instrument whose entire pitch is that anyone can have one. NU Boston published CAD drawings with dimensions and tolerances as figures. UBC-Vancouver published `.glb` meshes, a render format. In every one of these cases the model exists; it simply never left the design tool in a format anyone else can open.

The six that cleared the bar all did one unglamorous thing: they wrote the build as a document with files attached, not a page with pictures attached. NCKU-Tainan's MIT-licensed repo holds 225 files — 75 STEP exports, 59 STLs, the parametric CadQuery Python they were generated from, an ESP32 sketch with its own AS7341 driver, a bill-of-materials CSV and a 12-step assembly order that a second builder checked against the real machine. Its costing is the most honest number in the census: US$160.62 for the printed build, broken down to the print-shop receipt, with the line "an estimate, not an account" and the NT$31.68/US$1 rate it was converted at. Lambert-GA shipped Gerbers, a drill file, a JLCPCB pick-and-place CSV and a BOM keyed to LCSC part numbers, so the board can be ordered without a human in the loop. UNILausanne's C.L.A.W. costs under CHF 10, ships five STLs and a 3.8 MB manual, and includes the calibration that matters: a thermometer in the tube bore reads about 10 °C above the display, so the thermostat is set to 52.5 °C, preheated ten minutes, and holds 62.7 ± 1.2 °C over 30 minutes across three runs.

Two links fail the moment you check them rather than read them. Toronto's bioreactor page points at a Google Drive folder called "Bioreactor CAD Files"; opened signed-out it shows the folder name, no files, and a prompt to sign in — so the CAD for a $204 CAD bioreactor is, in practice, unavailable, while the firmware beside it is public and Apache-2.0. HongKong-JSS does the opposite: its Onshape document loads for anyone, 28 parts and a full feature tree, while `github.com/hkjssplkchc2026/mercurysense` — the firmware, the C12880 spectrometer driver and the acquisition instructions, as named on their own wiki — returns 404, and that GitHub account has no public repositories at all. Costs deserve the same scepticism. NU Boston's FLARE leads with "as low as $300 vs $10,000", then publishes two bills of materials totalling $499.80 and $344.18, **neither of which contains the Raspberry Pi 5 or the Arduino that run the instrument**. By contrast HongKong-JSS states plainly that its USD 357 build missed the USD 40 its stakeholders asked for, and TU Darmstadt records that the oxygen sensor is 83% of its €114.60 monitor.

Outside use is bleaker than it was for software. Across every hardware repository checked the fork count is zero and the star count is zero, with one exception: Bist-China's seven STLs on GitHub have two stars — and no licence file, so nobody may legally reuse them. The single genuine case of a device leaving its makers is Lambert-GA's, and it is a high-school team: they shipped Vapor-X to the Biochemical Genetics Laboratory at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, where John Moore measured 38 of 43 compounds recovered within 5% of undried controls, and to the Styczynski Lab at Georgia Tech, which checked GFP fluorescence after drying DNA and lysates. Both labs' raw data are downloadable. **One team in twenty asked an outsider to use the thing, and the one that did was the one with Gerbers.**

### Vapor-X — the only device an outsider has used
Lambert-GA's $80.07 vacuum dryer (a Mason jar, a 12 V pump, a polyimide heater and a Raspberry Pi Pico W on a custom PCB) is the only instrument in this cohort with third-party evidence. The team shipped it to the Biochemical Genetics Laboratory at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, where John Moore recovered 38 of 43 measured compounds within 5% of undried controls, and to the Styczynski Lab at Georgia Tech for GFP fluorescence after drying. The release matches: three STLs, a complete Gerber and drill set, a JLCPCB pick-and-place CSV, a BOM keyed to LCSC part numbers, MicroPython firmware under Apache-2.0, and an 8.5 MB construction manual. It is the only release here that a board house could execute without a human reading the wiki.

### NCKU-Tainan shipped the source, not just the export
225 files under MIT: 75 STEP assemblies, 59 STLs covering 66 printed pieces across two builds, and the parametric CadQuery Python the geometry was generated from — so another team can change a dimension rather than reprint yours. Alongside it sit an ESP32 sketch with its own AS7341 driver, a bill-of-materials CSV, a bench schematic with measured values, and working sensor settings (AGAIN 512x, ATIME 255, ASTEP 280). The costing is itemised by basis — print-shop receipts, costing sheet, distributor list prices — totals US$160.62 for the printed build and US$53.70 for the laser-cut one, and is labelled "an estimate, not an account". They also publish what failed: the laser-cut build could not tell the AHL sensor strain from cells without sfGFP.

### The Best Hardware winner published no CAD at all
Cornell's Arachne electrospinner won Best Hardware (Undergraduate) with a genuinely excellent bill of materials — 40 priced line items in three groups, from the $419.00 Analog Technologies AHV24V30KVR5MAW 30 kV supply to $0.08 M5 screws, subtotals $681.76 / $416.87 / $114.72, total $1,213.35 — and a fabrication-and-assembly guide and safety manual that both download. What never appeared is the geometry: no STL, no STEP, no circuit schematic file and no ESP32 firmware anywhere on the hardware, circuitry, encasement or contribution pages. The page still carries the sentence "we plan to provide a bill of materials, CAD files, circuit diagrams, assembly documentation, and an operation manual." Half of that shipped.

### An empty Drive folder and a 404 repository
Toronto's hardware page links a Google Drive folder named "Bioreactor CAD Files". Opened without a Google account it renders the folder title, lists nothing, and asks you to sign in — so the CAD for its $204 CAD, 96-unit bioreactor array is effectively unavailable, while the firmware next to it is public under Apache-2.0 and the BOM and assembly PDFs both download. HongKong-JSS has the mirror-image failure: its Onshape document is genuinely public (28 parts, full feature tree, view-only) but github.com/hkjssplkchc2026/mercurysense — named on its own wiki as holding the ESP32 firmware, the Hamamatsu C12880 driver and the acquisition instructions — returns 404, and the account has zero public repositories. Only its extraction-unit firmware survived, on a different personal account, with licence "NOASSERTION".

### The computer is missing from the bill of materials
NU Boston's FLARE soil chamber leads with "a build cost of as low as $300 vs. $10,000" and then publishes two bills of materials: $499.80 for the entire system and $344.18 for the UV module. Neither total includes the Raspberry Pi 5 that runs the imaging, the Arduino that drives the pumps, the printed and laser-cut enclosure, or the tubing — the module BOM lists a "Raspberry Pi 5 breakout board, $7.50" but not the Pi. So the headline is below both published totals, and both published totals are below the real one. Compare HongKong-JSS, which states outright that its USD 357 core-component build overshot the USD 40 its stakeholders asked for, and TU Darmstadt, which notes that the sensor alone is 83% of its €114.60 oxygen monitor.

### Eighteen STLs, six manuals — and meshes instead of models
GEMS-Taiwan clears the bar, and it is worth being precise about how narrowly. On the credit side: 18 STL files that download (verified, served as model/stl), six assembly guides of 10 to 16 pages for the bioreactor, both photometers and the light plate, a user manual and brochure, a 6.8 MB hardware notebook covering 23 March to 17 October, print settings recorded next to the files (Bambu Lab X1 Carbon, 0.2 mm, 20% gyroid, PLA Matte with TPU 95A cuvette slots), a published SiO2 OD600 calibration, and CC BY 4.0 on everything. Against: the files are STL meshes, not STEP or parametric source, so a second team can print the photometer but not change its light path; the costs are totals (NT$16,450 in parts; about US$360 for the photometer against roughly US$15,000 for the benchtop instrument it replaces) rather than a priced line-item table; and of the four devices only the reactor rig's sketch.ino is in the MIT digital-twin repo — the photometer and LPA firmware were never released as source. Nobody outside the team has built one.

**Checklist**

- Export every part to STEP as well as STL before the wiki freeze. ReLEAF ships 18 STL meshes; a mesh prints but cannot be edited, so nobody can move the photometer's light path. NCKU-Tainan shipped 75 STEP files plus the CadQuery source that generated them.
- Publish one itemised bill of materials per device — supplier, part number, quantity, unit price, extended price, subtotal — not a total. Cornell's 40-row table is the model to copy even though Cornell published no CAD; ReLEAF currently gives NT$16,450 and about US$360 with the parts named only inside the assembly guides.
- Put all four devices' firmware in the GitLab repo under MIT, not just the reactor rig's sketch.ino. If a file extension is blocked, do what KAUST-KSA did: upload the sketch as .js with a header telling the reader to save it as .ino.
- Ship each device as one versioned archive — STEP, STL, BOM CSV, firmware, manual, LICENSE — instead of eighteen loose links on a contribution page. HK League's three zips with a per-file print count are the pattern.
- Put the licence inside the bundle, not only in a sentence at the bottom of the page. Bist-China's seven STLs are the only hardware files in the cohort with any stars, and nobody may legally use them because there is no licence file.
- Never host design files on Google Drive. Toronto's "Bioreactor CAD Files" folder shows a signed-out visitor nothing at all, which is indistinguishable from publishing nothing.
- Write a calibration page per device and keep the honest number in it. The SiO2 OD600 calibration and the leaf-sensor +0.47 to +1.71 degC offset over 540 paired readings are exactly right; add the same for the LPA's per-LED output and the Pro-versus-Slim scale difference.
- Cost the whole instrument, including the computer. NU Boston's two BOMs both omit the Raspberry Pi that runs the device; the GEMS cost sheet should state explicitly what the NT$16,450 does and does not cover.
- Send one device to one outside laboratory, ask them to run something real, and publish their raw data. Lambert-GA is a high-school team and did this twice, at UAB and Georgia Tech — it is the only outside-use evidence in the entire cohort.
- Re-check every hardware link a month after the Jamboree. HongKong-JSS's firmware repository was named on the wiki and is now a 404; a single curl would have caught it.

_Method and limits. Twenty instruments were graded: the fourteen Best Hardware winners and nominees across all three sections, plus the six Best Measurement and Best Alternative Platform teams that actually built a device (UNILausanne, Princeton, CalPolySLO, SDU-Denmark, McMaster-Canada, Labi-Taiwan). The remaining Measurement and Alternative Platform teams checked — William-and-Mary, XJTLU-China, WageningenUR, CHINAGuangdongShimen, HangzhouFourteenAP, Yucai-SZ, UOttawa, Marburg, BGI-College — released no instrument and are excluded from the base rate; William-and-Mary's hardware page is still an unfilled iGEM template. Each instrument was scored on seven checkable things: a bill of materials naming parts with prices or part numbers; a total cost and whether it is credible; geometry or electrical source files that actually download; firmware with a licence; an assembly guide a non-author could follow; a calibration or validation protocol; and any evidence of outside use. The pass bar was all of files, priced parts, an assembly guide and a validation protocol, plus firmware where the device needs it. Server-rendered wiki pages were read with curl; client-rendered React wikis were read either from their JavaScript bundles or in a browser — and the browser mattered: a stale deployed chunk on Hongwen School's site still contained the team's own unexecuted editorial placeholders where the CAD link should be, while the live page serves a working 8.56 MB STEP file, so bundle evidence was always confirmed in the browser before being treated as a finding. Every claimed download was fetched and its HTTP status, content type and byte size recorded; Google Drive and Onshape links were opened signed-out. Repositories were queried through the GitLab and GitHub APIs for file tree, licence, stars, forks and last activity. What could not be checked: the contents of bill-of-materials and assembly PDFs, because no PDF text extractor was available in this environment — those files were verified to exist, download and carry the right media type, and their line items were only quoted where the wiki page itself reproduces them. Nor can a link check tell you whether a device reads true, whether an assembly guide is actually followable, or whether anyone has quietly built one; zero stars and zero forks mean no public signal, not certainly no users._

## Calibrated, but never checked

_Seven checkable habits of measurement discipline, scored by reading 39 decorated 2026 wikis directly. The cohort calibrates well, almost never defines its own error bars, and only twice in 39 teams does anyone measure the same thing twice._

We read the wikis of 39 decorated teams — all 14 Best Measurement winners and nominees across the three sections, plus the 30 Top 10 teams, 5 of which overlap — and scored each on seven things a reader can check: a calibration curve into an absolute unit, replicates named by type, an error bar whose meaning is stated, a limit of detection computed for the team's own assay, a negative control or blank, a second instrument or lab measuring the same sample, and a protocol that names the instrument.

**The easy half is done and the hard half is not.** A negative control or blank appears in **38 of 39** wikis (97%) — only Lambert-GA has none. A protocol naming the instrument appears in **35 of 39** (90%). A calibration curve or an absolute-unit anchor appears in **28 of 39** (72%). Then it falls away. Replicates are named by type — biological or technical, not a bare *n* = 3 — in **23 of 39** (59%). An error bar whose meaning is stated in words is in **23 of 39** (59%). A limit of detection computed from the team's own data, with a number on it, is in **6 of 39 (15%)**: WageningenUR, William-and-Mary, UNILausanne, Labi-Taiwan, GCGS and GEMS-Taiwan. And the same sample measured twice, by a second instrument, operator or lab, with the two numbers compared, is in **2 of 39 (5%)**.

**An error bar whose meaning is unstated is itself a finding.** Twenty-three of the 39 wikis print the phrase "error bars"; three of those never say what the bar is. Princeton captions a standard curve "fitted over 0–250 µg/mL with error bars on each standard: y = 0.0013x + 0.2726, R² = 0.9968" — the fit is reported to four decimals and the spread is not reported at all. One sentence does it: McMaster-Canada's BCA figure reads "BSA standard curve from nine blank-corrected standard means, 0–2000 µg/mL, measured in technical triplicate … Error bars show sample SD." Same assay, same chart type, a different reader experience. Six of the 39 never use any dispersion word — SD, SEM, confidence interval, ± — anywhere we could read. One of them is **CalPolySLO, the undergraduate Best Measurement winner**: across nine pages and 124,000 characters, including the most carefully written protocol set in the whole cohort, the characters "±", "error bar" and "standard deviation" appear **zero** times, and its headline PPK2 enzyme curves are labelled "averages of experimental duplicates (n = 2)".

**Nobody checks the instrument.** The word *inter-lab* appears in **0 of the 106 team files** in this report. On the 39 wikis, two teams did it. GEMS-Taiwan ran its inline photometer against a BioDrop benchtop spectrophotometer twice, with TiO₂ and then SiO₂ particle ladders — 45 paired points in August, 40 steps in October, slope 1.018, R² 0.995, residual SD reported for both instruments — and separately compared its leaf and air temperature sensors across **540 paired readings** at three sites, finding a site-dependent offset of −0.2 to +1.8 °C. Athens, an Overgraduate Top 10 team that was never nominated for Measurement, repeated a failed restriction digest with enzymes that had been verified at another laboratory, explicitly "to introduce an independent reference for the digestion step". Honourable third: HongKong-JSS, which names the gap instead of hiding it — "we did not run our samples on a calibrated fluorometer or plate reader alongside the box, so the workflow is unvalidated against a reference instrument" — and, on the same page, explains that "CV = 100 × SD/mean. Lower CV indicates lower relative signal variability, not greater detection accuracy." That is a high-school team teaching what a statistic does *not* mean.

**Does any of it buy you a podium? No.** Scored out of seven, the Best Measurement cohort averages **4.36** and the 25 Top 10 generalists average **3.76** — a gap of six tenths of one checkbox. Split by outcome instead of by award, the effect vanishes and reverses: the 30 Top 10 teams average **3.93**, and the nine decorated teams that did *not* reach a Top 10 — all of them Best Measurement nominees — average **4.11**. The cheap pass over all 106 team files says the same: of 22 teams whose files mention calibration work, 6 made a Top 10 (**27%**); of the 84 that do not, 24 made a Top 10 (**29%**). There is no effect to report. Measurement discipline earns the Measurement prize; it does not move you up the table. The honest version of the dry-lab roadmap's claim is therefore not *uncertainty wins medals* — it is *uncertainty is what makes a number worth keeping after the medals*.

**Where the award itself falls short.** The Best Measurement cohort really does lead on the converting half: calibration **12/14 (86%) against 16/25 (64%)**, and a numeric limit of detection **5/14 (36%) against 1/25 (4%)** — LOD is the single check that cleanly separates the specialists. But on the uncertainty half it does not lead at all. Stating what an error bar means: **8/14 (57%) for the Measurement cohort against 15/25 (60%) for the generalists**. Naming the instrument: **12/14 against 23/25**. WageningenUR, the Overgraduate winner, writes out LOD = 3.3σ/b and LOQ = 10σ/b, builds a separate calibration line per growth medium in µM fluoride, re-zeroes each line on the plate's negative control, and warns that "R² is only descriptive per situation, since it rises with the width of the concentration range" — and then calls its instrument "a microplate reader", with no make, model or wavelength settings. The prize is being awarded for turning a reading into a unit, not for saying how sure you are of it. By section the three tiers are nearly level — Undergraduate 4.07, Overgraduate 3.92, High School 3.92 — and high-school teams actually calibrate most often (10/13, 77%) while naming their replicate type least often (6/13, 46%).

### 2 of 39 measured it twice
Only GEMS-Taiwan and Athens put the same material in front of a second instrument or a second laboratory and compared the two numbers. GEMS-Taiwan has the only quantitative version: 45 paired points of its inline photometer against a BioDrop benchtop spectrophotometer, slope 1.018, R² 0.995, plus 540 paired leaf-versus-air sensor readings at three sites. Everyone else's instrument is trusted because it is the only one they used.

### 23 draw error bars, 3 never define them
GU Frankfurt, Princeton and Stanford all print the phrase "error bars" without ever saying whether the bar is a standard deviation, a standard error or a confidence interval. Six more wikis — CalPolySLO, ETH-Zurich, GHCIS, HongKong-HS, LYON, Stanford — contain no dispersion word at all. The cure is one clause in a caption, and McMaster-Canada shows exactly what it looks like.

### 4.36 against 3.76, out of seven
The Best Measurement cohort beats the Top 10 generalists by six tenths of one checkbox. It leads clearly on only two of the seven: calibration (86% against 64%) and a numeric limit of detection (36% against 4%). On stating what an error bar means it is level or behind, 57% against 60%. The prize currently rewards converting a reading into a unit, not reporting how sure you are of it.

### 7 of 7 on the checklist, n = 1 on the headline assay
GEMS-Taiwan is the only team in the 39 to tick all seven, and it earned that on hardware: a calibration analysis plan committed to the repository before the first measurement, with bias, repeatability, LOD, LOQ and hysteresis thresholds fixed in advance. The wet lab is weaker and the team says so. Its headline secreted ACC deaminase figure, 7.25 mU/mL, is n = 1 and is labelled by the team "below quantitation"; the light-induction error bars are technical wells on a single plate; and for containment it writes that "the detection limit was not recorded and replicate experiments were not performed". Its real contribution is provenance labelling, not replication. The cheapest next step for GEMS is also the most obvious one: run the key assay on three separate days.

**Checklist**

- Every axis carries a unit a reader outside your lab can interpret. If the unit is RFU, OD or a fold-change, say on the figure that it is instrument-relative and not comparable to anyone else's — Labi-Taiwan does exactly this.
- One calibration curve per assay and per medium, plotted and shown rather than described. Give the fit equation, the R², and the concentration range over which it holds.
- Say where your samples sit on that curve. If a point falls outside the standards, label the number an extrapolation and state the error you are accepting, the way William-and-Mary reports a ±15% extrapolation.
- Name the replicate: "n = 3 biological replicates, separate colonies on separate days" or "n = 3 technical wells on one plate". A bare n = 3 tells a reader nothing.
- Every error bar gets a clause in its caption — SD, SEM or 95% CI, and over what. If the figure has no bar because n = 1, write n = 1 on the figure.
- Blanks and negative controls appear in the plot, not only in the methods paragraph.
- Compute a limit of detection from your own blanks — mean + 3 SD, or 3.3σ/b — and report the limit of quantification beside it. If you cannot, write that the lowest concentration tested is not a validated detection limit, as HongKong-JSS does.
- Once per project, measure one sample twice: a second instrument, a second operator, or a second day. Plot the two against each other and report the slope and the residual spread. Two of 39 decorated teams did this; it is the cheapest way to be unusual.
- Name the instrument: make, model, wavelength, gain, integration time, path length. "A microplate reader" is not a method, even in an award-winning wiki.
- Publish the protocol so a reader can repeat the measurement without emailing you, and record who took each measurement and on what date.

_Method and limits. Two passes. Pass one pattern-matched the English dry-lab and science-for-good prose of all 106 team files in research/teams/, which is cheap and covers the whole decorated field but cannot see a practice a team performed and did not write up, nor one the researchers did not record. Pass two read the wikis directly for 39 teams: the 14 Best Measurement winners and nominees (CalPolySLO, McMaster-Canada, Princeton, William-and-Mary, XJTLU-China; WageningenUR, KAUST-KSA, SDU-Denmark, UNILausanne; GEMS-Taiwan, CHINAGuangdongShimen, HangzhouFourteenAP, Labi-Taiwan, Yucai-SZ) and the 30 Top 10 teams, of which Princeton, WageningenUR, KAUST-KSA, GEMS-Taiwan and HangzhouFourteenAP are in both lists, giving 39 distinct teams. Most 2026 wikis are client-rendered, so page text was recovered from the published JavaScript bundles and their lazy-loaded chunks; the static-HTML wikis were fetched page by page over measurement, results, engineering, model, proof-of-concept, experiments, notebook, contribution, description and parts. The two routes are not symmetric: a bundle yields the whole wiki at once, while a static site yields only the pages we asked for, so a static-site team can be undercounted. All headline rates come from pass two. Pass one is reported only where it is stated as such, because against the 39 verified wikis it recovers 39% of the calibration work, 23% of the limit-of-detection work and just 13% of the replicate typing — it is a floor and a ranking, not a measurement. Counting rules: a calibration counts when a standard or calibration curve is described, or when an absolute anchor such as fluorescein, CFU/mL or cells/mL appears at least twice. An error bar counts as defined only when a caption or sentence ties a named statistic (SD, SEM, 95% CI) to the plotted spread. A limit of detection counts only when the team computes one for its own assay and gives a number with a unit; informal uses such as "below the detection limit of the gel" and limits cited from the literature were excluded, which is why the strict count is 6 of 39 while 20 of 39 use the phrase. An inter-instrument check counts only when the same material is measured by a second instrument, operator or laboratory and the two results are compared. The seven-point score gives one point each for calibration, replicate typing, a defined error bar, a numeric limit of detection, a negative control or blank, an inter-instrument check, and a protocol that names the instrument. What this cannot see: a figure. Error bars drawn on a plot whose caption never names them score as undefined, which is the point of the exercise, but a caption baked into an image file is invisible to us, and so is anything in a linked PDF or a supplementary file. Nor can it see work done and not published. All 39 teams are decorated, so none of these rates describes the competition as a whole; they describe the teams that already won something. GEMS-Taiwan is the report author's own team and was scored on the same seven criteria as everyone else._

## Everyone disclosed their AI use. The argument is over what counts as AI.

_We read the official attributions record of all 106 decorated teams. The expected finding was 'almost nobody'. The actual finding is 106 of 106 — because iGEM 2026 made AI Tool Use a required block of a Bronze medal deliverable. What stays invisible is the half nobody was asked about._

We went looking for a hole and found a floor. **iGEM 2026's Attributions Form carries a first-class *AI Tool Use* block**, listed by iGEM itself alongside Team Member Contributions, iGEM & Partner Offers, External Contributions and Project Timeline — and the Attributions Form is a Bronze medal criterion that, in iGEM's words, "must be filled out completely, accurately, and honestly". We opened the canonical record for every one of the 106 decorated teams in this report at `teams.igem.org/wiki/<id>/attributions`. **106 of 106 have a non-empty AI Tool Use section, and 106 of 106 name at least one general-purpose assistant.** ChatGPT appears in 80 records, Claude in 68, Gemini in 30, Doubao or Kimi in 21, DeepSeek in 18, Copilot in 6. The median section is about 1,230 characters; the shortest is 99, the longest 7,418.

This is not confined to tidying prose. Counting the task tags teams selected: **Writing 80, Wiki Coding 78, Visualization 78, Background Research 64, Analysis 60, Software 59, Conceptualization 40**. Fifty-nine of 106 decorated teams state that an assistant touched their code, and 60 that one touched their analysis. A reader who assumed the dry lab was hand-written is reading 2026 wrong.

**Then the gap.** Three different things get filed under one word. (a) Scientific machine learning a team built or trained itself. (b) Third-party foundation models used as instruments — AlphaFold, ESM, ProteinMPNN, RFdiffusion, Boltz. (c) General-purpose assistants writing code and prose. Category (c) is disclosed universally, because a form field asked for it. Category (b) mostly is not: **40 of the 106 team files name a third-party structure-prediction or protein-design model** — the technique census on this site counts AlphaFold in 32 files, ProteinMPNN in 14, and RFdiffusion, ESM and Boltz in 8 each — but **only 19 of 106 name any such model inside the AI Tool Use block, and of the 40 teams that used one, only 15 listed it there.** Category (a), a team's own trained model, almost never appears in the AI field at all; it lives on the Model page as science. That is not dishonesty, it is a genuine conceptual disagreement: teams treat running AlphaFold as structural biology, not as using an AI tool. The consequence for a reader is still real — **the attributions record reliably tells you who helped write the wiki, and not what produced the structure you are looking at.**

**Quality varies far more than presence.** Seventy-two of 106 records include review, verification or human-oversight language. Only **4 of 106** state a negative boundary — what the AI did *not* do: UOregon, GEMS-Taiwan, Uni-Padua-IT and Athens. The best disclosure of the season is not on the form at all. **Al-Nahrain-IRAQ** wrote a *Responsible AI use* section on their own attributions page: a table of use, tools and **who reviewed the result**, with model versions named, an honest row reading "An AI assistant (which one was not recorded)", a line that Gemini was used only for prototypes and "none of its output is published here", and a closing boundary — "No scientific claim, data figure, simulation result, quote, or citation on this wiki was generated by AI." **Toronto** comes second with a per-task list and the single best sentence in the cohort: "We used the raw outputs, not the AI summary, as the record." At the other end, ICJFLS files 99 characters ("Deepseek — Translate Chinese document and the content for Wiki to English") and **PSI Korea** attributes the analysis of its optical characterisation data, its wiki images and its promotion video to ChatGPT in 182 characters with no statement that anyone checked the result.

**Did anyone test a model's output at the bench and say so?** Yes, and the high-school example is the strongest. **NBJF** ran a full generative pipeline — RFdiffusion backbones, ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN inverse folding, ESMFold and AlphaFold refolding checks, TemStaPro and SaProt scoring — then **expressed 85 de novo sequences, got detectable SDS-PAGE expression for 25, and published that as an application dataset rather than a success claim**. **HangzhouFourteenAP** is the honest inverse: FoldX ranked Y166Q top at −1.63 kcal/mol, the DNS activity assay put Q172P first at net OD 1.881 with Y166Q last at 0.629, **below wild type at 0.996** — the computational winner was worse than doing nothing. They normalised by BCA to rule out protein load, revised the published ranking, and demoted Y166Q to a mechanistic probe instead of deleting it. The other end exists too: **UMA Malaga** states outright that Diana's ranking order, substitution rule and pooling layout are untested in the lab and that the lab contradicted the substitution rule; **BAID-China**'s RFantibody designs received "computational screening and virtual validation" and no bench test; **ABOA** hands over a 28-part Golden Gate set that is designed but untested.

**Reported AI failures are rare and worth naming individually.** **Toronto** found that under homology-component-grouped splits their ESM-C embeddings lost to a single sequence-length column, reported that the random-split rho = 0.72 had been an artefact, and won Best Model for it; their Claude Sonnet literature-extraction pipeline is benchmarked against double-scored human curation at 95.0% precision and 87.1% recall with zero hallucinated enzymes across 32 doubly-scraped papers. **UPF-Barcelona** built iGEMforge, a Claude Code plugin of four skills, evaluated it over two cycles (28 cases, three runs per arm, an LLM judge against team-written rubrics, including deliberately planted flaws and silence cases), found no clear gain — experimental-design −0.11, scientific-evidence +0.04 — at roughly double the token cost, and **published that they therefore did not use it for project decisions**. **Jilin-China** ran a prespecified out-of-distribution test, found all 12 candidate-task combinations out of distribution, and declined to use the model scores at all. **Al-Nahrain-IRAQ** publishes Engine 1 as failed (2.4 g/L predicted at 13.25 h against 7.6 g/L measured) and states that parameters were read from papers with AI assistance and have not yet been re-checked by a team member. **XJTLU-Software** built delivery reconciliation into AMPilot on the premise that "a fluent closing message is not a delivery receipt". Five negative reports in 106 files. That is the scarce good.

**GEMS-Taiwan, assessed on the same scale.** The team's record names three tools — Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), ChatGPT (OpenAI) — with task tags, and closes with one of only four negative boundaries in the cohort: "All AI outputs were verified by team members against primary literature or experimental data before use. No experimental data, results, or citations were AI-generated." That is above the median. What it does not do: the same paragraph is repeated verbatim under all three tools, so the record never says what each one actually did differently; no model versions are given and no reviewer is named for any item; **AlphaFold, which the project ran with a pre-set confidence gate, is not in the AI field at all**, so the team reproduces exactly the category-(b) blind spot described above; and the LLM-assisted QGIS workflow over 346 farming townships — the one place the team did something a reader would want the prompt for, and did publish the data-preparation prompt — is covered only by a generic *Analysis* tag that does not point at it.
