The team's own page at `2026.igem.wiki/gems-taiwan/attributions/` is also nothing but an embedded frame of the iGEM form: a reader whose browser blocks the frame sees a banner and no attribution at all. **Verdict for the whole cohort, GEMS included: the disclosure on display is *at* what iGEM asked for, and only rarely above it.** iGEM asked which tools and which tasks, so teams supplied tools and tasks. iGEM did not ask who reviewed each output, which model version produced it, or what the AI did not do — so almost nobody said.

### 106 of 106 — because a form field asked
Every decorated team in this report has a non-empty AI Tool Use section in its official iGEM attributions record, and every one names at least one general-purpose assistant. The median entry runs about 1,230 characters. This is the one place in iGEM where a disclosure norm already exists and is universally obeyed — and the reason is simply that the deliverable has a box for it.

### AI Tool Use is part of a Bronze medal criterion
iGEM's own deliverables guide lists five submission blocks for the required Attributions Form: Team Member Contributions, AI Tool Use, iGEM & Partner Offers, External Contributions, Project Timeline. The medals page makes the Attributions Form Bronze criterion 2 and says it "must be filled out completely, accurately, and honestly". So AI disclosure in 2026 was not optional and not a special-prize flourish — it was the price of a bronze medal.

### AlphaFold is filed as biology, not as AI
Forty of the 106 team files name a third-party structure-prediction or protein-design model. Only 19 teams name any such model inside the AI Tool Use block, and only 15 of the 40 actual users put it there. Teams read "AI tool" as "chatbot", so the record tells you who drafted the wiki text and not what produced the structure in the figure. A disclosure norm that only catches assistants catches the cheaper half.

### Al-Nahrain-IRAQ wrote the table everyone else should copy
Their wiki carries a Responsible AI use section beyond the form: a table of use, tools and who reviewed the result; model versions named; a row that honestly reads "An AI assistant (which one was not recorded)"; a note that Gemini was used only for prototypes and "none of its output is published here"; and the boundary "No scientific claim, data figure, simulation result, quote, or citation on this wiki was generated by AI." They also publish their own failed model engine on the same wiki.

### 85 designs expressed, 25 detectable, published as a dataset
NBJF, a high-school team, ran RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN, ESMFold, AlphaFold, TemStaPro and SaProt, then took 85 de novo sequences to the bench, got detectable SDS-PAGE expression for 25, and reported the result as an application dataset rather than a success claim. Compare UMA Malaga, which says plainly that its ranking order, substitution rule and pooling layout are untested in the lab — and that the lab contradicted the substitution rule.

### The prediction that lost, and the plugin that did not help
HangzhouFourteenAP: FoldX picked Y166Q at -1.63 kcal/mol; the assay put it last at net OD 0.629, below wild type at 0.996, and they revised the published ranking. UPF-Barcelona built a Claude Code plugin, A/B tested it over 28 cases with planted flaws, found no clear gain at double the token cost, and said so. Toronto reported that a homology-grouped split made their embeddings lose to sequence length. Jilin-China ran an out-of-distribution check and declined to use the scores. Al-Nahrain-IRAQ published a failed engine.

### GEMS-Taiwan is above the median and below its own standard
The team's record names Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT with task tags and one of only four negative boundaries in the cohort. But the same paragraph repeats verbatim under all three tools, no model versions or per-item reviewers are given, the project's AlphaFold work is absent from the AI field entirely, and the published LLM-assisted QGIS prompt is not pointed at. The attributions page itself is an embedded frame of the iGEM form, so a reader whose browser blocks it sees no attribution at all.

**Checklist**

- Record it the day it happens, not in October. One line in the dry-lab notebook per session: date, tool and version (Claude Opus 5.1, not "AI"), what you asked for, what you kept, and who checked it. The 2026 teams with the best records are the ones who logged as they went; the one who wrote "an AI assistant (which one was not recorded)" is the honest cost of logging late.
- Disclose all three kinds, not just the chatbot. (a) A model you trained or fitted yourself goes on the Model page with its data split. (b) A third-party model you ran as an instrument - AlphaFold, ESM, ProteinMPNN, Boltz - goes in the methods AND in the AI record, with version and settings, because 2026 shows 25 of 40 teams left it out of the AI record entirely. (c) A general-purpose assistant goes in the AI record with the task it touched.
- A tool is a tool; nothing is a co-author. Name the tool, name the human who is answerable for the output. Every GEMS artefact - a figure, a script, a paragraph, a parameter - has exactly one named human reviewer, and that name goes next to the tool, as Al-Nahrain-IRAQ did.
- Mark every model output UNVALIDATED until a bench result exists, in the text and in the figure caption. A predicted structure, a designed sequence, a ranked shortlist, a fitted parameter read out of a paper: all unvalidated until measured. Write the status, not the hope - UMA Malaga's three honest categories (automated tests / real services / wet lab, with "not shown" recorded as a result) are the model to copy.
- Publish the prompt or the script whenever the AI produced data rather than prose. If an assistant extracted parameters, prepared a GIS layer or read numbers out of figures, the prompt is part of the method and belongs in the repository with the code.
- Write the negative boundary explicitly: what AI did not do. Only 4 of 106 decorated teams did this in 2026. One sentence - no experimental data, no result, no citation, no scientific claim was AI-generated - is cheap to write and is the single line a sceptical reader is looking for.
- Benchmark the assistant when it does scientific work, and publish the number. Toronto measured their extraction pipeline at 95.0% precision and 87.1% recall against double-scored human curation. An unbenchmarked extraction pipeline is not a method, it is a hope.
- Report the failures. The AI prediction that lost to the bench, the designed sequence that did not express, the plugin that did not beat the base model, the hallucinated reference caught in review. Five teams in 106 did this in 2026 and one of them won Best Model for it. Log every caught hallucination with its citation so the count exists at the end of the season.

_Method and limits. Base rate: we opened the canonical iGEM attributions record for each of the 106 decorated teams in this report at teams.igem.org/wiki/<id>/attributions - the same record their wikis display - rendered it in a browser (the pages are client-side React and return an empty shell to a plain fetch), and extracted the AI Tool Use section verbatim. All 106 returned a page and all 106 had a non-empty AI Tool Use section; none was missing or truncated. Tool and task counts are regex matches on those extracted sections, so a tool named only in an attached document or on a Model page is not counted here, and 'review language' means the section contains words such as review, verify, check, validate or oversight, which is a weaker test than actually reviewing. Foundation-model use (40 of 106) is counted from the dry-lab fields of the 106 team files on this site; the per-tool figures quoted (AlphaFold 32, ProteinMPNN 14, RFdiffusion 8, ESM 8, Boltz 8) are the technique census page's numbers, not ours, and we report them so the two pages agree. The iGEM requirement is quoted from competition.igem.org/deliverables/guides and the medals page; the detailed Attributions Form requirements page is behind a team login and we did not read it. The hard limit: this method can only see what a team wrote down. Undisclosed assistant use is invisible by construction - we cannot detect it, we did not try to infer it, and nothing here should be read as a claim about which teams 'probably' used more AI than they said. Equally, a disclosure is a statement, not evidence: we checked what teams wrote, not whether it is complete. The 106/106 figure therefore measures compliance with a required form field, not the true extent of AI use, and the 4-of-106 negative-boundary figure and the 5 reported failures are the numbers that actually distinguish teams, because those were not asked for. The sample is decorated teams only, so this is not a base rate for the competition._


# Science for good

## Science for Good is a programme, not a judging category

_At GEMS, Science for Good means a club-form programme with no competition deadline: a few well-chosen problems, worked continuously and from several directions, for as long as they take. iGEM's Human Practices criteria are evidence we can learn from. They are not the definition._

A competition season is nine months long and ends in a rubric. That shape is useful — it forces a team to finish something — but it decides a great deal that nobody intended. It decides that a problem is worth working on if it can be closed by October. It decides that the output is a wiki. And it decides who you talk to, because a judge recognises a professor's authority faster than a farmer's.

**The evidence on this page is the cost of that shape.** Of 21 award-winning software tools from 2026, 8 are still usable today, and across every repository checked there are zero stars and zero forks — nobody came. Not one team in the 106 ran an inter-lab measurement ring, the one form of collaboration that would have produced a number other people could reuse. Of 106 decorated teams, 71 closed a stakeholder-to-design loop, but only nine or ten closed it with someone who was not a credentialled expert. None of this is because the teams were careless. It is because the deadline rewards an artefact and a defensible story, and all three of those things take longer than a season.

**So Science for Good at GEMS is the container for the work the competition cannot hold.** It is open membership rather than a selected team, it carries problems across years rather than seasons, and it is allowed to arrive somewhere with no method in hand. The first visit is listening. The solution does not have to be a construct — it can be an instrument, a dataset, a protocol, a piece of software, or a way of organising something that already exists. Sometimes the honest finding is that synthetic biology is the wrong tool, and a programme that cannot reach that conclusion is not doing research.

iGEM still matters, but the direction of supply reverses. *The programme feeds the competition, not the other way round.* A problem that has been lived with for two years makes a far better nine-month project than a problem invented in January to fit a village.

### It matters to someone who is not us
A problem someone outside GEMS already has, and would still have if we never showed up. The test is whether a specific person can describe it to you in their own words, unprompted, before you offer anything.

### It can actually be put somewhere
There is a real site, a real operator and a real route to getting it there. The analysis on this page found the loops that closed were closed where a non-specialist physically operates the thing — a stall, a hive, a field. Deployability is not a later phase; it selects the problem.

### The effect can be counted
Before starting, you can name the number that would move and say how you would measure it. If the only available outcome is that people felt positive about science, it belongs in education, which is good work but a different programme.

### The second one is cheaper than the first
Scaling is a property of the design, not an ambition stated at the end. If helping the tenth farm costs what the first one cost, it is a service, not a solution — and the programme should know which it is building.

### Not an iGEM incubator, and not outreach
A problem does not enter because it would make a good project, and it does not stay because it photographs well. Outreach and education are separate, valuable, and measured differently. Confusing the two is how a programme ends up with a lot of activity and no result.

**Checklist**

- Write the four criteria down and score every candidate problem against them in public, inside the programme.
- Give each live problem one owner and a dated file that anyone in GEMS can read.
- Make the first visit to any new partner a listening visit with no method proposed.
- Require a named number before work starts: what would move, and how it gets measured.
- Review the pipeline twice a year and close problems deliberately, with a written reason.
- Let iGEM teams draw from the pipeline; do not let the iGEM calendar decide what enters it.

_Method and limits. This section states GEMS Research's own definition of its Science for Good programme; it is not a finding about iGEM. The figures quoted in support — 8 of 21 software tools still usable, zero stars or forks, no inter-lab measurement ring in 106 teams, 71 of 106 loops closed with nine or ten closed by non-experts — come from the analyses further down this page and on the dry-lab tab, each of which states its own method and limits. They are offered as evidence that a nine-month container has predictable costs, not as proof that a club-form programme avoids them. That part is untested, and GEMS is the test._

## What is actually in the pipeline right now

_Two live entries, both inherited from relationships the ReLEAF season happened to create, and three proposals that come from this report's evidence rather than from a person. That is an honest picture of a programme at the start, and the asymmetry is the most useful thing on this page._

A pipeline is only worth keeping if it distinguishes between a problem **someone brought you** and a problem **you thought of**. The first kind already passes criterion one; the second kind has to earn it, and most never do. Both belong here, but they must be labelled, because a programme that forgets the difference quietly fills up with its own ideas.

Right now GEMS has two of the first kind, and both arrived the same way: not through a search for projects, but because a team spent a season in a place and kept talking to the people there. That is worth noticing, because it is the actual mechanism by which this pipeline will fill. **Relationships generate problems; project searches generate topics.** The implication for 2027 is not to brainstorm harder but to go back, without a proposal in hand, to the places the 2026 season already reached.

The three proposals below come from the report and are marked as such. Each one passes the four criteria on paper, which is exactly their weakness: nobody outside GEMS has yet said they want any of them. They are candidates for a listening visit, not plans.

*The partner behind both live entries is named here, at GEMS's decision: Chen Hui-wen (陳惠雯), who farms and teaches by natural-farming principles.* What is not written down here is what that farm's specific difficulties actually are — not out of discretion, but because nobody has asked yet. That is what the first entry below is for. When those constraints are finally recorded, they should be recorded in the farmer's own words and published only with their agreement.

### Go back to Chen Hui-wen's farm without a method
The ReLEAF season put the team in contact with Chen Hui-wen (陳惠雯), a teacher who farms by natural-farming principles. The next visit should carry **no synthetic-biology requirement at all** — the point is to hear what that farm's actual constraints are and write them down before anyone proposes anything. It is entirely possible the answer is not biology. That outcome is a result, not a failure, and the programme has to be able to publish it.

### A seed-exchange platform
Raised by Chen Hui-wen, the same partner. Worth taking seriously precisely because it is **probably not a synthetic-biology problem** — it looks like a matching, trust and record-keeping problem, which is to say software, logistics and governance. If GEMS can only work on things that need a construct, it is a competition team with a longer deadline. The first question is not how to build it but who else is already trying, and why seed savers would use a new one.

### The shared measurement standard nobody built
Not one of the 106 decorated teams of 2026 ran an inter-lab measurement ring. GEMS holds Best Measurement and Best Hardware, so it can credibly ship a calibrated construct and a written protocol to other Taiwanese labs and publish the between-lab variance. Passes all four criteria on paper. Untested against a real person's stated need — nobody has asked for it.

### An instrument a school can afford and rebuild
The hardware analysis on the dry-lab tab asks whether a stranger could rebuild any award-winning 2026 device. Taiwanese school labs are a real population with a real budget ceiling and a real operator who is not an engineer — which is the deployability condition the human-practices analysis found actually matters. Scales by documentation rather than by manufacturing.

### A characterised part someone else actually uses
Taiwan took zero parts nominations in 2026, and the registry is the one artefact designed to outlive a project. A well-documented part is small enough for a club to finish between seasons and is reused by definition if it is any good. Weakest of the three on criterion one: it serves the field rather than a named person, and the programme should be honest that this makes it a different kind of entry.

**Checklist**

- Keep the two columns separate forever: problems a person brought, and problems GEMS thought of.
- Before any proposal is written for a partner, record their constraints in their own words, dated.
- Return to every place the 2026 season reached, without a project in hand.
- For each proposal, find one person outside GEMS who will say they want it — or close the entry.
- Ask a partner before publishing what they told you — naming someone is one thing, publishing their difficulties is another.
- Review twice a year; closing an entry with a written reason is a success, not an admission.

_Method and limits. The two live entries come from GEMS Research's own 2026 season and are reported from the programme's account of them, not from any published source; the partner is named at GEMS's decision, and no specific difficulty of the farm is described here because none has been recorded yet. The three proposals are derived from analyses elsewhere in this report — the collaboration network, the hardware reproducibility census and the parts census — and each states there what it can and cannot see. No proposal here has been validated against a stated external need, which is recorded in the table as a No rather than smoothed over. This section is a plan, not a finding, and should be read as one._

## Who actually let the outside world change the science

_Across 93 teams, closing the loop has stopped being the distinction and become the norm — and almost every loop that closed was closed by a credentialled expert rather than by anybody the criterion is rhetorically about._

A score of four is a sentence, not a stakeholder list: a name, a specific thing said, and a design that is visibly different afterwards. Wageningen's Triton has three modules rather than one because Peter Fischer of Aqualab Zuid explained that trifluoroacetate can only be measured by LC-MS at a central lab, which forced an on-site biosensor, and because Bert van der Waal and Peyman Salehian showed that even tenfold reverse-osmosis concentration leaves it far too dilute, which forced a capture module. **GEMS-Taiwan** was releasing engineered Bacillus into soil until Prof. Chen Wen-Liang told them it could be neither contained nor made to sense temperature precisely; the hollow-fibre perfusion reactor and the electronic AIoT sensing layer both came out of that one April conversation. UCAS-China dropped NKX2-1 as a cargo and put SLPI in its place because Professor Huaiyong Chen said the first matters in development and barely in adulthood. RDFZ-China built bcsABCD in both BL21(DE3) and C41(DE3) and switched host after Professor Haibo Zhang warned that a working genetic module does not imply an efficient one; WUXI-DSAS excised gtdT on Dr Tengfei Hu's advice and recovered the linear dose-response its first-generation sensor could not give; IISER-Kolkata rebuilt its kill-switch trigger around the hypochlorite-sensing regulator RclR after a wastewater engineer pointed out that Indian plants disinfect with sodium hypochlorite rather than UV; and Oxford gave up a living Snodgrassella symbiont for heat-inactivated yeast because regulators pushed back against the beekeepers who had asked for it, then published what that cost its own users.

The three Best IHP winners share a method, and it is organisational rather than intellectual: the practice is wired into the engineering, not appended to it. **TU Delft** ran Value Sensitive Design in three declared passes and translated values into requirements, labelling the ones it could not meet as Future Perspectives rather than dropping them quietly; UCAS-China built its RCSF cycle as a deliberate parallel to DBTL and gave the human practices group the standing job of tracking every subteam's bottleneck; GEMS-Taiwan ran four thematic expert pipelines with five continuously engaged experts. What the winners do not have is a monopoly on depth. Oxford, Wageningen and UFABC-Brazil were nominees with chains at least as traceable, and UFABC declared its confirmation and refutation rules before seeing its survey results, then redrew its own SWOT when two assumptions failed. **Madrid-UCM**, which published the only genuine closure criterion in the cohort, got no human practices nomination at all.

The formats that changed designs are narrow and unglamorous. One of them is a single conversation with whoever operates the thing: Veolia's technical director for LYON, a sulfur-recovery engineer of thirty-three years for UOttawa, an optometrist for UAlberta, wet-market vendors for HongKong-JSS who demanded a number and got a wavelength-resolved spectrometer in place of a 14-channel colour sensor. Another is protocol-level consultation with whoever actually runs the technique, which is where chassis and construct changes come from: DTU to Komagataella phaffii, NFLSHS-CHINA from two plasmids to one, Heidelberg to a Serratia expression cassette. Add regulators contacted while the design is still open, peer teams handing over negative data as Darmstadt 2025 did to Padua on pcrABCD's oxygen sensitivity, and written-scorecard pitch events, which are cheap and work: Stanford's BIOME Shark Tank produced the microneedle segmentation pipeline. Against that, the school workshop, the museum stand, the carnival booth, the panel discussion and SDG mapping produced headcounts and nothing traceable, and the large public survey changed vocabulary with near-perfect reliability and hardware almost never.

The high-school tier is fully competitive wherever the work is user-facing and iterative. HongKong-JSS's farm-driven hardware revisions, measured as a drop from 7.41 to 1.95 per cent coefficient of variation, are better user-led engineering than most collegiate teams managed; **Hongwen School** struck three marketing claims on a gastroenterologist's evidence ladder and changed its selection antibiotic on a professor's re-annotation; HFI, NFLSHS-CHINA, RDFZ-China and WUXI-DSAS all changed circuits or hosts for a named reason; and QingdaoAcademy compressed twenty-two activities into thirteen numbered decisions that split a one-pot process in two and abandoned a planned pH-based function switch outright. Where the tier is not competitive is institutional reach: nothing in it approaches Oxford's EPA-FDA-USDA-CBD mapping, Wageningen's analysis of the non-viable-GMO approval route, UCL's Water UK discharge gap or DTU's correspondence with the European Environment Agency, and formal ethics infrastructure is rare, with Baltimore's community-lab board the main exception; the tier also almost never publishes failures of access the way DTU names the turbine makers who never replied.

The uncomfortable finding is who actually caused the changes. Of 64 teams that closed a loop, the loop was closed by a credentialled technical expert in nearly every case; the publics, patients and communities that the criterion is rhetorically about overwhelmingly changed the vocabulary and not the vector. Cornell's burn survivors changed what the team promises, Princeton's myeloma patients changed the word 'virus', HFI's 434 respondents changed 'genetically modified' to 'engineered' — all real, none of it touching a construct. Genuine counter-examples number six or seven in 93: LYON removed every living cell from its filter because the public objected, ICJFLS turned public fear into a four-layer containment design, HongKong-JSS re-specified a sensor because farmers wanted a number, UFABC-Brazil routed its seizure alert to a caregiver because a psychiatrist in the public system pointed out that patients who cannot recognise an aura cannot act on one, a beauty-salon manager's distrust of local seaweed put ultrafiltration desalting and endotoxin limits into QingdaoAcademy's plan, and a landfill worker of six years gave Hongwen School the handling cost that made local processing a hard constraint. Two further discomforts: the branded cycle acronym is now universal and predicts nothing, with Jilin-China's Social Shaping Loop and GreatBay-SCIE's five-stage framework scoring 2 while plain tables score 4; and awards track legibility rather than consequence, since **KIT** won Inclusivity and GreatBay-SCIE was nominated for Best IHP on evidence that scores 2, while Madrid-UCM, Hongwen School, GYHS and WUXI-DSAS closed loops nobody rewarded.

### Two of three modules were somebody else's idea
Wageningen set out only to degrade trifluoroacetate. Peter Fischer at Aqualab Zuid, one of six labs legally tasked with assessing Dutch drinking water, explained that the compound can only be measured by LC-MS on samples shipped to a central lab, so the bioreactor could not be operated at all without an on-site readout: that created the biosensor module. Bert van der Waal and Peyman Salehian then showed that tenfold reverse-osmosis concentration takes 2.2 micrograms per litre only to 22, against a milligram-per-litre target, which created the capture module. Frank Schoonenberg of Vitens moved the whole deployment target to reverse-osmosis concentrate, and Tue Kjaergaard Nielsen changed the readout to released fluoride because measuring TFA disappearance mistakes adsorption for degradation.

### The conversation that moved sensing out of the cell
GEMS-Taiwan's original design put engineered Bacillus subtilis in the soil with a DesK-DesR system reading temperature directly. On 10 April, Prof. Chen Wen-Liang and bioprocess experts said two things were wrong: the bacteria could not be contained, and biological sensing was neither precise nor controllable enough. Sensing moved out of the cell into electronic sensors and an AIoT model, and a hollow-fibre perfusion bioreactor was built to hold the bacteria in while letting the protectants out. A later public forum with natural-farming advocates, who argued that a crop protected from every stress never builds tolerance, became the specification for the release threshold rather than an objection to be managed.

### When the regulator overrules the user
Danny Le Feuvre of the Australian Honey Bee Industry Council and Mike Allerton of Amateur Beekeepers Australia both wanted a persistent living Snodgrassella alvi gut symbiont because it minimises beekeeper labour. Oxford did not simply comply: it took the question to Scottish and Australian regulators and the Soil Association, who pushed the other way, and switched to heat-inactivated dried yeast. The team then stated plainly what that cost — the persistence the beekeepers valued, meaning repeat dosing and more labour. A joint meeting with EPA, FDA and USDA staff stopped them treating the inactivated route as a universal regulatory shortcut, forcing jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction mapping instead.

### A farmer asked for a number
HongKong-JSS built a mercury biosensor with a visible colour readout. Koo's Farm and local wet-market vendors said they wanted numerical readings, not qualitative colour, which is the direct reason the AS7343 14-channel sensor was replaced by a wavelength-resolved Hamamatsu C12880 with a numerical display. Users then reported excessive syringe force on the V1 filter stack, so manual delivery became pump-driven dosing, improving the coefficient of variation from 7.41 to 1.95 per cent. More Happy Farm said plainly that not every farmer wants to own a device, which pushed them to a service model — and after a 195-person demonstration found high perceived confidence, the team separated device status from safety judgement in the interface because confidence is not accuracy.

### The only team that defined what 'closed' means
Madrid-UCM built a five-rung integration ladder with an explicit closure criterion: a loop counts as closed only when the revised design goes back to the person whose input triggered it and their response produces a further change. They then demonstrated it on materials — Carmen Garcia Payo and Loreto Garcia Fernandez proposed core-shell capsules, the team built them but could not see the internal structure, took that problem back to the same researchers, and got magnetite as an optical tracer plus cryosectioning, which became a wall-thickness and leakage pipeline. Aurelio Hidalgo's point that a single-use biocatalyst is neither economical nor recoverable killed both placeholder designs and moved the enzyme panel onto a reusable solid support. They also document a change they chose not to make, on the grounds that not adding a pathway is a design decision too. No Best IHP nomination.

### The survey that changes your vocabulary
Large public surveys are the most common instrument in the cohort and the least consequential for design. HFI's 434 responses replaced 'genetically modified' with 'engineered' across all materials and rebuilt the education from basics. Peking's 539 respondents named three priorities the team concedes already outlined the finished project. UCAS-China's 419 public respondents and HongKong-HS's 420 produced awareness statistics and workshop plans. The honest version is GHCIS, which found that its price and speed questions branched into samples too small to use and explicitly refused to convert 'within RMB 30' into a product requirement, carrying it forward as a question for frontline users instead.

_Method and limits. Every team in this report is a Top 10 or special-prize winner or nominee, so this is the most decorated tenth of the competition and not a representative sample. Read '64 of 93 closed the loop' as 'closing the loop is normal among teams that win things', not as a statement about iGEM at large. Every team file with any good.ihp content was scored on the four-point rubric from what the file itself states: a 4 required a named stakeholder, a specific thing said, and a change to the build, the deployment, the readout, the safety design or the business model that the file ties to that input. Teams whose only documented consequence was a change of framing, language, education material or evidence package scored 2 or 3 however elaborately the process was branded, and awards were ignored throughout. The rubric cannot verify that a change was made because of the advice rather than attributed to it afterwards, cannot see the wiki behind the summary, and cannot distinguish a thin causal chain from a thin write-up of a thick one. Files continued to land while the scoring ran; all 93 present at the end were read and scored, so the set is complete as of writing but not closed. Since this was written the set closed at 106 files. A later analysis on this page, Who the loop actually closes with, rescored the thirteen that landed late and recounts 71 of 106 closing a loop and nine or ten closing it with a non-expert, against the six or seven in 93 reported here. The extra non-expert loops are the late files plus two formulation and delivery-route changes this pass had read as framing. The shape of the finding is unchanged; the denominators there are the current ones._

## What separated real engagement from outreach theatre

_Across the 2026 field, the teams whose Science for Good work counted did four things the rest did not._

**They designed education from data, then measured it like an experiment.** UCAS-China did not start from "raise awareness". It ran clinician interviews and a 461-person questionnaire, found that patients stop medication once they feel better and that parents refuse to start it for children out of fear of side effects, and made *compliance* the target instead of awareness. UOregon wrote three separate curricula for three audiences with different prior knowledge and ran them as three DBTL iterations across June, July and October, carrying each round's lessons forward. HFI ran everything through a five-step cycle it named CLEAR, in which **every activity had to report a measured outcome and a change for the next iteration**.

The sharpest version of this is publishing the results when they are bad. GEMS-Taiwan ran pre- and post-lesson surveys with 140 students across five schools and published per-question accuracy charts including the failures — only 30% of students got DNA base pairing right. That number is worth more to the next teacher than any photograph of a full classroom.

**They trained themselves before training anybody else.** Nineteen GU Frankfurt members took the "Basics of Science Communication" workshop run by NaWik, Germany's national institute for science communication, and used its core-message and cloverleaf tools as the basis of everything that followed. Most teams treat communication as something you already know how to do because you can talk.

**They put disagreeing people in the same room.** Oxford's *Buzz In* podcast is the most quietly radical format in the 2026 field: rather than interviewing stakeholders separately and summarising, it deliberately paired people who disagree — a Varroa-resistance academic with a commercial beekeeper on whether to treat at all, then an industry council CEO with amateur beekeepers. Disagreement is the thing most human-practices pages are built to smooth over; Oxford made it the content.

KIT won Inclusivity by turning the same honesty inward. It read the iGEM Diversity and Inclusion Committee's own writing, surveyed five previous iGEM gender-equity projects, and noticed that nearly all of them face **outward** — role models, outreach to girls, awareness — and almost none examine the team itself. So KIT examined the team itself.

**They quantified the need, and built a business model that was not "sell the product".** Oxford states the problem in numbers rather than adjectives: Australia's failed Varroa eradication cost A$101 million and destroyed about 30,000 hives; surveyed US commercial operations lost roughly 62% of colonies in 2024–25. DTU-Denmark anchors on a date and a measurement: the Danish wind industry's voluntary landfill ban took effect on 1 January 2026, and a Danish EPA screening detected bisphenol A in every tank leaching test on blade material.

Then the models themselves. HongKong-JSS sells **Certification-as-a-Service** — farmers subscribe annually, the team tests soil on site, passing farms get a "Heavy Metal-Free" logo for supermarket packaging that earns a premium, and surprise re-tests throughout the year are affordable precisely because the test is cheap. GEMS-Taiwan deploys through farmer collectives rather than direct sales, because its own fleet analysis shows a reactor owned by a single farm sits idle most of the season. GU Frankfurt chose exclusive licensing over a start-up because an autologous cell therapy's facility and specialist-salary costs cannot be carried by a spin-out, and has a letter of support from Miltenyi Biotec to show for it. XJTLU-China gives catmaOS away, on the argument that accessibility *is* the commercial thesis.

UAlberta's case is the most evidentially careful: demand is tabulated by customer role **with the strength of each piece of evidence named** — two clinician letters of support, a signed letter of intent from one clinic, 86% of 38 surveyed dry eye patients interested, an application at interview stage with Nucleate Canada. And UCAS-China opens its commercial section by stating outright that the case must rest on a defined unmet need rather than on technological novelty, then tabulates the strengths of the existing drugs it would have to displace. A team willing to argue against itself is a team worth believing.

### Oxford's Buzz In: put the disagreement on the record
A three-episode podcast that deliberately paired stakeholders who disagree, rather than interviewing them separately and summarising. Episode one put a Varroa-resistance academic opposite a commercial beekeeper on whether to treat at all. Most human-practices pages exist to smooth disagreement away; this one makes it the content, and it is far harder to fake than a list of meetings.

### Publish the question your students got wrong
GEMS-Taiwan surveyed 140 students across five schools before and after each lesson and published per-question accuracy — including DNA base pairing, where only 30% answered correctly. Reporting the failure makes the whole dataset credible and hands the next teacher something actionable. A photograph of a full classroom does neither.

### Train the team before training the public
Nineteen GU Frankfurt members took the Basics of Science Communication workshop from NaWik, Germany's national science-communication institute, and built everything afterwards on its core-message and cloverleaf tools. Science communication is a craft with a literature; almost every other team treats it as something you can already do because you can talk.

### Sell the certificate, not the instrument
HongKong-JSS does not sell its mercury assay. Farmers subscribe annually, the team tests on site, passing farms get a 'Heavy Metal-Free' logo for supermarket packaging that commands a premium, and surprise re-tests through the year keep the certificate honest — affordable precisely because the test itself is cheap. The cheapness of the science becomes the business model rather than a weakness.

### Name the strength of each piece of evidence
UAlberta tabulates demand by customer role and says how strong each item is: two clinician letters of support, one signed letter of intent, 86% of 38 surveyed patients interested, one application at interview stage with Nucleate Canada. A letter of intent and a survey response are not the same kind of evidence, and saying so is what makes the table worth reading.

### Argue against yourself in public
UCAS-China opens its commercial section by saying the case must rest on unmet need rather than technological novelty, then lists what the existing drugs do well. GEMS-Taiwan publishes a 68-year payback against a partner's 4.9-year figure and names the disagreement instead of resolving it. This is the practice that most distinguishes the 2026 podium, and it costs nothing but nerve.

_Method and limits. Drawn from the Science for Good fields of the team files in this report, each researched from the team's own 2026 wiki. Audience numbers and survey sizes are the teams' own figures and are not independently verified. The judgement about what 'counted' is ours; the team files and the wikis behind them are linked so a reader can disagree. GEMS-Taiwan is the report author's own team and appears here on the same terms as the rest._

## The commercial work that was worth reading argued against itself

_Across the 2026 field, the teams with credible real-world plans are the ones that published a model showing their own product losing._

Almost every iGEM team produces a business model canvas. Very few produce a number that could have gone against them. The difference is the whole of what separates a credible 2026 commercial section from a template.

**Worldshaper-Shanghai** published a recomputable net-present-value model and reported the result honestly: their own enzyme gives a **negative NPV**. They did not bury it, soften it, or quietly change the discount rate. **BGI-College** did the same with arithmetic instead of finance — a break-even calculation comparing 6.70 against 4.0 mol H₂ per mol glucose disproved the team's own premise, and forced a redesign around byproduct valorisation. **DTU-Denmark** ran a prospective life-cycle assessment in SimaPro with ReCiPe 2016 H and found its enzymatic route emits 2.1 kg CO₂-eq/kg against 1.4 for solvolysis and 0.9 for pyrolysis, with cement co-processing beating them on almost every indicator — then converted each losing indicator into a named engineering target. **Madrid-UCM** published an ISO 14040/44 openLCA result that currently rules against its own technology.

**Stockholm** went furthest. Its safety advisory board killed the open-water release the project was built around, so the team dismantled the venture, retreated to a contained membrane bioreactor on a smaller industrial stream, and made the deliverable **reusable safety infrastructure** instead: an STPA hazard analysis, a nine-system wastewater containment guidebook, and a measurement-uncertainty toolkit. Giving up the product and shipping the method is a result, and it was recognised with the Safety and Security Award.

Set against that, the template is easy to spot once you know the tell: **the cost side is real and the revenue side is fantasy**. ZJU-China itemises equipment at CNY 7.45 million, media, IPTG and labour, and publishes a downloadable cost sheet — genuinely good work — then assumes **100% capture of its serviceable obtainable market** to reach a USD 427 million NPV. The discipline applied to the inputs evaporates at the outputs.

The high-school tier is not behind here, and in places it is ahead. **SUIS-SFLS** built the only full financial model in the high-school set: capital expenditure of CNY 6.8 and 11.65 million across two scenarios, CNY 71 and 163.5 per litre, 34% against 15.9% margins, break-even years, and the spreadsheets published as downloadable PDFs, on a dual NMPA and ISO 13485 regulatory track. **ICJFLS** works bottom-up from unit economics — RMB 0.8 per dose against RMB 199 retail — with a 745-response survey and a named CDMO. **NFLSHS-CHINA** has a filed and accepted patent on a CsCCD2 mutant, two physical minimum viable products with formula tables, and labels its partnerships as prospective rather than implying they are signed.

The second thing the credible teams do is **name the stage of each claim**. Baltimore runs Venture Creation Labs OKRs with numeric gates and IRB-approved trilingual surveys, and says plainly that its letters of intent and grants are targets rather than commitments. McGill has a full techno-economic analysis — $11.83 to $20.58 per kg of rare earth oxide, an Ashram project NPV of +USD 51 million, seven sensitivity analyses — an accelerator place, a venture-capital mentor, two letters of support and secured tailings samples, and states that it is not yet incorporated. Nobody is penalised for an early-stage venture. Teams are penalised, correctly, for presenting an aspiration in the grammar of an achievement.

And a reminder that not every project should become a company. **HBUT-China**, **WHU-China**, **Squirrel-Beijing** and **BASIS-China** have no venture at all. Their deliverable is infrastructure other teams can use: 34 parts in four independently reusable modules with measurement parts built in and honest terminator read-through annotations; a five-layer characterisation of Neo-IL-2 including surface plasmon resonance and high-passage stability; a tunable bile-acid kill switch with a measured 0.1–0.2 mM threshold compared against real sewage and soil concentrations, plus a published five-step framework for characterising kill switches. That is a real-world contribution with a longer half-life than most business plans.

### Publish the model that says no
Worldshaper-Shanghai's recomputable NPV model finds their own enzyme gives a negative NPV, and says so. DTU-Denmark's prospective LCA finds cement co-processing beats their enzymatic route on almost every indicator, then turns each losing indicator into an engineering target. Madrid-UCM's ISO 14040/44 assessment currently rules against its own technology. A model that could only ever have agreed with you is not evidence.

### Real costs, fantasy revenue
ZJU-China itemises CNY 7.45 million of equipment, media, IPTG and labour and publishes a downloadable cost sheet — then assumes 100% capture of its serviceable obtainable market to reach a USD 427 million NPV. This is the most common failure mode in iGEM commercial sections: rigour on the inputs, where the team has data, and none on the outputs, where it does not.

### Stockholm dismantled its own venture
A safety advisory board killed the open-water release the project was built on. Rather than argue, the team retreated to a contained membrane bioreactor on a smaller stream and shipped reusable safety infrastructure instead — an STPA hazard analysis, a nine-system wastewater containment guidebook, a measurement-uncertainty toolkit. It won the Safety and Security Award. Giving up the product and publishing the method is a result.

### SUIS-SFLS built the only full financial model in its tier
Capital expenditure of CNY 6.8 and 11.65 million across two scenarios, CNY 71 and 163.5 per litre, 34% against 15.9% margins, break-even years, spreadsheets published as downloadable PDFs, on a dual NMPA and ISO 13485 track. ICJFLS works bottom-up from RMB 0.8 per dose against RMB 199 retail with a named CDMO. The census found high-school teams do more techno-economic analysis than undergraduates; this is what that looks like up close.

### Name the stage of every claim
Baltimore says plainly that its letters of intent and grants are targets, not commitments. McGill has a full techno-economic analysis, an accelerator place, a VC mentor, two letters of support and secured tailings samples — and states it is not yet incorporated. NFLSHS-CHINA labels its partnerships prospective. Nobody is penalised for being early. Teams are penalised for writing an aspiration in the grammar of an achievement.

### Not every project should become a company
HBUT-China, WHU-China, Squirrel-Beijing and BASIS-China have no venture at all. They shipped infrastructure instead — 34 parts in four reusable modules with measurement parts built in, a five-layer Neo-IL-2 characterisation, a tunable kill switch with a measured 0.1–0.2 mM threshold checked against real sewage concentrations, and a published five-step framework for characterising kill switches. For an institution building a reputation, that has a longer half-life than a business plan.

_Method and limits. Drawn from the realWorld fields of the team files in this report, each researched from the team's own 2026 wiki. Financial figures are the teams' own and are not independently audited; where a team's assumptions looked unsupported that is noted as our reading, not as a finding of error. Teams that published a model unfavourable to themselves are over-represented here because that is exactly what the analysis is about — it is not a claim that most 2026 teams did so._

## The experts-only pattern is not about medicine. It is about who operates the thing.

_The obvious hypothesis — that therapeutics teams talk to clinicians because they have to, while agriculture and bioremediation teams get real knowledge from farmers and residents — does not survive the counting. Medical villages closed 6 of 21 loops with a non-expert; land, water and food villages closed 8 of 24. The gap that is real is a different one, and it is wide._

Across the 106 decorated teams on file, 71 closed a stakeholder-to-design loop and 16 of those 71 closed at least one with a non-expert — a farmer, beekeeper, patient, resident, frontline worker, vendor, artisan or volunteer rather than a professor, clinician, regulator, company scientist or official. Sorted by village, the medical/agricultural split the hypothesis predicted is almost flat. **Therapeutics** is 5 of 12, a higher rate than **Bioremediation** at 1 of 8. **Conservation** is 2 of 8 and **Food & Nutrition** 2 of 4. Only **Agriculture**, at 3 of 4, behaves as predicted, and four closed loops cannot carry an inference on their own. Reported honestly: the hypothesis as stated is wrong, and the earlier *ihp-depth* finding that nearly every loop is expert-closed holds inside every large village without exception.

What the table does show is a split the hypothesis did not anticipate, and it is not close. The **platform villages** — Foundational Advance, Biomanufacturing, Space, Software & AI, Fashion & Cosmetics — closed 26 loops and 2 of them involved a non-expert. Foundational Advance is 0 of 8, Space 0 of 3, Software & AI 0 of 1, Biomanufacturing 1 of 11. The **applied villages**, medical and agricultural together, closed 45 loops with 14 non-expert among them. Where a project has no identifiable person downstream of it this year, nobody outside the lab closes a loop, and no amount of survey work substitutes: Heidelberg, Marburg, Princeton, ETH-Zurich, Vilnius, William-and-Mary and XJTLU-China are all score-4 teams whose every consequential input came from somebody with a doctorate.

The structural reason, where the files support one, is not the village but **who physically operates the thing being changed**. Compare the two villages the hypothesis treated as equivalent. An Agriculture or Conservation deployment ends in a hive, a plot or a market stall that a beekeeper, a grower or a vendor runs with their own hands, so the operator *is* the non-expert and the loop closes through them. A Bioremediation deployment ends inside a wastewater plant, a refinery or a biodiesel works, where the operator is a process engineer with a degree — ABOA's loop closed through the Turku plant's process engineer, UOttawa's through a sulfur-recovery engineer of thirty-three years, Madrid-UCM's through Bio-Oils Huelva and Repsol, Wageningen's through Vitens and Aqualab Zuid. The residents the hypothesis imagined are present in those files and they do change something, but they change communication: Madrid-UCM's Inmaculada Alonso, who had watched a reservoir eutrophy for decades, moved the team toward perceptible restoration outcomes and clearer explanation; UZurich's residents below the slopes made ecological cost something to investigate. Twelve of the 71 teams that closed a loop have a documented non-expert input of exactly that kind — real, named, and stopping short of the build. That is the same vocabulary-not-vector result the earlier analysis found, now located precisely: it happens wherever the public lives *near* the deployment instead of *running* it.

The best non-expert loops are worth naming because they are all the same shape. **Athens** states that two conditions were fixed before any construct was designed — the protein must reach the brood, and it must survive the larval gut — and says plainly that neither would have come from a literature search; beekeeper Peter Kasztelewicz's gentler practice (requeening, partial clean-out) is why delivery moved from spray to feed, and the team published what that cost. **HongKong-JSS** replaced a 14-channel colour sensor with a wavelength-resolved spectrometer because Koo's Farm and wet-market vendors wanted a number, then replaced syringe delivery with pump dosing after users complained about the force needed, measuring the result as a fall from 7.41 to 1.95 per cent coefficient of variation. **Hongwen School** got the handling cost of wet spent grain (70-80 RMB per tonne, driven by leachate, odour and liner) from Master He, a municipal landfill worker of six years, and turned localised processing from a preference into a hard constraint; separately Mr Shen of a Chongming ecological farm said 'I never look at the price per ton — I look at the cost per kilogram of gain', and the feed route became a standardised premix judged on feed conversion ratio. **LYON** removed every living cell from its filter because the public objected, and ruled households out as customers entirely. **QingdaoAcademy** put ultrafiltration desalting and endotoxin limits into its plan because a beauty-salon manager said she would hesitate to trust Qingdao Ulva. **TAU-Israel** is the medical exception that proves the rule: Shir Parchef's eighteen-year wait for an endometriosis diagnosis and Netta Ben Moshe's being told that incapacitating pain was ordinary cramps set the goal as eliminating pathology without systemic hormonal ablation — patients setting a constraint on the mechanism, not on the wording.

Two cautions against over-reading. First, the non-expert loops cluster not only by operator role but by **what kind of change they produce**: of the 16, ten changed something physical — a sensor, a delivery route, a formulation, a containment architecture — and six changed only deployment scope, target user or a selection criterion. Oxford is in the second group: about twenty chemical-free hobbyists of the Oxfordshire Natural Beekeeping Group argued against the entire premise, and Oxford's response was to narrow the target user to commercial operations and write that they had changed 'not the molecular mechanism of NECTAR, but the problem we believed NECTAR should — and should not — try to solve'. That is honest and it is real, but it is not the same act as changing a part. Second, legibility may be doing some of the work the villages appear to do: a judge can verify that a professor said something, and several teams that did consult non-experts recorded the result as an honest null. **IISER-Kolkata** asked Mr Mohadep Dutta, who has fished the Ganga since he was seven, about a shift in fish sex ratio, and published that he could not see one — evidence the effect needs instrumentation, rather than a loop. **Stanford University**, Grand Prize winner in Therapeutics, looked for keloid patient groups, found almost none, was told by the one that replied to talk to clinicians instead, and states outright that physicians cannot stand in for lived experience. Those two entries are better practice than most of the surveys in the cohort and they close nothing.

For an agriculture-adjacent team the operational reading is narrow and uncomfortable. The teams worth copying are not the Best IHP winners as a class — **TU Delft**, **UCAS-China** and **GEMS-Taiwan** all won and all had their architecture set by credentialled experts. **GEMS-Taiwan** should be held to its own standard here: sensing moving out of the cell, the hollow-fibre perfusion reactor, the abandonment of proline delivery, the narrowing to heat and salinity, the WB800 strain and the shift from continuous to periodic operation were closed by Prof. Chen Wen-Liang, Dr. Paul Verslues, Dr. Elizabeth Sattely, Prof. Huang Chieh-Chen and CH Biotech. The only non-expert input that reached the design was the natural-farming forum of 5 September, whose argument that a crop protected from every stress never builds tolerance became the specification for the release threshold, and a farmer's question about organic certification, which bounded the market rather than the machine. **Muenster-University**, nominated for Best Agriculture, reached farmers through the WLV agricultural association and changed its education strategy. That is the default outcome for an agriculture team that talks to farmers, and avoiding it takes a deliberate act: put the device in the hand of the person who will hold it, and ask for a number.

### A negative result, stated plainly
The hypothesis was that the experts-only pattern is worst where the stakes are most medical and best where non-specialists hold decisive practical knowledge. It does not hold. Medical villages (Therapeutics, Diagnostics, Oncology, Infectious Diseases) closed 21 loops with 6 non-expert among them, 29 per cent. Land, water and food villages (Agriculture, Bioremediation, Conservation, Food & Nutrition) closed 24 loops with 8 non-expert, 33 per cent. Four percentage points is not a pattern. Bioremediation, the village singled out for residents near contaminated sites, is the weakest applied village at 1 of 8.

### Platform villages have nobody downstream
Foundational Advance 0 of 8, Space 0 of 3, Software & AI 0 of 1, Biomanufacturing 1 of 11, Fashion & Cosmetics 1 of 3. The five platform villages between them closed 26 loops and 2 involved a non-expert, against 14 of 45 across the applied villages. This is not a failure of effort - Heidelberg, Marburg, Princeton and ETH-Zurich ran some of the most traceable chains in the cohort. It is that a tool with no named user this year has no lay stakeholder to be wrong in front of. For a team whose project is a platform, the honest move is Uni-Padua-IT's: take the hardware manual to an instrumentation professor and weaken your own claim.

### Two conditions, fixed before any construct was designed
Athens writes that the requirements for ApiconIASIS came from beekeeping, not from the team: the protein must reach the brood, and it must survive the larval gut. Neither, they say, would have been prioritised from a literature search, and both now define what counts as success. Beekeeper Peter Kasztelewicz, whose own hive footage is on the wiki, worked by requeening and partial clean-out, and that practice is why delivery moved from spray to feed - the adjuvant surfactants harm bees, and separately the person holding the sprayer inhales it, so protective equipment went into the protocols and not into the product. They then chose a purified non-replicating enzyme over a live phage knowing it is weaker and more expensive.

### The man who knew what a tonne actually costs
Hongwen School's register of changes is specific, attributed and sometimes negative. Master He, a municipal landfill worker of six years, gave them 60-90 tonnes a month at nearly 80 per cent moisture and handling costs of 70-80 RMB per tonne driven by leachate, odour, liner and labour, persisting not from indifference but from absent local off-takers. The team deleted both of its extreme narratives, fixed 70-80 RMB per tonne as a local baseline, and upgraded localised processing from a business preference to a hard environmental constraint, because a route relying on high-energy drying or long-haul transport would eat its own gains. Separately Mr Shen of a Chongming ecological farm reframed the unit of account - cost per kilogram of gain, not price per tonne - and the feed route became a standardised premix pourable into an existing mixer, judged on feed conversion ratio, diarrhoea rate and mortality.

### GEMS-Taiwan's architecture was closed by professors
GEMS-Taiwan won Best Integrated Human Practices in the high-school section on an agricultural project, and on this measure it sits with the majority rather than the exceptions. Sensing moving out of the cell and the hollow-fibre perfusion reactor came from Prof. Chen Wen-Liang on 10 April; abandoning proline delivery from Dr. Paul Verslues; narrowing to heat and salinity from Dr. Elizabeth Sattely; the WB800 strain and periodic rather than continuous operation from Prof. Huang Chieh-Chen; the costing and regulatory work from CH Biotech. The one non-expert input that reached the design is the natural-farming forum of 5 September, where the argument that a crop protected from every stress never builds tolerance became the specification for the release threshold, and a farmer's question about organic certification that bounded the market rather than the machine. The Ghanaian farmers who supplied the origin question have no documented design consequence.

**Checklist**

- Ask who will physically hold the device or run the process on the day it is used. If that person has a degree in your field, your non-expert loop will not happen by accident.
- Make the non-expert ask for a number. HongKong-JSS's sensor swap and Hongwen School's 70-80 RMB per tonne both started as a quantity somebody named out loud.
- Fix one or two success conditions from practice before the construct is designed, as Athens did, and write down that they did not come from the literature.
- Recruit the people who disagree with the premise. Oxford's twenty chemical-free hobbyists narrowed the target user; GEMS-Taiwan's natural-farming forum set the release threshold.
- Record non-expert input that changed nothing, and say so. IISER-Kolkata published a fisher who could not see the effect; Stanford published that it could not find patients. Both are better than a survey that only changed a word.
- Check the type of change before claiming a loop: a part number, a concentration, a format, a delivery route or who may buy it counts. A changed word, a new leaflet or a reframed slogan does not.

_Method and limits. Population: all 106 team files on disk, every one of them a Top 10 or special-prize winner or nominee, so this is the most decorated tenth of iGEM 2026 and not a sample of the competition. Loop scores: the 93 teams scored in the earlier ihp-depth analysis keep that analysis's score unchanged, and 'closed a loop' means its score of 4 - a named stakeholder, a specific thing said, and a change to the build, deployment, readout, safety design or business model. Thirteen files landed after that scoring ran (BASIS-China, BGI-College, Bist-China, Michigan, NCKU-Tainan, NU Boston, Squirrel-Beijing, TU Darmstadt, Tsinghua-T, UBC-Vancouver, UiOslo-Norway, WHU-China, XJTLU-Software); I scored those thirteen myself on the same rubric and seven reached 4, so 71 of 106 against the earlier 64 of 93. Non-expert rule, written before classifying: a person counts as a NON-EXPERT when their standing in the exchange rests on lived experience or hands-on practice rather than on a credential, a research post, a regulatory office or a technical role in a company - farmers, growers, fishers, beekeepers, residents, patients and their families, carers, frontline manual workers, market vendors, shop and salon staff, artisans, consumers, students, volunteers, indigenous community members. EXPERT covers professors and researchers, physicians, dentists, nurses and medical technologists, regulators and officials, company scientists, engineers, technical directors, QA and regulatory-affairs staff, investors and corporate managers, lawyers, ethicists and social scientists, peer iGEM teams and alumni. The hard case the brief names - a farmer with a degree - I resolved toward NON-EXPERT when the person speaks about running their own operation, and toward EXPERT when they are employed to advise other people's operations. Mr Lu of Worldshaper-Shanghai, described as a grower and extension author, is counted non-expert on that rule and is the clearest instance of it; Yusong Shi of GYHS, a doctoral student who is also a stony-coral hobbyist, is counted expert on the same rule, and GYHS's Conservation cell would move if that call reversed. A team counts in the last column if at least one documented loop was closed by a non-expert; ten of the sixteen changed something physical (sensor, delivery route, formulation, containment architecture) and six changed deployment scope, target user or a selection criterion. Twelve further teams have a documented non-expert input that changed only claims, language, education material or success framing, and those are counted as expert-closed, which is the same line the earlier analysis drew. Counting only physical changes gives nine or ten rather than the earlier analysis's 'six or seven in 93'; the difference is thirteen extra files plus formulation and delivery-route changes I counted and it did not, and this is the one place the two analyses differ. Villages: 50 of the 106 files carry no village string, and the high-school section does not have fine-grained villages at all - it competes in four merged clusters, so GEMS-Taiwan's agricultural project sat in the Space / Foundational Advance / Software & AI / Biomanufacturing cluster. I therefore assigned every team to one of the thirteen collegiate villages by where the technology is deployed and who it affects, using the official label from results2026.json where one exists. Several assignments are genuinely arguable - Cornell's smart bandage sits in Fashion & Cosmetics because that is the village it won, QingdaoAcademy and MIT-MAHE could be read as Food rather than Biomanufacturing, Mingdao and TU Darmstadt as Bioremediation rather than Biomanufacturing - and a different reading would move single teams between rows without changing the platform-versus-applied result. What this cannot see: whether a change was made because of the advice or attributed to it afterwards; the wiki behind the file summary, except for Athens and HUST-China, whose pages I read directly to check two borderline calls; whether a loop recorded as expert-closed had an unrecorded non-expert behind it; and whether judges preferred credentialled stakeholders, which is a plausible alternative explanation for the platform-village result that these files cannot settle. Nine of the thirteen village cells have fewer than eight closed loops and are flagged in the table; Agriculture at 3 of 4 is the single most quotable cell and the least load-bearing._

## Nobody measured an escape rate

_Zero of 106 decorated teams report a measured escape frequency. Nineteen built a containment device; three knew the metric well enough to say they had not measured it. The teams worth copying are the ones that turned a safety claim into a number, tested the safeguard until it broke, or gave up a design because the safety answer came back wrong._

**The base rate first, because it sets the bar low.** Across the 106 decorated teams researched for this report, 19 describe a genetic containment device — a kill switch, an auxotrophy, a toxin–antitoxin pair. Four discuss dual use or misuse at all. Two name how their synthesised DNA was screened. And **zero report a measured escape frequency**, the one number that converts a containment claim into evidence. Two teams in the environmental cohort — **UCL** (6381) and **WageningenUR** (6222) — have no safety page in their site navigation at all, while proposing water treatment and drinking-water deployment respectively. The Safety and Security Award itself tells the same story: no nominees at all in the Overgrad and High School sections, only a winner. Almost nobody enters this category, and the ones who do are not competing against a crowd.

**What a real safety page does that a recitation does not.** The recitation is: BSL-1, non-pathogenic chassis, a risk-group table, autoclave at 121 °C, gloves and closed-toe shoes. Everything on that list is true and none of it is about the project. The minority do one of five harder things. They convert the containment claim into a threshold and compare it against the receiving environment in the same units — **BASIS-China** (6123) measured its bile-acid suicide switch at a threshold of roughly **0.1–0.2 mM taurocholate**, then looked up feline duodenal bile salts at 15–42 mM, sewage total bile acids at 184–356 µg/L (which they convert to 4.7×10⁻⁴–9.1×10⁻⁴ mM) and 13.3 pmol/g deoxycholic acid in soil, and showed the gap. They test the safeguard until it fails — **William-and-Mary** (6243), the Undergrad winner, took a published triple-toxin kill switch off Addgene and ran it longitudinally; it was *the first of their circuits to lose function*, failing weeks before the others, and the entire project became an argument that kill switches need the failure analysis that bridges and aircraft already get. They measure non-target harm rather than asserting it — **Peking** (6366) screened its dsRNA in 21-nt sliding windows against RefSeq, found the longest uninterrupted match in any non-target homolog was **13 nt** (10–11 nt for the pharaoh ant), then actually expressed the ant's homologous fragments in S2 cells and measured relative expression of **1.22 and 1.30** after dsRNA treatment: no knockdown. They choose inactivation against the actual agent — **Bielefeld-CeBiTec** (6221) found that autoclaving and NaOH are of limited effect on α-synuclein fibrils, so they used 10% SDS *and* autoclaved, worked without preformed fibrils after asking the genetic engineering authority, and ran the lab on electronic access tokens with one-way transport and lab coats that never leave the culture room. And they publish an evidence ledger: a "what our results establish" column beside a "what remains before real-world use" column, which BASIS-China, Peking and IISER-Kolkata all do and most teams do not.

**The escape-rate question has a clean answer, and it is zero.** The strongest teams know exactly what is missing. **IISER-Kolkata** (6450) writes it out: *"the figure that matters for biocontainment is the escape frequency, i.e., the proportion of cells surviving induction... Values below 1 in 10⁸ cells are the benchmark used in the synthetic biology biocontainment literature. This has not been measured."* **UCSC** (6215) projects a **10⁻¹²** combined escape risk by multiplying a cited 10⁻⁶ per-plasmid transfer probability by itself, against a cited 10⁻⁸ standard — arithmetic, not measurement — and then says the honest thing about its own uracil auxotroph: the mutation is H99P, a single base substitution, *"among the most readily reversible,"* and *"any containment claim based on this strain needs a measured reversion frequency, obtained by plating a large population on medium lacking uracil and counting the colonies that grow."* **Madrid-UCM** (6124) notes that the strongest engineered systems report undetectable escape near two parts in 10¹². What teams measured instead were kill assays: **NU Boston** (6300) invalidated its own OD₆₀₀ kill-switch readout after discovering CcdB induces filamentation, which changes light scattering, and moved to flow cytometry live/dead and CFU counts, showing a drop at 0.2% arabinose across the 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁷ dilutions. That is good practice, and it is still not an escape rate.

**Three teams gave something up, and that is the strongest evidence in the category.** **Stockholm** (6292), the Overgrad winner, is verified: its own wiki records the largest change in the project as *"Open municipal deployment was dropped for a contained bioreactor on a defined, concentrated stream, with physical containment in place of a kill switch."* The trigger was a named advisory board member, Gunaratna Kuttuva Rajarao, telling them wastewater plants are not closed systems, plants will not accept GMOs, and a kill switch alone would probably not be enough. The venture went with it: no company, no pricing, no customer, and the chassis they now point at for production is not even yeast. **Oxford** (6391) is the second case and states the cost out loud: they chose heat-inactivated yeast over a living *Snodgrassella alvi* gut symbiont for containment and regulatory reasons, *"and in doing so gave up the persistence that made S. alvi attractive, which means NECTAR needs repeat dosing and therefore more beekeeper labour. Some of the beekeepers we spoke to preferred the option we dropped."* **Bielefeld-CeBiTec** is the third and the only one that dropped work on dual-use grounds: *"We dropped work on blood-brain-barrier-crossing LNPs because of its dual-use potential."* Smaller versions exist — ICJFLS (6098) binned a high-leakage kill-switch design after another team shared leakage data, BGI-College (6345) swapped chassis from *C. butyricum* to *C. beijerinckii* at an early safety review, GCGS (6242) documented a rejected pH-sensitive switch with a reason.

**DNA ordering is where this report's roadmap item actually has a worked example — exactly one.** **CalPolySLO** (6405) writes the paragraph GEMS needs to copy: *"We order synthetic DNA from IDT and Twist Bioscience, both members of the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, which screens orders for sequences of concern. We use nothing from Risk Group 3 or 4."* They then publish a four-step provenance chain from order to purified protein, and they got there because Dr Hank Greely told them to publish their safety thinking *before* starting work and Dr Keith Robison raised dual-use scenarios, which produced a benefits-versus-misuse framework. **TAU-Israel** (6196) is the other, and goes further by building screening into software: their design tool runs **commec**, the IBBIS Common Mechanism, on every generated sequence before release, holds the output when screening is incomplete or unresolved, and states plainly that a clean result *"does not establish that a sequence is harmless"* and that the frontend panel is not fully connected and live deployment is unverified. That last sentence is what makes it credible. **BASIS-China** names Sangon Biotech as its synthesis house and emailed safety@igem.org before collecting animal-derived material rather than assuming an unavailable form meant the work was impossible.

**On environmental release, the bar is visibly different and most teams do not clear it.** **Peking** designed physical screening into the hardware: two offset slit layers forming a tortuous passage sized against springtails at 0.5–10 mm, an attract-first-load-later deployment sequence so engineered yeast is only loaded after termite activity is confirmed on a load cell, and a removable inner cartridge so the material is retrievable — while declaring that its FAR1–Tet-Off proliferation brake *"remains at the design stage"* and that the two environment-responsive promoters *"do not yet constitute a combined dual-signal control system."* **Athens** (6478) traced the real regulatory fork: marketing authorisation under EU Regulation 2019/6 versus the biopesticide regime, EFSA alongside national authorities, and the fact that European foulbrood is WOAH-listed and compulsorily reportable in Greece, so any alternative to destruction must clear that first. **Madrid-UCM** had containment made a precondition by an industrial partner — Repsol said living GMOs would not be acceptable without evidence that release had been prevented — and answered with encapsulated cells plus a culture-and-qPCR monitoring campaign with a divert-and-inactivate protocol. **GHCIS** (6166) sidestepped the problem by going cell-free, so there is no replicating organism to contain. Against these, **Toronto** (6187) — whose human practices work is genuinely strong — has a safety page that is a laboratory incident risk register, and **NU Boston** has a live contradiction worth naming: its alginate beads are *designed to degrade in soil and release the bacteria*, while the kill switch is described as the thing that justifies release.

**GEMS-Taiwan, held to the same bar.** ReLEAF (6072) has exactly one measured containment result, and it is real: lumen-side medium sampled after 24 hours in the bioreactor grew colonies, shell-side medium grew none across a 0.2 µm hollow-fiber membrane retaining cells of 0.25–1.0 µm, backed by transmembrane-pressure and droplet leak detection. That is more than most teams have. It is also the whole case, and the gaps are large for a system that sits on a farm. There is no genetic containment layer at all — no kill switch, no auxotrophy, no second barrier if the membrane fails, which is the single failure mode the whole design depends on. The test is one timepoint, presence/absence, with no CFU count, no plated volume, no detection limit, no replicates and no stressed or fouled-membrane condition; the wiki nonetheless says the membrane *"ensures containment."* Antibiotic resistance markers (erythromycin) are used with no stated plan to remove them before field use. The DURC section identifies no misuse pathway, only a commitment not to misuse. There is no DNA-order screening statement and no supplier named anywhere — precisely the NSTM-6 gap the roadmap flags. And although the team correctly notes that cell-free agricultural biologics may fall between the biopesticide and synthetic-biology classifications, no Taiwanese authority is named as having been asked. CalPolySLO's one paragraph and BASIS-China's one email are each a week's work; both are missing.

### BASIS-China measured a threshold, then looked up the real environment
The suicide switch keeps cells alive above roughly **0.1–0.2 mM taurocholate** and suppresses growth below it, measured across four Anderson promoters with empty vector alongside. They then converted published concentrations into the same units: feline duodenum 15–42 mM, sewage total bile acids 184–356 µg/L (4.7×10⁻⁴–9.1×10⁻⁴ mM), soil deoxycholic acid 13.3 pmol/g. Two to three orders of magnitude of margin, stated as a comparison rather than a claim — and they add that their microcapsules are designed to release cells in the intestine and must not be counted as physical containment.

### William-and-Mary's kill switch broke first
They took a published triple-toxin kill switch from Addgene and followed it longitudinally alongside other circuits. It was the first to lose its intended function, failing weeks before the rest. CFU counts were used instead of OD₆₀₀ or fluorescence, on the reasoning that a kill switch's output is loss of viability, not loss of signal. Their conclusion is the uncomfortable one: a system designed as the last line of defence had never been subjected to the failure analysis that mature engineering disciplines apply as routine.

### Stockholm dismantled its own deployment plan, and Oxford named the cost
Stockholm's wiki records the project's largest change as open municipal deployment dropped for a contained bioreactor, physical containment replacing the kill switch, after a named advisory board member said plants are not closed systems and will not accept GMOs. The venture went with it. Oxford did the same thing one level down: heat-inactivated yeast instead of a living *Snodgrassella alvi* symbiont, for containment and regulatory reasons — *"and in doing so gave up the persistence that made S. alvi attractive... Some of the beekeepers we spoke to preferred the option we dropped."*

### CalPolySLO wrote the paragraph the roadmap is asking for
*"We order synthetic DNA from IDT and Twist Bioscience, both members of the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, which screens orders for sequences of concern. We use nothing from Risk Group 3 or 4."* Then a four-step provenance chain from order to purified protein. It exists because an ethicist told them to publish their safety thinking before starting work and a biosecurity scholar raised dual-use scenarios. Two of 106 teams name a screening regime at all; this is the cleaner of the two to copy.

### TAU-Israel put the Common Mechanism in the release path
Their design tool runs **commec**, the IBBIS Common Mechanism, over every generated sequence and holds the output when screening is incomplete or leaves an unresolved concern.
