What makes it credible is the disclaimer: a result without a finding *"does not establish that a sequence is harmless, suitable for an experiment, or approved for synthesis,"* the frontend panel is not fully connected, and live deployment has not been verified. They dated the audit and named the source revision.

### Peking measured what its bait does to the wrong insect
21-nt sliding windows against RefSeq with one-mismatch tolerance; longest uninterrupted perfect match in any non-target homolog was **13 nt**, 10–11 nt for the pharaoh ant. Then they expressed the ant's homologous fragments in S2 cells, treated with the termite dsRNA for 48 h, and measured relative expression of **1.22** and **1.30** — no knockdown. Hardware does the rest: offset slits sized against springtails at 0.5–10 mm, bait loaded only after termite activity registers on a load cell. The proliferation brake is declared unbuilt.

### Three teams named the metric and said they had not measured it
IISER-Kolkata: *"the figure that matters for biocontainment is the escape frequency... Values below 1 in 10⁸ cells are the benchmark... This has not been measured."* UCSC on its uracil auxotroph: H99P is a single base substitution, among the most readily reversible, and *"any containment claim based on this strain needs a measured reversion frequency."* Madrid-UCM notes the strongest systems report undetectable escape near two parts in 10¹². Naming the number you are missing is worth more than a table of risk groups.

**Checklist**

- **Suppliers.** Order synthetic DNA and oligos only from International Gene Synthesis Consortium members, and name them on the safety page the way CalPolySLO does — supplier, consortium membership, and the fact that they screen orders for sequences of concern.
- **Screen what you order.** Run commec (the IBBIS Common Mechanism) over every ordered construct of 50 nucleotides or more before the order goes out. A hold is not a pass: an incomplete or unresolved screen blocks the order until a human resolves it.
- **Record, and keep it eight years.** One register row per order: date, supplier, construct name, full sequence, length, requester, screening tool and version, result, approver. Eight-year retention, matching what NSTM-6 asks of certified suppliers, because a GEMS order inside a US-funded collaboration inherits the requirement.
- **One named signer.** A single GEMS biosafety officer approves every synthesis order and every new chassis before work starts. Two signatures for anything above Risk Group 1, anything on a select-agent list, and any sequence the screen flags.
- **Say what you will not do.** No release of viable engineered cells outside a sealed device; no Risk Group 3 or 4 material; no work with uncharacterised environmental isolates; no construct whose purpose is increased transmissibility, virulence or host range; no antibiotic resistance marker in anything intended to leave the lab.
- **Measure the containment number, don't project it.** For any strain that could leave a device, report an escape or reversion frequency per cell per generation: plate a large population under the restrictive condition, count survivors, state how many cells were plated and the detection limit. The literature benchmark is below 1 in 10⁸.
- **Compare against the real receiving environment.** Any threshold — bile acid, salicylate, temperature, nutrient — gets converted into the units of the soil, water or field where the organism would land, with a cited source. A containment claim is only as good as that comparison.
- **Publish the evidence ledger.** Two columns on every safety page: what these results establish, and what remains before real-world use. Name horizontal transfer, circuit drift over passages, and extracellular DNA explicitly, because genetic containment addresses none of them.
- **Ask someone outside, in writing, early.** Email the institutional biosafety committee, the relevant Taiwanese authority for field deployment of an engineered agricultural input, and safety@igem.org — and publish the question, the answer, and what changed. An unavailable form is not the same as an impossible experiment.

_Method and limits. Two passes. First, a keyword sweep of research/teams/*.json — the researched prose on all 106 decorated teams — for kill switch, auxotroph, biocontainment, containment, escape, BSL, dual-use, screening, risk assessment, Nagoya and release. Counts from that pass are: 19 of 106 describe a genetic containment device, 28 use the words biosafety or biosecurity, 28 name an institutional biosafety body or officer, 4 discuss dual use, 2 name a DNA-synthesis screening regime, and 0 report a measured escape frequency. Those counts are a floor, not a census: the files are researcher summaries, so a practice a team carried out but did not write up prominently — or wrote up only on a page the researcher did not quote — is invisible here. Second, direct verification on the teams' own 2026 wikis for 21 teams: the six Safety and Security Award winners and nominees (William-and-Mary 6243, Bielefeld-CeBiTec 6221, Peking 6366, UCSC 6215, Stockholm 6292, BASIS-China 6123) plus the environmental-release cohort (LYON, Madrid-UCM, RUM-UPRM, UCL, UOttawa, WageningenUR, DTU-Denmark, Toronto, Athens, Oxford, Muenster-University, Lambert-GA, GHCIS, Squirrel-Beijing, GEMS-Taiwan). Most 2026 wikis are client-rendered React applications that return an empty shell to curl; where that happened the page text was recovered from the site's own JavaScript bundle, and the static wikis were read directly. Every number quoted here was read off the team's own page. Bielefeld-CeBiTec 6221, UCSC 6215 and RUM-UPRM 6282 are not in the 106-team on-disk corpus and were read only from their wikis. UCL 6381 and WageningenUR 6222 have no safety page in their site navigation, which is a statement about their navigation, not proof they did no safety work — both completed iGEM's safety forms, which are not public. What none of this can see: the safety form every team files with iGEM, institutional biosafety committee records, and anything a team did at the bench and never wrote down._


# Team analysis

## Taiwan at iGEM 2026

_Taiwan fielded thirteen competing teams in 2026 and won six awards, more than any territory in East Asia except China, but every technical award came from the high-school tier and the island is invisible in parts, software and collegiate modelling._

Taiwan registered fifteen entries with iGEM in 2026 and thirteen of them competed — eight high-school, four undergraduate, one overgraduate — returning **eight golds, five silvers and no bronzes**, one Top 10 place, six outright award wins and seven further nominations. The wins were GEMS-Taiwan's Best Measurement, Best Hardware and Best Integrated Human Practices, Labi-Taiwan's peer-voted iGEMers Prize, NYCU-Taiwan's Best Project Promotion Video and NCKU-Tainan's Best Infectious Diseases Project; the nominations added Mingdao for Model, NCKU-Tainan for Hardware, NTHU for Food & Nutrition, Labi-Taiwan for Measurement, and GEMS-Taiwan for Presentation, Wiki and Best Village Project. Against the region that is strong in volume and weak in altitude: China fielded 176 competing teams for 24 wins and five Top 10 places, Hong Kong 16 for three wins, three Top 10 places and the high-school Grand Prize first runner-up in HongKong-JSS, Japan seven for nine nominations and no wins, Korea six for none and Singapore four for none. Taiwan therefore out-won Hong Kong six to three on fewer teams and was the only territory outside China to win more than once, but it took a single Top 10 and placed nothing in any Grand Prize at any tier.

The strength is **instrumentation**: six of the thirteen teams built and documented a device — GEMS-Taiwan's hollow-fibre perfusion bioreactor and two in-line photometers, NCKU-Tainan's CAPTURE-Screen fluorescence reader at US$54–161 against the US$3,500 open-source plate reader it substitutes, NTHU's four-channel frequency-tagged reader with digital lock-in detection, NTHU Taiwan's open-source moving-bed biofilm reactor, Mingdao's single-frame fermentor and Labi-Taiwan's portable electrochemical reader — with human practices and communication a clear second, carrying three of the six wins. The weakness is just as sharply defined: **not one Taiwanese nomination in any of the four parts awards, and none in Best Software**, where even Hong Kong managed one through HK-Joint-School, despite GEMS-Taiwan, NCKU-Tainan and NYCU-Taiwan all releasing licensed code; Best Model appears once, at high-school level, for Mingdao; and the collegiate tier produced no technical special award at all, NYCU-Taiwan's win being a video and NCKU-Tainan's a village category. The clearest symptom is NTHU Taiwan's CatharSys, whose four models dropped a screening factor on a predicted 6% separation, reversed an enzyme-engineering plan when formaldehyde was projected to five times chassis tolerance, stated a falsifiable prediction before the build and reversed a nozzle geometry on first-principles hydraulics — and which won a gold medal and nothing else.

GEMS-Taiwan's three wins and Top 10 place are the island's best result of the year, and they were earned on provenance rather than biology: an input ledger marking every number measured, cited or modelled, a growth rate pre-registered on 1 October and later scored at 0.286 ± 0.010 h⁻¹, and an autoencoder that named a failing photometer 26.7 hours before the channel died. Measured against the collegiate Top 10 sections the dry lab is thin in four named places — there is no inferential statistics, the central secreted-activity figure standing at **n = 1, 7.25 mU/mL, below quantitation** with two induction runs disagreeing on the sign, where NCKU-Tainan a tier up fits mixed models with plate as a random intercept and holds out a treatment to predict; the entire control architecture rests on a published CcaSR Hill curve assumed valid at 20 L although every induction ran at a single light intensity, so nothing in the project tests its own transfer function; the digital twin is an admitted digital shadow, replaying recorded runs with a person making every decision and green-light induction not integrated; and the economics are negative on the team's own numbers, 68 years to payback at perfect efficacy against a partner's 4.9. The step up needs depth in three places rather than more scope: replication and intervals on the central claim with a pre-registered **effect size** rather than a pre-registered growth rate; an in-house CcaSR dose–response across light intensities and scales in absolute fluorescein-calibrated units, which would simultaneously turn 35 contributed SubtiToolKit parts into a collection with the transfer curves a parts award actually rewards; and a twin that controls a run instead of replaying one, with one external software user whose complaints are written down.

The collaboration map begins with an uncomfortable fact: **GEMS-Taiwan is not in the island's network**. NYCU-Taiwan hosted the 2026 Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up at its Bo-Ai campus on 27 July for 53 students and advisors from NYCU-Taiwan, NCKU-Tainan, HIA-Taiwan, VIS and WIST, and NCKU-Tainan's collaboration page adds Mingdao, CCU-Taiwan and NTHU — while neither GEMS-Taiwan nor Labi-Taiwan appears on either list and the GEMS wiki carries no collaboration page at all. The partners therefore follow from complementarity, not goodwill: NTHU Taiwan shares the *Bacillus subtilis* chassis and the open-hardware habit, NCKU-Tainan holds the statistics and the cheap reader, CCU-Taiwan works the rice leafroller on the same crop and the same island, NTHU's AeroSense group has the cohort's deepest computation and admits its decoder was validated on external metal-oxide sensor datasets rather than its own cells, Labi-Taiwan is the only other high-school programme with a real computational stack, and NYCU-Taiwan convenes.

Taiwan's state-backed push is manufacturing-led — the Taiwan Bio-Manufacturing Corporation broke ground on a 15,000 m² GMP facility in Hsinchu Biomedical Science Park in June 2025 with operations from Q2 2026 including Taiwan's first GMP mRNA capability, biomedicine sits inside the 5+2 Innovative Industries Plan, a 33-company delegation went to BIO 2026, and this research found no Taiwan-specific synthetic-biology design programme or funding figure at all. Singapore and Israel are funding precisely that missing layer, with DayOne launching Singapore's first biological data centre prototype in August 2026 and Israel's Innovation Authority committing roughly NIS 70 million in July 2026 to national infrastructure for AI models built on biological data. The 2026 cohort is both the evidence of the gap and the evidence that it can be filled: thirteen teams, six instruments built, zero parts nominations, zero software nominations. GEMS should position itself as Taiwan's dry-lab pipeline rather than as a smaller wet lab, and say so to the Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical Industries Promotion Office and the Ministry of Economic Affairs with Singapore and Israel named as the comparison, to TBMC in Hsinchu as it ramps twenty minutes from NYCU and both NTHU teams, and to the Industrial Technology Research Institute, where NTHU Taiwan already holds a working relationship GEMS would not have to build from scratch.

### GEMS-Taiwan — ReLEAF
An optogenetic Bacillus subtilis WB800 bioreactor that reads field sensors and weather forecasts, sets a green-light dose through the CcaSR two-component system and secretes plant-protective proteins beside a Taiwanese paddy. Taiwan's only Top 10 place in 2026 and the island's only triple winner: Best Measurement, Best Hardware and Best Integrated Human Practices, plus nominations for Presentation, Wiki and Best Village Project. The award case rests on provenance rather than biology — a pre-registered growth rate scored after the fact, an autoencoder that named a failing photometer 26.7 hours early, an input ledger marking every number measured, cited or modelled, and a wiki that withdraws its own claims. The hole is that the published CcaSR transfer function the whole control architecture depends on was assumed, never measured, and the central activity figure is n = 1 below quantitation.

### Labi-Taiwan — BlueCatcher
A nucleic-acid biosensor for major depressive disorder, built by Labi Education, the programme formerly entered as Taipei-KCISLK. The dry lab is the most data-heavy of any Taiwanese high-school team: differential expression, miRNA–mRNA networks, GSEA and WGCNA narrowed 2,656 mature miRNAs to sixteen candidates and then to miR-124-3p as the first engineering target, with machine learning used to prioritise three-way-junction probes and toehold switches, and thermodynamic and kinetic modelling behind the readout. It won the iGEMers Prize, the award the other teams vote for, and was nominated for Best Measurement on a portable electrochemical reader. Like GEMS, it is a Taipei-area commercial-organiser programme and appears on no other Taiwanese team's collaboration page.

### NYCU-Taiwan — BITE
A modular food-safety biosensor combining magnetic-bead DNA enrichment, CRISPR-Cas12a recognition and G4–hemin colorimetric readout against synthetic DNA from the Salmonella enterica invA region. The dry lab is organised as SeekProbe_Designer for capture-probe design plus a four-layer model stack from bead capture through Cas12a activation and hairpin-G4 colour to end-to-end prediction, with a Y-shaped multi-chamber device concept. It won Best Project Promotion Video — the island's only collegiate win outside a village category — on a silver medal, which is the gap between communication and technical recognition in one team. NYCU is also the convening institution: it hosted the 2026 Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up for 53 people from five teams and built the exchange website behind it.

### NCKU-Tainan — Capture
Two engineered E. coli systems reading the same Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum-sensing signal: one reports AHL as fluorescence, one deploys aptamers to sponge it out of circulation, aimed at healthcare-associated infection in Taiwanese intensive care. It won Best Infectious Diseases Project and was nominated for Best Hardware for CAPTURE-Screen, a single-cuvette fluorescence reader at US$54–161 against US$3,500 for the plate reader it substitutes, paired with LasReader for 4PL calibration with approximate 95% intervals. The statistics are the best in the Taiwanese cohort — mixed models with plate as a random intercept, geometric-mean ratio effect sizes, and the Cb-2 treatment held out and then predicted. It is also the island's mentoring spine, having run a session for Mingdao in March with three of its own members as Mingdao alumni.

### NTHU — AeroSense
A biohybrid olfactory platform: Drosophila odorant receptors with ORCO in HEK293 cells, GCaMP6f fluorescence reporting, a four-channel frequency-tagged optical reader with digital lock-in processing, and a fly-inspired network for decoding odour patterns, aimed at early fungal-risk screening in stored bananas. This is the deepest computational work in the Taiwanese cohort — PCA and projection-neuron coding, measured infrared and quantum-vibration features, an OpenPOM comparison, mutation-robustness and cross-species transfer tests, and molecular-dynamics pocket-entry studies. Nominated for Best Food & Nutrition Project and nothing else. The team states its own limit plainly: the decoder was evaluated on external metal-oxide sensor datasets, not on its own cells.

### Mingdao — Waste-to-Watt
Laminated paper food containers from a 7,000-student campus turned into bioethanol by simultaneous saccharification and fermentation, with Zymomonas mobilis acting as a glucose sink so that BglA β-glucosidase never becomes product-inhibited and cellulase never sees accumulating cellobiose. Nominated for Best Model on three stacked models — enzyme-inhibition kinetics characterised under fermentation-compatible conditions rather than the thermophilic optimum, Monod growth for Z. mobilis, and a coupled ODE comparing closed and open systems. The hardware is a single 45 × 45 × 60 cm frame carrying shredding, hydrolysis, fermentation and distillation with the vessel riding to the distillation station on its own hotplate, so the mixture is never transferred. The clearest high-school modelling case in Taiwan after GEMS, and the only Taiwanese Best Model nomination at any tier.

### NTHU Taiwan — CatharSys
A second, separate National Tsing Hua University team, distinct from the overgraduate NTHU entry: engineered Bacillus subtilis forming biofilms on suspended carriers in a moving-bed reactor to treat TMAH and trimethylamine waste from Hsinchu's semiconductor lithography lines. Four models, and each one changed a decision — dissolved oxygen was dropped from the screen at a predicted 6% separation below flask noise, strengthening the bottleneck enzyme alone was shown to drive formaldehyde to five times chassis tolerance so a matched hxlAB upregulation was carried instead, a biofilm model stated a falsifiable prediction before the build, and first-principles hydraulics reversed a nozzle geometry for the pump already bought. CathaBench, its three-tank open-source benchtop MBBR with ESP32 control and an offline Wi-Fi dashboard, was iterated on feedback from ITRI and industry. Gold medal, zero nominations — on this evidence the most under-recognised dry lab in Taiwan in 2026, and the closest technical match to GEMS.

### CCU-Taiwan — NoFold
National Chung Cheng University against the rice leafroller, Cnaphalocrocis medinalis, which folds a rice leaf and eats it from inside and is described as a predominant foliage feeder across Asian rice ecosystems. The framing is the same economic argument GEMS makes: only about 12% of world rice crosses a border, so an Asian yield loss cannot be covered by imports, and the moths arrive on spring winds from overwintering areas such as Hanoi and Nanning with Taiwan on the route. Gold medal, no awards or nominations. Same crop, same island, same pest-pressure problem as ReLEAF, approached from entomology rather than abiotic stress — the most obvious untapped adjacency in the cohort.

### WIST — ultrasound-reporting probiotic
Washington International School, Taichung: an engineered E. coli that answers two chemical clues at once, lactate and nitrate, and reports the AND condition by filling with gas vesicles and becoming visible to ultrasound, as a swallowable early screen for colorectal cancer. The acoustic-reporter approach is the same gas-vesicle technology Heidelberg built its collegiate Top 10 project on this year, which makes it an ambitious choice for a high-school team. It carries both a Model and a Software page and declares every figure on the home page a diagram of method rather than acquired data. Gold medal, no awards; it attended the NYCU Meet-Up and appears on NCKU-Tainan's collaboration list.

### AEI Prep-Taiwan — SynPETic
Engineered E. coli making PETase and MHETase side by side on one scaffold — a 'PETosome' — to depolymerise PET in water at 37 °C with no extruder and no metal catalyst, framed around the roughly 2,500 kg of plastic waste the ISS generates a year and the up-to-US$20,000 cost of lifting a kilogram to orbit. One of only two commercially organised Taiwanese high-school programmes besides GEMS and Labi, and it carries Model, Software and Hardware pages. Silver medal, no awards or nominations. The Space village framing makes it the nearest cohort neighbour to GEMS's own village placement.

### VIS — Cadture
VIS@betterworld Lab, testing whether engineered metallothioneins can capture cadmium from industrial wastewater, with a modelling page on cadmium removal. The notable feature is epistemic honesty of the kind GEMS also practises: the home page states that current work measures bacterial growth and GFP response and that direct cadmium removal remains to be tested, rather than implying a result it does not have. Silver medal, no awards or nominations. It attended the NYCU Meet-Up and is on NCKU-Tainan's collaboration list, so it is inside the island network that the Taipei commercial programmes are outside.

### HIA-Taiwan — Aiy-U-Ready
Hsinchu International Academy in Zhubei, working on aiyu, Ficus pumila var. awkeotsang, a fig endemic to Taiwan that yields hundreds of tonnes a year and is almost unknown outside it. The project is built around that asymmetry — a locally owned crop nobody else is characterising — which is precisely the 'own a dataset nobody else has' logic the industry trend research identifies as a small institution's only durable asset. Silver medal, no awards or nominations, with a Dry Lab model page. It attended the NYCU Meet-Up and is on NCKU-Tainan's collaboration list.

### KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei — Herculyeast
Kang Chiao International School's Xiugang campus, running a yeast project with both Model and Software pages under its Dry Lab, plus Entrepreneurship, Inclusivity and Sustainability sections. Silver medal, no awards or nominations. Its sibling campus at Linkou entered separately as Taipei-TWN and was recorded as not eligible, so the Kang Chiao group fielded two high-school entries in 2026 and converted neither — and Labi-Taiwan, the iGEMers Prize winner, is the same Linkou programme's earlier lineage under a new organiser.

### Taipei-TWN and Oros Biotech
Two Taiwanese registrations that never reached the competition floor and so are missing from every results table. Taipei-TWN (Kang Chiao International School, Linkou campus, high school, Taipei) carries the status 'not eligible' with no medal and no wiki content. Oros Biotech of Taichung entered the venture-foundry track rather than the competition, has no section, no medal and a 404 wiki — meaning Taiwan's only 2026 entry into iGEM's startup pathway left no public record. Both matter for the denominator: fifteen Taiwanese registrations, thirteen competing teams, and an entrepreneurship route the island used once and did not document.

### Taiwan against China, Hong Kong, Japan, Korea and Singapore
On accepted competing teams: China 176, Hong Kong 16, Taiwan 13, Japan 7, Korea 6, Singapore 4. On outright wins Taiwan placed second in the region with six, behind China's 24 and ahead of Hong Kong's three, with Japan, Korea and Singapore returning none at all — so Taiwan was the only territory outside China to win more than once. On altitude the ranking inverts: China took five Top 10 places and a Grand Prize first runner-up, Hong Kong three Top 10 places and the high-school Grand Prize first runner-up through HongKong-JSS, Singapore one through NUS-Singapore, and Taiwan one through GEMS-Taiwan, with no Taiwanese Grand Prize placing at any tier. In kind the regions differ sharply: China dominates the parts awards and the Registry layer, Hong Kong spreads thirteen nominations across parts, model, software, hardware, education, presentation and wiki, Japan accumulates nominations without converting any, and Taiwan concentrates in hardware, measurement and human practices while taking zero parts and zero software nominations.

_Method and limits. The tally is built from research/results2026.json (captured from competition.igem.org/results/2026 on 19 November 2026) cross-checked team by team against iGEM's own public API — api.igem.org/v1/teams?year=2026 for the full 463-team roster with countries, cities, sections and acceptance status, and api.igem.org/v1/teams/<id>/awards for each team's medals, nominations and wins — which is how nine Taiwanese registrations absent from the results table were found, including NTHU Taiwan (6416), CCU-Taiwan (6408), WIST (6062) and AEI Prep-Taiwan (6200). Project detail comes from the teams' own 2026 wikis, read directly where server-rendered and through a browser for the client-rendered single-page sites (Labi-Taiwan, CCU-Taiwan), plus the existing researched file at research/teams/6072.json for GEMS-Taiwan and research/trends/industry.json for the TBMC, DayOne and Israel Innovation Authority figures. Two Taiwanese registrations could not be verified beyond their API records: Taipei-TWN (6142) is marked not eligible and has no wiki content, and Oros Biotech (6543) returns a 404 wiki, so nothing is claimed about either project; KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei's project could only be identified by name and navigation structure because its wiki ships a largely unmodified template, and Mingdao's medal-level claims rest on the API rather than on a wiki statement._

## What the Best Wiki winners did differently

_The four 2026 Best Wiki winners did not win on visual polish or page weight; they won by building an executive layer that tells a judge where the evidence is, and then by being unusually specific and unusually honest underneath it._

Three of the four winners ship pages whose text exists in the HTML before any JavaScript runs: **Heidelberg** writes static HTML by hand, **Uni-Padua-IT** prerenders SvelteKit, **Lambert-GA** builds with Astro. TU Delft is the exception, a Vite single-page app behind a 3.4 MB bundle, and it compensates deliberately with an `llms.txt` at the wiki root and a plain-Markdown mirror of every page at `/tu-delft/<page>.md`. Against that, the control group — Princeton, Cornell, LYON, UAlberta, UCNZ, Athens, GU Frankfurt and Eton-College-UK, all winners of serious 2026 science prizes — serves near-empty shells of 486 bytes to 15 kB, as little as seven characters of text without JS.

The real differentiator is an explicit executive layer. Uni-Padua-IT and Lambert-GA both ship a `/judging` page that walks medal criterion by criterion, summarises each in two or three sentences and deep-links the evidence — Padua pointing straight at its own negative results, Lambert stating in the summary that fifteen minibinder designs produced no confirmed hits before a second campaign of twenty produced one binder at roughly 604 nM. TU Delft reaches the same place with an illustrated module map on Results where hovering highlights a module and clicking jumps to it, over the same five modules that organise the project; Heidelberg puts three summary cards above the fold and gives every nav link a one-line subtitle, so "Results" reads "Where data tells the story".

Underneath, the winners are simply more specific. **Heidelberg**'s captions carry panel letters, 547 ng and 433 ng transfection masses, 18,000 × g, and an effect size quoted with its range — 5.6×, 4.3 to 6.4× depending on the haze setting — while Padua photographs the plate that grew nothing, numbers it as a figure, and explains why an earlier transformation failed. **TU Delft** built a content system rather than a set of pages: 1,604 reference tags over 735 unique DOIs, 724 glossary calls against 102 definitions, 307 auto-numbered figures, and one unvarying Background → Results → Discussion → Future Perspective spine. Its decision matrix tags every cell as Factual, Inferred, Estimated or Speculative, with a legend saying the tag records the strength of the evidence behind the cell rather than the judgement — epistemic honesty rendered as a UI component, and I saw nothing like it elsewhere.

What did not decide it is as instructive. Page weight spans two orders of magnitude inside the winners' circle, from Lambert-GA's 78 kB homepage to TU Delft's 3.4 MB. None of Heidelberg, Uni-Padua, Lambert-GA, Stanford, UCAS-China or Toronto declares a `prefers-color-scheme` rule, and meaningful alt text ran at 27 to 48 per cent across the winners while HongKong-JSS, ProFuture-China and WageningenUR hit 90, 86 and 81 per cent and won nothing for it. The winners do all honour `prefers-reduced-motion` — thirteen blocks in Heidelberg's stylesheet, eleven in TU Delft's bundle — and Heidelberg goes further, sniffing for a software WebGL renderer and dropping to a lite mode automatically, with `?lite=0` and `?perf=1` for anyone who wants to look: the motion budget goes to figure interactions and graceful degradation, not to hero spectacle.

### Build a judging page and make it the front door
Uni-Padua-IT and Lambert-GA each ship a `/judging` route that indexes every medal criterion and every award they apply for. Each entry is two or three sentences of plain summary followed by a deep link into the page that holds the evidence. Padua links directly to its own failed Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles under Silver; Lambert quotes the binding affinity and the two failed design campaigns in the Gold section. It costs one page and it converts a pile of required sections into a reading order.

### Label the provenance of every number you did not measure
TU Delft's entrepreneurship page scores four candidate applications against eleven weighted parameters. Every single cell carries a bracketed tag — [F]actual, [I]nferred, [E]stimated or [S]peculative — and the legend states that the tag records how strong the evidence behind the cell is, not the score, because every score is a judgement applied to sourced facts. The weights sum to 100 per cent and the weighted total is given to two decimals. It is the single most copyable device I found in 2026.

### Date every pivot and name who caused it
Lambert-GA applies one named framework, H.I.V.E. — Hear, Inquire, Validate, Evolve — identically to every stakeholder, then closes with a Project Pivots timeline. Five entries, each with a date, the named expert whose feedback caused it, and a literal before-and-after: nanobody changed to minibinder, P-domain in general changed to specific hotspots. The caption says every change shown came directly from stakeholder feedback rather than internal decisions. It makes integration auditable instead of asserted.

### Mirror the wiki as plain Markdown
TU Delft's wiki is a Vite single-page app and the heaviest I measured, yet it publishes an `llms.txt` at the wiki root listing twelve pages, each mirrored as plain Markdown at `/tu-delft/<page>.md`. That gives a JS-free fallback, a machine-readable corpus, and a diffable source of truth for the content, all from one build step. If you insist on a client-rendered framework, this is the tax you should pay for it.

### Write captions that stand alone, and number the negative control
Heidelberg's captions carry panel letters, exact reagent masses, exact centrifugation and pressure conditions, and effect sizes quoted with a range across settings — a reader can take the figure out of the page and still understand it. Uni-Padua-IT goes one better on controls: the plate that grew nothing gets its own numbered figure with the full condition in the caption, sitting beside the plate that grew two colonies. Showing the control is cheap and it is the fastest way to look like you know what you are doing.

### Keep content out of components
Stanford University — Grand Prize winner and a Best Wiki nominee, though not a winner — stores each page as a single hand-written JavaScript object with a documented block grammar of p, sh, gal, list, table, steps, math and quotes, plus a per-page accent colour and icon. TU Delft does the equivalent in MDX with a fixed component vocabulary. Either way the layout is written once and the copy is written by people who are not touching layout, which is why neither wiki drifts between pages.

### Degrade on purpose, not by accident
Heidelberg's wiki detects a software WebGL renderer on load and automatically switches to a lite mode, with `?lite=0` and `?lite=1` to force it either way and `?perf=1` to load a performance reporter. Its stylesheet carries thirteen `prefers-reduced-motion` blocks; TU Delft's bundle carries eleven. The winners treat a judge on a tired laptop as a real user. Nobody built a dark mode, and nobody needed one.

**Checklist**

- Ship HTML that already contains your words — prerender, or mirror every page as Markdown with an llms.txt, as TU Delft did.
- Build a /judging page that answers each medal criterion in two or three sentences and deep-links the evidence.
- State the controlling question on the first screen and repeat it in the same words on every summary layer.
- Put a three-card or five-module summary above the detail on every long page, before any subsection.
- Fix one spine for every results subsection — Background, Results, Discussion, Future Perspective — and never vary it.
- Write captions that stand alone: panel letters, exact conditions, units, n, and the effect size with its range.
- Photograph the negative control and give it a figure number of its own.
- Name your failures with numbers, and name them in the executive layer rather than burying them.
- Tag the provenance of every number you did not measure yourself — factual, inferred, estimated or speculative.
- Keep content in one data file per page with a documented block grammar; let layout be written once.
- Date every human-practices pivot, name the person whose feedback caused it, and show before and after.
- Honour prefers-reduced-motion and spend the motion budget on figure interactions, not on the hero.

**Effort that did not pay off**

- Dark mode and theme toggles. Not one of Heidelberg, Uni-Padua-IT, Lambert-GA, Stanford, UCAS-China or Toronto declares a prefers-color-scheme rule, and all of them placed well.
- A late alt-text compliance sweep. The four winners ran 27 to 48 per cent meaningful alt text while HongKong-JSS (90 per cent), ProFuture-China (86) and WageningenUR (81) all beat them and none was a Best Wiki winner — it is a floor, not a differentiator, so do it early and cheaply.
- Huge homepage media galleries. Toronto pulls 214 images and 252 .avif references on the homepage alone and ETH-Zurich serves a single 1.9 MB HTML page; neither won Best Wiki.
- A client-rendered SPA with no text fallback. This is the default in the control group — Princeton, Cornell, LYON, UAlberta, UCNZ, Athens, GU Frankfurt and Eton-College-UK all serve near-empty shells despite winning major science prizes.
- Per-page mascots, bespoke icon sets and per-page accent colours. Stanford invested in all three and placed as a nominee; none of the four winners has a mascot system.
- Treating the mandatory section list as the information architecture. A deep-linked judging index does the same job in one page and reads as an argument rather than a form.

_Method and limits. I rendered and read the four winners in full — Heidelberg, Uni-Padua-IT, TU Delft and Lambert-GA — by fetching their page HTML directly where it is server-rendered, by reading TU Delft's Markdown mirrors, and by loading the client-rendered pages in a browser; counts of references, figures, components, image formats, alt attributes and prefers-reduced-motion rules were taken from the shipped source. I sampled around thirty nominees and controls more shallowly, measuring framework, rendered text length, asset weight and alt-text coverage for all of them, and reading Stanford's and UCAS-China's content in detail as the closest nominees. I could not render several Vite single-page nominees deeply — Oxford, UCSC, NUS-Singapore, KAUST-KSA, Muenster-University, IISER-Kolkata and UOttawa among them — because a shared browser pane kept being navigated away mid-session, so they are excluded from the table and their design is not characterised here; I also did not measure real-world load time, mobile layout or screen-reader behaviour beyond the markup._

## Who worked with whom in 2026

_Sixty-nine of the 106 decorated teams record working with at least one other iGEM team; thirty-seven record none. Almost all of it is meet-ups. Not one team in the cohort ran an inter-lab measurement ring, and the team that offered to run the nearest thing got no replies. GEMS-Taiwan has no collaboration page and appears on nobody else's — and still took Top 10 and three wins, which is the uncomfortable part._

Across the 106 researched team files, **69 teams document working with at least one other iGEM team and 37 document none**. The forms are not equally weighted. The dominant one by a wide margin is the **regional meet-up**: BFH's European Meet-Up in Hamburg on 15–17 May (third edition, co-run by Bielefeld, Frankfurt and Hamburg), KIT's first iGEM Baden-Württemberg Meetup on 13 June with eight German teams, HUST-China's First Central-China iGEM Forum on 12 July with fifteen teams, Uni-Padua-IT's Italian Meet-Up in the Botanical Garden of Padua on 25 July with Bologna and Milan, NYCU-Taiwan's Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up on 27 July, Labi-Taiwan's TGEM at National Taiwan University on 22 August, Grand APiC at SUSTech and the University of Hong Kong on 16–19 August, ETH-Zurich's Swiss iGEM Meetup for five teams, Baltimore's Mid-Atlantic Meetup with nine regional teams, TAU-Israel's online Mini-Jamboree with eight. Below that sit mentorship of school teams by university teams, co-authored community publications, peer review, and a long tail of poster boards and podcast guest slots.

Sort them by whether a third party can use the output and the list gets short. **What survives contact with a stranger**: JLU-FBH's myth-busting handbook *Together with iGEM: Across Villages, From Myths to Facts*, chief-edited across submissions from 17-plus teams; HBUT-China's five-school joint biosafety manual for anti-tumour projects, written with ZJU-China, BNU-China, JLU-FBH and ZJUT-China and released as a downloadable PDF with deliberately differentiable risk protocols because the five teams use different carriers; SJTU-BioX-Shanghai's cross-team Education Activity Handbook, where they took responsibility for Part 7; the MSP Vector peer-reviewed iGEM journal run from Maastricht, where Madrid-UCM refereed three other teams' papers and Stockholm contributed a literature review and reviewed in turn; McGill's BIOME Book, to which NYCU-Taiwan supplied the text and concept for an LbCas12a entry and McGill supplied the artwork; and KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei and HKSSC splitting the central dogma between them into two physical teaching models over two planning calls on 20 August and 19 September, sharing prototypes through a common Drive, then each adapting to its own audience — KCIS rebuilding HKSSC's flat felt translation framework as a 3D tactile box with slotted E, P and A sites for seven students at the Taipei School for the Visually Impaired. **What does not**: icebreakers, rock stacking, beanbag toss, community blackboards, 'we met other teams and exchanged ideas'. NYCU-Taiwan says the quiet part itself on its own wiki: documenting an event does not by itself demonstrate its long-term impact.

The biggest hole in 2026 is technical. **Not one of the 106 teams ran an inter-lab measurement ring** — the same construct or sample measured by several teams on several instruments, with the between-lab spread published. The closest anyone came was negative. Uni-Padua-IT, who went on to win Best Software Tool and Best Wiki in the Undergraduate section, wrote on their software page: *"On 9 August 2026 we published an open call for collaboration to validate the software and shared it in the two ways that actually reach people: on our social media channels and directly with other iGEM teams. The offer was simple: tell us your chassis, and we will optimise a sequence for it and send the result back. Unfortunately, we did not receive any replies."* The only genuine independent replications in the cohort came from outside iGEM — four mechanical engineering students at Hanyang University rebuilt PSI Korea's reader from the released documentation alone — or across years, where HongKong-HS generated its toehold candidates with miRADAR, the tool Wageningen released in 2024, and Mingdao re-characterised the cenA part lineage (Edinburgh 2008, CAU_China 2019, XMU-China 2019, SYSU-CHINA 2021) at 34 °C in Bis-Tris pH 6.4 instead of the standard 50 °C acidic assay. Live part or sample exchange between two 2026 teams: essentially absent.

**Does it correlate with placing? Honestly, no.** Coding the 106 files three ways — substantive co-production (S, n = 48), attendance or visibility only (A, n = 21), nothing documented (N, n = 37) — gives Top 10 rates of 14/48 (29%), 10/21 (48%) and 6/37 (16%), and at-least-one-win rates of 29/48 (60%), 10/21 (48%) and 15/37 (41%). The hypothesis that substantive beats attendance runs the wrong way and is not significant (Fisher exact p = 0.17). The only thing with any signal is the crude contrast — any documented inter-team work, 24/69 Top 10, against none, 6/37 — and that is p = 0.069, suggestive at best, and confounded by the fact that teams who write more win more. The two biggest connectors in the whole network, Bielefeld-CeBiTec, which ran the European Meet-Up and the Community Blackboard that roughly 37 teams passed through, and JLU-FBH, which chief-edited the 17-team handbook, each took a Gold medal and nothing else. **One award does correlate, and it is the one other teams vote for.** Both 2026 iGEMers Prizes went to the most documented community builders in their tier: HUST-China, which hosted a fifteen-team forum and wrote entries into two other teams' publications, and Labi-Taiwan, which runs TGEM. Judges did not reward collaboration in 2026. Peers did.

Taiwan ran **two** national events and GEMS-Taiwan was at neither. NYCU-Taiwan hosted the 2026 Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up at Xian-Qi Hall on the Bo-Ai Campus on 27 July: 53 students and advisors, five Taiwanese teams (NYCU-Taiwan, HIA-Taiwan, NCKU-Tainan, VIS, WIST) plus Okinawa joining online, four icebreakers, five roundtable themes, two guest speakers, five fifteen-minute mock presentations, and — the part that matters — an iGEM Team Operations Guide compiled from the roundtable notes plus published preparation SOPs, registration templates and schedules for future organisers. Labi-Taiwan ran the fourth TGEM on 22 August at the Boya Building, National Taiwan University, co-hosted with NTU's Department of Biochemical Science and Technology: a mock competition of five-minute pitches and twenty-minute interrogation by professors, PIs and industry judges. TGEM has run annually since 2023, founded by Kang Chiao International School Linkou, Labi-Taiwan's own predecessor. Its named 2026 participants include NTHU Taiwan, Claremont CA, AEI Prep-Taiwan and KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei. NCKU-Tainan is the busiest Taiwanese partner on record: Mingdao mentorship on 7 March, the NYCU meet-up in July, a full online session with WIST on 17 September covering wet-lab bottlenecks and a dry-lab model comparison, CCU-Taiwan on 19 September, HIA-Taiwan on 20 September, and TAU-Israel's eight-team Mini-Jamboree on 8 October alongside NTHU. **GEMS-Taiwan has no /collaborations page, no /partnership page, and no other iGEM team named anywhere on its wiki.** Its one listed 'partner team' is Geospatial Analysis, an internal sub-team.

A closing warning about the evidence. **Collaboration claims in 2026 are frequently one-sided.** NCKU-Tainan documents mentoring Mingdao in March and a detailed technical session with WIST in September; neither Mingdao's nor WIST's wiki mentions NCKU-Tainan. ASIJ-Tokyo lists KCIS Xiugang among eight partner teams; KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei's collaboration page names only HKSSC. NYCU-Taiwan lists WIST as a meet-up attendee; WIST's pages do not mention the event. Where a claim appears on one wiki and not the other, the collaboration was usually real and the documentation was unilateral — which is itself the lesson. The partner who writes it up gets the credit and the reusable artefact; the partner who does not gets a photograph.

### NYCU-Taiwan's Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up
53 students and advisors from five Taiwanese teams — NYCU-Taiwan, HIA-Taiwan, NCKU-Tainan, VIS and WIST — at Xian-Qi Hall, Bo-Ai Campus, with Okinawa joining online for a sixth. Four icebreakers, five roundtable themes, two guest speakers, five fifteen-minute mock presentations. The reusable outputs are an iGEM Team Operations Guide compiled from the roundtable notes, plus preparation SOPs, registration form templates and event schedules published for future organisers. NYCU reached Okinawa by flying there in person first. HIA-Taiwan ran a separate bilateral exchange with NYCU on 21 July and surveyed it: 73.3 percent of participants rated their understanding of the other team's project 4 or 5.

### TGEM, the fourth Taiwan iGEM Meetup
Hosted by Labi-Taiwan at the Boya Building, National Taiwan University, co-hosted with NTU's Department of Biochemical Science and Technology. Format: a five-minute project overview followed by twenty minutes of questions from professors, principal investigators, industry professionals and advisers, then ten-minute village presentations. Running annually since 2023, founded by Kang Chiao International School Linkou — Labi-Taiwan's own predecessor, which competed as Taipei-KCISLK V1 to V3. Named 2026 participants include NTHU Taiwan, Claremont CA, AEI Prep-Taiwan and KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei, whose wiki records the full judging transcript and the four engineering changes it forced. Labi-Taiwan won the peer-voted iGEMers Prize in the High School section.

### Nobody answered Uni-Padua
On 9 August 2026 Uni-Padua-IT published an open call offering to codon-optimise any team's sequence for its chassis with ReTIsigner and send the result back, pushed through social media and directly to other iGEM teams. They received no replies, and they say so on the wiki. They went on to win Best Software Tool and Best Wiki in the Undergraduate section anyway. Read alongside the fact that not one of the 106 decorated teams ran an inter-lab measurement ring, the conclusion is that 2026's network carried people and slides but almost no reagents, constructs or measurements.

### KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei × HKSSC
Two virtual planning sessions, 20 August and 19 September. They split the central dogma: KCIS built a sequential LEGO track for transcription and gene regulation, HKSSC built an mRNA translation model with slotted E, P and A sites. Prototypes were exchanged as photo and video logs through a shared Google Drive, then each team deployed to its own audience — HKSSC for general science teaching in Hong Kong, KCIS rebuilding HKSSC's flat felt framework as a 3D tactile box with pipe-cleaner tRNA and Styrofoam amino acids for seven students at the Taipei School for the Visually Impaired. KCIS reports the limits too: N = 7, no pre-test, 4 of 7 found the tactile markers helpful. This is the only Taiwan-linked collaboration in 2026 that produced a physical object two teams can both hand on.

### HUST-China: fifteen teams, one forum, one peer prize
On 12 July 2026 HUST-China independently hosted the First Central-China iGEM Forum at the Qiming College Maker Space, replicating the Jamboree's own structure — opening speeches, keynotes, a LiveStage block, judge comment sessions and poster booths — for fifteen online and offline teams, of which fourteen presented and received targeted commentary. They then wrote a full entry into JLU-FBH's 17-team myth-busting handbook and specialised content into BUCT's air-to-protein publication, mutually reviewed and published on BUCT's wiki. They won the peer-voted iGEMers Prize. The other 2026 iGEMers Prize, in the High School section, went to Labi-Taiwan, which runs TGEM. Two for two: the prize other teams vote for went to the two biggest community builders.

### Bielefeld-CeBiTec, JLU-FBH, Lund, Okinawa
The teams that carried the 2026 network were not rewarded for it. Bielefeld-CeBiTec (6221) co-ran the BFH European Meet-Up in Hamburg on 15–17 May and the Community Blackboard that roughly 37 teams passed through: Gold plus one Safety and Security nomination. JLU-FBH (6056), chief editor of the handbook 17-plus teams wrote into: Gold, nothing else. BUCT (6055), co-producer with HUST-China: Gold, nothing else. NAU-CHINA (6419), which ran the nationwide ICII initiative that HUST explicitly copied: Gold and one part nomination. Lund (6160), whose podcast The Sequence featured about twelve teams including NYCU-Taiwan: Silver. Okinawa (6155), the one Japanese team that joined Taiwan's meet-up: no medal at all. Verified team by team against api.igem.org.

### Zero edges, three wins
GEMS-Taiwan has no /collaborations page and no /partnership page — both return 404 — and no other iGEM team is named anywhere on its wiki. Its one listed partner team, Geospatial Analysis, is an internal sub-team. It appears on no other Taiwanese team's collaboration page: not NYCU-Taiwan's, not NCKU-Tainan's, not KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei's, and it is not among the teams Labi-Taiwan names at TGEM. It still took High School Top 10 with wins in Measurement, Hardware and Integrated Human Practices. State that plainly: in 2026 collaboration did not buy placing, and GEMS is the proof. The case for building a network is not the medal — it is that GEMS currently has nowhere to send a construct and nobody to check its numbers.

**Checklist**

- March 2027 — the GEMS human practices lead emails Labi-Taiwan and the NTU Department of Biochemical Science and Technology to register for TGEM 2027. TGEM has run every August since 2023 and is held in Taipei, where GEMS already is; the 2026 edition judged teams with a five-minute pitch plus twenty minutes of questions from professors and industry. Ask for a slot in the high-school division and offer, in the same email, to run a thirty-minute measurement clinic using the Best Measurement work.
- April 2027 — email NYCU-Taiwan. They published their meet-up preparation SOPs, registration form templates and event schedules explicitly for future organisers to adapt, and wrote on their own wiki that next time they want a collaboration interest form rather than a poster. Take them at their word: offer to co-host the 2027 Taiwan iGEMers Meet-Up in Taipei, or to run the measurement session at theirs.
- May 2027 — propose the inter-lab measurement ring nobody ran in 2026. Write to four named teams at once: NCKU-Tainan 6379 (Best Hardware nominee, the US$54-161 CAPTURE-Screen fluorescence reader, and already the busiest technical partner in Taiwan), NTHU 6460 (four-channel frequency-tagged reader with digital lock-in detection), Labi-Taiwan 6511 (Best Measurement nominee, portable electrochemical reader) and Mingdao 6105, the only Taiwanese team that has already re-characterised another team's part at new conditions. The offer is concrete: GEMS ships one calibrated reference construct plus its photometer protocol, each team measures it on its own instrument, and the between-lab spread is published jointly.
- May 2027 — before any team says yes, put the ring protocol on the GEMS wiki as a dated, versioned page with the calibration curve, the acceptance criteria and the raw-data template. Uni-Padua-IT's open call failed with nothing attached; an offer that arrives with a finished protocol and a shipping plan is a different object.
- June 2027 — copy the KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei and HKSSC method for the cross-border attempt, because it is the only one in the 2026 Taiwanese record that produced a shared artefact: two scheduled planning calls six weeks apart, an agreed split of the work, prototypes exchanged through a shared drive, then each team adapting to its own audience. Approach HKSSC 6053 (High School Top 10, Best New Basic Part winner, already in the APiC and iGBA communities) or ASIJ-Tokyo 6338, which ran activities with eight teams across eight countries and already has a Taiwanese tie.
- July 2027 — write to Okinawa 6155 and HG-Tokyo 6352. Okinawa joined Taiwan's meet-up online after NYCU flew there, and won no medal in 2026; HG-Tokyo hosts the Japanese meet-up that UTokyo, TUS, Waseda, Keio, Oakridge and ASIJ attend. Both are reachable, and both have an incentive GEMS can serve.
- August 2027 — apply to Grand APiC. The first Asia-Pacific Synthetic Biology Youth Conference ran 16-19 August 2026 at SUSTech and the University of Hong Kong; Peking took Best Project there and HKSSC and HKU-HongKong sit inside the APiC and iGBA community. It is the regional umbrella a Taiwanese high-school research centre can enter without an invitation from any one team.
- Throughout — build /collaborations as a page with dates, named counterparts and outputs, not a gallery. And adopt a reciprocity rule: every exchange gets a one-paragraph record on both wikis, agreed before the call ends. In 2026 NCKU-Tainan, ASIJ-Tokyo and NYCU-Taiwan each wrote up partners whose own wikis stayed silent; the partner who writes it up keeps the credit and the reusable artefact.

_Method and limits. The first pass was on disk: all 106 researched team files in research/teams/ were grepped for collaboration signals (collaborat, meet-up, meetup, partner, exchange, inter-lab, interlab, conference, mentor, jointly, shared, co-hosted, iGEM team, other teams), returning hits in 74 files, and every good.partners[] entry naming an iGEM team or meet-up was extracted separately. This cannot see a collaboration a team did but did not write up, and it demonstrably misses some: NCKU-Tainan's file contains no collaboration signal at all, yet its wiki carries five dated exchanges. The classification behind the correlation (S = substantive co-production, n = 48; A = attendance or visibility only, n = 21; N = none documented, n = 37) is therefore a documentation proxy, not a census of behaviour, and the Fisher exact tests reported are two-sided on those counts. The roster and every award cited were taken from iGEM's public API — api.igem.org/v1/teams?year=2026 for all 463 registrations across 24 pages, and api.igem.org/v1/teams/<id>/awards for individual teams including Bielefeld-CeBiTec 6221, JLU-FBH 6056, BUCT 6055, NAU-CHINA 6419, Lund 6160, Okinawa 6155 and Claremont CA 6317 — not from any hand-written list. Wiki verification ran over /collaborations, /collaboration, /partnership, /partnerships, /collaborations-and-partnerships, /collaboration-partnership and /public-outreach-and-collaboration for 131 slugs: 568 of 917 returned 404, and many of the rest are client-rendered single-page apps that return HTTP 200 for any route, so the browser was used for Labi-Taiwan, CCU-Taiwan and Uni-Padua-IT while NYCU-Taiwan, NCKU-Tainan, KCIS-Xiugang-Taipei, Squirrel-Beijing and others were read directly. GEMS-Taiwan's absence was checked positively: /collaborations, /collaboration and /partnership all return 404, and its human-practices, education and contribution pages name no other iGEM team. Reciprocity was spot-checked in both directions and three one-sided claims are reported as findings. Pages were read on 19 November 2026._

## What makes a part worth other people's time

_A census of the four 2026 parts awards. Taiwan took six awards from thirteen teams and not one parts nomination — so we read the registry pages themselves. The winning parts are not the clever ones. They are the ones carrying a datasheet._

Four awards, eleven winners across the three sections, and one thing separates them from the forty-odd nominees: **what is actually on the registry page**. The 2026 registry (now at registry.igem.org, with every part reachable as a server-rendered page and a public read API) gives each part a Design, Experiment, Characterisation, Application and Discussion slot. The winners fill them. We measured the characters of documentation on each part page we could resolve. The winners' headline parts carry between **10,000 and 83,000 characters** across three to six documents. The nominee parts we sampled carry **440 to 2,500 characters**, usually a single Design note — and several carry nothing at all.

The empty pages are the real finding, because they belong to *nominated* teams. QingdaoAcademy's ulvan lyases (BBa_26QJCNH8, BBa_26ZVH9D0, BBa_265B8WZF) were nominated for Best New Basic Part at high-school level and each page has **zero documentation**: a title, a sequence, nothing else. HKU-HongKong's aTi-14 peptide (BBa_265GWS2B, 45 bp) was a Best New Composite Part nominee with zero documentation. Bist-China registered PdhR (BBa_26OKC42U) and LldR (BBa_26S2KNZ1) with no documentation at all, and put the real material on two near-duplicate variant pages instead. Nomination is cheap. A page is not.

**Novelty loses to documentation, decisively.** The high-school Best New Basic Part winner, HKSSC, won with BBa_262HI0IB — a *247 bp native promoter and RBS lifted straight out of GenBank AY077721.1*. Nothing about the sequence is new. What is new is that nobody had ever registered or characterised it: the team said so, predicted the promoter with BPROM (LDF 5.30, −10 box TATAAT at position 163, −35 box TTGAAA at 142), cloned it into the promoterless distribution-kit vector BBa_J435300, and reported the gels, the band sizes (974 bp insert, 2,680 bp vector) and the NanoDrop triplicates. The GFP read-out lives on the composite BBa_26MSEOFB, linked from the basic part. That is an entire award won on a promoter trap, a free web tool and honest bookkeeping. It is the single most copyable result in the whole census.

The best datasheet in the cohort is TU Darmstadt's GeoEsterase (BBa_269NN9UX, Best New Basic Part, Overgrad): activity on *p*-nitrophenyl hexanoate read at 396 nm with the extinction coefficient stated (ε = 18,100 M⁻¹cm⁻¹), 0.5 µM enzyme against 0.5/1/2/4 mM substrate, at 22, 32, 37, 42 and 47 °C, **every value the mean of a triplicate**, Michaelis-Menten fitted by least squares, and a table of V_max, K_M, k_cat and k_cat/K_M (894 M⁻¹s⁻¹ at 42 °C in buffer). It also reports that the engineered ThermoGeoEsterase *underperformed* the parent at every temperature and that the thermal shift assay found no improvement — and says the plate reader could not exceed 47 °C. Winners write down what did not work, in units.

Does the evidence live in the registry or link back to a wiki that will rot? **In the registry.** Across seven winning parts we counted the image hosts: 4 to 21 figures per part, every one served from registry.igem.wiki/documentation — the registry's own asset store, not the team site. Only TU Darmstadt and WHU-China link out to 2026.igem.wiki at all, and then as cross-references for extra detail, not as the place the data lives. The same holds for Best Part Collection: all three winners carry collection-level documentation (GHCIS 25,665 characters, Heidelberg 76,231, GU Frankfurt 111,681), while **eight of the twelve nominated collections have no collection page text whatsoever** — ETH-Zurich, Bonn, UTDallas, Marburg aside, Tsinglan, HFI, ASIJ-Tokyo, YHA-HWFLA and UCS-A simply list parts. A bag of parts with a title is not a collection.

One hypothesis fails. **Nothing in the 2026 registry shows a winning part being reused by another team.** Every non-zero *Used in* count on a 2026 winner points back at that team's own composites: Neo-IL-2 (BBa_26WNS0EJ) feeds BBa_26V37TWZ and BBa_26VH4F2F, both HBUT-China's; BBa_262HI0IB feeds HKSSC's own BBa_26MSEOFB; Michigan's M1 thermometer feeds its own geneblock. Reuse runs the other way, and it runs *backwards in time*: GCGS improved BBa_K2315014 from Shanghai_tech 2017 and borrowed Prhl(LR) (BBa_K1529310) from Tokyo_Tech 2014; Kyoto's Leucine ZipPart collection folds in five prior-year zippers and re-measures them. A part built in 2026 pays out in 2028. That is the actual timescale of a durable asset, and it is an argument for starting now rather than against it.

### 10,000 characters versus 440
Every winning headline part we resolved carries 10,388–83,030 characters of registry documentation across 3–6 typed documents (Design, Experiment, Characterisation, Application, Discussion). Squirrel-Beijing's high-school composite winner BBa_26BFFCJG tops the list at 83,030 characters and 12 registry-hosted figures. Sampled nominee parts: Vilnius-Lithuania 442–2,495, DTU-Denmark 520–1,188, mostly Design-only. Volume is not sufficient — UCAS-China's BBa_263ZN48F has 146,670 characters across 16 documents and only placed as a nominee — but below about 5,000 characters nothing in this cohort won anything.

### An unremarkable 247 bp, documented properly
HKSSC won high-school Best New Basic Part with prbA's native promoter and RBS (BBa_262HI0IB), copied from GenBank AY077721.1. The argument was that nobody had registered it. BPROM gave LDF 5.30 with a TATAAT −10 box at position 163 and a TTGAAA −35 box at 142; the fragment went into the promoterless distribution vector BBa_J435300 by HindIII/KpnI; gels, 974 bp and 2,680 bp band sizes and triplicate NanoDrop A260/A280 are all on the page; the GFP read-out sits on the linked composite BBa_26MSEOFB. Total cost: one gBlock, one free web tool, one reporter.

### Units, replicates, conditions — and the failure
TU Darmstadt's GeoEsterase (BBa_269NN9UX) is the reference datasheet of 2026: p-nitrophenyl hexanoate at 396 nm with ε = 18,100 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ stated, 0.5 µM enzyme against 0.5/1/2/4 mM substrate at 22–47 °C, every point n = 3, Michaelis-Menten fitted by least squares, k_cat/K_M = 894 M⁻¹s⁻¹ at 42 °C. The Discussion then reports that the ProteinMPNN-redesigned ThermoGeoEsterase was worse than the parent at every temperature, that the thermal shift assay showed no gain, and that the plate reader could not exceed 47 °C so the test stopped there.

### Two winners, zero nominees
Nobody else entered. Both improved-part awards — Michigan at undergrad, GCGS at high school — were given with no nominee list at all. GCGS shows the template: name the parent (BBa_K2315014, Shanghai_tech 2017), name the defect (basal leakage without C4-HSL), make two stated changes (an SsrA-ASV degron on RhlR; swap wild-type Prhl for Tokyo_Tech 2014's Prhl(LR), BBa_K1529310), then benchmark the improved part BBa_26QSD9SO side by side against the parent and four other tag variants across a 0 / 10 µM / 100 µM / 1 mM C4-HSL gradient, normalised as RFU/OD₆₀₀, with growth curves showing no metabolic burden.

### A shared grammar, or a bag of parts
Winners name their parts to a rule. Heidelberg's 18-item VOYAGE collection prefixes every entry with its function — GV-core:, Sensing:, Multiplexing:, Organize: — and GU Frankfurt's 25 items split cleanly by role into 4 HLA targets (Biological Region), 9 synNotch receptors (Engineered Region) and 12 shRNAs (NcRNA Gene): bind, trigger, silence. GHCIS's high-school winner is a 3 × 3 matrix: three AMR genes (mcr-1, blaNDM-1, blaKPC-2) × trigger RNA and reporter plasmid. Marburg's nominated CLiPPR, the largest collection at 246 parts, is the only one to state its assembly standard outright (MoClo, BsaI/BsmBI) — and still did not win.

### Eight of twelve nominated collections have no page text
All three Best Part Collection winners carry collection-level documentation: GHCIS 25,665 characters in 4 documents, Heidelberg 76,231 in 4, GU Frankfurt 111,681 in 7. Of the twelve nominated collections we checked, only Kyoto (40,761), NUS-Singapore (51,083), Princeton (68,005) and Marburg (58,778) have any — and Princeton's seven documents are all typed Design, with no characterisation document at all. ETH-Zurich, Bonn, UTDallas, Tsinglan, HFI, ASIJ-Tokyo, YHA-HWFLA and UCS-A registered a collection and left the page blank. Several of them, Tsinglan included, documented the individual parts well; nobody wrote the page that explains why the parts belong together.

### 'Used in' is self-citation — so far
The registry now shows a Used in count on every part page, which is the closest thing to a reuse metric iGEM has. On the 2026 winners it only ever points at the same team's own composites. Nothing in this cohort was picked up by a stranger inside the competition year. But the winners themselves are heavy consumers of old parts: GCGS built on a 2017 part and a 2014 promoter, HKSSC used a distribution-kit vector, and nine of the fourteen items in Kyoto's leucine-zipper collection are prior-year BBa_K parts re-measured. The registry pays out on a two-to-ten year lag. That is a reason to start, not a reason to wait.

**Checklist**

- Target Best New Improved Part first. In 2026 it had two winners and zero nominees across the whole competition — the only parts category where showing up is most of the work. It also needs no novel sequence, which suits a team without a protein-design pipeline.
- Pick a parent part that already exists in the registry, has a stated defect, and runs in E. coli. Write its accession down on day one (GCGS used BBa_K2315014 from Shanghai_tech 2017). If you cannot name the parent and its defect in one sentence, you are not entering this category.
- State the improvement as a list of discrete, named changes to the parent — not 'we optimised it'. GCGS's whole case is two lines: add an SsrA-ASV degron to RhlR, replace wild-type Prhl with Prhl(LR). Each change gets its own sub-part accession on the page.
- Measure the parent and the improved part on the same plate, on the same day, with the same reporter. A side-by-side benchmark against the unmodified parent is the single non-negotiable requirement of this category.
- Produce a dose-response or transfer function, not a yes/no. At least four inducer concentrations plus a blank and a solvent-only control, three biological replicates per point, output normalised to OD₆₀₀ (RFU/OD₆₀₀) or to enzyme concentration.
- Write the conditions a stranger would need to repeat it: strain and chassis, medium, temperature, induction OD, time points, instrument and wavelength, and the extinction coefficient if you convert absorbance to concentration (TU Darmstadt: ε = 18,100 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ at 396 nm).
- Put the figures in the registry, not on the wiki. Upload every plot and gel through the registry documentation editor so it is served from registry.igem.wiki/documentation. A figure that only exists on 2026.igem.wiki dies when the wiki does. Cross-link to the wiki for extra detail only.
- Fill all five document slots — Design, Experiment, Characterisation, Application, Discussion. Eleven of eleven winners used at least three; most nominee parts used one. Empty slots are visible on the page.
- Write the limitations into the Discussion and keep them. Michigan published that M3 produced no detectable protein and that its comparison rests on a single unreplicated blot; TU Darmstadt published that their engineered variant was worse than the parent. Both won. Hiding a null result does not buy an award, and reporting one apparently does not cost you a category.
- Register a collection as well, with a collection-level page of its own. Give every part a name built to a rule (prefix by function: GV-core:, Sensing:, Multiplexing:), state the assembly standard and overhangs explicitly, and write the one document that says why these parts belong together. Eight of twelve nominated 2026 collections skipped that document.
- Check every accession before you publish it. BBa_26SZRX0Y contains a zero, not the letter O; a single wrong character makes the part unfindable, which is the one failure mode that undoes all the work above.
- Budget the writing as a work package, not an afterthought. The median winning part page in 2026 is roughly 25,000–35,000 characters with ten-plus figures: that is one person for two to three weeks, and it has to be scheduled before the wiki freeze, not after.

_Method and limits. Started from the 106 researched team files on disk, which named exact accessions for several cohort teams. Then read the 2026 registry directly. parts.igem.org now redirects to registry.igem.org, a React application backed by a public read API (api.registry.igem.org/v1) that the site itself calls; we drove it through a browser tab and used only the endpoints the registry's own pages request — part by slug, documentation, composition, used-by, collections, collection items. Every accession quoted here was confirmed to return HTTP 200 from /v1/parts/slugs/<slug>; BBa_26SZRXOY, as transcribed in one team file, 404s — the real part is BBa_26SZRX0Y with a zero. We resolved documentation for all eleven winners' headline parts or collections, for all fifteen Best Part Collection cohort collections, and for sampled parts from eleven nominee teams. Documentation size is the character count of the markdown stored in the registry's own documentation records; figure counts are markdown and HTML image references in that same text. Limits: the award lists name teams, not parts, so for teams that registered several parts we inferred the award-winning one from the team file, the part's documentation depth and the project description — Muenster-University's Best New Composite Part winner in particular we could not pin down, and the Blocker_PCS series we found carries no documentation at all, so that row may be the wrong part. We also could not see team files for XMU-China, NNU-Nanjing-China, China-HUBU-Wuhan, RUBochum, NAU-CHINA, LZU-Northwest and VUB-Brussels, so those nominees are not represented in the depth figures. Rate limiting on the registry API (HTTP 429) capped the sampling, so nominee counts are samples of three to five parts per team, not full inventories. No team wiki was used as a source for any number here._

## What 106 decorated teams actually built in

_Exactly 1 of the 106 decorated teams used light to control a *Bacillus subtilis* culture, and that team is GEMS-Taiwan itself — 5 teams used light as a control input in any organism, 5 worked with *B. subtilis*, and the two sets overlap in one place. The companion test returned a null: among these decorated teams a non-model chassis neither helped nor hurt the odds of a Top 10 place (9 of 27 against 21 of 79, Fisher exact p = 0.62)._

**E. coli is still the house organism.** 51 of the 106 decorated teams put a construct into *E. coli*, and 24 of those 51 name a strain — BL21(DE3) most often, then DH5-alpha, then Nissle 1917, MG1655, Rosetta(DE3), SHuffle, C41 and BL21-AI. The other 27 write only "E. coli" and stop there, which is enough to describe a project and not enough to repeat one. Yeast is a distant second at 13 teams: 8 name *S. cerevisiae* (EBY100, BY4741 and three-plasmid builds among them), 3 use *Pichia pastoris* or *Komagataella*, and 4 write "yeast" with no species at all. Mammalian cell lines appear in 8 teams and are overwhelmingly HEK293, with CHO, a piggyBac reporter line and an oncolytic HSV-2 complementing line making up the rest. *B. subtilis* appears in 5.

**The tail is more interesting than the head.** 14 teams built in a named non-model organism and almost none of them chose the same one: *Pseudomonas putida* four times (KT2440 three times, F1 once), then *Streptococcus salivarius* K12, *Zymomonas mobilis*, *Komagataeibacter rhaeticus*, *Sporosarcina pasteurii*, *Magnetospirillum magneticum* AMB-1, *Shewanella oneidensis* MR-1, *Clostridium beijerinckii* S63 (isolated from a wetland by the team and made transformable from scratch), the thermophile pair *Acetivibrio thermocellus* and *Geobacillus thermocatenulatus*, *Photorhabdus* virulence cassettes, and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Add *Nostoc* sp. PCC 7120, *Chlamydomonas reinhardtii* twice, *Nicotiana* and a *Stevia* hairy root, Sf9 insect cells and M13 phage. 9 teams ran cell-free systems, 6 worked only with purified enzymes or in vitro nucleic-acid chemistry, and exactly 1 decorated entry had no wet lab at all. 18 teams used more than one chassis.

**The null, stated plainly.** Splitting the 106 into the 27 that used a chassis outside *E. coli*, *S. cerevisiae* and standard mammalian lines against the 79 that did not, 9 of 27 reached a Top 10 place versus 21 of 79 — 33 percent against 27 percent, Fisher exact p = 0.62. There is no effect here. The honest boundary on that sentence is that the sample is decorated teams only, so it says that among teams which already won something, chassis choice does not separate the Top 10 from the rest; it says nothing about whether a non-model chassis helps a team get decorated in the first place, because this analysis has no undecorated baseline and never could.

**The white space, tested against iGEM.** The academic trend review puts it in one line: light has become a real-time actuator for feedback control of fermentation, with reported 60 percent titer gains in a 1 L photobioreactor, *while optogenetics in Bacillus subtilis remains almost unexplored — twelve papers in all of PubMed*, and no published light-controlled *B. subtilis* bioreactor at all. The industry review arrives from the other side: Fermeate raised seed money to control gene expression with light so existing stainless-steel fermenters can be retrofitted instead of replaced, which is the cheapest route past the capital-cost wall. Against iGEM 2026, the counts are these. **5 of 106** used light as a control input in any organism: McGill (VP16-EL222 / C120 driving flocculation in *S. cerevisiae*), GEMS-Taiwan (CcaSR green light in *B. subtilis* WB800), WHU-China (EL222 with pBLI in *E. coli*), Princeton (an AsLOV2 optomonobody releasing cargo at 450 nm on M13 phage), and William & Mary, who measured dark and light curves on one of four pre-existing circuits they were stress-testing. Marburg is a sixth near-miss: they investigated optogenetic induction with the PULSE system and called it the most attractive long-term inducer on safety grounds, then did not build it. **5 of 106** worked with *B. subtilis*: GEMS-Taiwan (WB800), UPF-Barcelona (rhizosphere colonisation, strain unnamed), Hongwen School (WB600 secretion host), KAUST-KSA (Dsup integrated for radiation resistance), and BGI-College, who cultivated a commercial strain on spent broth rather than engineering it. **1 of 106** did both. Four of the five *B. subtilis* teams induce with something other than light — a promoter, an osmolarity switch, a genomic integration — and four of the five light teams are working in an organism where the technique is already routine. Excluding GEMS-Taiwan, the intersection is **0 of 105**. The white space the Drylab roadmap points at is real inside iGEM as well as inside PubMed, and nobody else in this cohort is competing for it.

### 5 of 106 used light as a control input
Four of the five work in organisms where optogenetics is already routine: *S. cerevisiae*, *E. coli*, and M13 phage displayed protein. Blue light accounts for four of the five systems (EL222 twice, AsLOV2 once, one unspecified); green light appears once. Only one of the five closes a control loop rather than switching a circuit on.

### 5 of 106 worked with B. subtilis, 4 engineered it
Two named a strain (WB800, WB600), one wrote only "B. subtilis", one integrated a cargo genomically across three hosts, and one cultivated a commercial strain without engineering it. A sixth team used *B. subtilis* only as a surrogate biofilm organism in an assay, which is a test subject rather than a chassis and is not counted here.

### 27 of 51 E. coli teams never name the strain
A chassis is not a species, it is a strain: BL21(DE3) and DH5-alpha behave nothing alike, and Nissle 1917 is a different proposition again. 24 of 51 say which one. Beyond that, 12 of the 106 dossiers describe bench work whose host organism is nowhere in the write-up at all.

**Checklist**

- Hold the B. subtilis optogenetics line for more than one season. The count is 1 of 106 and that one is us; no other decorated team in 2026 is in this space, and the published literature is twelve papers.
- Publish a full CcaSR transfer function in WB800 — light intensity crossed with duty cycle crossed with growth phase — because no other team in this cohort has B. subtilis light data to compare against, and a single induction intensity cannot test a Hill curve.
- Write the strain in every sentence where others write the species. 27 of 51 E. coli teams never do, and 1 of 5 B. subtilis teams never does. "B. subtilis WB800" costs five characters and is the difference between a description and a protocol.
- Put the host organism on the Description page, not only in the notebook. 12 of 106 decorated dossiers describe bench work with no host named anywhere — judges and readers should never have to infer it.
- Do not pick a non-model chassis to score points. Among decorated teams it moves nothing (p = 0.62). Pick B. subtilis for secretion and for light, and write down that reason.
- Record the induction method as a measured variable, not a protocol footnote. Four of the five B. subtilis teams in 2026 induce with a promoter or an osmolarity switch; the argument for light is only as strong as the dose-response data behind it.

_Method and limits. Sample: all 106 team dossiers in research/teams/, one per decorated team — every 2026 Top 10 team, special-prize winner and nominee. This is not the competition at large and nothing here describes undecorated teams. Counting: regular-expression sweeps for organism, strain, cell-line and light-control vocabulary across the English prose fields of each dossier (tagline, summary, dry, good, gemsTakeaway, award list), then every hit read in its surrounding sentence and classified by hand. Gene donor organisms, surrogate test organisms, rejected alternatives, modelling references (iML1515, iBsu1147) and education-activity mentions were excluded, which removed roughly a third of raw matches — "laccase" matches CcaS and "Jaccard" matches CcaR, so the unverified counts were wrong by several teams in both directions. A team is counted once per chassis category, so the table sums above 106: 18 teams used more than one chassis. Cloning and propagation hosts are counted where named. The B. subtilis count includes BGI-College, who cultivated a commercial strain without engineering it, and excludes HangzhouFourteenAP, who used it only as a surrogate biofilm organism in an assay.
