The light count includes William & Mary, who measured dark and light curves on a pre-existing light-responsive circuit although optogenetics was not their subject, and excludes Marburg, who investigated optogenetic induction in human practices and did not build it, and McMaster-Canada, whose only match was a blue-light transilluminator used for imaging. The placing test compares Top 10 placement against everything else using a two-sided Fisher exact test. What this cannot see: the dossiers are summaries of wikis, not the wikis themselves, so a chassis a team used but did not write up is invisible to this count. 12 teams describe wet-lab work whose host organism appears nowhere in their file; they are counted as "not stated" rather than assigned to E. coli, even though E. coli is the likely answer for most of them. The E. coli figure of 51 is therefore a floor, not a ceiling, and the same applies to every other category. Strain-naming counts reflect what the dossier records, not what the team's wiki or notebook may contain._


# Roadmap

## GEMS measured against its own report

_Every finding in this report, turned back on the team that commissioned it. Some of it is flattering and some of it is not, and the roadmap only means anything if both are said plainly._

**Start with what already meets the standard, because it is more than expected.**

The report's central result is that teams which close the model–data loop reach a Top 10 at 53% against 23%. GEMS-Taiwan closes it, and in one respect goes beyond anything else in the 2026 field: the crop-stress index was *fitted* to Taiwan's own harvest record — 25 years of county rice yields against ERA5 reanalysis, all 32,767 combinations of fifteen candidate terms scored on held-out years — and then tested **prospectively**, frozen on 26 September before any county published. County error came in at 365 kg/ha against 419 for a plain trend line. Separately, a growth rate of 0.2986 h⁻¹ with a 90% interval was registered in writing on 1 October, before a single bioreactor run; run 6 landed inside it at 0.286 ± 0.010.

No other team in this report pre-registered a quantitative prediction and scored it afterwards. It is the single highest-credibility item on the wiki and it cost nothing but committing in writing before the data arrived.

The provenance discipline is likewise at the top of the field, alongside TU Delft's. The honesty is real too: run 7 was excluded from scoring with the reason given, the curve-shape endpoint was recorded as not scored, and a 68-year payback was published against a partner's 4.9-year figure with the disagreement named rather than resolved. The human-practices loop closes properly — Prof. Chen Wen-Liang said in April that the organism could not be contained and that biological temperature sensing was not precise enough, and both the hollow-fibre perfusion reactor and the entire electronic sensing layer came out of that one conversation. Education was measured with pre- and post-surveys and the failures published, including the 30% who got DNA base pairing wrong.

**Now the gaps, each tied to a finding in this report.**

*The software has no front door.* The report found that 8 of 21 award-winning tools survive, and that the one habit separating them is a hosting decision made months early — every live tool was up on wiki-freeze day, every source-only tool lists localhost. The digital twin is MIT-licensed on GitLab and genuinely substantial, but it is a reactor controller: there is nothing a stranger can open. A simulator mode running on recorded data, at a URL, would move it from the source-only column to the live one. Two **high-school** teams managed exactly this in 2026.

*The structure-prediction stack is a generation behind.* The census found AlphaFold still dominates iGEM at roughly a third of teams while the research literature has moved to open models. GEMS used AlphaFold with a pre-set confidence gate, which is better practice than most — but Boltz-2, Chai-1 and the MPNN family are where Lambert-GA, Heidelberg and Princeton were working. This is the cheapest capability gap to close on the list.

*No parts contribution.* Taiwan took zero nominations in any of the four parts awards across both tiers in 2026, and GEMS is part of that zero. The report found that teams with no venture at all — HBUT-China, WHU-China, Squirrel-Beijing, BASIS-China — still contributed infrastructure other teams can reuse, and that this has a longer half-life than a business plan. A characterised, documented *B. subtilis* optogenetic part is the obvious candidate, and it is the same work as the Phase 3 research line.

*The model is not yet fitted at the scale it is used.* The CcaSR Hill transfer function is assumed to hold at 20 L when every induction run was at a single light intensity. By the report's own loop-closure test, that step is modelled rather than measured — and the wiki's amber rail says so, which is to its credit, but saying so is not the same as fixing it.

*The integration gaps are stated and still open.* Green-light induction tested but not wired in; dissolved-oxygen calibration did not hold; the protectant amount cannot be measured. These are the honest limits of a nine-month competition, and they are exactly the work an institution — rather than a team — exists to finish.

*No collaboration page.* GEMS appears on no other Taiwanese team's collaboration page and has none of its own, while NYCU-Taiwan's July meet-up drew 53 people from five teams. Being findable is a precondition for everything in Phase 4.

**The summary, stated plainly.** GEMS-Taiwan's weakness is not rigour — on provenance, pre-registration and honest reporting it is at or near the top of the entire 2026 field, high school and collegiate alike. The weakness is **reach**: a tool nobody outside can open, a part nobody else can order, a page nobody can find. That is a different problem from the one most teams have, and it needs a different year.

### The only pre-registered prediction in the report
A growth rate of 0.2986 h⁻¹ with a 90% interval, registered in writing on 1 October before any bioreactor run; run 6 landed inside it at 0.286 ± 0.010. The crop-stress index was frozen on 26 September and tested against county yields nobody had published yet. No other team in this report did either. Keep doing it, and make it a house rule rather than one person's idea.

### The digital twin has no front door
MIT-licensed on GitLab and genuinely substantial — live OD600, pH, four pressure channels, an autoencoder alarm, a Kalman forecast, a hydraulic fouling model and the BLASTAM infection rule. But it is a reactor controller: there is nothing a stranger can open. A simulator mode running on recorded data, at a URL, moves it from source-only to live. Two high-school teams managed that in 2026.

### Zero parts nominations, and Taiwan's zero is shared
Taiwan took no nomination in any of the four parts awards across both tiers in 2026. Teams with no venture at all still contributed parts other teams can reuse, and that outlives a business plan. A characterised, documented *B. subtilis* optogenetic part is the obvious candidate — and it is the same work as the Phase 3 research line, not extra work.

### The Hill curve is assumed at 20 L, not measured there
Every induction ran at a single light intensity, so the CcaSR transfer function is modelled rather than measured at the scale it is used. The wiki's amber rail says so, which is to its credit — but saying so is not fixing it. A dose–response series across intensities at working volume is a term's work and would close the loop at the step that currently carries the most weight.

### The weakness is reach, not rigour
On provenance, pre-registration and honest reporting, GEMS-Taiwan sits at or near the top of the entire 2026 field, high school and collegiate alike. What it lacks is a tool anybody outside can open, a part anybody else can order, and a page anybody can find. That is a different problem from the one most teams have, and it needs a different kind of year.

_Method and limits. Compares the GEMS-Taiwan team file in this report against the findings of the other nine analyses. The file was researched from the team's own 2026 wiki on the same terms as every other team, and much of the critical material here is the team's own stated limits rather than our discovery — the wiki is unusually candid, which is what makes this comparison possible at all. Where we say a gap exists, it is a gap relative to practice elsewhere in the 2026 field, not a judgement that the work is poor._

## Why the dry lab is the roadmap

_GEMS Research is becoming an institution, not a team. Institutions are defined by what they can still do after the current students graduate._

A wet lab is bounded by its benches, its reagents budget and the hours its students are physically present. A dry lab is bounded by what its people know and what they have written down. That asymmetry is the whole argument: computational capability compounds across years in a way that pipetting skill does not, because a model, a pipeline or a calibrated measurement protocol survives the student who built it.

This is also where the field has moved. Protein design, metabolic modelling and measurement standardisation are no longer the specialist corner of a project — in 2026 they are frequently the project. The teams on the 2026 podium did not win because they ran more gels.

So the roadmap below is deliberately about capability, not about any single 2027 project idea. Pick a phase and start.

## Two independent analyses, one answer

_The academic trend review and the industry trend review were run separately, from different sources, with no knowledge of each other. They landed on the same white space._

From the literature side: light has matured from a laboratory curiosity into a real-time actuator for closed-loop control of fermentation, with reported titre gains around 60% in a 1 L photobioreactor — and optogenetics in **Bacillus subtilis** is a twelve-paper literature in the whole of PubMed.

From the industry side, reached by an entirely different route: optogenetics is becoming the control and cleaning layer of bioprocessing, because light lets you retrofit an existing steel fermenter instead of building a new one. That makes it the cheapest route past the capital-expenditure wall that is currently the binding constraint on biomanufacturing.

GEMS Research already stands in that gap. ReLEAF was a CcaS/CcaR optogenetic circuit in *Bacillus subtilis* driving a bioreactor, and it won Best Measurement and Best Hardware at high-school level for exactly the instrumentation this line needs. The competition project is over; the research line it opened is not.

There is a second, blunter finding underneath this. Taiwan's state-backed biotechnology push is a manufacturing play — contract development and manufacturing, GMP capacity — with no visible synthetic-biology **design** layer, while Singapore and Israel are explicitly funding exactly that layer. A small institution cannot out-build a CDMO. It can occupy the design position that nobody in Taiwan currently holds.


# Academic trends

### Structure and complex prediction became free infrastructure, and open weights beat the flagship
AlphaFold3's architecture was reproduced and surpassed in openness by Boltz-1/Boltz-2, Chai-1, Protenix and OpenFold3, so predicting a protein-ligand complex is now a commodity step, not a project.

AlphaFold2 made monomer structure free; the 2024-2026 wave made co-folding (protein plus ligand, nucleic acid, ion and modified residue) free as well. AlphaFold3's weights remain gated to non-commercial use through a restricted-access agreement and its outputs may not be used to train competing models, which directly provoked an open counter-movement: MIT's Boltz-1 and then Boltz-2 shipped under MIT licence with weights, Chai Discovery released Chai-1, ByteDance released Protenix, and the OpenFold consortium released OpenFold3. Boltz-2 is the practically important one for engineering because it folds binding-affinity prediction into the same model rather than requiring a separate docking or free-energy pipeline. The downstream effect visible in the 2026 Nature literature is that structure prediction has stopped being the contribution and become the substrate: Nature Communications papers such as RASSCCoL (rapid physics-based design of small-molecule-binding proteins, 19 Oct 2026) and DeltaCata (geometric deep learning for mutation-induced changes in enzyme kinetic parameters, 5 Nov 2026) assume accurate structures and compete on what is predicted next - chemical complementarity, kcat/KM shifts, hydrogel stress relaxation. The honest caveat, raised repeatedly in 2026 benchmarking write-ups, is that co-folding models interpolate the PDB rather than learn physics, so they are strong on natural-like complexes and weak on genuinely novel chemistry and on affinity ranking within a congeneric series. For a teaching institution the significance is cost: the entire structural step of a project now runs on one GPU in seconds to minutes.

**GEMS action.** Stand up a single shared GPU box (or a modest cloud budget) running Boltz-2 and ColabFold behind a simple internal queue, and make 'fold it, then check the confidence metrics' a required step in every student project rather than an optional extra. Build one hard institutional skill that most undergraduate programmes lack: reading pLDDT/PAE/ipTM honestly, including a written rule for when a prediction is too low-confidence to act on. Within 12 months GEMS should be able to show a project where a Boltz-2 affinity prediction was experimentally checked, right or wrong - the negative result is as valuable a teaching artefact as the positive one.

### Generative protein design crossed from 'does it fold' to 'does it work', including design from plain English
RFdiffusion2, LigandMPNN and BindCraft made de novo binders and enzymes routine enough to benchmark, and Pinal now designs functional proteins from a natural-language prompt.

The 2026 state of the art is no longer backbone generation but functional success rate, and the field has started reporting it honestly. BindCraft (Nature 2025) reported per-target success rates spanning 10 to 100 percent with a mean of 46.3 percent, while independent commentary puts the realistic cross-target rate nearer 25 percent and notes that the most comprehensive single-target dataset - the Nipah G binder competition - came in under 10 percent. On the enzyme side, a March 2026 preprint benchmarked RFdiffusion2 (which depends on LigandMPNN for sequence design followed by RF3 refolding) at 30/41 on an enzyme design benchmark, with the challenger model reaching 41/41. The Baker lab's De novo design of miniproteins targeting GPCRs (Nature, 21 May 2026) is the clearest proof that this now reaches hard, membrane-embedded, therapeutically relevant targets: designed miniprotein agonists and antagonists against receptors implicated in itch, pain, cancer, metabolic disease and migraine, validated through a receptor-diversion microscopy screen. The genuinely new modality is language-conditioned design: Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter model from Fajie Yuan's group at Westlake University (Nature, 21 Oct 2026), was trained on roughly 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein-text pairs and designs candidates from a written functional description; its validated outputs span GFP, a PET-degrading enzyme, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a glycine-cleavage H-protein, where the designed version raised final product concentration to 1.7x the natural E. coli protein. Preprint versions report Pinal recovering roughly 77 percent of requested functional keywords against about 12 percent for ESM3 on keyword-only design, though the figure shifts between versions and should be treated as indicative.

**GEMS action.** Run one contained design-and-test campaign in the next 12 months with a deliberately cheap, unambiguous readout - a de novo binder or a light-responsive switch against a target GEMS already has an assay for - using BindCraft or ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN for design and ordering 10 to 20 constructs rather than hundreds. Record and publish the success rate including the failures, because calibrated in-house hit rates are the single most useful number an institution can own and almost nobody reports them at this scale. Treat Pinal-style natural-language design as a literacy exercise for students, not yet as a production tool.

### Biological foundation models and the race to a virtual cell
Evo 2, Arc's STATE and a Nature Perspective on a virtual yeast have turned 'simulate the cell' from rhetoric into a funded, benchmarked programme with an open prize.

Three strands converged in 2026. First, DNA foundation models: Evo 2, published in Nature in March 2026, was trained on 9.3 trillion bases from more than 128,000 genomes across all domains of life, scaled to 40 billion parameters, handles context windows up to one million bases, and shipped with open weights. Second, perturbation models: Arc Institute's STATE, its first virtual cell model, was trained on observational data from roughly 170 million cells plus perturbational data from over 100 million cells across 70 human cell lines, split into a State Embedding model for the transcriptome and a State Transition model for predicting perturbation-induced shifts; it is released under a non-commercial licence with State 2 in development, and Arc added an in-context-learning successor in January 2026. Arc has made this a community sport through the 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge, which scores models on predicting gene-knockdown responses in six cell lines they never saw in training, with a 100,000 USD prize. Third, and most relevant to synthetic biology, the microbial virtual cell: Towards the construction of a virtual yeast (Nature Perspective, 1 July 2026, Qian, Zhou and Guo) proposes decomposing S. cerevisiae into eight function-centred modules - genetic, metabolic and structural - each as a domain-specific AI tool coordinated by an LLM orchestration layer over three data pillars (mechanistic knowledge, subcellular architecture, dynamic states), inside a closed loop that autonomously designs and runs experiments. Nature Methods separately highlighted a 4D whole-cell model of a minimal cell (14 April 2026), and bioRxiv work is already building virtual viruses inside a JCVI-syn3A-based spatial minimal cell. The honest status: none of these predicts a novel engineered phenotype reliably, and the Virtual Cell Challenge exists precisely because generalisation to unseen contexts is unsolved.

**GEMS action.** Enter a GEMS student team in the next Virtual Cell Challenge cycle: it is a free, externally scored, genuinely unsolved benchmark with a public leaderboard, which is the cheapest credible way for a young institution to demonstrate dry-lab capability. In parall, pick one microbial model system GEMS already runs wet (ideally Bacillus or yeast) and start assembling the three data pillars for it - curated mechanistic knowledge, growth and expression time-series, imaging - so that GEMS owns a dataset rather than only consuming models. Reach out to Arc Institute's tools community and to the virtual-yeast authors; both are actively recruiting benchmark contributors.

### Genome-scale generative design: models now write whole genomes that boot
Genome language models have gone from annotating DNA to authoring viable bacteriophage genomes, and Nature Reviews is already publishing how-to pieces on it.

The landmark result is the Stanford and Arc Institute phage work: Evo 1 and Evo 2 were used to generate complete bacteriophage genomes modelled on the 5,386-nucleotide phiX174, roughly 700,000 candidate genomes were sampled, 285 were chemically synthesised and transformed, and 16 yielded viable, bacteria-killing phages - the first AI-authored genomes that function. Nature Reviews Genetics ran a Tools of the Trade piece by Samuel King on 17 November 2026, Generative genome design with DNA language models, walking through design, synthesis and validation, which is a reliable marker that a technique has moved from stunt to method. This sits alongside a hard-engineering track on the same problem: Nature Reviews Bioengineering published De novo design of synthetic microbial genomes (23 February 2026, Koster, da Costa Oliveira and Claassens) on rational genome design and genome-scale organisation; a bioRxiv group reported Generating E. coli 0.5 controlled by a half-sized genome by fleshing out an imperfect minimal genome through genome-scale debugging; Nature Biotechnology covered the Sc2.0 synthetic yeast chromosome programme; and Nature news reported both a genome transplant reviving 'zombie cells' (24 March 2026) and bacteria running key machinery on 19 rather than 20 amino acids via AI-guided redesign (30 April 2026). Nature also ran a Book Review by Kate Adamala in February 2026 asking directly whether AI genome design will upend how life evolves. Note the biosafety design choices embedded in the phage work: viruses infecting humans and close relatives were excluded from training, and only non-pathogenic E. coli hosts were used.

**GEMS action.** Teach genome language models as a reading-and-critique unit rather than a build project: have students generate and computationally evaluate sequences (promoters, regulatory DNA, small operons) without synthesising anything, which captures nearly all the educational value at zero biosafety cost. Where GEMS does build, stay at the part and pathway scale and adopt the phage paper's conventions explicitly - non-pathogenic hosts, excluded sequence classes, documented rationale. Write that stance down now as a one-page institutional policy; it will be required for collaborations and funding within the year.

### Agentic AI moved from literature assistant to experiment designer and robot driver
Robin, Biomni, Co-Scientist and cloud biofoundries closed the loop from hypothesis to robot to analysis, and the 2026 question is no longer whether agents can run experiments but how to validate what they conclude.

A 2026 Cell review on agentic AI for autonomous science classifies three paradigms that all landed in top venues within about a year. Robin, a multi-agent system published in Nature in 2026, linked hypothesis generation to data analysis in a lab-in-the-loop cycle and identified ripasudil and KL001 as enhancers of RPE phagocytosis, proposing ripasudil for dry age-related macular degeneration. Biomni (Science, 2026) is a general-purpose biomedical agent released open source as an environment (Biomni-E1), architecture (Biomni-A1) and RL-trained models (Biomni-R0), reporting generalisation across causal gene prioritisation, drug repurposing and rare-disease diagnosis. Google's Co-Scientist (Gottweis et al., 2026) is a Gemini-based tournament of agents validated on AML drug repurposing with in vitro confirmation, novel target discovery and antimicrobial resistance mechanisms. Synthetic biology specifically is getting its own instances: an October 2026 bioRxiv preprint describes iCloudBiofoundry, a cloud-accessible platform pairing agentic AI with robotic execution through a layer that translates protocols into automation workflows, with three experimentally validated case studies; MicroGrowAgents (bioRxiv, June 2026) is an agentic system for microbial cultivation optimisation; a Scientific Reports paper (8 September 2026) integrates LLMs with knowledge graphs for metabolic pathway design in food synthetic biology; and a bioRxiv group is using LLMs for ontology-driven generation of SBOL knowledge-graph software with Beal, Myers and Misirli as authors. The counter-evidence matters: a 2026 arXiv study of agentic self-driving microscopy found that benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalise to unseen tasks, and an Experiment-as-Code paper documents the real integration tax - one major orchestration framework maintains 28 device instances across 16 device types, each needing a hand-coded adapter. Emerald Cloud Lab remains the proof that fully programmable cloud labs are commercially viable and the warning that the ecosystem is closed and proprietary.

**GEMS action.** Adopt one open agent stack (Biomni is open source and the natural choice) on institutional infrastructure and make every student project run a documented agent-assisted literature and hypothesis pass whose outputs are then manually checked, with disagreements logged. Build the verification habit as the deliverable: a standing rule that no agent-proposed claim enters a report without a human-traced primary citation. For automation, do not buy a biofoundry - instead negotiate time on an existing cloud lab or a regional biofoundry and write protocols in a machine-readable form from day one so GEMS work is portable when it does scale.

### ML-guided DBTL and 'digital cell factories' now beat intuition on real titers
Machine learning over genome-scale models has stopped being a methods paper and started delivering multi-fold titer gains in a handful of cycles, with the field explicitly pivoting from biological realism to economic prediction.

The numbers are now concrete enough to plan around. Carruthers et al. (Nature Communications, 2025) coupled lab automation with ML to optimise isoprenol in Pseudomonas putida: CRISPRi downregulation of combinations of up to four gene targets raised titer five-fold over six consecutive DBTL cycles, while ML reduced a design space of roughly 800,000 combinations to about 400 priority constructs, with high-throughput proteomics used to validate the mechanism. Van Lent et al. (ACS Synthetic Biology, 2026) ran two DBTL cycles on p-coumaric acid in S. cerevisiae over a library of 18 genes and 20 promoters spanning about 170 million possible designs, and showed a gradient-bandit exploration-exploitation recommender beating greedy feature-importance selection, reaching 1.23 g/L - a 2.37-fold improvement; an earlier Moreno Paz study reached 0.52 g/L with a 68 percent gain in two cycles. The framing is also shifting: Chen, Li and Nielsen's Comment Digital cell factories for biomanufacturing (Nature Reviews Bioengineering, 4 November 2026) argues for metabolism-centric digital cell factories that privilege predictions of production performance and economic outcomes over biological detail - an explicitly pragmatic turn. Supporting infrastructure arrived too: Persephone (Nature Protocols, 5 November 2026) is an automated pipeline for personalising and evaluating human whole-body metabolic models coupled to community microbiome models; Canopy (ICML 2026) is a heterograph foundation model for metabolic engineering that beats tabular baselines on fermentation titer prediction; ML4SD (bioRxiv, September 2026) runs active learning over genome-scale-model scores for growth-coupled knockout design with explicit uncertainty; and iModulon-based engraftment (Nature Communications) uses ML decomposition of transcriptome compendia to transfer functions across species. A June 2026 bioRxiv preprint benchmarks LLM competence on genome-scale model analysis and finds they surface structural and data-quality limitations in the models themselves.

**GEMS action.** Make genome-scale metabolic modelling a core taught competency within 12 months: COBRApy plus flux balance analysis plus one published Bacillus subtilis GEM, with students reproducing the van Lent exploration-versus-exploitation comparison in silico before touching a flask. Then run one real two-cycle ML-guided DBTL campaign on a small combinatorial library in GEMS's own chassis, with the recommender written by students and the design space documented - two cycles is enough to produce a publishable, honest result. Seek a collaboration with an Agile BioFoundry-style or regional biofoundry group for the build step rather than buying liquid handlers.

### The Build step is being industrialised: cell-free prototyping, one-pot gene synthesis and million-scale design-space mapping
Robotic cell-free platforms, hybridisation-driven gene synthesis and long-read multiplexed profiling have broken the DNA-construction bottleneck that used to set the pace of every synthetic biology project.

Four 2026 papers together redefine what a 'build' costs. Automated prototyping of genetic codes (Nature, 26 August 2026, Radford, Sapers and Church) is a robotic cell-free platform that rapidly prototypes redesigned genetic codes, translating proteins with reassigned codons and non-standard amino acids without modifying any living genome - cell-free as the fast lane that avoids the viability constraint entirely. MOSAIC (Nature Biotechnology, 19 August 2026, Wu, Sun and Wei) replaces enzymatic processing with hybridisation: self-assembly of complementary oligonucleotides during thermal annealing, exploiting the full capacity of microchip oligo synthesis to produce over 1,000 distinct gene fragments and mutant libraries in a one-pot reaction. CLASSIC (Nature, 14 January 2026, Rai, O'Connell and Bashor) combines long- and short-read sequencing to quantitatively profile pools of arbitrary-length constructs with diverse genetic part compositions, which is how you actually map a genetic design space rather than sample it. Nature Biotechnology also published a microchip-based massively parallel DNA synthesis system, and Nature ran a Technology Feature on made-to-order DNA doubling achievable sequence length. The frugal end is advancing in parallel and matters more for GEMS: DropSynth-Gold (bioRxiv, June 2026, Plesa lab) extends emulsion-based multiplexed gene synthesis to longer genes via Golden Gate in droplets, and the Salis lab posted A Low-Cost, High-Throughput Design-Build-Test Pipeline for Engineering Genetic Systems (bioRxiv, June 2026) stress-tested on complex structural proteins - explicitly motivated by high DNA synthesis costs and assembly inefficiency. Also notable for throughput of measurement rather than build: Nature Biotechnology's Highly multiplexed mammalian metabolic engineering with a shotgun approach (Boeke lab, 6 October 2026).

**GEMS action.** Implement one frugal high-throughput build method end to end - the Salis low-cost DBTL pipeline or DropSynth-style pooled assembly - as a flagship capability project, and publish the cost-per-construct GEMS achieves. Pair it with cell-free (TXTL) prototyping as the default first test for any new circuit, because cell-free removes transformation, growth and biosafety friction and is ideal for a student-paced institution. Budget for long-read sequencing access rather than more pipetting capacity; CLASSIC shows that measurement depth, not construct count, is what converts a library into knowledge.

### Biosensors are now machine-designed, not discovered - including the receptor itself
Nature Biotechnology published fully synthetic allosteric switches whose ligand-binding receptors were designed by machine learning, which turns biosensing from a search problem into a design problem.

Artificial allosteric protein switches with machine-learning-designed receptors (Nature Biotechnology, 15 April 2026, Guo, Smutok and Alexandrov) is the pivotal result: ML-engineered minimal ligand-binding domains work as efficient receptors in single-component allosteric switches despite lacking global conformational change, yielding colorimetric, luminescent and electrochemical biosensors for small molecules, peptides and proteins, which the authors then compile into intramolecular YES and AND logic gates. They report fully synthetic switches built from artificial receptor plus artificial reporter domains, use HDX-MS and 19F NMR to attribute the mechanism to ligand-induced reduction of conformational entropy raising reporter catalytic activity, and demonstrate utility by engineering E. coli with steroid-dependent antibiotic resistance and bioelectronic devices that quantify steroid hormones. Around it sits a dense 2026 biosensing literature: Synthetic microbial co-cultures for modular bioelectronic sensing in diverse environments (Nature Biotechnology, 17 April 2026, Li, Zhu and Ajo-Franklin) modularises whole-cell electrical sensing across environments; Bacteria as living biosensors for DNA (Nature Reviews Bioengineering, 30 October 2025) benchmarks bacterial DNA biosensors against in vitro ones in unpurified samples; Nature Methods highlighted Engineering gut biosensors (12 March 2026); Nature published engineered magneto-sensitive fluorescent proteins for multimodal quantum-spin-resonance sensing (21 January 2026, Abrahams, Stuhec and Steel); and Scientific Reports published a Corynebacterium glutamicum glutamate-binding protein as a fluorescence probe (13 November 2026). On the cell-free diagnostics side, 2026 reviews converge on lyophilisation compatibility as cell-free's decisive advantage, with reported lyophilised Cas12a wearable and face-mask formats reaching femtomolar detection in 56 to 78 minutes, and a January 2026 microfluidic paper device integrating lyophilised RPA plus Cas12a across seven functional zones for colorimetric HPV16 E7 detection - but field validation, shelf life and sensitivity remain the stated gaps, and I found no deployed field trial.

**GEMS action.** Make ML-designed biosensing GEMS's declared niche and build the Alexandrov-style workflow in house: take a published minimal binding domain, redesign its specificity computationally, and validate with a colorimetric or electrochemical readout - a project that fits a student timescale and produces a real number. Standardise on lyophilised cell-free (TXTL) as the delivery format so the output is a shelf-stable field test rather than a plate reading, and pair it with a low-cost reader. Approach the Alexandrov group (Queensland) and Ajo-Franklin lab (Rice) for a protocol-level collaboration; both publish open and both work on sensor modalities GEMS could extend to agricultural targets.

### Optogenetics grew up into closed-loop bioprocess control - and Bacillus is nearly untouched
Light has become a real-time actuator for feedback control of fermentation, with reported 60 percent titer gains in a 1 L photobioreactor, while optogenetics in Bacillus subtilis remains almost unexplored - twelve papers in all of PubMed.

Cybergenetics - closing a control loop around a live culture using light as the manipulated variable - matured in 2026 from proof of principle to bioprocess tool. A Trends in Biotechnology study reported closed-loop optogenetic feedback on the yeast unfolded protein response in a custom 1 L photobioreactor, adjusting alpha-amylase expression from real-time measurements and achieving roughly 60 percent higher product titers. LEMOS (ACS Synthetic Biology, 2026) is an LED-equipped microplate integrating programmable illumination with continuous growth and gene-expression measurement for closed-loop control, paired with GEAGS, a model accounting for how gene expression changes across growth stages - which is the practical answer to the fact that optogenetic dose-response curves are steep enough to push systems to fully on or fully off, making intermediate setpoints hard, hence the emergence of pulse-width-modulated switching-time control. Light-controlled Corynebacterium glutamicum fermentation has been reported at 6.2 g/L for chitooligosaccharides. The protein-engineering side advanced too: Nature Methods published Design and optimization of a kinase-controlled allosteric switch (21 July 2026, Cao and Toettcher) and previously ProDomino, an ML model predicting domain insertion sites from sequence alone to accelerate design of light- and drug-triggered protein switches; Nature Biotechnology published a photoactivatable A-to-I RNA base editor for in vivo gene therapy; Advanced Science (2026) reported engineered optogenetic circuits in yeast with self-sustained outputs. The striking gap, which I verified directly: a PubMed search for optogenetics plus Bacillus subtilis returns twelve records in total, across all years, with the foundational work being a CcaS/CcaR green-red system ported from cyanobacteria. There is no published light-controlled B. subtilis bioreactor, and no published optogenetic control of Bacillus biocontrol or plant-growth-promoting function.

**GEMS action.** Commit to the gap: make 'optogenetic control in Bacillus subtilis' a multi-year institutional line, starting by porting and properly characterising a CcaS/CcaR or LOV-based light-inducible cassette in B. subtilis with full dose-response and growth-stage characterisation - that alone is a publishable contribution to a twelve-paper field. Build or buy an LEMOS-style LED microplate (the design is published and cheap) so GEMS owns closed-loop capability rather than open-loop induction, and implement a simple PI or model-predictive controller as a joint dry-lab/wet-lab student project. Then connect it to the plant-protection application by putting a biocontrol-relevant output, not a fluorescent reporter, under light control.

### Agricultural synthetic biology hit the deployment wall, and the blocker is market and acceptance, not science
A Nature Biotechnology assessment of 77 agricultural biotechnologies found that market viability and social acceptance, not technological readiness, are the binding constraints - while engineered nitrogen-fixers entered real field trials.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture (Nature Biotechnology Perspective, 10 November 2026, Mishra, Lui and Arkin) is the most strategically useful paper of the year for anyone building an agricultural synbio programme. It applies a Balanced Readiness Level assessment across technological, market, regulatory, acceptance and organisational dimensions to 77 biotechnologies in eight domains (crops, soils, livestock, watersheds, aquaculture, health and security, food loss and waste, frontiers) and concludes that market viability and social acceptance - not technological readiness - are the primary constraints. The high-readiness technologies share a profile: drop-in, contained, transient and perceived as natural. The authors name GMO containment as a concrete lever and set out a roadmap toward 'living infrastructure' - predictively designed multicomponent biological communities functioning at the ecosystem level - backed by a Fermi analysis of microbial fertilizers. The field evidence matches: Nature news (November 2026) reported a Nature Biotechnology comment arguing engineered bacteria could eventually displace up to half of synthetic fertilizer while requiring multi-species cooperation and more rigorous field trials, and noted that Brazil approved a transgenic bacterium for field testing for the first time; Switch Bioworks has permits and multi-state US corn trials with switchable nitrogen-fixing microbes, targeting a deliberately modest 25 percent nitrogen replacement. Plant-side tools advanced too: a modular extracellular contractile injection system repurposed from a bacterial nanomachine for receptor-mediated protein delivery into plant cells (Nature Nanotechnology, 18 November 2026, Legendre, Muchenje and Demirer); a synthetic gibberellin receptor giving spatiotemporal control of GA signalling in roots (Nature Plants, 22 October 2026); a modular high-throughput Chlamydomonas chloroplast engineering platform (Nature Plants, 2025); and Genome synthesis in plants (Nature Reviews Bioengineering, 2025). Containment research is advancing in step - a bioRxiv preprint from Nyerges and colleagues reports a firewalled synthetic commensal that blocks horizontal gene transfer in the gut.

**GEMS action.** Score GEMS's own optogenetic Bacillus plant-protection concept against the Balanced Readiness Level dimensions from the Arkin paper and publish the assessment as part of the project write-up - it costs nothing and immediately distinguishes GEMS from teams that only report titers. Design for containment and transience from the start, since light-dependence is itself a containment mechanism (no light, no function) and that is a genuinely novel argument worth making. Seek a Taiwanese agricultural research partner (an agricultural research institute or university plant-pathology group) for a contained greenhouse trial, because the Arkin analysis says field and acceptance data, not lab data, are what the field is short of.

### Biosecurity became a compliance requirement with teeth, and screening itself became a research field
The US tied federal life-science funding to buying DNA only from adherent suppliers, while Nature Communications published algorithms to defend synthesis screening against order-splitting evasion.

Governance moved from voluntary norms to funding conditions. The White House issued NSTM-6 on 5 November 2026 with an attached National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening, replacing the 2024 Framework and, on full implementation, the 2023 HHS Screening Framework Guidance; it conditions federal life-sciences funding on procuring synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop synthesis equipment only from designated Adherent Suppliers, with a phase-in reaching customers in 2027, and it supplements rather than replaces export controls and the Select Agents regulations. The international picture is uneven: order screening is now central policy in the US, EU, New Zealand and UK, but IBBIS data indicate only a small fraction of more than 700 known providers worldwide maintain publicly identifiable screening, and the International Gene Synthesis Consortium remains voluntary. Crucially, screening is now a legitimate and publishable technical research area: Defending synthetic DNA orders against intra-order splitting-based obfuscation (Nature Communications, 28 September 2026, Tayouri-Attia, Kogan and Puzis) tests a Gene Edit Distance algorithm that detects obfuscated orders regardless of fragment length, and Evaluating AI-Assisted Customer Verification for Synthetic Nucleic Acid Screening (bioRxiv, 2026, with Nelson among the authors) studies the legitimacy-screening step - verifying who is ordering and why - as the primary human safeguard. Governance of the AI layer specifically is being worked out in Navigating regulatory fragmentation in the convergence of synthetic biology, artificial intelligence, and automation (Nature Communications Perspective, 29 August 2026, McLennan, Freemont and Pretorius), which analyses national regulations and proposes a SynBioxAI regulatory interoperability toolkit explicitly aimed at giving research institutes the capacity to navigate divergent regimes. Nature also kept the harder questions open with Ting Zhu's Comment on whether mirror-image molecular biology research should be stopped.

**GEMS action.** Within 12 months write and publish a short GEMS biosecurity and biosafety policy covering three things: ordering synthetic DNA only from IGSC-member or adherent suppliers, a documented internal review step for any sequence design work, and an explicit scope statement excluding pathogen and toxin sequences - then use the SynBioxAI toolkit framing to structure it. Teach screening as curriculum, not compliance: the Gene Edit Distance paper is an outstanding student exercise in sequence similarity and adversarial thinking that builds real bioinformatics skill. Nominate one staff member as biosecurity point of contact, because collaboration agreements will increasingly require a named person.

### Standards, FAIR data and equitable access became the field's self-identified weak link
Synthetic biology is confronting the fact that its data are not machine-readable enough to train the models it now depends on, while a parallel movement works on who gets to participate at all.

The dependency is explicit: ML-guided DBTL and foundation models need consistent, annotated, cross-site data, and synthetic biology does not reliably produce it. A January 2026 ACS Synthetic Biology paper by Vitalis, Myers and colleagues proposes a standards-enabled FAIR data management workflow spanning the actual data types labs generate - sequences, models, protocols, images and time-series measurements. The SBOL ecosystem is modernising around SBOL3's fully graph-based, JSON-LD-aligned data model, with a 2026 Journal of Integrative Bioinformatics paper describing an SBOL converter that minimises data loss across versions, and a decade-review of SBOL Visual documenting growing adoption of the diagram standard. A 2026 FEMS Yeast Research review of high-throughput yeast engineering in biofoundries argues directly that alignment on QC thresholds, metadata standards and FAIR principles is now necessary for machine learning and cross-site validation. The access strand is equally substantive and more immediately relevant to a growing institution: Reclone, the Reagent Collaboration Network (Nature Methods Comment, 22 June 2026, Molloy, Federici and Rosca), builds regional distribution hubs and nodes for open sharing of biomaterials, protocols and knowledge to address the global R&D asymmetry; Nature Biotechnology ran Expanding global access to synthetic biology (12 October 2026, Karki and GC) on cost, logistics, local expertise and educator motivation; and Nature Communications previously published the frugal CRISPRkit, a smartphone-quantified CRISPR education kit explicitly designed so high-school students can do gene editing affordably and safely. Scientific Reports published A simplified modelling protocol for synthetic biology (16 September 2026, Alvarez, Turjanski and Sanchez), which is the methodological counterpart - lowering the barrier to doing the modelling at all. What is still missing, and I could not find 2026 work on it, is measurement metrology: calibrated, unit-bearing reporter measurements comparable across labs.

**GEMS action.** Adopt SBOL3 and a FAIR data layout as GEMS's native format now, before there is legacy data to migrate: every student construct gets a machine-readable record, every assay gets structured metadata, and the whole thing lives in a versioned repository. Fix the metrology gap locally by calibrating all fluorescence measurements to absolute units (fluorescein or MEFL equivalents) so GEMS data are comparable with other labs - a cheap, concrete practice that very few teaching institutions follow. Apply to become a Reclone node or hub for Taiwan and East Asia, which converts GEMS's educational mission into international standing at close to zero marginal cost.


# Industry trends

### The AI protein-design wave has its own capital market now, and it is spilling out of pharma
De novo protein design went from a 2023 proof of concept to a funded product category in 2026, with Chai Discovery at a $3.8B valuation and design agents being sold to biologists who cannot code.

Chai Discovery closed a $400M Series C in July 2026 at a reported $3.8B valuation, roughly 25x its September 2024 seed valuation, bringing it to about $630M raised across four rounds. Below that tier, 2026 produced a steady drumbeat of design rounds: BigHat Biosciences took a $75M Series C in September ($223M total), MoleculeMind in China reported a Series A over $100M in June backed by Cathay Biotech, Galux in South Korea closed a $29M Series B (KRW 42bn, $47M total), Scala Biodesign in Israel raised $16M led by Grove Ventures, and Lithuania's Biomatter closed an $18M Series A led by Astanor on 12 November for AI enzyme design with a Vilnius facility planned for 2027. The product is shifting from models to agents: Latent Labs released Latent-Y in October 2026, which it calls the first lab-validated drug design agent, built on its Latent-X2 frontier model for antibody and peptide design, and claims a 56x faster computational antibody workflow versus expert protein designers, with ~4,300x on literature and PDB structure review and ~350x on epitope selection (company technical-report figures, unverified by SynBioBeta). UC Davis's Yarov-Yarovoy lab used the Latent Labs platform to design nanobodies against a human ion channel, with four of five designs inhibiting current and the best at 30 nM IC50 in the first round without optimisation. At SynBioBeta 2026, Xaira CEO Marc Tessier-Lavigne dated the inflection to Baker-lab de novo design in 2023 and said companies can now generate high-affinity antibodies against large fractions of tested targets, while explicitly rejecting one-button drug design. The spillover is the newest part: Quercus Biosolutions raised a $5M seed led by Serra Ventures in July 2026 to design mini-protein binders against herbicide targets, in a crop-protection market where 21 of 31 known sites of action are already compromised by resistance and a new product averages 11+ years and ~$307M (AgbioInvestor for CropLife International, 2026).

**GEMS action.** Stand up a design-and-validate module in which students take a defined target, run binder design through a hosted platform (Latent Labs' web interface, Cradle, or open ESM/RFdiffusion-class tooling), and then measure something: binding, inhibition, or expression. Insist every design project ends in a wet-lab number, because the market premium in 2026 is on people who can falsify a model's output, not generate more of it. Approach one Taiwan or Asia-Pacific academic protein-design group as a validation partner so GEMS students can send designs somewhere that will test them.

### Biological foundation models became a product category, and the moat moved from architecture to proprietary data
Evo 2 is free and in Nature while Basecamp raised $140M on the claim that its biodiversity data is what public databases cannot give you, which tells you exactly where the value sits.

Arc Institute's Evo 2, trained on 9.3 trillion DNA base pairs from over 128,000 genomes, was published in Nature in March 2026 and is distributed fully open (weights, training data, inference tools) including via NVIDIA BioNeMo; Arc reports 200+ citations, 88,000+ downloads and over 8 million API requests in its first year. Arc also released its first virtual cell model (State) trained on ~270 million cells and ran the 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge, which asked models to predict post-perturbation expression after CRISPRi knockdown and 10x Flex profiling in cell contexts the model has never seen, sponsored by NVIDIA, 10x Genomics and Ultima Genomics with winners targeted for November 2026. Because the architectures are commoditising, money is going to data: Basecamp Research announced a $140M Series C on 23 September 2026 led by Bill Maris's S32 with NVIDIA and Menlo Ventures participating, explicitly on the premise that its biodiversity-derived BaseData gives its EDEN models training signal unavailable in public databases (totals reported inconsistently at $200M-$225M; an $800M valuation figure appears in one aggregator and is unconfirmed). Ginkgo Datapoints sells that same thesis as a service and told investors it serves 10 of the top 20 pharma companies with repeat training-data orders. Pharma is paying model-licence prices for data too: one aggregator reports GSK paying $50M upfront plus licence fees for non-exclusive access to Noetik's cancer virtual-cell models, and a $200M AstraZeneca-Tempus multimodal oncology data deal, while Tempus itself launched an effort in September 2026 to build the largest multimodal whole-genome dataset. The open-source counter-move is real: Outpost Bio open-sourced a microbiome foundation model, its data and its benchmark in September 2026, showing a model trained only on soil, ocean and wastewater still improves prediction of human gut outcomes, which is the first evidence that microbiome structure is universal enough to support one shared model. GenBio AI announced a world model of the human cell in August 2026. I could not find published per-token or per-seat API rate cards for EvolutionaryScale, Profluent or Basecamp; treat any specific API price as unverified.

**GEMS action.** Pick one narrow, locally-sourced dataset GEMS can own and release properly (subtropical soil or coastal microbiomes, local crop pathogens, a defined enzyme family from Taiwanese isolates), with a public benchmark task attached, following Outpost Bio's model-plus-data-plus-benchmark pattern. Teach students to fine-tune and probe Evo 2 or an ESM-class model through NVIDIA BioNeMo rather than training from scratch. Treat the benchmark paper, not the model, as the publishable output.

### The execution layer: autonomous labs became federal infrastructure, and narrow agents became the sellable product
The Genesis Mission is paying Ginkgo $47M for a 97-robot autonomous lab inside a national lab, while the actual product-market fit in software is narrow agents that do the boring parts of one specific person's week.

Ginkgo Bioworks won $4.6-4.7M for AMP2, an 1,800 sq ft anaerobic autonomous lab at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's EMSL with 14 Reconfigurable Automation Carts and 18 instruments, plus a $47M award for M2PC, a 32,000 sq ft Microbial Molecular Phenotyping Capability with 97 robots and 100+ instruments, breaking ground in 2026 and opening as a user facility by 2030. Both are among the first concrete projects under the White House Genesis Mission executive order directing the Department of Energy to build robotic laboratories for AI-directed experiments; Jason Kelly compared it to Manhattan and Apollo, and critically both run as user facilities open to competitive academic and industry access, so the capacity is rentable rather than captive. On the venture side the AI-scientist companies carry valuations well ahead of published output: Lila Sciences has disclosed roughly $550M (a ~$200M seed in March 2025, a ~$350M Series A in October 2025) and Bloomberg reported it in June 2026 in talks for ~$2B at a ~$8.5B pre-money valuation, while Periodic Labs raised a $300M seed in September 2025 and Forbes reported advanced talks in May 2026 at $7.5B. Neither close was confirmed in what I could read. The first-generation cloud labs are a cautionary tale: Strateos folded or restructured after an April 2023 announcement (its current status is reported inconsistently), Emerald Cloud Lab still operates from Austin but has had prolonged outages, and March 2026 analysis counts only a handful of commercial cloud labs accessible to outside scientists. The layer that actually sells is narrower and cheaper, and it shares one architectural principle. Potato launched Tater, an AI scientist, in autumn 2025, heard from users that it was not solving their real problem, and narrowed to Optimizer in August 2026, which converts an assay spec sheet plus a statement of available hardware into a multivariable design of experiments, a written protocol, plate maps and Opentrons worklists, using deterministic calculation for volumes, concentrations and dilution series rather than letting a language model guess. Roebling makes the identical claim for process engineering, with CEO Edward Shenderovich saying biological performance goes straight into mass and energy balances, equipment sizing, CapEx and OpEx, and that the calculations are deterministic, not guesses from a language model. Potato's Merrit Savener is explicit that the opportunity is not Ginkgo-scale throughput but better use of the 96-well plates a lab already runs, and that even large organisations skip design of experiments because the available tools are too hard. Alongside these: Transfyr launched a physical-AI platform for science with a $25M seed on 1 September 2026, Latent Labs' Latent-Y automates the literature review, PDB analysis and epitope selection that previously needed an expert designer, Weave Bio partnered with Takeda on AI regulatory automation in September 2026, Schrodinger unveiled the Bunsen AI co-scientist in August 2026, and Arc's genomic intelligence models were integrated into Biomni Lab in July 2026. Latent Labs supplies the structural consequence: when design gets cheap the binding constraint moves to wet-lab testing, target choice and the quality of the data used to judge candidates, and researchers start running experiments that never justified the time before, such as dozens of targets in parallel or several epitope hypotheses on one target at once.

**GEMS action.** Adopt one agentic design tool this year and build curriculum around it rather than treating it as optional: pair Potato's Optimizer (or equivalent) with an open, scriptable liquid handler such as an Opentrons OT-2, and require every student project to submit an executable protocol and a design-of-experiments plan alongside its notebook. Explicitly teach the deterministic-versus-generative distinction by having students hand-check a tool's dilution maths and audit a predicted structure, and require each project to state what the tool got wrong. Track EMSL/PNNL user-facility calls and Genesis Mission access terms, and identify an Asia-Pacific equivalent to apply to within 12 months.

### The post-Ginkgo correction: the platform company is dead, the picks-and-shovels company is compounding
Ginkgo's revenue roughly halved year-on-year while Twist Bioscience grew 22% to $459M and hit positive adjusted EBITDA, which is the clearest statement the market has made about what the 'platform' business model is actually worth.

Ginkgo Bioworks reported Q2 2026 revenue of $20.2M against $39.1M a year earlier, attributing the drop to a reduced scope of services for a large agriculture customer and fewer pharma and biotech enterprise programs; aggregator summaries put Q3 2026 at about $28M, down 6% year on year with the sequential rise partly a catch-up on a modified contract. Losses are narrowing but not gone: Q3 net loss from continuing operations improved 44% and adjusted EBITDA improved 58%, yet adjusted EBITDA remained negative at $22M, with quarterly cash burn of $27M, nine-month burn of $120M and full-year burn guidance of $125-150M against liquidity reported between $285M and $373M depending on the date. The company has repositioned around autonomous labs, with Cloud Lab, Datapoints and Solutions as the three businesses feeding it, but management is not breaking out revenue by line, which makes the pivot unmeasurable from outside. Contrast Twist Bioscience, which reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $459.4M, up 22% from $376.6M, gross margin up to 52.4% from 50.7%, record Q4 revenue of $126.6M (up ~28%, its fifteenth consecutive quarter of sequential growth), positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4, and FY2027 guidance of $550-560M. Twist's fastest-growing segment is DNA Synthesis and Protein Solutions at 39% growth versus 12% for NGS Applications, and management explicitly guides AI-related orders from $25M in FY2025 to $50M in FY2026 to a $100M target in FY2027. That is the shape of the correction: the company selling the reagent to every AI design shop is profitable, the company that promised to be the design shop is not. A third model is emerging in between, in which partners stitch together a single contract across the stack rather than one firm owning it: Saku Biosciences and Sable Fermentation announced in September 2026 a single agreement covering US customers from strain engineering through scale-up, and Cemvita partnered with Roebling in October 2026 to put biology, process engineering and techno-economics into one deterministic model.

**GEMS action.** Build a short financial-literacy strand into the programme: have students read the Ginkgo 10-Q and the Twist FY2026 8-K side by side and write the one-page memo explaining the divergence, which is a genuinely employable analytical skill. Define GEMS's own niche as narrowly as Twist defines its: one capability done reliably, with a measurable output, rather than an end-to-end platform claim. Use the Cemvita-Roebling techno-economic framing when evaluating any student project that proposes a product.

### The cost-of-goods wall is now an engineering problem with government money behind it
Nobody is short of strains; everybody is short of a tank they can afford, and in 2026 the US Department of War started paying to redesign the tank itself.

Biosphere received $21M from the Department of War through the Defense Industrial Base Consortium to build, run and prove a 20,000-litre bioreactor sterilised with UV light instead of steam, targeting operation by late 2027 at roughly 100 tons of product per year. The economics are the whole point: engineered microbes making enzymes, food ingredients or specialty chemicals get overrun by contaminants, so they need near-pharmaceutical cleanliness, but steam sterilisation forces pressure-rated steel, a boiler and extensive clean-in-place plumbing. A new 2,000-litre stainless tank alone runs $500,000 to $1,000,000 (figure from cocoa startup California Cultured), and industry estimates put surrounding piping, utilities and cleaning systems at several times the tank cost. CEO Brian Heligman notes biopharma abandoned steam sterilisation as too expensive and unreliable in favour of single-use plastic bags, which cap out at a few thousand litres and can cost tens of thousands of dollars per batch in consumables, economics that work for medicine and not for chemicals. The scale-up record supports the diagnosis. Liberation Labs' 600,000-litre Richmond, Indiana plant has taken three-plus years and $126.5M against an original end-of-2024 production target. Perfect Day's plant was due to reach mechanical completion in September 2026 with first commercial truckloads targeted in Q4 2026 after roughly 20 months of construction. Formo took a €35M (about $36M) EIB loan for biomass and precision-fermentation cheese. Plantible Foods raised $35M helped by a USDA-backed loan to scale Rubisco protein fivefold. Capra Biosciences got $17M from HHS in August 2026 to onshore essential API production, and the Department of War backed Visolis for bio-based solvents in February 2026. The counter-example that proves scale-up is tractable when you instrument it: Cemvita ran a 75,000-litre FermOil campaign at Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant in Ghent in May 2026 with consistent results from 30 litres to 75,000 litres, a 2,500-fold scale increase, and is now feeding that data plus its failures into a Roebling model that connects strain performance directly to mass and energy balances, equipment sizing, CapEx and OpEx.

**GEMS action.** Add a compulsory techno-economic analysis step to every applied student project: titre, rate, yield, and a one-page cost model including feedstock, utilities and downstream recovery, following the Cemvita-Roebling logic that biological improvements only matter where they move plant economics. Teach bioprocess basics on small instrumented benchtop fermenters with real data logging rather than more flask work. Approach Taiwan's food, enzyme or amino-acid fermentation industry for a scale-up site visit and a student data-analysis project on an existing production dataset.

### Agricultural and food synbio got its regulatory unlock, and the winning pitch is economics not sustainability
USDA conditionally licensed the first engineered microbe that manufactures antibodies inside an animal's gut, it is already in 35 million broilers, and the sales argument is feed conversion rather than fewer dead chickens.

On 29 September 2026 USDA's Center for Veterinary Biologics conditionally licensed BiomEdit's BE-101, a Limosilactobacillus reuteri strain engineered to secrete llama-derived single-domain antibodies against Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin and NetB; it is now in more than 35 million broilers. The design choices are instructive: the expression cassette is chromosomally integrated rather than plasmid-borne for genetic stability, the chassis is two chicken-derived strains from the same clade, and delivery exploits the one day a chicken's gut is nearly empty, via a spray cabinet at hatch, with colonisation in about a day and roughly three weeks of protection from one application. The market framing matters more than the biology: necrotic enteritis costs global poultry production an estimated $6 billion a year, mostly through feed conversion and weight gain rather than mortality, and antibiotics are the wrong tool twice over because C. perfringens is a normal gut resident and because antibiotics have been pulled from broiler production. BiomEdit went to USDA in early 2023, months after launch, and co-created the regulatory path, choosing USDA over FDA and EPA jurisdiction up front so one agency could issue the Finding of No Significant Impact. The rest of the sector shows the same pattern of commercial pragmatism: Leaps by Bayer led Robigo's Series A in September 2026 on engineered microbes for crop protection; Quercus raised $5M to design mini-protein herbicides; Pivot Bio, now valued at roughly $2 billion on about $697M raised and reporting use on more than 15 million corn acres (13 million in its 2024 impact report), cut prices, raised production and announced a price and supply assurance programme spanning the 2026, 2027 and 2028 seasons as fertiliser costs spiked, and moved its headquarters from California to Minnesota; its PROVEN G3 trials report replacing an average of 33 pounds of synthetic nitrogen per acre, a company figure I could not independently verify. C16 Biosciences expanded its Palmless brand into food and beauty in August 2026, and Proxy Foods AI raised a $6M seed for a food R&D platform.

**GEMS action.** Run one student cohort project on a locally relevant agricultural target (a Taiwanese crop pathogen, an aquaculture gut health problem, or a feed-conversion question) and require a regulatory pathway memo naming the responsible Taiwanese agency alongside the science, mirroring how BiomEdit chose its agency before developing. Build a relationship with one Taiwanese agricultural research institute or an aquaculture or poultry producer so projects have a real end user. Teach students that the pitch is cost per tonne or per bird, not sustainability.

### DNA synthesis competition moved from price per base to length, turnaround guarantees and supply security
Ansa sells 50 kb clonal constructs from $0.13 per base pair with an on-time guarantee while Twist advertises fragments from $0.07, which means the differentiator is no longer cost per base but what you can get, when.

Ansa Biotechnologies, which uses enzymatic synthesis that binds nucleotides to a DNA polymerase before extension, launched a 50 kb clonal DNA product in October 2025, raised a $54.4M Series B with the industry's first guaranteed on-time service, priced from USD 0.13 per base pair across its 100 bp to 50 kb range per its April 2026 announcement, and partnered with Integrated DNA Technologies, with an upgraded joint e-commerce platform for complex constructs announced in September 2026. Twist Bioscience advertises Gene Fragments from USD 0.07 per base pair and has argued that chemical synthesis remains cheaper, more accurate and capable of longer strands, with CEO Emily Leproust previously calling cost the real fatal flaw of enzymatic synthesis; Twist's own answer has been to cut the expensive nucleoside triphosphate consumption in enzymatic routes. Twist's FY2026 numbers show where demand actually is: DNA Synthesis and Protein Solutions grew 39% versus 12% for NGS Applications, and the company targets $100M in AI-related orders in FY2027 from $25M in FY2025. Elegen launched a Gen II cell-free DNA platform in October 2025 and ENFINIA IVT-Ready DNA for mRNA workflows. Benchtop synthesis remains an awkward value proposition: a DNA Script Syntax-class instrument is cited at around $200,000, against commentary that per-base synthesis cost has fallen to roughly €0.1-0.3 from about €10 in the 1990s, so the instrument only pays back for labs with sustained, security-sensitive or turnaround-critical demand. Market sizing is unreliable: 2026 reports for enzymatic DNA synthesis range from USD 0.47 billion to USD 3.77 billion with a quoted 23.5% CAGR, and a November 2026 report flags tariffs raising prices for imported enzymes, reagents, microfluidic components and synthesis cartridges, which is a new and material cost pressure for any lab outside the US supply chain.

**GEMS action.** Negotiate an academic or education account with one long-DNA vendor (IDT, Twist, Ansa or Elegen) and one regional distributor, and publish internal lead-time and landed-cost benchmarks so students plan to real timelines. Teach design-for-synthesis explicitly: codon optimisation, repeat and GC avoidance, modular assembly, and ordering fragments you can assemble locally rather than one long construct. Do not buy a benchtop synthesiser in the next 12 months unless a security or turnaround case justifies the roughly $200,000 instrument cost.

### Nucleic acid synthesis screening became binding US policy, and it reaches anyone who sells to US-funded labs
The November 2026 National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening forces federally funded researchers to buy only from certified providers that screen orders of 50+ nucleotides with NIST-verified tools and keep records for eight years.

The White House released the National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening on 5 November 2026 alongside NSTM-6, implementing Executive Order 14292 of May 2025 which had directed OSTP to revise or replace the 2024 framework. Under it, federally funded researchers must purchase from certified providers; providers must screen sequence orders of 50 or more nucleotides using NIST-verified tools, verify customer identity, report flagged orders and retain records for eight years, with implementation phased in over roughly a year. Separately, a revised BIOSECURE Act became law in December 2025 as Section 851 of the FY2026 NDAA, prohibiting US entities holding relevant federal contracts, grants or loans from using equipment from specified Chinese biotechnology firms in their supply chains; a July 2026 implementing policy exists but ambiguity over what counts as prohibited research has created real uncertainty for collaborations. Congress is pressing further: the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S.3741, with House companion H.R. 3029) was introduced in January 2026 to require Commerce to issue binding regulations for nucleic acid synthesis security, and had not passed as of what I could verify. The commercial layer is appearing alongside the policy: Praio launched an environment screening panel at SynBioBeta 2026 in May, and Neion Bio brought Barnwell Bio's biosurveillance into its egg-based manufacturing flocks in October 2026, which is the beginning of screening and surveillance as purchasable services rather than compliance overhead. Note the coupling to the previous trend: AI protein design plus cheap synthesis is precisely the dual-use pairing these rules target, and Belfer Center analysis frames AI-enabled biotechnology as a governance problem the current regime only partially addresses.

**GEMS action.** Write and publish a one-page GEMS sequence-ordering and screening policy that mirrors the NSTM-6 requirements (certified providers, 50-nucleotide screening threshold, identity verification, record retention) and have every student sign it before their first order, which both protects the institution and signals seriousness to partners. Teach a short dual-use and biosecurity module using the Belfer and NSTM-6 documents as primary texts rather than generic ethics material. Audit instrument and reagent suppliers for BIOSECURE Section 851 exposure before any US-funded collaboration.

### The centre of gravity in engineered biology is shifting to Asia, and Taiwan is positioned on the manufacturing side rather than the design side
China holds about 70% of world fermentation capacity and supplied 44.5% of global pharma licensing deal value in H1 2025, while Taiwan's state-linked bio-manufacturing push is a CDMO play with no visible synthetic-biology design layer.

SynBioBeta's analysis frames China's bioeconomy as three sequential waves now running simultaneously: a completed first wave of amino acids, bulk chemicals and food ingredients built by Meihua, Fufeng, Cathay, Anhui Huaheng Bio and CABIO on cost and operational discipline, which industry sources say displaced Ajinomoto and Kyowa Hakko from significant shares of global amino acid markets (market-share figures explicitly unverified by the author); a second wave built on the 2015 CFDA overhaul, the MAH system and ICH accession in 2017, producing the therapeutics licensing boom in which major pharma in-licensed 31% of their innovative pipeline assets from China in 2024 and China accounted for 44.5% of global licensing deal value in H1 2025; and a third wave now forming. The headline fact underneath all of it is that roughly 70% of world fermentation capacity sits in China. Deal evidence: GSK's 2025 Jiangsu Hengrui agreement at $500M upfront and up to $12B with milestones, AstraZeneca's $2.5B Beijing R&D and manufacturing commitment plus a CSPC research collaboration at $110M upfront with up to $1.62B development and $3.6B sales milestones built on CSPC's AI drug discovery platform, and Cathay Industrial Biotech's reported $500M Wusu expansion in long-chain dicarboxylic acids where China holds about 30% of global production. SynBioBeta separately concluded that 2026 was the year China surpassed the USA in biotech innovation, deal value and clinical output. Taiwan's own posture is manufacturing-led: the state-linked Taiwan Bio-Manufacturing Corporation broke ground on a 15,000 m2 GMP facility in Hsinchu Biomedical Science Park in June 2025 with operations expected from Q2 2026, including Taiwan's first GMP mRNA capability, biomedicine sits inside the 5+2 Innovative Industries Plan, the government acquired National Resilience's advanced pharmaceutical production platform, and a 33-company delegation went to BIO 2026 in San Diego led by the Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical Industries Promotion Office. Regional peers are moving on the dry-lab side instead: DayOne launched Singapore's first biological data centre prototype in August 2026, and Israel's Innovation Authority committed roughly NIS 70 million in July 2026 to national infrastructure for AI models built on biological data. I found no Taiwan-specific synthetic-biology policy programme or funding figure.

**GEMS action.** Position GEMS explicitly as Taiwan's dry-lab synthetic biology pipeline rather than a smaller wet lab, and say so to the Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical Industries Promotion Office and the Ministry of Economic Affairs when seeking support, pointing at Singapore's DayOne biological data centre and Israel's NIS 70M biological-AI infrastructure as the comparison Taiwan currently lacks. Open a concrete relationship with TBMC in Hsinchu for student visits and a data project, since it is physically close and its ramp from Q2 2026 means it needs people. Build one regional partnership (Japan, Singapore or Korea) for compute or model access rather than trying to replicate it locally.

### Therapeutics is where the capital is, and where the dry lab's claims are finally being tested in patients
Isomorphic Labs raised $5B in November 2026 without disclosing a single human trial, while Insilico's AI-originated drug is in a 320-patient Phase III, which is the whole credibility gap in two sentences.

Isomorphic Labs announced a $5 billion Series C co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia in mid-November 2026 while disclosing no human trial, no named clinical candidate and no valuation; Demis Hassabis had said at Davos in January 2026 that first trials would begin by the end of 2026, and that remains unconfirmed. A claim that Isomorphic advanced a wholly AI-designed candidate to Phase 2 in June 2026 appears in one secondary source and conflicts with better-sourced reporting, so treat it as unverified. The genuinely advanced programme is Insilico Medicine's rentosertib (ISM001-055), a TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which showed a mean forced vital capacity improvement of +98.4 mL at 12 weeks on 60 mg once daily versus a 20.3 mL decline on placebo in Phase IIa, and whose 320-patient Phase III (NCT07687459) was registered on 7 July 2026. Recursion's clinical story is thinner: REC-4881 in familial adenomatous polyposis is Phase 1b/2, REC-994 and REC-2282 are Phase 2 in cerebral cavernous malformation and NF2-related schwannomatosis, REC-2282's failure removed a near-term catalyst, and the company guides additional clinical data to the first half of 2027. No AI-designed drug has FDA approval. Around that core, 2026 was busy: TwoStep Therapeutics closed an oversubscribed $62.5M Series A with FDA IND clearance for a first-in-class peptide-drug conjugate from a Nobel-laureate spinout, Moonwalk Biosciences raised a $70M Series B for adipose-targeted RNAi in obesity, Aureka raised a $100M Series B, Ridge Biotechnologies expanded its investor base on AI-designed bioconjugates, Owkin partnered with Boehringer Ingelheim and Envisagenics partnered with Boehringer on RNA splicing targets, Weave Bio partnered with Takeda on AI regulatory automation, and Recursion partnered with Genentech on neuroscience targets. Anthropic's life sciences lead Eric Kauderer-Abrams told SynBioBeta 2026 that the company aims to compress life-sciences R&D timelines tenfold, has opened wet labs, acquired the eight-month-old Coefficient Bio, and described Opus 4.6 as its first model with extensive biology training, while conceding that biology often has no single unambiguous source of truth to train against. Xaira's Tessier-Lavigne argued the next step is causal models, built by perturbing cells and organoids and measuring outcomes, with a recent paper spanning 16 cellular contexts, and noted two-thirds of clinical failures come from not identifying the right patients.

**GEMS action.** Run a recurring journal-club format in which students compare a company's press release against its clinical trial registry entry or SEC filing and write the discrepancy memo, using Isomorphic and Insilico as the opening case. Teach the target-validation question (why this target, in which patients) as seriously as the design question, since that is where Tessier-Lavigne locates two-thirds of failures. Point interested students toward causal-perturbation data analysis, which is the skill Xaira and Arc are both hiring for.

### The funding climate is up in dollars and down in companies: capital is concentrating into fewer, larger, dry-lab-flavoured rounds
Synbio funding was up 79.5% to about $1.33B through late September 2026, but the number of funded companies fell from 67 to 62, and excluding rounds over $50M growth was only 34.8%.

One tracker puts synthetic biology funding at $1.327 billion through 22 September 2026, up 79.5% on the comparable 2025 period, and then undercuts the headline: excluding rounds above $50M, 2026 ran only about 34.8% ahead, while funded companies fell from 67 to 62 and deals from 68 to 64. Concentration is extreme within quarters too, with Q2 2026 the largest at $501.5M of which NewLimit's $435M round was 86.7%, against Q1 2026 at $263.7M across 14 deals. Therapeutics took $874.4M, 54.5% of the total, from only eight deals. These are vendor trackers with inconsistent definitions, and a separate tracker counting broader biotech reports 232 VC rounds and $30.9B in 2026, so the absolute numbers should not be quoted without checking PitchBook or Dealroom.
