Wettability was tested by measuring water contact angle on the gas-facing wall face. (2) An in silico evolution pipeline for GvpC: AlphaFold2 predictions of a Serratia GvpA tetramer and a GvpC repeat aligned onto the experimental Dolichospermum GvpA-GvpC complex and repacked, then LigandMPNN redesigning interface residues across four tiers from fully native to all ten positions, with candidates screened by Boltz-2 co-folding, AlphaFold2 in initial-guess mode and PyRosetta relaxation. (3) A de novo binder pipeline: RFdiffusion3 generating backbones against four adjacent GvpA chains, ProteinMPNN designing eight sequences per backbone, AlphaFold2 re-prediction, then filtering on interface PAE, binder pLDDT and RMSD. (4) A biosensor pipeline where RFdiffusion3 designs a blocking latch fused to the binder at freely chosen hotspots, ProteinMPNN redesigns it, and AlphaFold2 scores three states — construct plus GvpA alone (should not bind), construct plus target alone (latch should displace by more than 3.0 A RMSD), and construct plus both (both bound, latch fully dissociated) — with PyRosetta interface delta-G estimates on each bound state.

**datascience.** The honesty is the distinguishing feature. The MD model predicts a 1.63-fold stiffness increase from truncated GvpC against 1.48-fold measured experimentally — close — but its absolute collapse pressure estimate of 124-137 kPa without GvpC sits well below the experimental 195 kPa, and the team states plainly that ATLAS is therefore suited to ranking variants rather than predicting absolute pressures, because a whole vesicle is not an idealised wall patch. The umbrella sampling gives 43.5 kJ/mol to remove one GvpC repeat (about 17 k_B T at 310 K) and notes that the free energy plateaus once the repeat has moved 0.55 nm, when only 24% of original atom contacts remain, so most of the cost is paid before the last contacts break. The wetting hypothesis was tested and rejected on its merits: 122.8 degrees without GvpC against 122.2 with, a 0.6-degree difference against the roughly 6 degrees a condensation mechanism would require. Screening thresholds were calibrated against controls rather than chosen by feel — the redesigned sequences were run alongside native Serratia GvpC repeat 3 and nine negative controls, and of all metrics tested only AlphaFold2 interface PAE separated them cleanly (135 of 200 designs passed the 12.0 gate, all nine negative controls failed, the native repeat passed at 11.42), with the team stating explicitly that only that one threshold is calibrated and the other three are a priori safeguards whose predictive value is unproven. PyRosetta interface energies are reported but excluded from selection because they did not discriminate the controls. GVSAM's evaluation was adapted to the problem: intersection over union is unsuitable for objects this small because a one-pixel shift wrecks it, so a hit requires the annotated box centre to lie inside the prediction within 2 px and the areas to differ by at most fourfold, each annotation matchable once, highest-scoring first — with recall, precision and F1 pooled across images and 95% confidence intervals bootstrapped over images. They report F1 rising from 0.2% (base CellSAM) to 42% (GVSAM) with false positives down 97%, and openly diagnose overfitting: validation loss bottomed at epoch 6 while training loss kept falling, so that checkpoint was taken. Two team members annotated independently to reduce single-annotator bias, images of deliberately varying quality and images with no vesicles at all were kept for robustness, and the 108 annotated images were split 70/20/10 at image level with vesicle and non-vesicle images split separately. Ultrasound analysis in GAS uses median intensity and median absolute deviation rather than mean and standard deviation because ultrasound speckle makes single-pixel brightness fluctuate with intensity, with background subtracted as the median recorded after all vesicles were destroyed, and collapse pressure taken as P50 from a four-parameter regression fit (R-squared above 0.99 on all curves).

**dataviz.** This is the Best Wiki winner and the visualisation is doing real work rather than decoration. Every technical term carries an inline definition on hover (acoustic contrast, acoustic pressure, xAM, acoustophoresis, DARPin, pLDDT, i_pAE), and every computational tool gets an 'Explore this software' panel explaining what it is, how it works and what its published benchmarks are — so a reader can follow the pipeline without already knowing LigandMPNN or CellSAM. Structures are interactive: a 'View in 3D' control turns the progression from one GvpA, to a rib inside its cryo-EM density (EMD-14238), to the 13,450-copy vesicle, to the GvpC cage; MD trajectories play as interactive animations of the wall rippling; and biosensor constructs can be rotated with and without bound GFP. The GVSAM results are presented as a ten-image gallery where the reader switches each test image between raw, ground truth, GVSAM prediction with true positives, false positives and false negatives marked, and the base CellSAM prediction — which lets a sceptic check the model rather than take the F1 score on trust. Design pipelines appear as schematic flow diagrams, and the binder filtering is shown as KDE plots overlaying all 1,429 designs against the 13 accepted ones on each metric, making visible that many designs pass individual gates while almost none pass all three.

**software.** ATLAS ships as a documented end-to-end pipeline with its own comprehensive user guide, covering the MD characterisation route, the GvpC in silico evolution pipeline and the de novo binder and biosensor design pipelines. GVSAM is a fine-tuned derivative of CellSAM (itself built on Meta's Segment Anything Model with an Anchor DETR based CellFinder detector and a ViT-B encoder) retrained to detect gas vesicle clusters rather than whole cells, trained with Dice plus binary cross-entropy with logits, batch size 3, learning rate 1e-4 (backbone 1e-5), weight decay 1e-4, annotated in napari and converted to bounding boxes by a Python script, with 90 and 270 degree rotation augmentation to cope with only 108 images. GAS is the physics-informed fitting model that converts raw cross-amplitude-modulation ultrasound data into pressure-dependent signal curves. On the wet side the team released the VOYAGE part collection (expression systems for D. flos-aquae gas vesicles in mammalian cells and Serratia gas vesicles in E. coli, plus characterisation and purification parts), an extensive collection of optimised gas vesicle protocols including AFM and darkfield imaging, and an accessibility guide for working with gas vesicles on a budget — which includes using the open-source 3D-printed OpenFlexure microscope for darkfield imaging of purified vesicles and live-cell imaging of producers, explicitly so that teams with limited resources can replicate the work. The Fail Forward Guide is the fourth released artefact.

**ihp.** The clearest example of stakeholder input changing method rather than framing came from Prof Dr Frauke Gräter, interviewed on modelling strategy. The team first built exactly what she proposed — two Martini coarse-grained sheets with gas between them, tested at different pressures — and it taught them something by failing: the flat patch collapsed even without any applied pressure, because it lacks the closed curved geometry that holds a real vesicle open. That killed the approach and, building on her point that relative differences are what matter for ranking and that a small wall section is representative, they switched to measuring bending stiffness on an all-atom repeating patch and converting it through shell theory. Her warning about sampling is why they chose bending rather than stretching as the primary measurement, ran every simulation at least three times and compared several GvpC variants rather than only wild type; her advice on pulling speed went into the steered MD, where they pulled at several speeds and used only runs in which GvpC genuinely came off. They also tried her suggested coarse-grained model as a fast pre-screen, found it could not distinguish the variants, and state that every reported result therefore comes from all-atom simulation. Elsewhere: Prof Pfeifer warned that GvpA is highly conserved and vulnerable to mutation, redirecting the whole engineering effort onto GvpC as the modular target, and explained which accessory genes the expression constructs needed. Dr Huber's feedback on how long even one sub-idea takes changed how many aspects they attempted and forced explicit prioritisation. A stakeholder conversation led them to replace the D. flos-aquae / P. megaterium expression mix with a Serratia-based cassette in E. coli, which is what finally gave them expression and purification and set the host for everything downstream. Protein design expert Paul Kittner diagnosed a real failure mode: hallucination tools like BindCraft are biased toward hydrophobic interfaces because their structure predictors are trained on natural ones, and GvpA's outward-facing surface is hydrophilic — he advised adding a custom penalty term to the generation loss, which worked and let them target the hydrophilic face, and also pointed them to diffusion models as less biased, which is why RFdiffusion3 became the backbone generator. Dr Michael Jendrusch told them bluntly that no existing pipeline suited their biosensing goal and sketched the binder-plus-latch architecture they built, including the multi-state scoring step and the advice to screen with pooled assays and Twist Oligo Pools rather than testing candidates individually. Prof Dr Karl Rohr's advice is why GVSAM fine-tunes CellSAM rather than training from scratch. Mentor Molina Ramirez moved from interview subject to collaborator, supervising imaging, adapting the xAM script to their specific transducer, and advising them to use beamformed rather than pixel data and median rather than mean normalisation to suppress outliers. Prof Dr Georg Schmitz gave them a falsifiable clinical test — look first with the transducer you already have at frequencies close to clinical scanners, and only go higher if nothing appears — which they followed and passed at 5-7 MHz. Dr Lakshmanan's practical warnings (closing a low-quality tube cap can generate enough pressure to collapse vesicles) shaped handling, and her advice to modify GvpC termini shaped the latch design.

**publicEngagement.** Heidelberg's education programme, Fail Forward, takes error culture in science as its subject rather than synthetic biology content, which makes it unusually distinctive. The centrepiece is the Error Bar, billed as 'a night of scientific f*ck ups': around 80 students and researchers in the university's student bar in July, with successful professionals telling their own stories of things going wrong and what they learned. It was deliberately not a lecture — a short presentation introduced structural problems including publication bias against negative results and mental health stressors in academia, then interactive activities invited participants to share their own experiences, and recreation therapist Brady Hughes ran a workshop on distinguishing a fiasco from a crisis, reappraising situations and using grounding exercises, ending with the group shredding their recent failures together. A panel discussion with around 120 participants extended the theme from personal to institutional failure in the healthcare system, bringing researchers, healthcare professionals, patient advocates and the public into one room, with one panellist making the publication-bias argument in concrete terms: unpublished negative studies mean the same approach gets tried repeatedly, wasting resources and re-exposing participants to risk. All of it was distilled into the Fail Forward Guide, which includes background on failure in academia, expert interviews, and a tutorial for hosting your own Error Bar anywhere in the world — and the team has already committed to making the Error Bar recurring, with an open-mic session planned and PIs who missed it asking to join the next one. Alongside this they ran a Science Cinema with the local student cinema Unikino Heidelberg (over 70 participants for GATTACA, followed by a presentation and open discussion on how realistic the scenario is and which elements of that society we can already find in our own), a documentary screening with gynaecologist Dr Kathrin Haßdenteufel providing medical context and a Q&A (40 participants, every seat taken), a Science Pub Quiz, a Science Slam, school workshops, a laboratory summer school, a lecture series, and a full-day alumni event at the Marsilius-Kolleg bringing around 45 current and former iGEM Heidelberg members from every year the university has competed.

**realWorld.** The target application is monitoring engineered cell therapies, chosen because the alternatives are genuinely inadequate: PET tracking needs suitable radioactive tracers and costly specialised equipment, with each scan requiring tracer administration so measurements are days apart rather than continuous; bioluminescence imaging needs no such infrastructure but cannot penetrate patient tissue; and biopsy is invasive, reports only the sampled site, and cannot show how therapeutic cells redistribute. Ultrasound is comparatively inexpensive, widely available and needs no ionising radiation or tracer, which is the whole argument for a genetically encoded acoustic reporter. Crucially they tested the frequency question rather than assuming it: all measurements were made at 5-7 MHz, a range clinical scanners use, so purified vesicles, GV-expressing bacteria and mammalian cells were all detected as clear scattering signals against a degassed negative control without resorting to high frequencies that would limit penetration depth — while stating openly that whether a therapeutic cell can accumulate enough vesicles for a detectable in vivo signal remains to be established. The team has patent work on a modular, reversible acoustic label: because interchangeable binding proteins attach vesicles to a chosen target, the target's acoustic properties change without genetically modifying it, which matters for cell-therapy manufacturing where the product must not be altered. Named next steps are specific — test one ATLAS binder against a marker with existing clinical use such as HER2 or PD-L1, and test two gas vesicle variants with distinct collapse pressures in a tissue-mimicking phantom to establish whether both signals can be read in one measurement, with a published liver phantom protocol cited as a starting point — plus quantifying sorting efficiency and validating cell viability after label removal. A collaboration with PHOENICS is sketched on shared mechanism: the PHOENICS cell computes through phosphorylation and the GvpC sensor turns phosphorylation into ultrasound, so together they would make an engineered cell's internal decision readable from outside the body.

**For GEMS:** The transferable dry-lab habit is calibrating your filters against negative controls before you trust them: Heidelberg ran nine deliberately bad sequences plus the real binder through the identical pipeline, found that only AlphaFold2 interface PAE separated them, said so, and refused to select on the metrics that failed the test — a discipline that costs nothing but compute and turns a pile of prediction scores into an actual decision rule. On the human side, copy Fail Forward: an evening where senior scientists tell students about their own failures, plus a written guide that includes instructions for running the event yourself. For a high-school-plus research centre whose students will mostly meet failure before success, an institutional format that makes failure discussable is worth more than another outreach workshop — and the guide means you can run it next term without inventing it.

### LYON — BioThetis
Undergrad · France · https://2026.igem.wiki/lyon/
BioThetis goes after trifluoroacetic acid, the smallest and most stubborn PFAS: an NGO found it in 34 of 36 tap water samples across eleven European countries in 2024, activated carbon barely retains short chains, ion-exchange resins are not approved for French drinking water, and reverse osmosis only concentrates TFA five to ten times at enormous energy cost — the elected official in charge of water at the Metropole de Lyon told the team a single installation would run to roughly one billion euros. Their alternative is a protein binder fused to the cellulose-binding module CBM3a, which sticks to ordinary microcrystalline cellulose with no chemical coupling, captures TFA, and gives it back when the column is heated to 65 C so the material is reusable. Because TFA weighs only 114 Da and no natural binder was on offer, they designed binders from scratch with BoltzGen — 10,000 candidates, 6,823 through the filters, top 5 kept, three taken to the bench in two anchor orientations each — and demonstrated dose-dependent TFA binding by nanoDSF that does not respond to difluoroacetic or acetic acid, so the recognition is TFA-specific. They also solved the fluoroacetate dehalogenase DAR3835 to 1.10 A, the highest resolution reported for that enzyme, and said plainly that no density on the processed datasets is attributable to TFA. It won Best Bioremediation and Best Presentation on an unusually honest project: 15 new Registry parts, 25 printable protocols, all code and all dead ends released CC BY 4.0, and a human practices record that names exactly which conversation changed which page.

**frameworks.** Two strands, both documented with their failures intact. Binder design used BoltzGen 0.3.2 (Stark et al. 2025) on the Neurosnap platform with protein length constrained to 80-120 residues: 10,000 candidates generated, 6,823 passing BoltzGen's geometric and energetic filters, then re-filtered with the documented parameters (alpha 0.2, RMSD threshold 3.0 A) to keep the top 5 — across that shortlist median RMSD 0.982 A, median pTM 0.859, median ipTM 0.859, which the team notes shows consistent confidence rather than one lucky outlier. Three binders (Galatea, Ianassa, Melite) went forward in two anchor orientations each. Separately, a rational-design pipeline for DAR3835 variants combined structure prediction (Boltz-2 and AlphaFold3 via Neurosnap), sequence redesign with LigandMPNN, and binding-energy scoring with AutoDock Vina, run first on the related dehalogenase RPA1163 and then on DAR3835. Its result was negative and reported as such: no automatically redesigned mutant beat its wild-type benchmark on either scaffold, backbone confidence stayed high so the losses were interface rather than folding effects, and with the ligand pose at pLDDT 46-48 on the fluorines a Vina difference of 0.4 kcal/mol sits below the method's noise and cannot rank designs. The nine variants were therefore picked on explicit structural reasoning and rotamer feasibility, with docking used only as a consistency check, and one design was dropped at review after a rotamer check. The second strand is a packed-bed breakthrough column model in MATLAB: advection, axial dispersion and binder capture along the bed, Danckwerts inlet condition at C0, zero outlet gradient, bed starting empty, solved by finite differences with the stiff solver ode15s, reporting the breakthrough curve, BV10 and BV50, empty-bed contact time, bed Peclet number, Damkohler number and total TFA captured. All AI-designed proteins were screened through ToxinPred2 and BLAST against known toxins before anything was ordered.

**datascience.** The honest handling of uncertainty is the real data science contribution. The team established an analytical limit case, a mass balance check and an independent re-implementation of the column model before trusting it, and published the parameter file with units and sources — flagging openly that some support and column parameters remain placeholders because they did not finish the model as intended. The conclusion they draw from it is genuinely useful and counterintuitive: affinity and capacity, not column geometry, decide how long a filter lasts. On the protein side they converted thermal shift assays into quantitative affinities (Ianassa N-term apparent Kd 25.0 +/- 4.9 mM, C-term 24.9 +/- 4.0 mM against TFA, versus 105.01 for wild-type DAR3835) and quantified the cellulose anchor by depletion assay (Bmax 1.18 +/- 0.11 nmol/mg, Kd 0.66 +/- 0.33 uM on microcrystalline cellulose). Engineering was run through explicit decision gates with pass criteria written in advance — TFA binding required a Tm shift of at least 0.5 C at 50 mM, reproducible and dose-dependent (met); thermal reversibility required at least 80% of the unfolding transition recovered on a second ramp (not met, for either DAR3835 or the de novo binders, and recorded as a failure with a proposed fix). They also list four checks required before the next synthesis round: redo the ligand pose by docking (AutoDock Vina or GNINA) on PDB 8SDC followed by 100 ns of molecular dynamics with recomputed RESP charges for TFA to test whether the Protenix pose reproduces; a rotamer scan on every bulky substitution; nanoDSF Tm plus post-cycle refolding yield for every variant; and acetate and propionate negative controls so affinity is attributed to the CF3 group rather than a generic carboxylate interaction.

**dataviz.** The dry lab page is built to be read and reused rather than admired. The column model is introduced by a single annotated schematic that shows water entering at concentration C0 and flow rate Q, the two state variables C(z,t) dissolved and q(z,t) captured, a front moving down the bed, the three things that happen to TFA (carried by flow, spread by mixing, captured by binder), and the breakthrough curve as the output — so the whole model is legible before any equation. BoltzGen's 10,000 designs are shown as three scatter plots against design length (predicted error, pTM, ipTM) with grey for all designs, red for top quality after filtering and blue for quality-and-diversity picks, which makes the funnel from 10,000 to 5 visible instead of asserted. Retained designs are presented as superpositions of four AlphaFold3 predictions each. Every figure's generating script is published alongside it. The wiki itself carries a light/dark theme the visitor chooses, and the human practices section is organised as a stakeholder ledger where each entry is tagged Opened, Changed or Confirmed, with the date, the topic, and the specific wiki pages that entry altered.

**software.** Everything is released under CC BY 4.0 on the team GitLab. The column model (MATLAB column_model.m, the parameter sweep scripts, a parameter file with units and sources, and the script behind each figure) is at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/lyon/-/tree/main/model/biothetis-column-model with an explicit invitation to plug in your own binder. BL21 is a browser video game that fits in a single 1.3 MB HTML file, runs entirely offline with no third-party assets, stores levels as data so the science is swappable (change the chassis and the target), takes about 15 minutes, works in French and English, and ships with 33 automated tests. The education kit adds three printable board games including an escape game with facilitator guides in English and French, colour-blind-safe design pairing every colour with a symbol, an experiments booklet, a handbook for school staff, and a before-and-after mind map to measure what pupils learned. They also published 15 new Registry parts (six binder constructs — Galatea, Ianassa and Melite each in two orientations — and nine DAR3835 variants, annotated region by region with one feature per mutated codon, numbered as PDB 8SDC plus 14 so mutations map straight onto the published structure), 25 bench protocols and three reference tables in one printable layout, and the survey questionnaire with anonymised aggregated results.

**ihp.** The human practices record is structured as a ledger where every stakeholder entry is tagged Opened, Changed or Confirmed, dated, assigned a topic, and linked to the exact wiki pages it altered — which makes the influence auditable rather than claimed. The largest change: public concern about releasing engineered organisms moved them to a system containing no living cells at all, only purified protein on cellulose. Residents at an Institut Ecocitoyen PERFAO workshop set the target — their first request was depolluting drinking water because their catchment is over-contaminated and the installed activated carbon does not work on TFA — and testimony from PFAS Contre Terre, the plaintiffs of the 'proces des 250' against Arkema and Daikin, and team members' own relatives confirmed that TFA specifically, and the polluter-pays principle, is what local people want addressed. Veolia's technical director for France and two engineers across July and September calls reshaped the commercial design: they confirmed activated carbon barely works on short chains, that ion-exchange resins lack French health-authority approval for drinking water, that reverse osmosis concentrates TFA only five to ten times while being energy and water intensive and leaving an unmanageable concentrate, that resins and carbon are usually single-use so a regenerable system is commercially interesting, and that factory outflows typically carry 1-10 ug/L; they validated heat elution and CBM3a anchoring and suggested using it on reverse osmosis concentrate. Hector Osuna at Applexion pushed scale-up and multi-column systems, which became the carousel design. A nature protection association's plant visit taught them which treatment plants could realistically adopt it — large and relatively recent ones — and that economics, regulation and political decisions, not just feasibility, govern deployment. Florence Besoin of a residents' association in Saint-Genis-Laval, who approached them after seeing a flyer, set their public tone: residents are genuinely anxious and need to see people taking the problem seriously without being promised an unrealistic fix, so the team adopted 'honest and encouraging, never triumphant' and states on every page what the approach cannot do yet. A utopia-or-dystopia workshop at the French Mini Jamboree surfaced the failure mode of selling to households — clean water for those who can pay, risk left with the most exposed — confirmed by the survey where 96.3% of respondents wanted PFAS producers and users to pay, so customers are companies and operators only, never households. They also voted at the outset not to contact PFAS emitters, fearing reprisal and being used for greenwashing, and say so openly. After an intellectual property warning from Claude Mabillat they took IP training and then chose to release everything under an open licence anyway.

**publicEngagement.** LYON built formats deliberately matched to audience rather than one activity repeated: children 6-14, high school students, adults, families, school staff, students, researchers and professionals, and anyone online from age 12. The flagship is four three-hour workshops run between 8 October and 19 November 2026 with a full ULIS class of 18 pupils in a primary school in Givors, south of Lyon, an area particularly affected by PFAS — ULIS being the unit that includes pupils with disabilities inside a mainstream school. Each session follows one line of reasoning: map environmental pollution with hands-on experiments, question filtration with a filter the pupils build themselves, define synthetic biology simply with a short video, and close with a board game. Pupils run the experiments themselves; the school aides who support them take part; the team adapts to children who need breaks and follows their rhythm rather than imposing a programme, and collects teacher and aide feedback after every session. They measured learning with a before-and-after mind map and published the experiments booklet, protocols and a school-staff handbook as a reusable kit, with partnerships continuing past the Jamboree and the guide left behind where the workshops happened. The materials are designed for reuse: three printable board games in French and English with facilitator guides, colour paired with symbols for colour blindness, and BL21, a single-file offline browser game with swappable science and 33 automated tests. A dialogue-free short film made with oKlama about the psychological impact of PFAS contamination carries no language barrier. They took shorter stand versions to Meet & Fabrik (winning two second prizes), visited three lycees, worked with biology, agriculture, dietetics, and history-and-geography teachers so PFAS gets studied from several angles, and organised an inter-school conference on 19 November where students present their own posters. A public survey drew 376 responses by 7 October, published anonymised with a frank list of what they would change. Community work included organising the French Mini Jamboree, a joint Jamboree talk with Berlin and Wageningen on PFAS, sending their game to iGEM Patras's community game library, joining Bochum's trading card project with 29 other teams, and a peer-reviewed article in Vector Volume 5 guided by Maastricht.

**realWorld.** The product is specified as a treatment skid in a container: two cellulose columns carrying the binder, one capturing while the other is heated to 65 C to release TFA into a small volume that goes to destruction, capacity added by extending the carousel, sold, rented or charged per cubic metre treated with binder cartridges as consumables. First roadmap targets are pharmaceutical peptide synthesis, fluorinated chemistry and agrochemistry — industrial emitters and treatment operators, explicitly never households. The economics are worked and bounded: destroying the concentrate adds about 0.80 EUR per cubic metre at a placeholder 300 EUR per cubic metre of concentrate, cost barely moves between 1 and 10 ug/L, and since the support holds at most about 0.13 mg TFA per gram of cellulose the filter stays cheaper than destroying the whole stream up to roughly 40 mg/L at pilot pricing and a few hundred mg/L at industrial pricing, so the dilute regime is where it works — consistent with 2022 state measurements around the Pierre-Benite platform finding long-chain PFAS in industrial outlets from ug/L to low mg/L. Incumbents are costed side by side (activated carbon 29-33 kWh per kg to manufacture plus re-calcination above 850 C; ion-exchange resin 18-24 kWh per kg to make and 4.4 kWh per kg to regenerate at USD 18-33 per kg of medium), and one billion euros is used as the order of magnitude for the reference reverse-osmosis solution at drinking-water scale. The team's stated ethical position is that remediation complements regulation and never replaces it, repeated on every page and in every talk, with restriction supported first. They are open to founding a start-up as the 2025 Lyon team did, but on an open-licence basis, and a film screening with debate is planned for January.

**For GEMS:** Steal LYON's human practices ledger: every stakeholder entry tagged Opened, Changed or Confirmed, with a date, a topic and a link to the specific project pages it altered — it turns 'we talked to people' into an auditable record and forces the team to admit when a conversation changed nothing. The second transferable habit is publishing failure as a deliverable: LYON state that their docking scores could not rank designs because the ligand pose confidence made a 0.4 kcal/mol difference meaningless, that thermal reversibility was never demonstrated, and that some column parameters are still placeholders — and release the code anyway so the next team starts further along. A high-school centre can adopt both tomorrow at zero cost, and both are exactly what judges and reviewers reward.

### HangzhouFourteenAP — DCO (Dental Calculus Obstructor)
High School · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/hangzhoufourteenap/
DCO is a three-module biological oral care system: an enzyme cocktail that degrades the organic matrix holding plaque biofilm together, a tooth-binding antimicrobial peptide that coats enamel to block re-colonisation, and a controlled-release system to coordinate them. The enzymes are two recombinantly expressed glycoside hydrolases — PmGH87 (alpha-1,3-glucanase) and CoGH66 (alpha-1,6-glucanase), which act cooperatively because CoGH66 removes alpha-1,6 branches and exposes new PmGH87 cleavage sites — plus commercially sourced DNase I and papain for extracellular DNA and protein. It addresses a real and specific burden: 96.7% of Chinese adults aged 35-44 have dental calculus, over 900 million have periodontal disease, only 20.1% of elderly people saw a dentist in the past year, and the dentist-to-population ratio is about 1:7,768. It won Best Village Project on a tight problem-to-product chain, a FoldX mutation-prioritisation pipeline whose prediction was wrong and whose failure is reported in full, and an unusually commercially literate entrepreneurship section that refuses to make anti-calculus claims it cannot support.

**frameworks.** Two computational pipelines, both modest in tooling but well-reasoned and, importantly, both reported against their experimental outcome. (1) A CoGH66 mutation prioritisation pipeline built to avoid screening hundreds of mutants in the wet lab. Starting from the substrate-bound structure PDB 8IUB (CoGH66 with isomaltotriose bound, so no re-docking was needed), they used PyMOL to extract all protein residues within 4.0 A of the substrate, giving an 18-residue binding pocket (Y166, D167, Q169, Q172, I190, Y217, L219, H250, L252, F256, I260, D293, L295, N395, K429, E430, Y431, N434) consistent with the published catalytic cleft and +2 to -4 subsites. Domain annotation came from CD-Search (Glyco_hydro_66 at residues 22-560, E-value 0) and InterPro (glycosidases at 104-440), with sequence translation via Novopro. They then layered evolutionary information: BLASTp against the NCBI non-redundant protein database, deliberately selecting homologs from different bacterial species at 30-70% identity to avoid over-representing near-identical sequences and to capture naturally tolerated substitutions, aligned with MAFFT and visualised as an ESPript conservation map. Of the 18 contact residues, seven (Y166, Q169, Q172, I190, H250, N395, K429) showed species-specific natural substitutions and were taken as plastic; the remaining eleven were conserved and deliberately left alone. Mutants were built in PyMOL, repaired and scored in FoldX for both stability change and binding change, with an operational priority threshold of binding delta-delta-G < -1 kcal/mol chosen explicitly because it exceeds typical FoldX error. (2) Antimicrobial peptide selection: after a literature review identified four hydroxyapatite-binding AMP candidates, they used AlphaFold Server to predict peptide-calcium ion coordination as a first computational filter, reasoning that hydroxyapatite presents Ca2+ as the primary interaction site, and ranked candidates by pTM and interface pTM (ipTM) scores. SHABP (21 aa, cyclic and disulfide-constrained) and G12R (18 aa, linear alpha-helical) both reached pTM around 0.4, above DNase-fused and HBAMP alternatives, and both were advanced into parallel experimental validation on the grounds of their distinct structural strategies (conformational stability versus membrane disruption).

**datascience.** The most valuable dry-lab content is a documented computational failure. The pipeline predicted Y166Q as the top candidate (the only mutant meeting the -1 kcal/mol binding threshold, at -1.63 kcal/mol) with Q172P as a secondary candidate retained despite only -0.38 kcal/mol because of its predicted stabilising effect and natural occurrence in homologs. Site-directed mutagenesis (reverse PCR with back-to-back mutation-carrying primers, DpnI digestion of methylated parental template, self-ligation), colony PCR at the expected ~1726 bp, and Sanger sequencing confirmed both constructs (Y166Q TAC to CAG; Q172P CAG to CCG). The DNS activity assay then inverted the ranking: Q172P gave the highest apparent activity at net OD 1.881, wild type 0.996, and Y166Q only 0.629 — the computational winner was worse than wild type. The team's response is the right one: they revised the ranking in the text, named Q172P the leading experimental candidate, reclassified Y166Q as a mechanistic probe rather than quietly dropping it, and had already flagged in advance that Q172P introduces a proline and may alter main-chain conformation so its FoldX estimate should be read with caution. They also controlled the comparison properly rather than letting protein load explain the result: BCA quantification gave WT 12.1, Y166Q 10.9 and Q172P 9.1 microgram/mL, crude lysates were normalised to equal total protein before the DNS assay, and the wiki explicitly notes that Q172P's lower total protein means its activity signal cannot be attributed to a higher load. The measurement work on the artificial dental calculus model is similarly self-critical. Gravimetric analysis of six treatment conditions (negative control, four single-component omissions, complete cocktail) found no significant weight-loss differences, and the team attributed this to balance sensitivity and to non-uniform mineralisation producing variability that masked the effect, then moved to more sensitive assays rather than reporting a null as a result. Crystal violet quantification at OD gave the complete cocktail a significant reduction against the negative control (p < 0.05), with the papain-omission comparison reported honestly as a trend toward significance at p = 0.08 and interpreted as papain playing a supporting rather than dominant role under single-treatment conditions. Acridine orange fluorescence with ImageJ quantification showed significance against the negative control and against the DNase-I-omission group, supporting the mechanistic model that eDNA cleavage lets the other enzymes penetrate, while the overall small between-group differences led them to conclude that the primary mode of action is structural matrix dismantling rather than direct bactericidal potency. Limitations are stated plainly, including that the B. subtilis surrogate model does not replicate the Streptococcus mutans-specific EPS composition the glucanases actually target. The AlphaFold peptide screen also carries its own caveat: the team notes that peptide-Ca2+ coordination cannot fully replicate crystal-surface binding, that pTM around 0.4 indicates only moderate confidence, and that the scores were used for relative ranking rather than as affinity estimates.

**dataviz.** The model page leads with a schematic workflow diagram of the whole mutation-prioritisation pipeline, so the logic from structure to alignment to energy calculation is readable before any numbers appear, and ends with a three-dimensional localisation figure placing the two prioritised positions in the pocket (protein green, mutated positions red with arrows, substrate yellow, other 4.0 A contacts cyan). The genuinely notable choice is an interactive 3D model of the CoGH66-isomaltotriose complex embedded in the wiki as a glTF file exported from PyMOL, so a reader can rotate the enzyme and inspect the contact residues rather than squint at a static render — a cheap but effective way to make a structural argument inspectable. Tables carry the natural substitutions observed per non-conserved position with counts, and the full FoldX energy results for every tested mutant rather than only the winners. Measurement figures pair the physical artefact with its quantification throughout: a 96-well plate photograph alongside the bar chart derived from it for the DNS reducing-sugar assay, the crystal violet extracts, and the acridine orange fluorescence images with the ImageJ intensity quantification in the identical group order so the reader can check the numbers against the wells. Standard curves are shown with their regression equations and R2 values (BCA at Y = 0.8964X - 0.2574, R2 = 0.9951).

**software.** No standalone released software tool; the dry lab is a documented analysis pipeline rather than a product, and the wiki itself is a React/Vite single-page application with GSAP animation. Released reusable resources instead: the full mutation-prioritisation methodology as a reproducible protocol, the interactive glTF structural model, PDF slide decks for all four education audiences (two elementary sessions dated 5-28 and 6-11, a high school deck, and an elderly-residents deck), a consolidated enzyme stabilisation and controlled-release guide offered as a generalised framework for multi-enzyme formulations across biocatalysis, food processing and environmental remediation, and a 'lessons learned for future iGEM teams' section. Constructs were expressed from codon-optimised genes in pET-32a via seamless cloning, carrying an N-terminal thioredoxin (TrxA) tag for soluble expression, a 6xHis tag for IMAC purification and an enterokinase site for optional tag removal, under T7 promoter control in E. coli Rosetta(DE3), with CoGH66 confirmed at approximately 76.54 kDa. The team also documented a safety-driven substitution they consulted the iGEM committee about: because Streptococcus mutans is not on the iGEM White List they used B. subtilis as a surrogate in the artificial calculus model, and because Aspergillus niger is not listed they used commercially available edible fungi as a material source.

**ihp.** Twelve named advisors spanning clinical dentistry, periodontics, microbial control, pharmaceutics, gene circuit regulation, management and marketing, and oral care product regulatory and quality management, engaged in a staged problem-framing process. Problem framing combined a 350-respondent user questionnaire, an in-depth clinical interview with Dr. Lei Lihong (Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine) and an industry interview with Mr. Fan Wenjun (healthcare investment), triangulated against the Fourth National Oral Health Epidemiological Survey specifically to avoid bias from a single interview source. The survey quantified both misconception and the knowing-doing gap: 61% worry that scaling damages enamel, 23% believe brushing removes calculus, only 6% claim to fully understand it; and separately, 52% know calculus forms at the gingival margin and in deep interdental spaces but only 25% floss or use an irrigator daily, 48% know brushing cannot remove calculus but only 38% get scaling once or twice a year, and 84% know calculus causes periodontitis but only 25% have a six-monthly examination. The project-defining intervention came from Dr. Wang Yongwu (Hangzhou First People's Hospital), who said that using enzymes to dissolve already-mineralised calculus is 'like an egg hitting a stone' — and the team did not just accept the efficacy point but derived a safety consequence from it: because calculus and enamel and dentin are both calcium phosphate mineralised tissues, any non-selective demineralising agent would risk enamel or dentin demineralisation, sensitivity or erosion. That reframed the entire target from mineralised calculus to the organic matrix of the early pre-mineralisation biofilm, which is the intervention window the whole project now occupies. Dr. Lei and Dr. Yuan Yifang (Affiliated Stomatological Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University) corroborated it and specified what to attack: the polysaccharide-protein cross-linking and the stabilising role of eDNA that together hold the biofilm's three-dimensional structure against salivary washing. Four design constraints emerged from the interview set — efficacy validation, penetration ability, cytotoxicity safety and stability assurance — which became the selection criteria for the enzyme cocktail and delivery system. A second concrete pivot: experts pointed out that enzymatic removal does not prevent recolonisation because salivary proteins form a pellicle within minutes, which is why the hydroxyapatite-binding AMP module exists at all; the computational peptide screen was conducted on their explicit recommendation. A third: on discovering that bovine pancreatic DNase I is already commercially available at roughly 80-160 yuan per 100 mg and widely used, they strategically stopped trying to recombinantly express it and concentrated the synthetic biology effort on the glycoside hydrolases where the EPS matrix offered a real opportunity. Dr. Lei also set a boundary the team kept: any active ingredient in a daily product must be safe and must not disrupt the normal oral microbiome or damage soft tissues.

**publicEngagement.** Four-tier education (primary school, high school, elderly residents, general public) with the explicit design principle that they did not just teach knowledge but recorded what changed after participants went home — brushing, flossing, denture care, diet, dental visits and attitudes toward synthetic biology. The best single tool is a tangible genetic circuit built from electronic building blocks: a touch sensor stands for the promoter, a toggle switch module for the lac operator, a button for lactose as inducer, an LED for the RBS, a small fan for the target gene and a manual power-off switch for the terminator, so children physically discover that touching the sensor alone does nothing because the operator blocks by default, and that the circuit only runs when the inducer is held. For younger children they wrote child-friendly science comics and ran plaque disclosing tablets as a reveal — children chewed the tablets, rinsed, saw red and blue patches on their own teeth, were asked to guess and ask questions first, and were then shown microscope images with the framing 'this is not dirt, this is a city'. The team records the emotional shift honestly: children moved from fearing bacteria to being curious about them and from passive listening to asking and designing. High school sessions used a full script and deck covering project background, enzyme mechanism, experimental process and application value, and specifically targeted the soft-plaque-versus-hard-calculus confusion. The nursing home session simplified everything into plain language and images and delivered concretely actionable care: a soft-bristled small-headed brush at 45 degrees to the gumline, gentle brushing with no horizontal scrubbing, bedtime brushing more important than morning, floss or interdental brushes rather than toothpicks, and denture care rules (rinse after meals, remove and soak overnight, never boiling water, never toothpaste, never sleep in them), with the explicit disclaimer that this is science communication and does not replace professional dental advice. Public outreach at Wushan Square used display boards, roll-up banners, hand fans and leaflets on plaque versus calculus and scaling misconceptions.

**realWorld.** The most commercially literate section of the five teams, and notable for restraint. The problem is scoped deliberately narrowly: the project does not aim to replace professional scaling, but to serve adults who cannot or will not undergo frequent scaling with a daily, safe, evidence-based product that interferes with plaque maturation and reduces mineralisation risk before it happens — daily prevention and risk reduction, not treatment of existing calculus or periodontal disease. Target segment is urban young people aged 20-30, students and people one to five years into their first jobs, chosen because they have purchasing power, care about social image and have not yet entrenched habits. Channels are specified rather than gestured at: online seeding on Douyin, Xiaohongshu and Bilibili, e-commerce subscriptions, and offline placement in convenience stores, beauty collection stores and supermarkets, with trial experience areas in beauty collection stores. A B-end clinic seed-trial path runs in parallel with the C-end consumer path, and contingencies are written down (if clinic repeat-purchase is below expectation, optimise usage instructions and physician script training; if C-end subscription retention declines, control ad spend pace and iterate the product experience). Six quarterly milestones run from improving the dual recombinant enzyme lab data and stability, patent drafting and seed trials in three to five clinics, through pilot scale-up and third-party safety testing, to daily chemical regulatory filing, first commercial production, retail rollout and a monthly subscription. A three-year P&L is projected (revenue 45 with net -30 and about 35% gross margin, then revenue 280 with net +120 and about 58% gross margin, then revenue 950 with net +530 and about 65% gross margin). IP strategy notes that existing Chinese patents in this space are mostly single-enzyme or simple multi-enzyme combinations and rarely apply microcapsule encapsulation systematically to oral enzyme care, and acquisition by listed biotech oral care entrants such as Bloomage Biotech or Weimeizi (Saky) is named as the exit after commercial validation. Most creditable: all marketing materials and product claims will state explicitly that the product does not replace professional scaling or periodontal treatment, and the portable chewing gum format is to be marketed only for post-meal freshness with no preventive or anti-calculus claim at all — a team voluntarily giving up its best marketing line because it has not earned it yet. Sustainability is argued concretely rather than with SDG slogans: all four actives are proteins expected to degrade to amino acids and peptides after use, and no live organisms are released.

**For GEMS:** Their best transferable move is reporting the computational prediction that lost: FoldX picked Y166Q, the bench picked Q172P, and the wiki revises its own ranking and demotes the failed candidate to a mechanistic probe while showing that BCA normalisation rules out protein load as the explanation. A high-school dry lab earns more credibility from one honestly scored wrong prediction with the confound controlled than from three unvalidated ones. Also copy the cheap inspectability trick — export the docked structure as a glTF so a reader can rotate it — and the commercial restraint of marketing a format with no efficacy claim until the evidence exists.

### Toronto — PetaBite
Overgrad · Canada · https://2026.igem.wiki/toronto/
PetaBite attacks PET and microplastic pollution by abandoning the field's usual strategy of engineering a handful of known enzymes and instead searching the natural sequence landscape at planetary scale. The dry lab rebuilt PETadex from scratch into PETadex V2: 1.74 billion plastic-degrading enzyme homologs recovered from NCBI nr and the Logan assembly of the entire Sequence Read Archive, filtered by 53 hand-curated catalytic HMMs to 291,922,243 complete catalytic ORFs, each annotated with the pH, temperature, salinity and environment of the sample it came from. They paired this with PETai activity labels scraped from literature by an LLM pipeline and by 20+ human curators, pretrained PlasticESM (LoRA adapters on ESM-C) on the corpus, and built a hardware bioreactor array to feed condition-specific measurements back into the model. They won Best Model largely for scientific honesty: a homology-component-grouped split showed that sequence length beats their own embeddings, and they reported that rather than the inflated random-split numbers.

**frameworks.** The PETadex V2 pipeline chains DIAMOND homology search against NCBI nr (42,053,081 hits down to 7,825,107 non-redundant sequences at E < 1e-5) with 53 catalytic profile HMMs built by a jackhmmer-analogous four-iteration loop that only advanced homologs retaining every canonical catalytic residue, then searched 2,740,458 catalytic-domain centroids against the Logan assembly of the SRA (87.0 Pb of raw reads compressed to 1.8 Pb of contigs) to recover 5.57 billion hits and 291,922,243 complete catalytic ORFs. Structures came from AlphaFold DB (575,770 hits, via UniProt idmapping) plus their own ESMFold2 run: 1,793,781 sequences folded in 16.6 hours on up to 80 GPUs (851.6 GPU-hours, median pLDDT 92.3), benchmarked against 244 experimental PDB structures to choose the full model under 150 aa and ESMFold2-Fast above it at 32 diffusion steps and 3 refinement loops. On the learning side they continued masked-language-model pretraining of ESM-C 300M on PETadex using LoRA adapters on all four projections of every transformer block (240 adapter tensors, 14.7M trainable parameters, backbone frozen) to produce PlasticESM, and probed its embeddings with ridge regression under homology-component-grouped cross-validation. Supporting layers include CATH and Pfam domain assignment, SignalP 6.0 secretion prediction over all ORFs, Biopython ProtParam biochemical properties, InterProScan plus HMMER accessory-domain analysis, and a reconstruction of the TED (The Encyclopedia of Domains) novelty-discovery pipeline adapted to PETadex HMMs.

**datascience.** Their central data-science contribution is turning a literature corpus into training labels and then proving honestly that the labels, not the corpus, are the bottleneck. An automated LLM extraction pipeline gathered 11,000 identifiers via the PAZy API, screened them to 900 seed papers, expanded by forward and backward citation to 50,000 candidates, filtered to ~4,600, converted full texts to structured JSON with Docling, Grobid and PyMuPDF, and extracted 51,455 cleaned measurement entries across 31,441 enzymes; Claude Sonnet benchmarked best (95.0% precision, 87.1% recall) with zero hallucinated enzymes across 32 double-scraped papers. In parallel, 20+ members spent 450+ hours hand-extracting 61 papers through a standardized interactive HTML schema with autogenerated IDs and built-in error checks, giving a ground truth where 78% of independent scraper pairs agreed within 10%. The benchmark result is the headline: under random five-fold splits stock ESM-C reached rho = 0.72 on kcat and 0.74 on melting temperature, but splitting folds by connected homology component dropped the same embeddings by 0.49 to 1.01 while a single sequence-length column lost at most 0.18 — because 90-92% of labelled sequences have a homologous relative elsewhere in the set. Length itself reached rho = +0.343 on kcat and beat both embeddings on all twelve target sets, so they reported the negative result, published the model card alongside the weights so nobody reuses the adapters expecting activity prediction, and designed round 2 to be chosen by model uncertainty rather than predicted activity.

**dataviz.** The wiki is the clearest dataviz work in the cohort: a 300-million-protein 'PETadex Model Landscape' rendered as three explorable layers (what we found, what we know, what we predict), a draggable component map of the 46 PETadex-PAZy families, a 3D structure viewer that highlights the catalytic triad, oxyanion hole and docked PET dimer for each of 16 CATH fold groups, and a BioSample viewer that drills from a real sample (e.g. SAMN03075713, Arctic tundra soil) down through its sequencing run to individual ORFs and their 90% identity clusters. The Sharded DIAMOND search and the per-enzyme record card both ship as live in-page demos that replay ten real searches, sped up from 45 seconds to two. There is also a 'PETadex Project Calendar' that walks week by week from March to October with an explicit 'What went wrong, and what we changed' panel per workstream, and a PETamon mini-game that teaches why no single enzyme cleans up every plastic.

**software.** Two tools released under MIT at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/toronto/petabite. LOBSTER (Library Optimization for Bioprospecting Sequences Through Economical Recombination) splits PETase cores into fragment positions and designs degenerate-codon oligos that combinatorially assemble by Golden Gate to cover as many natural cores as possible — it synthesized a 1,744-sequence library at 45% of individual-synthesis cost (55% nucleotide reduction) for the IsPETase and LCC 90% identity clusters. Sharded DIAMOND Search splits the 307M-sequence corpus into 32 shards searched in parallel by serverless cloud workers, returning ranked neighbours for a pasted protein in under a minute with nothing to install, live at petadex.net. Datasets are on Zenodo (PETadex catalytic ORF corpus v1.1 + sharded search DB, 23.8 GB, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23457986) and Hugging Face (petadex/plasticesm-dualseed, petadex/catalytic-orfs-90pid, petadex/petai-activity-labels, each label source published separately); analysis notebooks live at github.com/petadex/igem-toronto and github.com/petadex/petabite. Hardware: a parallel bioreactor array, up to 96 units, at about $204 CAD per reactor, with PID temperature control holding 37 C within +/-0.3 C, dual-photodiode OD600 with three-point quadratic calibration (R^2 = 0.993 on yeast), peristaltic pumps under Arduino PWM control, 150 RPM stirring, and a single-file Python dashboard over USB serial; it grew E. coli over 4 hours in the final test.

**ihp.** Roughly 70 stakeholders across four continents, and the changes are specific. A public event where biosafety dominated the questions told them containment has to come before technical detail, so every subsequent public-facing event opened with containment. Regulatory and ethics conversations led them to prioritize enzyme candidates with close homology to naturally occurring proteins and to lead with a contained bioreactor rather than dosing enzymes into open process streams. A researcher's clarification that PETases are only a subset of plastic-degrading enzymes made them explicitly define scope throughout the documentation. Hardware feedback on optical channels led them to separate the optical-density path from the colorimetric degradation readout so dye cannot corrupt cell-density estimates, and a GFP recommendation gave them a route to reporting activity per enzyme rather than per cell; the same conversations reframed the 40 mL reactor as the directed-evolution and Michaelis-Menten instrument and split off the 1,000-to-50 intermediate screen as a separate smaller-format problem. A CGM-adjacent interviewee's distinction between sensor and adhesive reshaped MVP scope. Indigenous knowledge holders reframed plastic pollution as a matter of relationships among people, land and water rather than a technical problem, which fed country-specific regulatory profiles for Pakistan, India, Nigeria, Indonesia and Canadian Indigenous communities addressing waste colonialism and ethics dumping. All of this was codified into a reusable MERGE framework (Multidisciplinary outreach, Education, Regulatory oversight, Global database, Environmental consideration) and a Regulatory Oversight Framework covering Canada's Roadmap for Open Science, FAIR, the Nagoya Protocol, dual-use research of concern, PIPEDA, the Directive on Automated Decision-Making and the EU AI Act.

**publicEngagement.** Toronto hosted three conferences, including a 'Rethink plastic' microplastics conference built around two questions (what happens to plastic once it enters the environment, and what can we realistically do about it), deliberately framing PetaBite as one approach among many alongside prevention, policy and community action. They mentored two high-school synthetic biology teams, ran sustained exchanges with four universities abroad, and carried out eight campus collaborations across the University of Toronto reaching over 800 students and community members. Outreach ran on humour rather than lecture: a promotion video combining live action with original animation and PETase-inspired axolotl mascots, a 'Road to Jamboree' Instagram Reels series using trends and familiar formats, and a newsletter, The Waterfront, with 300+ subscribers. Instagram content drew over 105,000 views, 250+ new followers, 2,500+ profile visits and 374 link clicks through to the project and the conference.

**realWorld.** PetaScale is the commercialization arm, explicitly framed as taking PetaBite from 0-to-1 to 1-to-n. The beachhead is wastewater treatment plants, validated through 20 feasibility conversations with operators, engineers and managers across Ontario, Alberta and Newfoundland, with PETases immobilized in packed-bed reactors so the enzyme stays contained. Three adjacent verticals are mapped: microfibre filtration, landfill leachate and textile effluent. Their differentiation is explicit against Carbios, Samsara Eco and Protein Evolution, all of which build around one engineered enzyme and one operating window (Carbios amorphizes PET and runs near 70 C) — PetaScale instead matches the enzyme to the site's existing temperature, pH and salinity so no heating or pretreatment is needed. Regulatory mapping covers CEPA, EPA TSCA Section 5 and provincial discharge permits, with tailwinds from EU Regulation 2023/2055, Directive 2024/3019 and Canada's Federal Plastics Registry. Validation signal: their associate RNAlab screened 161 randomly selected natural enzymes and two outperformed FAST-PETase. They tested the model across five Canadian national and four global competitions plus two international conferences, placed top 3 in six, attended Y Combinator Startup School, Web Summit Vancouver, SynBioBeta Global and the Canadian Food Forward Summit, completed the Wilbe incubator sprint, opened early discussions with three Canadian VC firms, and raised support from 17 sponsors.

**For GEMS:** Copy their evaluation discipline, not their compute budget: grouping train/test splits by homology component and forcing every model to beat zero-parameter controls (sequence length, amino-acid composition) is free, and it is what turned a plausible-looking rho = 0.72 into an honest negative result that reviewers rewarded. Pair that with their hybrid labelling pattern — an LLM extraction pipeline benchmarked against a small, double-scored, schema-driven human corpus — which is exactly the right shape for a school research centre that has many students and little GPU time.

### GCGS — PathoLogic
High School · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/gcgs/
PathoLogic engineers E. coli Nissle 1917 into a living sensor that fires only when it detects two simultaneous signals of the cystic fibrosis airway — low iron (via Fur) and high C4-HSL quorum-sensing molecule from Pseudomonas aeruginosa (via RhlR) — wired as an AND gate. On dual activation, Lysis E lyses the cells to release alginate lyase, which degrades the alginate-based extracellular polymeric matrix that shields P. aeruginosa from antibiotics and immunity. The product concept is a spray-dried, matrix-protected inhalable live biotherapeutic positioned as an adjunct, not a replacement, for inhaled antibiotics. It won Best New Improved Part on a genuinely instructive two-cycle engineering story: adding SsrA degradation tags to RhlR killed the leakage but also killed the induction, and only replacing the weak wild-type Prhl with the engineered Prhl(LR) recovered a working sensor. The dry lab is the thinnest of the five high-school Top 10 teams; its strength is wet-lab characterisation discipline and an exceptionally thorough regulatory and stakeholder analysis.

**frameworks.** GCGS has no dedicated model or software page (both routes 404) and this is the clear weak point relative to the other four Top 10 high-school teams. The one modelling claim is a circuit-level simulation of the Fur-RhlR dual-response AND gate, which predicted that the low transcriptional activity of the native rhl promoter would prevent the full circuit from functioning — consistent with the 2016 Tokyo_Tech iGEM team's finding of weak native Prhl activity — and which therefore justified upgrading to the engineered Prhl(LR) (BBa_K1529310) in design cycle 2b. The simulation's structure, parameters, equations and software are not documented on the wiki, so it reads as a design-justification step rather than a reproducible model. No protein structure prediction, docking, molecular dynamics, flux analysis or machine learning appears anywhere on the wiki; the alginate lyase and Lysis E modules were taken from literature rather than computationally designed. Quantitative analysis is instead concentrated in assay-level fitting: the dual-response circuit's C4-HSL response under low-iron conditions was fitted by linear regression against log concentration (Y = 2.582X + 39.04, R2 = 0.894), yielding a limit of detection of 53.1 nM that the team mapped against physiologically relevant C4-HSL concentrations measured in clinical sputum, plus cross-reactivity testing against related signal molecules and a growth-curve validation in artificial lung fluid over 48 h showing the engineered strain remains viable with a moderate relative growth decrease on dual-signal stimulation, consistent with Lysis-E-driven conditional autolysis.

**datascience.** The genuine intellectual contribution is a clean design-build-test-learn argument about a trade-off, which is a form of data reasoning even without computation. Cycle 2a fused four SsrA degradation tags (LAA, LVA, ASV, AAV, spanning a range of known degradation kinetics) to the C-terminus of RhlR on the wild-type Prhl, assembled all five constructs including the untagged control onto pTrc99k by homologous recombination, and ran 8-hour time-course dose-response experiments across blank, solvent-only, 10 micromolar, 100 micromolar and 1 mM C4-HSL in sequence-verified DH5-alpha. The result was interpreted carefully rather than selectively: growth curves showed only LAA suffered a small but significant final-density reduction (p < 0.05), consistent with its fastest protein turnover imposing extra proteolytic burden, while LVA, ASV and AAV showed no significant growth penalty — so the tags are not generally toxic. Fluorescence showed all tags reduced basal background as intended, but LAA, LVA and AAV lost induction so completely that no statistically significant difference remained between blank control and 1 mM C4-HSL, and only the moderate-rate ASV tag retained weak but distinguishable induction. The team drew the correct general conclusion: when a promoter's maximal transcriptional output is weak, the SsrA-driven degradation rate can exceed the synthesis rate, so tuning protein turnover cannot compensate for inadequate transcriptional capacity — background suppression and induced output cannot both be optimised from the degradation side alone. Cycle 2b tested that inference by swapping in Prhl(LR) and re-characterising the whole panel, identifying RhlR-SsrA-ASV-Prhl(LR) as the combination achieving both low leakage and robust induction, which was then integrated into the final AND gate. Human practices also drove a methodological change: because experts noted iron limitation varies across patient airways, characterisation was switched from a single fixed low-iron concentration to a dose-response design, and because the public survey flagged off-target activation concerns, low uninduced leakage became an explicit selection criterion rather than a nice-to-have.

**dataviz.** Figures are conventional but competently used and consistently paired with their physical source. The engineering and improve pages present AND-logic characterisation as four-condition bar panels, growth curves across the full C4-HSL dose gradient per construct with 8-hour endpoint comparisons and significance annotation, and a dedicated analytical-performance figure carrying the dose-response regression, limit of detection and cross-reactivity results together. Agarose gels, transformation plates, colony PCR and Sanger traces are shown for every construction step rather than asserted. The circuit designs are drawn side by side as 'existing part BBa_K2315014' against 'the improved part', so the specific change in each cycle is visible rather than described. Human practices and education present survey data as high-resolution chart figures (398 valid responses on the public survey). The landing page uses an animated scroll narrative structured as Sense / Respond / Restore to make the AND gate legible before any biology, and a dual-response system diagram carries the mechanism. There is no interactive or computational visualisation, no dashboard and no in-browser tool.

**software.** No software released and no software page. Contributions are biological and documentary: the optimised composite part pCon-RhlR-SsrA-ASV-Prhl(LR)-GFP (BBa_26QSD9SO) submitted to the Registry as a reusable C4-HSL biosensor for future teams, an improvement on the existing part BBa_K2315014 originally characterised by Shanghai_tech_2017, and a part collection page documenting the Fur and RhlR sensing modules, the Lysis E effector-release module and the alginate lyase cargo. Alginate lyase expression was confirmed at the theoretical ~42.2 kDa with supernatant and pellet fractionation. No repository link appears on the wiki for either code or hardware.

**ihp.** Seven structured expert interviews plus a 398-response bilingual public survey, organised around a self-designed reflective model and reaching into regulation, manufacturing and finance rather than stopping at academia. The clearest documented change is a scope reduction the team accepted against its own interest: Dr. Guangquan Chen (Tongji University School of Medicine, with clinical and research experience in CF) gave candid feedback that the VOC diagnostic module, while feasible, was not innovative because existing research already confirms CF patients exhale characteristic VOCs without engineered bacteria. The team de-emphasised the VOC module, repositioned it as a future extension, and refocused entirely on biofilm degradation and antibiotic-adjuvant therapy. Dr. Ran An (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) identified four biosafety risks and ranked horizontal gene transfer highest; the team added a temperature-sensitive kill switch as a second containment layer on top of the existing mission-complete self-lysis system, and explicitly declined the pH-sensitive switch as technically challenging — a documented rejection with a reason, echoed independently by Dr. Xin Wang (Henan University of Technology), who noted insufficient pH difference inside and outside the body and pressed for multi-layered containment including auxotrophy against pulmonary over-colonisation, leakage to the digestive tract and horizontal gene transfer. Dr. Wang also raised that long-term antibiotic therapy already disrupts the CF lung microbiota and an engineered probiotic may interfere further, which the team adopted as a named safety endpoint: monitoring the impact of the engineered strain on respiratory microbial composition in future studies. Dr. An separately forced a positioning correction, stressing that the product must clearly present its adjunctive role because the biofilm is the target, not standalone infection treatment — language that now runs through the whole wiki. Dr. Baoshan Xu (Hospital of Stomatology, Sun Yat-sen University, rare genetic diseases) set the communication priority order as eliminating stigma first, building inclusion second, sharing disease knowledge third, and recommended person-first language, avoiding emotional narratives and letting patients review content, which became the education ethics policy. Two experimental design changes came from stakeholder input: dose-response characterisation across a low-iron gradient instead of a single fixed concentration, to reflect heterogeneous airway iron limitation between patients, and low uninduced leakage elevated to a critical selection criterion because the public survey showed off-target activation was a top concern. Commercial and regulatory engagement included Ms. Qing Yao (co-founder and chairwoman of Guangzhou Hanguang Pharmaceutical, a 25-year-old top-50 Chinese OTC pharmaceutical company), an anonymised biopharmaceutical R&D and industry strategy expert, HSBC investment and commercial banking professionals, Prof. Tao Wei (Guangdong Shaohe Biotechnology and South China Agricultural University, computational biology) and Dr. Huihui Bao (China National Center for Food Safety Risk Assessment).

**publicEngagement.** Audience-segmented education from primary school through university students to industry professionals, governed by a self-designed GCGS reflective cycle (Gather information, Construct and conduct, Synthesize and sustain) applied after every activity, with the content depth and communication strategy varied per group. The distinguishing feature is a written ethics policy for rare disease communication, derived directly from expert advice rather than invented: person-first language, participants review any content referencing their stories before publication, no overly emotional narratives, no framing that implies patients are a burden, anonymity respected, and no fabricated data. A WeChat official account was launched in Chinese to serve the Chinese-speaking general public after the survey showed over 60% of respondents had never heard of cystic fibrosis and nearly half were unaware of the biofilm mechanism; it publishes rare-disease knowledge aimed at patients' psychological needs and gives patients a platform to connect and support each other, which is unusually thoughtful for a high-school outreach channel. Objectives are differentiated by tier — sparking curiosity in young students through hands-on activities, helping non-biology-major students grasp synthetic biology principles, reducing stigma through responsible communication with the public, and giving professionals and industry stakeholders technical and translational insight. Education strategy was explicitly treated as an output of the human practices work rather than a parallel track.

**realWorld.** A rare-disease market analysis grounded in Chinese reimbursement reality rather than global TAM arithmetic. CF is in China's First Rare Disease Catalog (2018), was once considered extremely rare in Asian populations at roughly 1 in 32,000 births against 1 in 3,300 in Caucasian populations, and is severely under-diagnosed — reported Chinese cases in the past decade reached 2.5 times the total reported in the preceding thirty years, with current estimates possibly exceeding 20,000 patients. Over 78% of adult CF patients develop chronic P. aeruginosa infection. The unmet need is stated precisely: no approved therapy directly targets and degrades the biofilm matrix, inhaled antibiotics cannot penetrate it, airway clearance improves symptoms without eliminating pathogens, and CFTR modulators (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) work only for specific genotypes, are expensive and cannot reverse established structural lung damage. The access model follows expert advice that rare disease drugs do not need broad distribution: regional CF diagnosis and treatment centres and expert networks are the efficient channel, with respiratory physicians at those centres as the prescribing decision-makers. Payer analysis is survey-grounded — over 90% of respondents preferred public or collective payment, with 51.26% supporting rare disease funds combined with charity and 40.45% supporting national insurance against only about 8% for self-pay — and expert input that commercial insurers show limited willingness to cover rare diseases led the team to prioritise the National Healthcare Security Administration and local rare disease funds. They identify that few inhaled live biotherapeutic products have been approved for clinical use in China, so the regulatory and clinical pathway is genuinely unclear, and name long-term platform expansion to other chronic P. aeruginosa lung infections such as COPD and bronchiectasis. The product form is a spray-dried, matrix-protected EcN formulation designed to reach deep lung tissue.

**For GEMS:** Copy the engineering logic, and read the gap as a warning. Their transferable asset is a two-cycle DBTL that isolates a real trade-off — SsrA tags cut leakage but, on a weak promoter, degradation outruns synthesis and kill induction too, so you must raise transcriptional capacity rather than keep tuning turnover — plus the discipline of running a growth-curve control so a signal loss cannot be mistaken for toxicity. The warning is that GCGS reached High School Top 10 with essentially no model or software page, and it is the one clear hole in an otherwise strong wiki: a modest, fully documented ODE model of their own AND gate, with parameters and code, would have cost little and closed it.

### Muenster-University — P.A.C. Immunity
Overgrad · Germany · https://2026.igem.wiki/muenster-university/
P.A.C. Immunity rewires plant immunity instead of breeding for it. A plant NLR immune receptor is held inactive by a synthetic blocker peptide containing a protease cleavage site; when a pathogen secretes its effector protease into the host cell - a step many viruses, bacteria, fungi and nematodes cannot skip - the protease cleaves the blocker, the NLR fires, and the plant mounts a hypersensitive response. Because only the cleavage site changes between pathogens, swapping one short sequence retargets the whole system, which is the modularity argument: classical resistance breeding takes years and pathogens overcome new resistances quickly. The bottleneck they hit is that almost no pathogen protease has a known cleavage motif, so the dry lab built ProTEUS (Protease Target Elucidation Using Structural Modeling), a de-novo-binder-style pipeline chaining AlphaFold3, RFdiffusion3 and LigandMPNN with a mechanistically grounded geometric scoring function to generate candidate cleavage peptides for proteases with no characterised substrates at all.

**frameworks.** ProTEUS repurposes the de novo mini-binder design stack for an unsolved problem - predicting cleavage sites for proteases whose substrates are unknown - which existing tools (PROSPER, PROSPERous, Procleave, iProt-Sub) cannot do, since they only predict where a given substrate is cut by a protease with 30 or more already-described sites. The pipeline, named as machines on the wiki: AlphaFold3 predicts the target protease structure (AF3 machine I), since no crystal structure existed for any of RipT, RipE1, RipBN or HopN1; the structure is inspected in ChimeraX and aligned by Matchmaker against papain (PDB 9PAP) and other characterised proteases to derive catalytic triads and specificity residues, whose solvent-exposed atoms become hotspot constraints (scanner); RFdiffusion3 generates 5,000 binder backbones per target (1,000 batches of 5) with atom-level rather than residue-level hotspot conditioning and 'is_non_loopy' set to false so no helical bias blocks accessible peptides, with gamma_0 raised from 0.2 to 0.6 to reduce duplicate sequences (RFD3 machine); a Python filter rejects backbones closer than 1.7 A to the protease or farther than 8.0 A from the catalytic centre, with target-specific pass rates of 94.2% for HopN1, 51.1% for RipE1, 48.1% for RipT and 12.3% for RipBN, which they attribute to differences in pocket depth and hotspot geometry (cannon I); LigandMPNN (checkpoint ligandmpnn_v_32_010_25, seed 111, sampling temperature raised to 0.3 from 0.1 for short-sequence diversity) designs 6-10 sequences per backbone with sidechain conformations (MPNN machine); AlphaFold3 re-folds each unique designed sequence in complex with the target protease (AF3 machine II); and a Python scoring script extracts binding geometry and ranks with selected weights (cannon 2), handing the top 100 per protease to wet-lab screening (portal).
