Everything ran on the PALMA II HPC cluster at Munster - RFdiffusion3 on an RTX 4090 (24 GB) node at about 14 h per protease, LigandMPNN on 8 CPU cores at about 10 h, AlphaFold3 on an A100 (40 GB). Confidence handling is deliberate: they analysed pLDDT and minimum binder-target PAE rather than pTM/ipTM, which have been reported as weaker predictors for protein-peptide interactions, found mean binder pLDDT of 39.73-49.00 across the four targets, and chose explicitly not to filter hard on confidence (a pLDDT > 80 cut would keep only a handful; a pLDDT > 50 intermediate filter changed nothing in the final 100 after structural assessment), reasoning that badly predicted designs would fail the geometric assessment anyway.

**datascience.** Their most transferable piece of work is converting enzymology into a scorable geometry, because no training data existed. Since their four targets have no known cleavage motifs, they could not fit a model; instead they derived scoring parameters from the catalytic mechanism of protein-nucleophile proteases - the nucleophile sulfur or oxygen within attack distance of the base nitrogen, the nucleophile-to-carbonyl-carbon distance, the hydrogen-bond distance from the oxyanion hole amide NH to the scissile carbonyl oxygen, the nucleophile's reactive rotamer (gauche- versus trans, which determines whether the oxyanion hole is formed by the nucleophilic residue's own amide NH or the one C-terminal to it), the near-universal angle between the nucleophile atoms and the base, and the nucleophilic attack angle, with the explicit correction that cysteine proteases take a different ideal attack angle than serine proteases because sulfur hybridises more weakly than oxygen. These were combined into a weighted score over AlphaFold3 complex geometry. They also engineered the cost down: profiling showed the jackhmmer MSA search accounted for over 86% of AlphaFold3 runtime, and because every binder in an iteration is co-folded with the same protease they cached the protease MSA and skipped MSA generation for the artificial peptides entirely (homologs of a designed peptide being meaningless), cutting time per prediction from about 13 minutes to 30 seconds and making a 5,000-30,000 prediction campaign feasible where the naive estimate was 45 to 270 days. Validation was retrospective: run on NIa-Pro, a protease with a known motif, the pipeline recovered the correct residues (E/P6, V/P4, Q/P1) among its top 100 candidates, and for the four uncharacterised proteases it pinpointed potentially important residues, with preliminary wet-lab signal for HopN1, RipBN and RipT that the team states needs a refined screening assay to confirm.

**dataviz.** The wiki is a single-page React application built as an explorable argument rather than a document. It opens with Gary, a farmer whose story carries the problem (30% of global yield losses to plant pathogens, pesticide treadmill, resistances overcome quickly) before any molecular biology appears, and that narrative thread was a direct result of human practices advice. The dry lab page presents the ProTEUS pipeline as a machine metaphor - scanner, RFD3 machine, cannon, MPNN machine, portal - with an animated workflow, and each of the four candidate proteases gets a card showing its AlphaFold3 prediction with per-residue pLDDT for each catalytic triad member and for the whole and core enzyme, plus the hotspot atoms chosen for diffusion. Quantitative figures include a pLDDT-versus-PAE hexbin density plot with the official AlphaFold confidence bands marked, before-and-after pLDDT bars showing what trimming disordered N-terminal secretion signals does to each protease's confidence (raising RipBN above 70), and side-by-side renders of a rejected design versus a kept one. An interactive 3Dmol viewer serves structures (including an AlphaFold3 resistosome model), Rive animations drive the cloning and engineering-cycle explanations, and inline tooltips expand every acronym. Education results are themselves visualised as radial comparison charts of pre- versus post-event survey answers.

**software.** ProTEUS is the team's software contribution, documented step by step on the model page with every tool version, checkpoint, seed, non-default parameter and HPC node specification stated - enough for another group to rebuild it - but no public repository link is given on the wiki. Their released artefact is instead the part collection on the iGEM Registry, which is where the Best New Composite Part came from: a modular toolkit for plant-immunity engineering comprising pathogen effector protease expression constructs (NIa-Pro from Potato Potyvirus Y with an N-terminal myc tag, plus AvrPphB, HopN1, RipT, RipE1 and RipBN from Pseudomonas syringae and Ralstonia with C-terminal myc tags), a blocker peptide that prevents NLR activity when fused to the N-terminus (experimentally demonstrated on autoactive AtNRG1.1 [D485V], BBa_26V5N8GY), graded series of protease cleavage sites for NIa-Pro, AvrRpt2 and AvrPphB with short, medium and asymmetric GS-linkers plus non-cleavable mutant negative controls, a FRET pair (mTurquoise / cpVenus173) for Nicotiana benthamiana, and synthetic BsaI, BsaI-with-internal-NdeI and PaqCI dropout segments designed so an insert can be swapped into a composite part by Golden Gate assembly - built specifically for pooled library cloning, which is what makes the collection modular 'for anyone to advance with standard cloning practices'.

**ihp.** They state their principle as treating criticism as an ally and letting unanswered questions dictate which experts to approach next, and the chain is traceable. Prof. Dr. Dirk Prufer (Institute of Plant Biology and Biotechnology, Munster) validated the concept but said a project is only as strong as its ability to be explained, which is why the work up to that point - almost entirely experimental - was rebuilt around a narrative thread, and why they distilled their science communication learning into a reusable form. Public-trust interviews produced the framing that their biggest challenge is outside the lab, since without public trust there is no foundation for engineered crops in Europe. The bottleneck conversation is the most consequential: with no reliable way to identify protease cleavage motifs, they interviewed Prof. Dr. Kummel's working group and Lasse Middendorf, Michel Westermann and Michel Stevens, who told them that AlphaFold predicting a peptide in a pocket is not evidence it will be cleaved, advised a screen-many-good-predictions approach over seeking a single best prediction, recommended validating the pipeline on a protease with a known motif, and warned that AlphaFold would struggle with short peptides - all four of which became design decisions in ProTEUS, including the separate geometric scoring layer and the NIa-Pro retrospective validation. They advised against an alternative N-terminal-binding-domain NLR engineering route on feasibility grounds, which the team dropped. Verification strategy changed too: they settled on Western blotting with the cleavage site placed between two differently sized tagged proteins, and on co-infiltrating the NLR construct with the protease construct to guarantee both are expressed, judging the live-pathogen route better suited to stably transformed plants later. Industry contacts advised focusing on crops with higher production margins and identifying which chemical pesticides are likely to be restricted so the technology can be positioned as a replacement. An early farmer-focused interview changed the education strategy outright: they contacted the WLV agricultural association to reach farmers directly, and used the resulting discussion to extract farmers' specific requirements for genetic engineering, quoting farmers' own statements back as design references.

**publicEngagement.** The broadest and most systematically evaluated education programme of the five teams, and almost every activity was measured with pre- and post-activity questionnaires decided on in advance. Formats: a stand on the MS Wissenschaft science exhibition ship (a German federal research ministry project visiting 33 cities across Germany, Poland and Austria) during its Munster stop, drawing on roughly 5,000 weekend visitors, where people isolated DNA from bananas with household chemicals, built DNA double strands from 60+ gummy-bear model kits (deoxyribose, phosphate and four coloured bases) and translated their own codon to an amino acid on a take-home worksheet with a QR code back to the project; a workshop series at the LWL Museum of Natural History over the summer holidays bridging microscopic to macroscopic DNA, with agar-plate cultures cleared in writing with museum management and lab management, ending with participants designing their own Petri dishes, and follow-up feedback collected from parents rather than only participants; a protease workshop series for 8th and 9th grade school classes using digestive enzymes - ginger-juice proteases curdling milk at different temperatures, fruit juices degrading gelatine - iterated after anonymous participant feedback that the first round's instructions were 'a little hard to understand'; a bio pub quiz with the question rounds embedded in a narrative frame; 'Design Your Crop', a 3-6 player card game in which players become plant breeders guarding a hidden genome, built as a scalable substitute for events that only reach as many people as the team's time allows; a children's book featuring a farmer and a planned primary-school reading-plus-worksheet collaboration; a bioethics lecture analysing P.A.C. Immunity as a case study under the new EU NGT Directive; 'A Mosaic of Opinions', a dialogue event designed against the finding that consumer fear of gene editing in the food chain comes from campaigns plus shallow understanding; and a Fishbowl discussion in Nottuln co-organised with the Westphalia-Lippe Agricultural Association (WLV), with roughly two rounds pairing critical and supportive voices - fruit grower and pomology expert Hans-Joachim Bannier and Bioland farmers against Prof. Jochen Schmid (IMMB Munster) and the team - attended by regional farmers, Bioland farmers, association representatives, science students and the general public. They also hosted their own three-day conference, Junior Jam Munster, at the Munster castle, with expert talks, interactive workshops, poster sessions, a panel discussion and a session on iGEM judging criteria, and reported the meta-lesson from participant feedback that interactive workshops retain more than frontal ones and that Zoom talks land far weaker than in-person. The most durable piece is curricular: they developed a lesson concept on proteases for 8th and 9th grade biology, refined with teachers at a partner school and compliant with North Rhine-Westphalia's rules on genetic engineering experiments in schools; recognising that thermocyclers, electrophoresis chambers and photometers are not available in every school, they designed a lending experiment-kit concept, and they are working to shape teacher training through a university module in which master's students build and trial a lesson plan with invited school classes - aimed partly at the fifth Abitur examination subject with experimental assessment arriving in 2027-28.

**realWorld.** There is no entrepreneurship page; the real-world case is made through regulation, agronomic positioning and safety. The project is timed against the EU's new genomic techniques regulation: they tracked the European Parliament debate through the season, committed in advance to analysing the outcome's effect on their project, and published a bioethics case study assessing P.A.C. Immunity under the new NGT Directive alongside a risk analysis, noting that it remains to be seen how the rules play out in practice. Their market framing is agronomic rather than financial - pathogens cause roughly 30% of global yield losses, pesticide dependence carries economic and ecological costs, classical resistance breeding is slow and resistances are overcome quickly, so the selling point is a platform that updates by swapping one short cleavage sequence - and industry advice pushed them toward higher-margin crops and toward positioning against pesticides facing restriction. Safety is addressed as a staged transition: current work is under laboratory containment, and they state explicitly that moving toward pathogen-resistant crops in the field introduces a fundamentally different risk picture. The honest limitation is published as its own section: not all crop pathogens secrete proteases into host cells, so the platform is not universal, and ProTEUS is positioned as what would let P.A.C. Immunity expand from a few pathogens toward broad-spectrum use. The modular part collection on the Registry, plus the documented ProTEUS methodology, are the handover to whoever continues it.

**For GEMS:** Two things are directly portable. First, when no training data exists, derive a scoring function from the mechanism instead of waiting for a dataset: Munster turned textbook protease enzymology - nucleophile-to-base distance, oxyanion hole hydrogen bonds, reactive rotamer, nucleophilic attack angle, with the serine-versus-cysteine correction - into a weighted score over predicted structures, and validated it by recovering a known motif. Second, copy their education evaluation habit: decide before each event how you will check whether the learning objective was met, run a short pre- and post-questionnaire, and publish the result including what failed - and copy the curricular endgame, where a workshop becomes a lesson plan for local schools plus a lending kit for schools without thermocyclers, which is how one season's outreach keeps running after the team disbands.

### HKSSC — Engineering E. coli to express prbA, a paraben-degrading esterase, as a pre-treatment for food waste recycling
High School · Hong Kong · https://2026.igem.wiki/hkssc/
HKSSC (St. Stephen's College, Hong Kong) noticed a bottleneck nobody was talking about: Hong Kong's O-PARK organic resources recovery centre runs anaerobic digestion on food waste, but the chemical preservatives already in that waste inhibit the very microbes doing the digesting. They cloned prbA, a paraben esterase from Enterobacter cloacae that hydrolyses parabens to 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and needs no complex cofactors, into pET22b+ under a T7 promoter with a pelB signal peptide directing it to the periplasm, then characterised it with CFU-based MIC assays, a pNPA esterase assay and HPLC. They won Best New Basic Part at high school level largely on the strength of the prbA part family - including the previously unregistered native promoter and RBS, which they located in silico with BPROM and then built into a promoterless GFP reporter construct. The dry lab and statistics are the standout: structure-guided mutant design in HotSpot Wizard on an AlphaFold model, and a Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis defended with two-way ANOVA, a Brown-Forsythe Levene variance check and Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction.

**frameworks.** Three distinct computational strands. (1) Structure and protein engineering: the prbA structure was taken from AlphaFold and visualised in UCSF Chimera, which revealed a long flexible N-terminal tail consistent with the 31-residue signal peptide and justified the Cycle 2 switch to pelB periplasmic targeting. HotSpot Wizard 3.1 (Loschmidt Laboratories) was then used for a full structure-guided mutagenesis workflow: stability hotspots were ranked by B-factor and relative accessible surface area (ASA), buried residues filtered out, and three candidates triaged - A198 (50% ASA, highest flexibility) rejected because the Correlated Positions tab showed it needs a compensating mutation elsewhere; P329 rejected because only one amino acid occurs at that homologous position; N240 (34% ASA) selected, with Amino Acid Frequencies showing histidine as the commonest homolog residue and Mutational Landscape giving Asp/His/Ser an 88% probability of preserving function. They used the Design Library function with a minimal frequency threshold of 10% to generate degenerate codons for saturation mutagenesis at N240 and back-translated an E. coli K12-optimised mutant sequence. A second, separate hotspot run targeted catalytic efficiency rather than stability, prioritising A221 and A140 (mutability score 6, both in the catalytic pocket and substrate access tunnel) and designing an RCY degenerate codon library giving 50% Ala / 50% Thr with ~94% chance of seeing both variants in 5 colonies. (2) Molecular docking: methyl-paraben (PubChem CID 117065203) was docked across the whole prbA structure using HotSpot Wizard's docking module and visualised in Chimera to confirm N240 is not in the ligand-binding region - and they honestly flagged that histidine ionises near pH 6, so the mutation could backfire. Earlier docking with CB-Dock2 in PyMOL identified the catalytic serines. (3) Promoter prediction: BPROM was run on the 247 bp upstream region of prbA, predicting a sigma-70 promoter with an LDF score of 5.30 (threshold 0.20), a consensus -10 box TATAAT at position 163 (score 68), a near-consensus -35 box TTGAAA at 142 (score 23), 21 bp spacing and TSS at 178. (4) Enzyme kinetics: a Michaelis-Menten model fitted to pNPA assay data, plus a 35-page mathematical modelling report, with Monod kinetics recommended by Professor Patrick Lee for future digester-scale work.

**datascience.** This is the most statistically disciplined high school dataset of the five teams reviewed. Because they could only measure enzyme input by total powder weight rather than molar concentration, they refused to report kcat/Km and instead defined a mass-normalised catalytic capacity metric Q = Vmax / (Cmass x Km), valid only in the low-substrate regime (S << Km), with units cancelling to L g-1 min-1. Recombinant prbA at 1 ug/mL scored Q = 9.518 L g-1 min-1 versus Q = 4.545 for commercial porcine liver esterase at the same mass concentration - a 2.09-fold advantage. They then proved the difference was not pipetting noise: a two-way ANOVA across 4 enzyme conditions x 7 non-zero substrate concentrations gave enzyme condition F(3,64) = 52.530, p = 3.01e-17; substrate F(6,64) = 92.111, p = 1.49e-29; interaction F(18,64) = 21.012, p = 3.15e-20. A Brown-Forsythe Levene test (median-based, chosen over mean-based Levene precisely because outliers drag the mean) returned p = 0.01898, rejecting equal variances - so rather than ignore it they switched to Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction for multiple comparisons, confirming significance at 0.25 mM (p = 0.03452), 0.20 mM (p = 0.04225) and 0.10 mM (p = 0.00408). Separately, they chose CFU plate counts over OD600 for MIC determination because OD600 is confounded by precipitation and dead cells, and built an OD600-to-CFU/mL standard curve for proper per-cell normalisation. MIC was bracketed empirically: 400-500 mg/L methyl-paraben for wild-type BL21(DE3), 1000-1500 mg/L for the Cycle 1 prbA-idt construct, and 500-600 mg/L for the Cycle 2 pelB construct - and they published the awkward finding that Cycle 2 was worse than Cycle 1, diagnosed it from faint SDS-PAGE bands as a protein-isolation methodology problem, and opened Cycle 3 with 6xHis-tag IMAC purification to fix it.

**dataviz.** The wiki carries a 35-page mathematical modelling PDF embedded inline for the kinetics section. More interesting is how they made the data defensible rather than merely pretty: initial velocity versus substrate concentration plotted for all four enzyme conditions (1 and 10 ug/mL porcine liver esterase control, 1 and 8 ug/mL recombinant prbA), Michaelis-Menten fits overlaid, and the statistical validation laid out as readable tables with the F statistics, degrees of freedom and p-values spelled out and each test explained in plain language for a non-statistician reader. Every chart in results is captioned with a complete alt text describing the plate layout or chromatogram, and both HPLC calibration chromatograms and time-course chromatograms (T0, T1, T2, T4) are shown rather than just a summary number.

**software.** Two released pieces of software, both genuinely built rather than mocked up. FoodSafe is a native iOS app in Swift (source at https://github.com/judeliucodex/Foodsave, initial scaffold AI-assisted then refined by the software team) with two features: a 60-second swipe-left/swipe-right food-sorting game (100 points per correct call plus combo bonuses, backed by a food library for post-game review) and an AI-assisted food safety checker that sends a photo to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's vision model and returns a danger-meter rating with the observations behind the judgement. They are explicit about the limits - a photograph cannot establish safety, pathogens can be invisible, and the meter is an AI estimate, not a measurement - and about distribution, noting it is on TestFlight for invited testers rather than the App Store. Microbe Wars is a browser-based 2D arena game written entirely in Python by the team and hosted at https://igem-game.vercel.app, where the player fights paraben enemies as prbA using weapons like an enzyme pipette, with campaign/endless/practice modes, four difficulty tiers and a levelling system. On the parts side they contributed BBa_26SZRX0Y (prbA CDS), BBa_264E443U and BBa_26XQ4J7K (stop/start-codon-free variants), BBa_262HI0IB (native promoter + RBS, the Best New Basic Part), composite parts BBa_26SU8KOK (pelB + prbA) and BBa_26MSEOFB (native promoter/RBS + GFPuv), colony PCR and Gibson primers, and a curated 'PrbA's Family' part collection (UUID 9f037d92-78bb-470b-b139-c4ce28d4cc86).

**ihp.** IHP ran on a six-step cycle of their own design, the iCycle (Identify, Initiate, Interact, Insight, Improve, and a sixth step, Inspire), with the deliberate twist that Improve feeds back into Interact so broad stakeholders can be revisited. Stakeholders were sorted into four functions - Information, Implementation, Safety & Technical, and iGEMer feedback - and they covered the whole disposal-to-treatment pipeline: public and restaurants (disposal), EPD (collection), O-PARK (treatment). The design changes are specific. CityU Professor Patrick Lee told them flatly that engineered microbes cannot legally be placed in collection bins in Hong Kong and must be used in a controlled environment with a kill switch, which reshaped their entire safety and implementation framing; he also said demonstrating paraben loss is stronger evidence than showing translation and told them to use both HPLC and the pNPA assay alongside Monod kinetics - which is exactly what the results page then does. HKU advised them they were over-engineering enzyme optimisation, that expressing the protein was enough to demonstrate the concept, that they should focus on the bacteria rather than the enzyme, and that instead of immediately adding a kill switch they should compare growth rates of wild-type versus transgenic E. coli and determine MIC by growing bacteria across paraben concentrations - which became the project's central experimental design. The Environmental Protection Department replied by institutional email with real operating data: food waste pH is 4-6 and varies with contents, impurities are removed and the waste slurried with process water, and the slurry stabilises in a buffer tank for 2-3 days before digestion. HKSSC acted on both constraints, testing their microbes under different pH conditions (which is also why pH stability became the target of the HotSpot Wizard work) and adding bin-contamination messaging to their education workshops. The HKUST Black Soldier Fly Bin team confirmed preservatives are a real but under-documented problem, endorsed pre-treatment in the bin before food reaches O-PARK, and pointed out HKSSC had not considered how to feed their E. coli - advising a layer of food replaced weekly. The KYS student survey revealed a misconception that catering, not households, produces most food waste, and that students knew about the problem but not the solutions, so the team added Smart Food Waste Bin content to the comic and to later activities. The elderly survey showed forgetting purchased food was a key driver of waste, which generated a planned 'food record' fridge-inventory reminder feature for the FoodSafe app.

**publicEngagement.** Education ran under a framework they called LITTLE GEM (Gauge, Engage, Modify), reaching ages 3 to 101 across one kindergarten (Pods Kindergarten, Wan Chai), two primary schools (SSCPS and Shap Pat Heung Rural Committee Kung Yik She Primary School), a senior centre run by Suicide Prevention Services, their own school, and partner high school teams. Formats were built per audience rather than recycled: a DNA rainbow coin-toss game booth at a public carnival that engaged over 170 participants in three hours; a 'Find a Match' food-waste card game and DNA clay-modelling for 3-6 year olds; strawberry and banana DNA extraction for primary students; a Kahoot quiz; a live beta test of the FoodSafe app; and an original comic book, 'The Tragedy of Margaret in Food Waste', which they also staged as a drama skit with Margaret the frog as the lead. For the elderly they ran a physical food-waste card-matching game and clay craft. Internally, the HKSSC iGEM Club ran 8 after-school workshops over 7 months for ages 11-16 (4 lab, 3 IHP, 1 software) covering DNA, pipetting and serial dilution with P200 and P10 micropipettes across 28 participants, gel electrophoresis, and DNA keychain making, with Wayground quizzes for review - a deliberate pipeline for future team members. They measured learning rather than attendance: at SSCPS, 0% of 20 students knew what iGEM was and 10% knew synthetic biology before the workshop, versus 100% able to state iGEM's core goal and define synthetic biology afterwards, with 100% successfully extracting visible DNA; at KYS the post-presentation Kahoot returned 90% (18/20) accuracy. They also moved from one-off baseline surveys to paired pre/post questionnaires after realising the carnival survey only measured perception, not learning gain.

**realWorld.** The intended deployment is a pre-treatment step dropped into infrastructure that already exists - the EPD's smart food-waste bins in public rental housing estates and the front end of O-PARK's anaerobic digestion line - rather than a new facility, and the team repeatedly checks the design against real operating constraints (pH 4-6, impurities, 2-3 day buffer-tank residence, and the legal bar on releasing GMOs into public bins). They frame the contribution as a reusable framework rather than a single product: parabens are one preservative class, and the enzymatic pre-treatment approach is pitched as adaptable to other persistent inhibitors and micropollutants. Impact is mapped to SDG 4 (target 4.7), SDG 7 (target 7.2, higher biomethane yield from more complete digestion), SDG 11, SDG 12 (targets 12.4 and 12.5) and SDG 13. There is no formal business model, revenue forecast or regulatory filing plan on the wiki, and FoodSafe deliberately stops short of public App Store release on cost and effort grounds - both stated plainly rather than overclaimed.

**For GEMS:** The copyable thing here is statistical honesty as a competitive advantage: HKSSC could not measure molar enzyme concentration, so instead of quietly reporting an invalid kcat/Km they invented and justified a mass-normalised metric (Q) valid only below Km, then ran a two-way ANOVA, discovered unequal variances with a median-based Brown-Forsythe test, and switched to Welch-Satterthwaite contrasts with Holm correction rather than ignoring the violation. Pair that with their habit of publishing the cycle that went backwards (Cycle 2's MIC was worse than Cycle 1's) and diagnosing why - a high-school-plus centre will gain more credibility from that than from any extra experiment.

### UAlberta — gleyeco
Undergrad · Canada · https://2026.igem.wiki/ualberta/
Dry eye disease affects an estimated 34.6% of people globally and 21.3% of Canadian adults, and the central problem is not the drug but the delivery: blinking and tear drainage clear a topical therapeutic within minutes. gleyeco treats the ocular glycocalyx as a docking site rather than a barrier, fusing a Galectin-3 carbohydrate-recognition domain (binding Core 1 O-glycans on mucins), a tandem pair of the 12-residue hyaluronic-acid-binding peptide HABpep, and IL-1RA (anakinra) as the therapeutic payload, delivered from a crosslinked PEG/hyaluronic acid hydrogel as a drop or a contact lens. The team built a five-stage dry lab pipeline with its own acronyms - GLARE, InSiGHT, VOIR, I-SPY, HOPE - that chooses the target, engineers the binder, sets the valency, predicts the yield and tunes the gel, and released GLARE as an installable Python package. It won Best Entrepreneurship on an unusually rigorous commercial case (38-patient survey, two clinician letters of support, a letter of intent from a clinic, competitor matrix against Restasis/Cequa/Xiidra, PESTEL, 10-year plan) and was nominated for the Inclusivity Award for an open-access Inclusivity in Research course, an Adaptive Technology Kit and a rural teachers' programme.

**frameworks.** Five named operations, each handing its result to the next. GLARE (Glycan-Lectin Analysis for Recognition and Evaluation) mines global glycan databases of 50,000+ catalogued sequences, filters to the 134 unique structures documented in ocular tissue (cornea, tear film, lacrimal gland), confirms O-glycans dominate, then screens Galectin-3's off-target risk across other organs and three cancers under identical statistics with multiple-hypothesis-testing correction, and finally re-runs the analysis under a dry-eye disease signature, finding the disease phenotype exposes over 2.5x more accessible binding sites. InSiGHT (In Silico Glycan Honed Targeting) engineers Galectin-3 to favour Core 1 over LacNAc: mutation sites were chosen from the literature (H46, N48, R50, N62, W69, E72 hydrogen-bonding residues plus nearby polar R32, E53, R74), a Clustal Omega multiple sequence alignment of all available mammalian galectins from PDB and NCBI (which excluded the perfectly conserved W69 and flagged the poorly conserved E53), and a PyMOL structural alignment of 12 galectin CRDs against Galectin-3 (PDB 3ZSJ, 0.86 Angstrom) that identified the E53-V58 loop and the I33/N31 positions as differentiators; a Python script generates mutant combinations, FoldX builds the structures, HADDOCK and Schrodinger dock Core 1 and LacNAc in parallel after AutoDock Vina proved unable to handle large flexible glycans, and GROMACS scores binding strength - batched across RunPod for parallel FoldX jobs. Ten mutants (Alpha through Kappa) went to the bench. VOIR (Valency Optimization and Integrated Retention) uses the valentBind model to compute bivalent avidity as a function of linker length and glycan target density, concluding that a second binding domain gives the largest gain, a third a moderate one, and a fourth nothing - and recommending (GGGGS)6-16 linkers. I-SPY (I Shall Produce Yield) curates the BL21(DE3)-based iBB1018 genome-scale reconstruction in COBRApy for the SHuffle T7 Express chassis, adds a demand reaction for the heterologous fusion protein, and runs flux balance analysis to locate metabolic bottlenecks. HOPE (Hydrogel Optimization for Pharmacokinetic Evaluation) models mesh size with the Peppas-Merrill and then the Canal-Peppas form of Flory-Rehner, using interpolated PEGDA swelling data and MeHA degree of methacrylation, and derives protein diffusivity from it.

**datascience.** The team repeatedly uses modelling to avoid spending bench time, and reports the limits of each prediction. GLARE's stated limitations are unusually frank: the database records which structures have been documented in a tissue, not how much is displayed, so enrichment results describe structural patterns and must not be read as surface density; the diseased-versus-healthy split is built from literature signatures rather than a labelled patient dataset, and the pipeline is written so a real patient-derived list can be dropped in unchanged; binding strengths come from published microarray data, not from their own fusion protein; the tissue panel is small, and the cervix moved along the same mucin O-glycan axis as the eye so other mucosal surfaces would need direct testing. In InSiGHT they caught their own pipeline's instability - mutating key polar residues to alanine did not abolish predicted binding as it should, and one HADDOCK run gave mutant Gamma -6.495 kcal/mol against Core 1 while a separate run of the same mutant gave -3.84, which they report as evidence the pipeline needs repeated runs. For VOIR they state the point is the optimal linker length range, not the headline avidity ratio, because the values are literature-derived estimates not validated in vitro. For HOPE the model behaved as theory predicts (mesh falling from 16 nm at 5% w/v PEGDA to about 10 nm at 25%, predicted protein diffusivity from about 60 to 37 micrometres squared per second against 97 in free water) and they say plainly they could not build the equivalent alginate model, and that an OpenFOAM CFD attempt failed because the corneal absorption boundary condition had to be written in C++ and did not run reliably, so they fell back to a 1D Python model for sensitivity analysis.

**dataviz.** The modelling page is organised as a relay: five labelled operations (Choose, Improve, Multiply, Produce, Deliver) in a flow a reader clicks into, each with its own write-up and its own Impressiveness/Design/Validation/Exemplarity framing. The software page embeds a live in-browser CLI simulator for GLARE with clickable example commands (--cell eye, --binding-galectins eye, --target-compare eye core1 stn, --disease-compare dry_eye) so a judge can run the pipeline's logic without installing Python. For audiences without a biology background the team built the gleyecobuddies: Lecto (Galectin-3, with the binding site built into the character design), Ana (IL-1RA, a red plus sign) and Happy (HABpep, a blue rectangle standing for a wall that holds the drug in place), deliberately layered on top of the standard Symbol Nomenclature for Glycans rather than replacing it, and justified as serving visual learners, neurodivergent people and children. All InSiGHT results are reported with the predictors' disagreements visible rather than averaged.

**software.** GLARE, released as an importable Python package (v0.2.0, Python 3.10+) at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/ualberta/software-glare, runnable from the command line with a clear module structure separating tissue validation, binding analysis, cross-tissue comparison, disease signatures and docking-structure generation behind a single pipeline interface, with generalised inputs so another team can point it at a different tissue, lectin or glycan. A browser-based CLI simulator on the wiki lets anyone try it without installing. The Adaptive Technology Kit is an open-source hardware release: 3D-printable PCR strip-tube and microfuge-tube openers (in multiple design variants, because user testing showed different researchers preferred different models), an agarose gel loader, an SDS gel loader, a braille stamper, a keyboard tool, a pencil holder, a non-slip tray, a microscope phone holder, and a tactile map of the iGEM lab with published blueprints. A Synthetic Biology Lab Manual and the full Rural Teachers Synbiosium materials are published as free PDFs, as is the DNA-as-Code Kit.

**ihp.** Every stakeholder entry is logged as a Key Insight paired with an Action Taken, and the actions are real design reversals. Dr Warren Wakarchuk (Scientific Director of GlycoNet) warned that small-molecule binding pockets hold cargo too tightly to release on the eye and that yeast adds problematic sugar tags, and noted eukaryotic tissue autofluoresces green under UV - so the team abandoned the binding-pocket release concept, chose E. coli over yeast, switched the reporter from GFP to mScarlet, and retargeted abundant normal ocular glycans instead of rare disease-specific ones. Dr Lisa Willis (glyco-immunology) raised immune safety and challenged them to test whether the Galectin-3 and HA domains cooperate or compete for binding - so instead of assuming more binding is better, they redesigned the experimental plan to measure each domain separately by isothermal titration calorimetry. Dr Carr advised narrowing from retinal delivery to corneal inflammation in dry eye with IL-1RA cargo and offered Xenopus eye tissue for ex vivo testing. An advisor recommended the SHuffle T7 strain and told them their fusion protein was not complex enough to justify a chaperone plasmid, so they dropped it. Dr Amandeep helped unify the five separate models into one pipeline and suggested using eye images as GLARE input to make it diagnostic - the team pursued it, found it infeasible, said so, and redirected to modelling; he also pointed them to RunPod, which is why FoldX now runs in parallel. Jezlyn warned that chemical and UV crosslinking would denature mScarlet, so they moved to physical ionic crosslinking with calcium chloride, wrote autoclaving protocols for sterility, and were pointed at the Peppas-Merrill and Flory-Rehner equations that became HOPE. Dr Cortez told them not to add a second nickel column but to optimise their existing HisTrap/FPLC wash stringency, which they did and documented on Coomassie gels. Optometrist Dr Abdo Kattan explained that his multi-product dry eye package (omega 3s, drops, lid wipes, goggles) has very low compliance because it is time-consuming, expensive and impossible to attribute benefit to - which refocused the whole project on one affordable single-product treatment. Separately, CD44 was dropped entirely as the HA-retention domain in favour of tandem HABpep after it kept appearing in the insoluble fraction and the literature revealed isoforms linked to cancer therapy resistance. On the inclusivity side, Nicholas Piroddi (a medical researcher with autism) was consulted, then consulted a second time to review how the course represented neurodiversity, which added the institutional reporting-pathways module; ASVI's input became the blind and visually impaired module; and user testing of the 3D-printed tube openers at the WinSTEM expo is why the kit ships multiple variants of the same tool.

**publicEngagement.** Three distinct, durable programmes rather than one-off booths. (1) The Inclusivity in Research Course, an open-access training run through Google Classroom, built from a nationwide survey and expert consultations, with modules on a Native Land activity, the team's own 'Just Ask' framework and neurodivergent inclusion, creating open spaces, blind and visually impaired inclusion, Deaf and hard-of-hearing inclusion, racialized people, women and 2SLGBTQIA+ and gender minorities, navigating reporting processes, and an accessibility resource bank - each with downloadable slides, infographics and interactive summaries. It was piloted with their own team, neighbouring labs and Canadian iGEM teams, and the three pieces of pilot feedback (offer multiple learning formats, add scenario-based practice, cover more groups) were each implemented as narrated audio and slideshows, self-reflection prompts and real lab case studies, and two new modules. (2) The Rural Teachers Synbiosium, a half-day online professional development event for rural Alberta teachers, mapped explicitly onto the Alberta middle and high school curriculum, covering case studies and how to secure funding, with three guest speakers including Amino Labs CEO Julie Legault, 9 free hands-on kits distributed (teachers chose between a one-day yeast-fermentation race car and a multi-day pigment-engineering agar art project) and all materials shipped in advance to lower the burden. (3) Public outreach at K-Days, an Edmonton summer festival, where visitors attempted lab tasks while simulating different visual impairments, plus a DNA-as-code bracelet activity, and tabling at Alberta's Women in STEM week after being invited by the Alberta Women in Science Network. The team also presented at the Canadian Glycomics Symposium, CNAS Research Day, Darwin Day, Cell Biology Research Day, the RE Peter Conference and the Canadian iGEM GCI Conference, and ran a hands-on workshop at Canmore Collegiate High School - which is what revealed the rural access problem and started the Synbiosium.

**realWorld.** The strongest undergraduate commercial case of the five. Evidence of demand is tabulated by customer role with the strength of evidence named: letters of support from Dr Abdo Kattan and Dr Matthew Benson (and a signed letter of intent from Kattan's clinic to work with them), 86% of 38 surveyed dry eye patients interested in a synthetic biology treatment, and an application in interview stage with the Nucleate Canada accelerator. The patient survey plus three clinician interviews produced five explicit unmet needs - fewer doses, longer retention, no burning or stinging, targeted anti-inflammatory action, contact lens compatibility - which the product is then measured against. A competitor matrix compares gleyeco line by line with Restasis (AbbVie), Cequa (Sun Pharma) and Xiidra (Bausch + Lomb) on mechanism, dosing, time to effect, clinical evidence, tolerability, lens compatibility, 30-day cost and Canadian availability, citing prescribing information and Drugs.com prices as of 15 October 2026, and crucially labels gleyeco's own entries as design goals that preclinical and clinical data must confirm. The gap identified is precise: every anti-inflammatory option is dosed at least twice daily and none occupies targeted once-daily treatment. TAM/SAM/SOM, regional opportunity, bottom-up dynamics, current distribution network, a Size-Potential-Access analysis, a beachhead market defined by role (users, decision makers, payers, pharmaceutical partners), a 10-year implementation plan and an exit strategy all follow. The PESTEL analysis is specific to Canadian biotech: Health Canada's Reliance Order syncing review with the FDA if filed within 120 days, Alberta Innovates and FAST cutting trial start-up from 90+ to 45 days, PMPRB price controls pushing them toward private payers first, over 75% of Canadian life-science investment coming from abroad so Phase 2 needs a partner, the USD/CAD rate at 1.4, and the fact that the RE Peter Conference and Jamboree disclosures start the novelty clock (12 months in Canada, absolute novelty required in Europe). Clinical milestones were set directly from a clinician's roadmap, and lab eye models have been offered by two separate researchers for the move from proof of concept to preclinical.

**For GEMS:** Copy UAlberta's two-column human practices habit - every conversation written as one Key Insight and one Action Taken, where the action is a concrete reversal (GFP to mScarlet, yeast to E. coli, CD44 dropped for HABpep, chemical crosslinking dropped for calcium) - because it forces a team to admit when advice changed nothing. The other directly adaptable asset is their rural pivot: they went in planning to help schools found competition teams, learned from the teachers that capacity was the real constraint, and instead built a curriculum-aligned half-day online session with pre-shipped kits and a free lab manual, which is exactly the model a Taiwanese research centre could run for under-resourced schools.

### UOttawa — Nulfur
Undergrad · Canada · https://2026.igem.wiki/uottawa/
Nulfur rebuilds the four-enzyme 4S biodesulfurization pathway (DszA, DszB, DszC plus a flavin reductase) from Rhodococcus erythropolis inside Pseudomonas putida KT2440, targeting dibenzothiophene (DBT) — the refractory sulfur compound that conventional hydrodesulfurization struggles to remove without running at 300-400 C and 3-6 MPa. Rather than replacing hydrodesulfurization, the team reframed the project after industry consultation as a modular side-stream polishing step on diesel. The project won on the strength of its alternative chassis work: because P. putida is a non-model organism, the team built the missing toolkit from scratch (a Golden Gate-compatible broad-host-range vector, a measured four-promoter set, and a working heat-shock transformation protocol) and published it as a handbook for other teams. That platform contribution, paired with an unusually deep dry lab (COBRApy genome-scale modelling, a FoldX/ThermoMPNN protein engineering pipeline, and an agentic AI research platform called Cofactor), won Best Alternative Platform and Best Wiki and Best Bioremediation Project nominations.

**frameworks.** Three distinct computational layers. (1) Genome-scale metabolic modelling: the published P. putida KT2440 model iJN1463 was extended in COBRApy with the heterologous 4S pathway reactions (DszA/B/C/D), and flux balance analysis solved through GLPK over a 1000-point sweep of the DBT exchange flux bound showed metabolism never bottlenecks uptake, while forcing DszB flux revealed an NADH-limited ceiling of 9.80 mmol gDCW-1 h-1 that formate co-feeding raises 25.5% to 12.30. (2) A first-principles mass-transfer model of the biphasic reactor combining Hinze-Kolmogorov droplet-breakup scaling, film theory at the stagnant-sphere limit (Sh = 2), micellar solubilization above the CMC and Michaelis-Menten uptake, solved by bisection for the steady-state free DBT concentration; it predicts rhamnolipid raises effective DBT availability 2.8- to 34-fold. (3) A protein engineering pipeline that screened over 1,100 candidate substitutions in DszB and DszC using ConSurf conservation grades, MD-derived backbone RMSF, and an ensemble of FoldX (empirical force field) plus ThermoMPNN (deep learning on ProteinMPNN embeddings) for ddG, then validated catalytic integrity with explicit-solvent GROMACS MD (amber99sb-ildn, TIP3P) and AutoDock Vina ligand docking before shortlisting five mutants per enzyme.

**datascience.** The headline data-science contribution is turning the protein engineering loop into a measured, auditable artefact. The team built a six-arm evaluation suite for Cofactor with four ablation regimes (bare, bare_prompt, tools, full) that add exactly one harness layer each, then scored outcomes: 37 deterministic probes in Arms A and B all pass, Arm C recorded zero workflow violations across 27 scorable runs under the phase machine versus two in the bare condition, and Arm D found the ungrounded condition hallucinated amino-acid positions while both grounded conditions did not. Arm E asked the agent to reconstruct the initial experimental designs of six published papers (three postdating the model's knowledge cutoff) and audited tool transcripts for contamination. On the wet-lab side, the promoter library was quantified as log-normalized mScarlet-i fluorescence per OD600 corrected for media background and P. putida autofluorescence, which revealed only three distinct expression tiers rather than the four reported in the literature.

**dataviz.** The wiki is a server-rendered-feel React site with a genuinely engineered visual layer: a WebGL/Three.js distillation-tower scene and animated pathway loop on the landing page, every equation rendered as its own labelled SVG so the derivation reads as a chain, and predictor-agreement scatter plots (Figure 9) that shade the quadrant where FoldX and ThermoMPNN both call a substitution stabilising and enlarge it to label the five mutations actually sent to the bench. The Human Practices page is built as a clickable stacked column where each band is one of seven kinds of conversation across 21 entries, so a judge can jump straight to the stakeholder group they care about. Every figure carries a long descriptive alt attribute that states the figure's actual numbers, not just its subject.

**software.** Cofactor, an agentic protein engineering platform released under MIT licence at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/uottawa/cofactor. It wraps a general-purpose LLM in an explicit phase state machine whose preconditions are checked against a 16-table SQLite store (.cofactor/research.sqlite3, WAL journaling, foreign keys) rather than against the model's claims, so runs resume across sessions and the research record stays readable without the tool. A deterministic tool layer covers sequence operations, RFC10 compliance checking, codon optimisation, restriction analysis, solubility scanning, and retrieval from UniProt, NCBI, RCSB PDB, AlphaFold, PubMed and Europe PMC; an ExecutionManager submits jobs to local, SSH or Slurm backends. Three frontends ship: a FastAPI web UI, a Textual TUI and a CLI, all bring-your-own-key and model-agnostic against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The team also released the P. putida handbook with protocols and the sanitized Golden Gate-ready pBBR1MCS-2 vector to the iGEM Registry.

**ihp.** 21 conversations across seven categories, each logged in the same three-part structure: why we went, what we heard, what we changed. The changes are concrete. Dr. Jinwen Chen (Natural Resources Canada, CanmetENERGY-Devon) and Dr. Stephen Larter (Calgary, petroleum geochemist) both told the team to abandon heavy diluted bitumen for diesel because of viscosity, mass-transfer and emulsion-separation barriers, and because diesel carries a hard <10 ppm sulfur limit and concentrated refractory DBTs - the team moved its entire target stream to diesel polishing. Dr. Rasha Maal-Bared warned that viscous crude mixes in localised laminar flow, which put static mixing elements and bioreactor sizing into the continuous-flow design. Patrick Lumley (Safe Sulphur Systems, 33 years in sulfur recovery) said the aqueous sulfite byproduct needs pH control to prevent SO2 release and that Claus-plant load reduction is economically worthless - so a pH control loop went into the P&ID and the business case was rebuilt around hydrogen savings and reduced hydrotreating severity instead of sulfur throughput. Larter's warning about microbially influenced corrosion added corrosion and material-compatibility criteria to the reactor design. Faculty of Engineering Design Day feedback forced the pivot from a full HDS-replacement narrative to the complementary polishing model. Dr. Corrie DaCosta, a protein chemist, was consulted specifically about what Cofactor's output report must contain to be usable by the person doing the engineering, and the report format changed as a result.

**publicEngagement.** Education is organised around four stated principles - Access, Adapt, Engage, Extend - and each initiative is written up against one of them. The team ran bilingual (English/French) sessions for 370+ children aged 4-13 in the Ottawa-Carleton District School Board's International and Indigenous Languages Program summer school, reached 70 more through the Ottawa Catholic School Board, and visited AcadeCap International School for ages 4-7. Original hands-on activities include Lava Lamps (oil properties), The Art of Consortia (a collaborative mural standing in for microbial division of labour), Mix and Match Genes, The Power of Bacterial DNA, and a Heavy vs Light Oil worksheet. For durability they published a free interactive children's magazine, Bio-Builder, distributed through local Ottawa public libraries explicitly to reach low-income families who cannot buy such resources, plus a demo list, infographics, a science and research podcast, and a full downloadable resource library of presentations and worksheets so the activities run without the team present. They also hosted the Great Canadian iGEM Incubator poster competition (with QGEM) and the Great Canadian Meetup pitch competition, both with published scoring rubrics.

**realWorld.** A fully worked commercialization case. Market sizing: TAM ~$3.1B (global HDS catalyst market), SAM ~$66M (Canada's 2.2% share, 16 refineries, ~2M bbl/day), SOM ~$1.4M from a single-refinery side-stream demo at a $0.40/bbl royalty on a 10,000 bbl/day stream. Revenue model is per-barrel licensing royalties, validated in conversation with an operations and project engineer. A techno-economic analysis compares BDS against HDS CAPEX of $16-42M USD for a 20,000-25,000 bbl/day refinery and projects 50-60% CAPEX reduction from eliminating high-pressure hydrogen hardware; a life cycle assessment with a declared system boundary and BDS/HDS inventories backs the environmental claim rather than asserting it. A staged timeline runs from proof of concept (2026) through publication and NSERC Alliance / Mitacs Accelerate / CRIN non-dilutive funding (2027), pilot demonstration on real feedstock plus formal pre-engagement with Environment and Climate Change Canada under New Substances Notification regulations for contained LMO deployment (2028-29), to licensing (2030+) and expansion into biodenitrogenation. The team deliberately targets smaller, older refineries facing Euro V limits with constrained hydrogen capacity rather than major oil sands operators, on Lumley's advice, and flags biogas producers as a faster early-revenue path. Risk analysis, SWOT, Business Model Canvas and a competitive positioning matrix are all published, and the team is explicit that Nulfur is harm reduction during the energy transition - "a bridge, not a destination".

**For GEMS:** Copy uOttawa's human-practices template literally: a single page where every one of 21 stakeholder conversations is logged in the same three fields - why we went, what we heard, what we changed - with the change written as a specific design edit (a pH loop in the P&ID, a switch of feedstock, static mixers). It costs nothing to adopt, makes a student team's reasoning auditable, and is the clearest way a school research centre can show that outside input actually moved the project rather than decorating it.

### NUS-Singapore — ORCHID
Undergrad · Singapore · https://2026.igem.wiki/nus-singapore/
Industrial bioreactors hold hundreds of thousands of litres and a single bad batch is expensive, yet conventional monitoring tracks only physical and chemical parameters such as pH and dissolved oxygen — nothing about what is happening inside the cell. Omics and LC-MS can see inside, but they are offline, destructive and slow enough that results arrive after the batch has finished, so they cannot act on anything. ORCHID puts biosensors for endoplasmic reticulum, oxidative and ATP stress into Saccharomyces cerevisiae as fluorescent reporters readable straight from a plate reader, solves the resulting spectral overlap with a linear unmixing model, and feeds the separated stress signals into SABLe, a neural-network framework that predicts growth, product and stress from process conditions and then proposes which culture to run next. It won nominations across parts, presentation, wiki and integrated human practices because the loop actually closed: SABLe's exploration rule proposed 27 C, the team grew that plate, and the measured product signal reached 491 mApple RFU/OD600 against 204 and 179 at the 24 and 30 C conditions it was trained on.

**frameworks.** Three layers, built in sequence. First, a linear unmixing model adapted from multispectral fluorescence imaging to plate-reader wells: each sample's readings are modelled as a mixture matrix with one column per reporter and one row per channel, with diagonal entries carrying a reporter's own signal and off-diagonal entries the crosstalk, inverted to recover each reporter's share. It was validated on mixtures of single-reporter strains including untransformed BY4741 for autofluorescence and water-only wells for background, six replicates per condition. Second, a mechanistic baseline: Hill dose-response curves fitted at each temperature for DTT against the stress reporter and galactose against the product reporter, plus simple ODE time-course equations. The ODEs tracked growth well (R-squared about 0.91-0.93) but fitted stress (0.33-0.47) and product (0.41-0.42) poorly, and the team uses that failure as the explicit justification for moving to machine learning rather than assuming ML was needed. Third, SABLe: a multilayer perceptron trained on 700 culture-time records from 40 unique condition combinations (two temperatures at 24 and 30 C, five DTT concentrations 0-1 mM, four galactose concentrations 0-0.2%, three independent plate cultures each, measured at 0, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 24-26 hours), predicting OD600, mApple/OD600 and mCitrine/OD600 without ever receiving their measured values as inputs. On top of the trained network they run gradient ascent (network frozen, 64 starting conditions, 500 steps each, 32,000 evaluations without growing a culture), a ten-member bootstrap ensemble for disagreement-based uncertainty, and UMAP projection of the 64-dimensional latent response to 20,000 queried conditions to inspect what the network learned.

**datascience.** The statistical discipline here is well above the usual standard. Cross-validation groups all biological replicates and time points from a single cultivation condition into one split, because splitting correlated measurements across train and test would inflate performance — so the reported scores (R-squared 0.955 for OD600, 0.891 for mApple/OD600, 0.842 for mCitrine/OD600) measure generalisation to genuinely unseen condition combinations. Channel selection asked how few reads are needed and found one well-chosen channel per reporter matches a full spectral scan (three channels as good as six for three reporters, four as good as eight for four), turning an hour-long scan into minutes so a bioreactor can be sampled routinely. A simulation study set the design rule for adding reporters: for each separation angle from 2 to 90 degrees they generated 3,000 random two-reporter mixtures with 5% noise and found median error stays within 5 percentage points once reporters are at least 28 degrees apart — which is why mCitrine and eGFP at 20 degrees are ruled out. Errors are diagnosed rather than reported: the consistent 3-point overestimate of mTurquoise2 and underestimate of mApple in three-reporter mixtures is attributed to sample preparation rather than the algorithm because noise alone would scatter in both directions, and the larger four-reporter errors are traced to the whole plate being 6-17 times dimmer, leaving mApple and mTurquoise2 only about 160 and 690 RFU above water. Then the model generated a biological hypothesis: UMAP showed conditions with more DTT clustering where both stress and product are predicted high (79% of high-predicted-product conditions were also high DTT, 81% high predicted stress, against 25% expected by chance), the team went back to the measured cultures and confirmed it (Spearman rho, p < 0.001), checked that mCitrine bleed into the mApple channel could explain at most 8% of the rise, and named the next mechanistic question. They also caught their own education-survey analogue of this problem in the model: the 27 C validation plate was read at 24 hours while earlier plates were read at about 25, and they say so.

**dataviz.** The wiki is a Three.js scrollytelling experience that walks a reader from the $2-4 trillion bioeconomy projection down to a single yeast cell, with hoverable bioreactors explaining Titer, Rate and Yield before the project is even introduced — the argument is built visually before any data appears. The dry lab page is laid out as a numbered slide sequence (raw extremes, normalisation, normalised trajectories, stress dose fit, product dose fit, time model fit, fivefold split, held-out scores, held-out trajectories, gradient search, ensemble uncertainty, exploration score, optimisation versus exploration, latent UMAP, measured DTT response, UMAP robustness), so the reasoning chain is the navigation. Two choices stand out. The exploit-versus-explore panel shows side by side that maximising predicted signal just returns to a corner already measured, while the exploration rule spreads eight proposed tests across under-sampled combinations — making the value of the method visible rather than argued. And the UMAP is drawn sixteen different ways with the caption telling the reader to compare colour gradients rather than outlines, with an explicit note that the map axes have no biological units, which is an honest treatment of a technique usually presented as if its shape meant something.

**software.** SABLe and the linear unmixing algorithm are released on the iGEM GitLab at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/nus-singapore/model, framed explicitly as a reusable framework rather than a one-project script — future teams can use the unmixing to quantify several fluorescent proteins at once and track multiple cellular processes from a single strain design. The part collection is the other deliverable: 17 modular basic parts (stress-sensing elements including altered and native Yap1 response elements, UPRE1 and UPRE2 Hac1 binding sites, biosensor tuning elements, promoters of differing strengths, terminators, and fluorescent reporters including a genetically encoded green ATP sensor) plus 12 composite parts for the ER, oxidative and ATP stress biosensors, designed for plug-and-play assembly. They also characterised leakiness-reduction design principles as a reusable pattern: Sko1 repression upstream of the TATA box, a cP_CYC1 core promoter to lower basal expression, an ODC degradation tag for continuous turnover of background protein, and an RPP2Bt terminator. Two education artefacts are software: a browser game in which players build genetic circuits in virtual yeast populations, with every number and equation documented by source category (published, game-balance tuned by scripted playtesting, or stated rule) and an honest statement that no value was fitted to a real culture so the game shows the shape of the biology rather than predictions; and SynVision, an app whose camera scanner links everyday objects to synthetic biology concepts and then runs DBTL-guided questioning.

**ihp.** The project's scope was set and then substantially narrowed by stakeholders. An application scientist at TJX Bioengineering established that a single failed batch causes substantial financial loss and shifted the team's attention from the product to the production process and the changing conditions cells experience; Anomaly Bio, a precision fermentation startup, established that conventional monitoring tracks physical and chemical parameters while the cell's inner workings are overlooked because they are hard to measure and hard to interpret. The largest single change came from Dr Bruce Li, Alan Yang and Prof Yong-Su Jin raising scale-up challenges, deployment barriers and startup resource constraints: in response the team moved ORCHID's primary intended application from continuous industrial monitoring to early-stage R&D, naming strain-engineering and process-development teams at startups as the primary users and dropping production-scale deployment as an immediate objective. Several design elements are individually attributable — Dr Jee Loon Foo's guidance set the initial oxidative and ER stress targets, Sheena Chan's feedback added the ATP depletion sensor, and Dr Bruce Li's concerns about whether the biosensors themselves perturb the cell led them to build parental-versus-biosensor-strain comparisons into the experimental design. Sook Wei explained how genome-scale metabolic models represent competition between growth and product formation but warned that conventional metabolic models may not match real cellular behaviour because of unaccounted byproducts, competing pathways and biological constraints, stressing that experimental data is what closes that gap and pointing toward combining genome-scale modelling with machine learning — advice visible in the final architecture, where a mechanistic ODE baseline is fitted first, shown to fail on stress and product, and only then replaced by a learned model. Later feedback also asked them to extend the model to weigh productivity, yield and cost together rather than optimising a single predicted output, which is recorded as future work rather than claimed as done.

**publicEngagement.** NUS treated their educational game as a research object, which is rare at any level. It was designed against Self-Determination Theory with autonomy, competence and relatedness mapped to specific mechanics (free choice of parts, a shared leaderboard, facilitated peer discussion), and every simulation value published with its provenance. Evaluation used paired pre- and post-surveys via Microsoft Forms where participants generated the same anonymous linking code on both forms from details only they would know, so before-and-after answers could be matched without collecting names or emails. They deployed across six settings — Project STEMpact Workshop 3 with secondary school students, NCEB Engineering Biology Week FUTURES Day with polytechnic students, two undergraduate modules (SP2718C and BN4501), NUS Telegram channels and a Raffles Girls' School email blast — getting 58 pre-surveys and 27 post-surveys between 5 September and 18 October 2026, of which 24 paired. The analysis is where it becomes exemplary: four Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales were shortened and reworded, then checked for internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha in their own data, which exposed that Perceived Choice at alpha 0.23 was not a single construct (its two items measured having choices and feeling obliged to play) so they reported them separately instead of averaging. Three items were negatively worded and reverse-scored to catch acquiescent responders. Attrition bias was tested — only 41% of pre-survey takers paired — and no item differed (all p > .18). Self-ratings on all three understanding statements rose 1.3-1.8 points (d = 0.76-0.95) and intent to pursue synthetic biology from 4.0 to 4.9 (d = 0.64), all surviving Holm correction. But they also scored free-text definitions as an independent check: promoters rose from 64% to 91% correct, sensors from 23% to 45%, genes stayed at 55%, and the overall written score moved only 1.4 to 1.9 out of 3 (p = .06). Crucially, self-ratings matched written answers before playing (rho = .65) and did not afterwards (rho = -.04) — participants felt they understood more than they could explain — so the team explicitly treats the self-reported gains as an upper bound. Their own headline finding is that participants valued the game more than they enjoyed it: the highest-rated statement in the survey was that the game is useful for understanding synthetic biology (5.5) and the lowest was about enjoying it while playing (4.3).

**realWorld.** The deployment story is deliberately modest after the industry reality check. ORCHID is positioned as an early-stage R&D platform for strain engineering and process development teams at startups, not as production-scale instrumentation, because the team accepted that industrial implementation carries technical and financial constraints they cannot yet meet. The workflow they specify is concrete: build or adopt modular biosensors for the analytes of interest in whatever chassis is being engineered, culture under varied process conditions, train the model on how conditions map to stress responses, use it to interpolate and recommend conditions, then run the organism under those conditions — with the intracellular data also making unintended effects on the host easier to spot. The framing they use for the value proposition is a grey box rather than a black box: in-line pH and dissolved oxygen sensors show how organism and environment affect each other, but when production is inefficient researchers still cannot tell which pathway is the constraint, and high-dimensional intracellular stress data gives a window into that. Because the biosensors are modular, they argue the collection builds toward a shared library: metabolic engineering teams can track the burden a heterologous pathway places on the cell, and environmental synthetic biology teams can assess strain robustness in harsh conditions. Troubleshooting is published as a first-class deliverable, with issues and fixes in segmented boxes down the results page specifically so later teams hit them less hard.

**For GEMS:** Two things are directly copyable and neither needs a bioreactor. First, NUS's active-learning loop: fit a simple mechanistic model, show where it fails, train a small neural net on your own plate data, then use ensemble disagreement plus distance from tested conditions to pick the next experiment — and actually run it, so the write-up ends with a measured confirmation rather than a prediction. Second, and more unusual, evaluate your outreach the way you evaluate an assay: paired pre/post surveys with anonymous linking codes, reverse-scored items to catch acquiescence, Cronbach's alpha on any scale you shorten, attrition checks, and a free-text knowledge score as an independent check on self-reports. NUS found their participants felt they had learned more than they could explain, and said so — that kind of honesty about one's own teaching is both rare and cheap to adopt.

### UZurich — SeisMIC
Overgrad · Switzerland · https://2026.igem.wiki/uzurich/
SeisMIC adapts microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) to Alpine slope stabilisation, where heavy rainfall is now 26% more frequent and 12% more intense and concrete anchoring is often out of proportion to the risk. Sporosarcina pasteurii hydrolyses urea so calcium carbonate crystallises around soil particles, filling pores and binding loose grains, and the team worked on the four limits that stop MICP transferring to the Alps: uneven cementation, scaling across large slopes, cold sensitivity and ammonium production. The distinctive contribution is the dry lab, which is a geospatial and economic decision system rather than a protein pipeline: an infinite-slope Factor of Safety model run across all of Switzerland on daily historical rainfall, a PHREEQC reactive transport model of calcite formation down a soil column, a QGIS MICP feasibility map, and an economic model using Flow-Py runout simulation to put a Swiss franc figure on damage avoided. The models are linked to each other and were reshaped by named expert feedback, which is what earned the Best Model nomination.

**frameworks.** Four models, explicitly chained so each one's output is the next one's input. (1) Slope Stability: an infinite-slope model computing the Factor of Safety from effective cohesion, effective friction angle, slope angle, soil unit weight and the pore-pressure ratio, split into a temporal model that drives soil saturation and pore-water pressure from daily historical rainfall through a bucket hydrology scheme and is validated against recorded landslide events, and a spatial model that runs the same calculation Switzerland-wide to find unstable pixels and, crucially, to output the additional effective cohesion MICP would have to supply - a direct, quantitative target the wet lab can be measured against. Root cohesion is modelled as a parallel natural source, with scenarios for bare soil, roots, MICP and roots plus MICP; the modelled unstable share falls from 82.8% to 28.9% under combined roots and MICP, stabilising 65.04% of initially unstable pixels. (2) Reactive Transport: an adaptation of the Razbani et al. model in PHREEQC, simulating a 52 cm sand column as ten stacked cells with bacteria pre-attached to grains and a urea/CaCl2 cementation solution pumped from below over ~52 hours, using Michaelis-Menten ureolysis kinetics (Rmax, Km, initial reactive surface area, biomass decay time td) and calcite precipitation rate constants k1 = 1.55e-6 and k2 = 0.501 mol m-2 s-1, reproducing both continuous-flow and stop-flow experiments; run with the wet lab's own recipe (1.015 M urea, 2 M CaCl2) it showed more than 2 M CaCl2 brings no benefit, and it predicts 77-79% of lab calcite still forms at 4 C, identifying acidic pH rather than temperature as the bigger obstacle. (3) MICP Feasibility: a binary suitability classification in QGIS combining public Swiss soil and terrain layers on stone content, water storage capacity, permeability and slope, giving 67.06% of Switzerland as technically feasible, then overlaid on landslide hazard and on the stability output to produce a MICP Injection Map - 67.32% of modelled unstable pixels fall inside feasible areas. (4) Economic: unstable cells (FoS <= 1) become release areas fed into the open-source Flow-Py gravitational mass-flow model, producing a runout envelope of 425.2 km2 from 568,627 release cells in the mpp = 1.0 scenario (62.0% of canton Glarus, 348.7-425.2 km2 across tested hydrological conditions); historical landslide frequencies and damage costs then give expected annual damage per asset class (roads, buildings, railways, forests, agricultural land), and tracing the highest-damage locations back to their contributing release areas says where treatment would pay. Combined roots and MICP lower estimated annual damage from CHF 583,000 to CHF 351,000, a 39.8% reduction. A directed evolution strand runs alongside, aimed at a non-GMO second strain.

**datascience.** Their strongest data-science moment is a debugging story they chose to publish. The adapted PHREEQC model initially would not run at all, failing with 'Model failed to converge for initial solution 0'; raising iteration counts, changing tolerances and step size and improving initial guesses did nothing, and removing the calcite-equilibrium constraint made it converge to a physically absurd pH of 1.5. They computed the charge balance at fixed pH from 1 to 12, found it never reached zero, inspected the species and discovered ammonium was almost entirely in its neutral form (5.67e-2 M Amm against 8e-11 M AmmH+) because the reaction AmmH+ = Amm + H+ in the phreeqc.dat database carried no equilibrium constant, so PHREEQC set it to 0 instead of about -9.25; they fixed it with the parameters of the database's own NH4+ = NH3 + H+ reaction. The stated lesson - always check the values a model produces, not just the absence of errors - is the reusable part. The rest of the pipeline is integration work: joining national rainfall records, landslide inventories, digital elevation models, land cover and soil property rasters into one framework, validating predicted instability against recorded events and against SilvaProtect, running sensitivity analyses, and carrying each model's limitations on its own page.

**dataviz.** The modelling work is presented as a prototype decision tool, not a figure dump. An Integrated Dashboard connects slope stability, MICP feasibility, rainfall and potential damage into a single interactive surface for deployment planning, and the team is unusually honest about its state: it currently covers slope stability and selected treatment scenarios and does not yet integrate all four models, so it is labelled a prototype of the intended end-user tool. The model landing page leads with four headline numbers (-53.9% unstable area, 67.06% of Switzerland feasible, 67.32% overlap, -39.8% annual damage, 77-79% calcite at 4 C) each linked to the model that produced it, with arrow navigation between models. Supporting visuals are decision-oriented rather than decorative: unstable share and p95 pore-pressure by canton (which ties instability to the cantonal offices that actually do prevention planning), seasonal cohesion requirements, a required-cohesion histogram, sensitivity analysis, an agreement map against the SilvaProtect reference dataset, and per-asset risk maps for roads, railways, buildings, forest and agricultural land. Derivations are offered as downloadable PDFs (infinite-slope FoS, critical saturation, bucket model) so the maths can be checked independently. An Awards page states plainly which awards the team is claiming and summarises the evidence for each.

**software.** Code is published: the rainfall-triggered slope instability and MICP modelling at https://github.com/Alizzie/RainfallTriggeredSlopeInstabilityMICP, with the team repository at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/uzurich. They did not build a standalone released application; the deliverables are the four validated models, the nationwide MICP Feasibility Map and MICP Injection Map (which they note did not previously exist for Switzerland in any public form), and the Integrated Dashboard prototype on the wiki. They also published a measurement framework for MICP experiments - biological screening, calcium measurement, powder recovery and soil analysis as several independent readouts rather than one, with assay limitations and validation checks documented so future teams can interpret MICP experiments more reliably.

**ihp.** The interview process itself is the method: prepare (write down why this person, what you hope to learn, which assumptions you want tested, and how their input could change SeisMIC), interview with enough flexibility to follow unexpected leads, then reflect back in an interview log on what actually changed, what challenged an assumption, what new concern it raised and who to speak to next. Stakeholders were mapped on a power-interest matrix used to decide how to approach each one rather than to rank importance, and ELSI was treated as a connected framework rather than three boxes. Concrete changes: a researcher told them to start from the environment rather than the organism rather than defaulting to E. coli because it is well characterised. A pore-scale fluid dynamics researcher listed the parameters no MICP model should omit (temperature, pH, oxygen, ion and calcite concentrations, urea hydrolysis, water saturation) and recommended sensitivity analysis to find which dominate - so they dropped a machine learning idea rather than spending the summer discovering it could not be trained, moved the reactive transport work onto established software instead of a custom implementation, and added the sensitivity analysis. Dr. Joaquin Jimenez-Martinez's feedback changed how they treat temperature, bacterial survival and pH. Stakeholders and their PIs repeatedly asking how much vegetation already contributes is why root cohesion was added to the stability model. A microbiologist corrected their premise directly - ammonia release makes soil more basic, not acidic - sending them back to locate the real problem, and suggested reading pH change around colonies with plate indicators; another suggested nitrification inhibitors to stop nitrate forming. An expert pointed out that innovative biological methods usually fail on political opposition rather than feasibility, technology or financing, and suggested they also consider protected natural areas. They dropped CLIMADA after Prof. David Bresch's guidance and reframed the economic benefit as fewer slope failures. Residents below the slopes said what they value most is the surrounding nature, which made the ecological cost of the treatment something to investigate rather than assume; their hesitation about engineered bacteria eased once biomineralisation was explained as a natural process, which told the team their job is explaining the mechanism rather than defending the idea.

**publicEngagement.** Education was run as a two-way exchange explicitly tied to the values the team set in its Human Practices work - transparency, honesty, communication and collaboration - and they state that those became practical criteria for how they communicated rather than abstract principles.
