Social media carried three recurring formats: 'What even is...?' deep dives into a single concept, 'Word of the Week' introducing one piece of terminology at a time without burying readers in project detail, and 'Myth vs. Fact' separating common assumptions about bacteria, biotechnology and climate change from what the evidence supports. In-person work included an Activity Fair stand and workshops, plus ZurichLernt, and across every activity they tried to distinguish three things for their audience: what is already known, what their own project demonstrated, and what they could not investigate within the time and resources available. They brought in a strategic communication professional to test their assumptions about how to build a campaign, since nobody on the team had communications training.

**realWorld.** The business case is built on a gap they verified rather than assumed: many at-risk Swiss slopes get no protection because concrete and anchors are disproportionate to the risk, and two cantons, Lucerne and Glarus, independently described exactly such slopes. Interviews with Marco Peyer (Risktec) and Prof. David Bresch (ETH Zurich) moved them off insurers and onto the real decision chain - the canton decides and pays, an engineering office proposes the method, the federal government co-finances - so the customer is cantonal natural-hazard offices and their consulting engineers. The offer is deliberately a bundle: a site-specific treatment delivered together with the modelling that shows how much damage it avoids, because as Ulrich Kaiser pointed out, prevention has a visibility problem - a stabilised slope produces no event, no headline and no credit, while the cost is immediate and concrete, so proving avoided damage has to be part of the product. Interest is reported honestly as interest, not sales: one canton offered to connect them with a suitable slope and another asked to follow the damage model, with the team stating plainly that neither is a customer yet. The roadmap is about five to eight years from lab to a first slope, with Swiss approval staged as lab, then field trial, then market. Risks are named with mitigations: urea run-off requires rinsing (one company converts the run-off to fertiliser) and they are investigating a lower-urea route while stating nothing is settled at field scale; containment is handled by a kill switch plus a second strain adapted by directed evolution without genetic engineering.

**For GEMS:** Steal their interview discipline, which needs no equipment: before every expert conversation write down why this person, what you hope to learn, which assumption you want tested and how their answer could change the project, then log afterwards what actually changed and who to talk to next - that single loop is what let them kill an untrainable machine learning idea in one conversation instead of losing a summer to it. Their published PHREEQC debugging story is the second lesson worth printing on the wall: a model that runs without errors can still be wrong, so check the values, not just the exit code.

### Eton-College-UK — ProteaSign
High School · United Kingdom · https://2026.igem.wiki/eton-college-uk/
ProteaSign is a disposable-cartridge electrochemical diagnostic that separately measures MMP-9 (which degrades the extracellular matrix) and human neutrophil elastase (which degrades the growth factors needed for repair) in chronic wound fluid, turning wound assessment from a visual judgement into a measurement. The sensing interface is a gold electrode carrying methylene-blue-labelled, protease-cleavable peptides whose cleavage is read by square-wave voltammetry, with an independently anchored ferrocene reporter providing internal ratiometric normalisation and a matched non-cleavable peptide control on a second working electrode. The peptide sequences were not guessed: the team built a seven-protease machine-learning substrate predictor trained on 10,472 curated cleavage windows, and validated the predictions with two reprogrammable recombinant sfGFP protease biosensors. It won on the rare combination of genuinely publication-grade dry lab (cluster-aware cross-validation, Laplace-transform kinetics derivations, a physics-based SWV forward model), working hardware, and a human practices programme with over twenty named clinical and industrial stakeholders that visibly moved the design.

**frameworks.** Three distinct modelling efforts, all unusually deep for high school. (1) A protease substrate predictor: for each of seven proteases (MMP-2, MMP-8, MMP-9, MMP-14, neutrophil elastase, LasB, and a pooled digestive serine protease group) they trained two additive scorers on 8-residue cleavage windows — an L2-regularised logistic regression on VHSE physicochemical descriptors (8 descriptors per residue, so 64 standardised features) and a BLOSUM62-smoothed position-specific scoring matrix — using 10,472 confirmed windows from MEROPS, Eckhard et al. 2016 proteomic MMP profiling, and a re-extracted LasB elastin-digestion table from Yang et al. 2015. Negatives were constructed 3:1 (half other proteases' real windows, half random Swiss-Prot 8-mers at natural amino-acid frequencies). (2) A surface-bound enzyme kinetics model: they derived both the steady-state solution and the exact biexponential solution for Michaelis-Menten kinetics on a surface-attached substrate using Laplace transforms and partial-fraction decomposition, then proved analytically and numerically that the steady-state approximation is only valid as their single parameter lambda approaches 1. (3) A square-wave voltammetry forward model (swv_forward_model.py) that computes net SWV current from probe-level physics — about 3.1e10 probes at 7.4 nm spacing, with a 1.4 nm methylene-blue lateral excursion used to justify treating probes as non-interacting.

**datascience.** The evaluation methodology is the real achievement and is more careful than most undergraduate iGEM dry lab. They recognised that near-duplicate cleavage windows cause data leakage under ordinary K-fold CV, so they defined Hamming-distance clusters (any pair with d_H <= 2, taken as connected components, found in near-linear time via a 3+3+2-block pigeonhole trick with union-find) and used stratified group 5-fold splitting whole clusters, with a nested 3-fold inner CV to pick the regularisation strength C per protease, and the null percentile distribution and PSSM rebuilt per outer fold to avoid leaking into the background. They separated two questions — Detection (held-out positives vs random background) and Discrimination (held-out positives vs another protease's confirmed sites), noting the latter is what actually matters for a multiplexed sensor. They derived and Monte-Carlo-verified an analytic ceiling on measured AUROC under false negatives (measured AUROC <= 1 - pi/2 for a fraction pi of mislabelled negatives), ran three controls (label shuffle collapsing AUROC to 0.49-0.53; composition-only ablation showing e.g. 0.664 vs 0.874 for MMP-2 but 0.886 vs 0.877 for LasB because 76% of its positives come from elastin; and random vs cluster-aware folds, where LasB drops 0.886 to 0.879 once leakage is removed). Scores from the two models are converted to percentiles against 100,000 random Swiss-Prot background windows so they are comparable across proteases, combined by harmonic mean (high only when both are high), and reported as a 'specificity margin' = target consensus percentile minus the strongest competitor's. They also published an explicit list of eight assumptions and limitations, including that additivity costs at most 0.007 AUROC against gradient-boosted trees, that VHSE PCA captures only 64-79% of the full positional signal, and that the harmonic-mean consensus was reasoned rather than validated.

**dataviz.** The substrate predictor page ends in a live in-browser scorer ('Try It — Score a Peptide'): you type a peptide, mark the scissile bond, and every protease in the panel scores it as you type, with warm/cool per-position attribution bars that sum exactly to the logit and the PSSM score, and grey bars for unknown (gapped) positions. The sensor probe itself is shown scored at every bond by the MMP-9 and elastase models, with the P4-to-P4' window shaded and the actual cut marked. The SWV page carries an interactive forward-model plot where moving across reads every predicted current curve at one potential. Results are presented as out-of-fold ROC curves, precision-recall curves against a 0.25 prior, and held-out percentile distributions against a uniform null, plus paired difference plots with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals where a filled marker means the interval excludes zero. Equations are rendered in KaTeX and the human practices page uses globe.gl.

**software.** The substrate predictor is released as a protease-agnostic Python package (modules spred.data, spred.model, spred.pssm, spred.train, spred.validation, spred.evaluation, spred.panel) that another team retrains on its own protease panel's known substrates on a basic laptop in a few hours; the team explicitly frames it as a reusable contribution. Hardware: a handheld reader built around the Analog Devices AD5940 electrochemical analogue front end with an nRF52840 microcontroller and a TI TMUX1104 4:1 precision multiplexer, sequentially interrogating four working electrodes against a shared reference and counter electrode, with full KiCad schematics (5 sheets) and an exported bill of materials released as PDF. The hardware builds on the open-source Biocoin wearable multiplexed biosensing platform (github.com/ProfDrewHall/Biocoin; Hack & Hall, npj Biosensing 2026). They also contribute two reprogrammable recombinant protease biosensors with swappable substrate 'cassettes': pES-01 (FLAG-sfGFP / peptide / C-terminal His6, read by Ni-NTA depletion, ELISA, Western blot or SDS-PAGE) and pDUAL (split-sfGFP with GFP11 embedded in an eglin c surface loop, giving a fluorescence readout). Code and wiki at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/eton-college-uk.

**ihp.** Over twenty named stakeholders across wound care, electrochemistry, health economics, regulation and patient advocacy, with a 'pinpoint / event / action' structure that states what changed. Concrete examples: Dr Anatoliy Markiv (King's College London) moved them off pET-24a(+) to pSB1C3 as a reusable starting plasmid, reviewed their primers and proposed a better substrate-swapping method, and pointed them to the split-GFP protease-sensing paper that became their second design cycle; he also required construct sequences for biosafety assessment before permitting experiments. Dr Ben Bullen (podiatry) cemented the reusable-reader / disposable-cartridge split and the ~20 microlitre sample volume, and set a 15-minute workflow target against the team's estimated 30 minutes — which the team records as an unmet goal requiring shorter incubation. Ms Kathleen Leak (tissue viability) and Trish Idensohn drove the requirement for fast readouts and simple operating procedures, which produced the cartridge's standardised metering, dilution and incubation steps before SWV acquisition. Dr Honda Hsu (plastic surgeon, Taiwan) confirmed the device fits a real clinical workflow and his account of delegated wound care created an explicit usability requirement that routine dressing-change staff, not just specialists, must be able to run it. Dr Kevin Lye (Accorto Regulatory Solutions) and Dr Douglas Queen (health economics of wound care) covered the regulatory and reimbursement path; Dr Martin Peacock (Zimmer and Peacock) and Professor Kevin Lam (synthetic electrochemistry, Greenwich) and Dr Ana Maria Totea advised on electrodes and liquid handling; Professor Keith Harding (Cardiff), Professor Steven Jeffery (Pioneer Wound Clinics), Professor Dato Harikrishna Nair, Professor Paul Davis (co-founder of Mologic) and Professor Eleanor Stride (Oxford biomedical engineering) reviewed the clinical and device case. Patient and charity voices included 'Bob', a person living with a chronic wound, Breakthrough T1D and Diabetes Scotland. Feedback also reinforced measuring cleavage rate with calibration across known enzyme concentrations. The anonymised 'David' narrative on the description page is explicitly constructed from real accounts heard through these conversations.

**publicEngagement.** A genuinely reusable education portfolio rather than a set of one-off visits. 'What If?' is a team-written and illustrated comic modelled on Marvel's What If...? series, built directly from the four ideas children drew at the Eton Porny workshop (colour-changing plants, bacteria making medicines, programmable cells, healing wounds); over 350 printed copies were distributed in two months and it was translated into two further languages. A 58-page Activities Handbook of printable exercises at graded difficulty, with instructions and answer keys written in conversation with a secondary school teacher, was inspired by Leiden iGEM 2025's approach to reusable materials. 'Bio-Detectives' is a museum-sabotage mystery workshop for Year 8 in which teams work five stations — reconstructing DNA sequences, exploring protein production, critiquing flawed experiments, comparing lab labels, and modelling genetic control through AND/OR/NOR gates — and must explain their reasoning to unlock each piece of evidence, ending in a fixed-budget redesign task; student and facilitator packs plus the presentation are released so it can be rerun. Year 11 volunteers facilitated and reported their own gains ('I'm not a science student but still really enjoyed it because of the mystery format'). They report honestly that the content was too hard for pupils who had not yet met DNA and recommend targeting Year 10/11 instead. Other sessions: a hands-on goat-DNA genetic modification build for 34 Year 5 pupils at St George's Windsor (physically assembling glowing / curly-hair / spider-silk gene templates from spare nucleotides), an edible animal-cell modelling workshop with a published allergen risk assessment, protease kits for a carers' workshop, street interviews (8 of N respondents had no personal experience of chronic wounds), and biosafety videos.

**realWorld.** The implementation page is a structured device risk assessment rather than a business pitch: it enumerates infection transfer through reusable components, pain or damage to fragile healing tissue, allergic reaction to wound-contacting materials, unnecessary anxiety or treatment escalation from false positives, and exposure of identifiable patient data, each with a named mitigation (prefer single-use patient-contacting components, biocompatibility assessment of all wound-contacting materials, clinically justified interpretation criteria with evaluated specificity and false-positive rates, calibration and quality-control procedures with error alerts and clear invalid-test instructions, minimised personal data collection with access restriction and retention policies). The intended route to market is a reusable reader plus disposable cartridge for community wound care — GPs, wound-care nurses, podiatrists and carers — positioned to guide selection of the existing protease-modulating dressings (e.g. UrgoStart) and to track proteolytic activity over time alongside wound size. Costing came from the KiCad bill of materials plus estimated enclosure and reagent costs. The team is candid that clinical validation, bacterial confounding of the chosen peptides, and testing on real clinical samples all remain outstanding. A Smith + Nephew work experience business insight day and an Imperial iGEM mini-jamboree (24 August, UK and European teams) fed the commercial framing.

**For GEMS:** Copy their evaluation discipline, not just their model: before reporting any ML metric, cluster near-duplicate sequences by Hamming distance and split whole clusters across folds, then run a label-shuffle control and an ablation that strips the information you claim to be using — three cheap steps that turn a high-school classifier from a number into evidence. Their second transferable move is shipping the model as a live in-browser scorer with per-position attribution bars, so a judge or clinician can interrogate the prediction instead of taking the AUROC on trust.

### UCNZ — NanoBrew
Undergrad · New Zealand · https://2026.igem.wiki/ucnz/
NanoBrew takes brewers' spent grain (BSG), which makes up about 85% of beer brewing waste by weight and is mostly landfilled or sold as cheap animal feed, and extracts nanocellulose from it enzymatically instead of with hot acid and energy-intensive mechanical grinding. The team expressed a Bacillus subtilis xylanase (XynA) to strip hemicellulose and open up the cellulose, plus an ancestrally reconstructed Cel5A endoglucanase fused to a carbohydrate binding module to cut cellulose down to nanofibrils, and tested six construct variants with and without the YebF secretion tag in E. coli. It was Top 10 and nominated for Presentation, Entrepreneurship and Biomanufacturing because the project is framed end to end as a New Zealand circular-economy story - built on a real brewery partnership, grounded in the Maori value of kaitiakitanga, with a full pilot-plant cost analysis and letters of support - and because the team is candid that it never managed to characterise its product. No previous iGEM team had extracted nanocellulose from lignocellulosic plant material rather than growing it bacterially.

**frameworks.** Modest but purposeful, and honestly scoped. Before ordering genes, all six constructs were folded with AlphaFold 3 and the predicted structures aligned in PyMOL against the unfused enzymes to check the YebF tag, linkers and CBM had not disturbed the catalytic core - RMSD came out at 0.101 and 0.117 Angstrom for XynA and YebF-XynA, and 0.183, 0.155, 0.173 Angstrom for the endoglucanase variants, all well under 2 Angstrom, with pTM reported per model and the flexible linker correctly flagged as an unstructured region. Enzyme assays were run as time-series DNS and fitted to Michaelis-Menten-like behaviour on both the control substrate (birchwood xylan) and on BSG, with enzyme inactivation used to freeze each timepoint. For the system-level question they built a causal loop diagram with 12 nodes linking the environmental, economic and social effects of an upscaled process, signed each causal link positive or negative, and decomposed the graph into balancing and reinforcing loops - while explicitly refusing to quantify link strength. The microfluidic viscometer was designed entirely in simulation (Capillarix, an unreleased capillary-microfluidics simulator supplied by its creator) with a simulated error table, and the absorbance sensor uses a machine learning calibration running on the device itself.

**datascience.** The dry lab's strongest quality is calibrated honesty rather than volume of computation. The team states plainly at the top of the entrepreneurship page that its market research targeted cellulose nanofibrils because that was the anticipated product from the literature, but that it was unable to characterise what it actually made; the FTIR comparison against a pure nanocellulose reference sample came back inconclusive, and they published that, named ATR-FTIR as the next attempt, and said they were waiting on expert advice as of the wiki freeze. For the absorbance sensor they ran out of nanocellulose and substituted guar gum, justifying it as shear-thinning with a similar concentration-opacity relationship, and tabulating the results as such. The viscometer error table notes that surface roughness is not modelled. They also report that only one student in their school talks had heard of iGEM, and that a 2019 survey of 9,000 New Zealanders found 30% opposed selling GM food at all - using measured baselines rather than assertions about public attitudes.

**dataviz.** The two devices are the visualization story: the project needed a way to read nanocellulose concentration from microlitre samples, and the engineering subteam built it. The differential microfluidic viscometer compares a sample against a reference fluid in a sealed channel to cancel out the variable hydrophilicity of PMMA, computing relative viscosity as the ratio of average length-times-velocity products over the first second of flow, then calibrating to the expected sample range so unknowns are read by linear interpolation. The optical sensor strobes red, green and blue LEDs sequentially and feeds the three absorbance values to a machine learning model on an onboard ESP32, which infers concentration - and is deliberately built so a biotechnologist can recalibrate it for whatever property they want to infer. The wiki itself keeps each page to a clear sectioned structure with a sidebar contents list, and the stakeholder work is presented as an influence-interest grid rather than a list.

**software.** No standalone software release. The hardware is the deliverable: two sensors for reading nanocellulose concentration in microlitre volumes, one a differential capillary-microfluidics viscometer validated in simulation, the other a built RGB-strobing absorbance/turbidity sensor with on-ESP32 machine learning calibration, both developed through two documented iterations of the engineering design cycle and integrated into University of Canterbury engineering students' coursework with some of those students joining as external collaborators. Parts are the other contribution: six constructs registered, with EG-CBM (BBa_26TOG7XZ) highlighted as expressing and purifying extremely well with good activity on complex substrates, plus Pichia/yeast-targeted versions using an OST1 signal sequence and T2A self-cleaving peptide bicistronic designs (BBa_266IKFQ3, BBa_26OB3D76), and a characterisation of the YebF secretion tag (BBa_K1610300, from TAS_Taipei 2015) intended to let future teams choose a secretion system on evidence.

**ihp.** Human practices is organised around kaitiakitanga, the Maori concept of guardianship, with Bree Bell (Kaiarahi for UC Science) consulted early on how the project interfaces with iwi and hapu, and further consultation explicitly deferred to the scale-up stage rather than claimed as done. Stakeholders are mapped on an influence-interest grid and the design changes are specific. The team was split between on-site plants at each brewery and one centralised facility; Professor Jack Heinemann and Dr Brigitta Kurenbach, both involved in international synthetic biology regulation, argued that a distributed model multiplies accidental-exposure risk and regulatory burden because each site needs separate approval, so the team went centralised. The same pair identified the circular-economy rebound effect - if BSG becomes valuable, beer gets cheaper to make, production rises and total waste could increase - and told them 'sustainable' depends on timeframe and is often marketing; the team consequently narrowed its claim to reducing environmental impact relative to alternative BSG disposal, up to a stated horizon, and no further. Materially Kiwi (a startup making leather from kiwifruit waste) independently warned that customers buy on performance, consistency and price, not sustainability, and that a free feedstock does not mean a cheap product once collection, processing, testing and equipment are counted - which moved yield confirmation and full process costing to the top of the priority list. Dr Stefan Hill and Dr Mathias Sorieul at the Bioeconomy Science Institute warned that BSG-derived nanocellulose may be indistinguishable from wood-derived, so the low-cost waste feedstock, not the material, is the selling point; they also reframed BSG's high hemicellulose as a possible advantage, citing an Australian spinifex grass result where hemicellulose remnants improved material properties, and prescribed the three characterisation methods (SEM for fibril width, sedimentation for aspect ratio, FTIR for purity) the team then attempted. Dr Andrew Prest at Foodstuffs Own Brands listed what a packaging buyer needs and confirmed food-contact use would need substantial safety assessment, which is why the team targets non-food packaging first. Lincoln Agritech's suggestion of rheology as a measurement route is what started the viscometer, and Professor Volker Nock was met at the BIC symposium after researchers there raised the energy cost of freeze-thaw cycles at scale.

**publicEngagement.** Outreach was built around a deliberate hypothesis: in New Zealand, synthetic biology means genetic modification and genetic modification means risk, so the team tested whether a local story changes how people engage. They gave three secondary-school talks (one at Burnside High School, two at Christchurch Girls' High School, both schools some members had attended) covering synthetic biology, iGEM, what a science degree looks like and how NanoBrew works, and structured them for dialogue - long question time, small-group breakout discussion, a quiz where answers were argued through rather than marked, contact details left for follow-ups, and teacher feedback collected. Their findings are reported as findings: students already knew breweries and brewery waste so the local hook carried the science; small groups worked far better than whole-cohort presentation; most questions were about science careers and preparing for university, where undergraduates were better placed to answer than any teacher; and only one student had ever heard of iGEM. For the wider public they worked with the university communications team on a press release framed as a local problem with a local solution, which reached The Press, NZ Herald, Radio New Zealand, NewstalkZB, The Breeze, The Platform and deliberately rural and regional outlets including the Ashburton Courier and Selwyn Times, with a team member and the PI giving radio interviews that explained containment in plain language; the Instagram account passed 23,000 views. They also presented at the Biomolecular Interaction Centre Winter Symposium. The published lessons for future teams are practical: get your institution's comms team involved early, and contact schools months ahead because they plan a year out.

**realWorld.** The commercial case is unusually complete for an undergraduate team and backed by two letters of support (Cassels Brewing Co. and Lincoln University). Local grounding: in Christchurch alone BSG accounts for an estimated 680-1,000 tonnes to landfill a year, costing breweries up to NZ$220,000 in disposal fees, and nationally roughly 13,700 tonnes to landfill producing 14,000 tonnes CO2-equivalent, which the promotional video renders as 3,300 petrol cars running for a year. Market: nanocellulose at US$947 million in 2026 growing at 23.74% CAGR to a projected US$6.4 billion by 2035, with the team noting that estimates vary between reports and stating which figure it uses throughout. Price reality from stakeholders sets the strategy: at around $100/kg nanocellulose suits high-value medical uses while broad uptake needs roughly $10/kg, so packaging is the entry market. The page carries a development roadmap, a commercial-scale cost forecast, a downloadable preliminary CNF cost analysis for a pilot-scale plant, financial analysis and timeline, a business exit strategy, minimum viable product definition, PEST, SWOT, risk and competitor analyses (including Nano-Sea/AgriSea making kelp-derived nanocellulose locally, which does not target packaging), and a pitch deck. On IP, the UC Technology Transfer Office told them a first filing runs NZ$10-15K and is only worth it if results look promising, that only novel elements need protecting, that much of their approach is already published so finding the novel element may be hard, and that they should BLAST their enzyme sequences against patented sequences to check freedom to operate - and that they should document negative results because that is how an invention's origin is evidenced. The team notes everything submitted to iGEM enters the public domain, so any filing had to precede the wiki. Continuation is real: the media coverage plus the results won University of Canterbury funding for a summer research project carrying the work on under Dr Kelsi Hall, one of only 18 scholarships awarded across all faculties in 2026. The team also commits to licensing the process to other agricultural and food-processing waste streams once protected, with documentation, stakeholder map and methods open now.

**For GEMS:** UCNZ shows how to publish an unfinished result well: they never characterised their nanocellulose, said so at the top of the page that depended on it, named the failed method (FTIR, inconclusive against a reference sample), the planned replacement (ATR-FTIR) and the substitute material they used when samples ran out - and still won Top 10. The second transferable move is the local hook: anchor the project in an industry students already recognise, then get the institution's communications office involved early enough that national and regional media carry the story, which is what converted their outreach into continuation funding.

### HongKong-HS — AmpliRen - a urine-based home screening kit concept for chronic kidney disease using urinary miRNA and hybridisation chain reaction
High School · Hong Kong · https://2026.igem.wiki/hongkong-hs/
HongKong-HS is a five-school joint team (Wah Yan College Kowloon, Pope Paul VI College, C&MA Sun Kei Secondary School, Tsung Tsin Christian Academy, St. Paul's School Lam Tin) tackling chronic kidney disease, which affects roughly 788 million adults worldwide, has risen past 405,000 recorded adult cases in Hong Kong, and is usually caught only at stage 3-5 because creatinine-based eGFR does not move until about half of kidney function is gone. AmpliRen detects two urinary microRNAs - miR-21-5p for fibrosis severity and miR-192-5p as an early warning, together reported at 89% sensitivity and 82% specificity - and amplifies the signal enzyme-free at room temperature with hybridisation chain reaction, whose G-rich hairpin loops fold into G-quadruplexes that bind hemin to form a DNAzyme and oxidise TMB into a colour change visible in natural light. The project is a genuine four-cycle engineering story: the team started with toehold switches designed in miRADAR and screened in NUPACK, found EGFP output too weak and invisible, pivoted to HCR, then to G-quadruplex-containing probes, then to hemin/TMB colorimetry. It was nominated for Best Wiki on one of the most ambitious scroll-driven, 3D-visualised wikis in the competition.

**frameworks.** The dry lab is nucleic-acid thermodynamics rather than protein design, and it is used as a hard screen at every cycle. Candidate toehold switches were generated with miRADAR, the design tool released by the 2024 Wageningen iGEM team - a deliberate reuse of another team's software rather than reinventing it - producing 9 candidates for miR-21-5p and 7 for miR-192-5p. Every candidate was then simulated in NUPACK (RNA mode, 37 C, default model options and algorithm settings, 1 uM toehold and 3 uM miRNA to keep the trigger in excess) and scored against five explicit criteria: bound-toehold equilibrium concentration, absence of unintended secondary structure downstream of the ribosome binding site (which would block the ribosome and cause false negatives), hybrid minimum free energy (HMFE) versus toehold minimum free energy (TMFE) so that the bound state is thermodynamically favoured and the switch does not prefer to dimerise with another switch, C-G content for hairpin stability, and RBS location. They tabulated the HMFE-TMFE difference for every candidate in kcal/mol and read NUPACK's base-pair equilibrium-probability plots to check that loop-maintaining base pairs drop to low probability on target binding so the switch can fully linearise - selecting toeholds 6 and 7 for miR-192-5p and 7 and 9 for miR-21-5p. The same NUPACK workflow was then reapplied to HCR: H1/H2 hairpin pairs (the miR-21-5p pair adopted from Miao et al. 2016, the miR-192-5p pair built in house) were simulated at 37 C with 1 uM hairpin and 3 uM miRNA, confirming long H1-H2 polymer formation with target but also predicting unintended H1-H2 binding in the absence of target - a background-leakage problem the model found before the gel did. Minimum-free-energy structures were computed for H1 alone, H2 alone, H1+miRNA and the full miRNA-H1-H2 complex for both targets. In Cycle 4, double-loop G4H1/G4H2 hairpins based on Peng et al. (2022) had InG4 G-quadruplex motifs inserted into the loops, and NUPACK was used to confirm both complex formation and that the InG4 sequences sit in the loops where they can fold and leave the polymer after HCR. The two probe pairs were deliberately given different geometries - longer stems and smaller loops for miR-192-5p, shorter stems and larger loops for miR-21-5p.

**datascience.** Analysis is modest in volume but correctly specified. Cell-free EGFP expression was compared with and without target miRNA across five repeats against both positive controls (pET-14b-EGFP with no toehold) and no-plasmid negative controls, read on a fluorometer at 488 nm excitation and 507-513 nm emission, with significance tested by one-sample t-test on fold change; the honest outcome was that miR-21 candidates showed no significant difference, miR-192-5p-6 was significant but minimal at 1.03-fold, and miR-192-5p-7 showed a more pronounced 1.51-fold increase that did not reach significance - and they reported that rather than spin it. ThT fluorescence and hemin/TMB colorimetric assays were analysed by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett post-hoc against the 0 pM control: miR-21 gave significant signal at 100 pM, 10 nM and 100 nM (n=3, p<0.001), while miR-192 was significant at 100 nM (p=0.01 and p=0.002) but also, unexpectedly, significantly lower than control at 1 nM - an anomaly they diagnosed as free miR-192-5p G4H1 self-folding into a G-quadruplex and producing colour without target, and then turned into a concrete future-work list (splitting the G4, stabilising the hairpin stem, tuning C-G/A-T content, optimising toehold length). Plasmid work was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and miniprep A260/280 purity, and gel evidence was escalated from agarose to PAGE when agarose smearing proved inconclusive.

**dataviz.** The wiki itself is the data-visualisation achievement and is why it was nominated for Best Wiki. The landing page is a scroll-driven narrative that zooms from two kidneys, through tissue and the filtration barrier, down to the molecular signal, with each stage labelled as an illustrative view rather than clinical eGFR categories. The HCR mechanism is animated across four scroll states - two locked hairpins, target binding and toehold opening, chain growth into a double-stranded nanowire, then potassium-dependent G-quadruplex folding with hemin - so a reader physically watches the amplification cascade instead of reading a paragraph about it. Epidemiology is presented as individually sourced stat cards, each carrying its own population, year and citation (788 million adults globally, GBD 2023/The Lancet 2025; 87% unaware, CDC 2026 NHANES 2021-2023; 405,833 Hong Kong adult cases 2021, Yue et al.; 2,571 on the transplant waiting list; 1,226 registered deaths in 2024) with an explicit note that one figure is a recorded-case count, not a current population estimate. The kit concept is presented as an interactive unboxing with three fitted compartments and a pannable close-up, and the team labels it openly as AI-assisted imagery and animation made with Higgsfield and as a research concept, not a validated diagnostic product. The engineering page is built as a clickable 22-note timeline across four Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles. Every figure carries a full descriptive caption and alt text.

**software.** No standalone software or hardware was released. The dry lab is the application of existing tools - NUPACK for thermodynamic simulation and another iGEM team's miRADAR for candidate generation - plus a bespoke wiki front end. Two toehold switch candidates per target were cloned into pET-14b-EGFP using XbaI and NdeI sites between the T7 promoter and the EGFP reporter and verified by Sanger sequencing, and an mCherry colorimetric variant was in progress when the season ended.

**ihp.** IHP was organised as four parallel two-way feedback loops (Public, Healthcare, Science, Industry) feeding both the wet lab and the education team, structured over three stages (Understanding the Problem, Identifying the Needs, Develop & Co-design) and processed through a four-step cycle they call LIVP (Locate, Iterate, Validate, Propose). The design changes are traceable to named people. Professor Chan Ting Fung (RNA biology) assessed the toehold-switch limitations and identified HCR as the alternative worth trying for signal amplification - the single biggest pivot in the project - and later recommended expanding the H1/H2 sequence design space to mask the ribosome binding site to eliminate background leakage, noted that lithium interference in urine is negligible, and told them to test sodium's effect on the DNAzyme experimentally. Professor Szeto Cheuk Chun (Head of Medicine and Therapeutics, CUHK, whose research is urinary biomarkers) confirmed miRNA as near-ideal for urine because of its stability, told them to run miR-21-5p and miR-192-5p in parallel as a complementary test (which is why the kit has two detection pathways and a six-well chamber), said biomarkers are detectable in urine that has not been high-speed centrifuged so they could drop centrifugation from the workflow, warned that urinary chromogens may interfere with a visible colour readout, set a user-experience target of roughly half an hour to result, and endorsed a colour change readable under natural light - which is precisely why the team ended up on G4/hemin colorimetry rather than ThT fluorescence, since ThT needs UV excitation and a fluorescence reader. Professor Ma Ming Yao established that the kit must be positioned as a screening flag prompting medical follow-up, never a diagnosis, and that false positives and negatives must be managed responsibly, and that high-risk patients are the target - which reshaped how the whole wiki speaks about the product and prompted a community education workshop for the elderly. A medical laboratory technologist insisted on a clear, reasonable cut-off concentration for the target miRNA, rigorous quality control, timely sample processing, and a larger sample size for credibility, which pushed the team towards a multi-target design. E-SENSE Innovation & Technology Limited said clinicians will only recommend a home test backed by real-world clinical data with low false-positive and false-negative rates, which pushed the wet lab to run the cell-free EGFP validation and the HCR sensitivity series. Public input was quantified: a street interview of 137 people and an online survey of 283 found 52% had never heard of CKD or diabetic kidney disease and only 28% had heard of both, 60% did not know or were unsure that early kidney disease can be symptomless, and 63.2% of street respondents cited absence of symptoms as their reason for not getting screened.

**publicEngagement.** Education reached over 800 participants and was built on three stated principles - a Cascading Peer-Educator Model, Gamified Educational Experiences, and Reflective Learning. The peer-educator model is the distinctive one: rather than only teaching end-learners, they trained non-iGEM junior-form Science Team members as Student Facilitators with both content and facilitation skills, then had those facilitators independently run workshops for their schoolmates, and published a training guide for holding a secondary school workshop plus a CKD brochure for older adults so the materials outlive the team. Activities were designed per audience and deliberately low-cost and replicable: at Salesian Yip Hon Millennium Primary School's STEAM Day (about 600 students and parents) they ran a micropipette drip-art station, a magnetic miRNA detection game in which only the target miRNA card hides a magnet so it alone sticks to a paper toehold-switch model, and a health-knowledge ping-pong ball toss into an illustrated face; at Shek Lei Catholic Primary School, strawberry DNA extraction delivered entirely in Cantonese with terms simplified ('cell walls' became 'the surface of the strawberry') and a 'Blood Vessel Clearing Game' using paper, drawing supplies and a hand-made wooden vessel model, with students drawing their own food items and testing whether they fit through. Secondary outreach covered St. Paul's School (Lam Tin) with 169 participants and Hoi Ping Chamber of Commerce Secondary School with 19, using a micropipetting precision-dyeing challenge and a 'Detective on Call' online DNA fingerprinting game. They also ran a card game for community-centre children including ethnic-minority children, an elderly workshop, a Hong Kong Joint Secondary Schools Science Fair booth, and regional middle-school outreach in the Greater Bay Area. Reflection was built in with structured worksheets, exit cards and open Q&A, and every activity records what they changed next - after noticing their terminology was too advanced for young children they switched to plainer language, more gestures and more Cantonese, and they adapted in real time when a student asked 'Why strawberries? Why not apples?' by adding an impromptu discussion.

**realWorld.** The intended product is an at-home urine screening kit, costed against a system where each Hong Kong dialysis patient runs about HKD 50,000 per year and where confirming CKD currently needs repeat clinic visits over a three-month window because uACR varies by 30% or more day to day and cystatin C is several times the price of creatinine and rarely reimbursed. Every design decision is pulled towards deployability: urine rather than blood, no centrifuge, enzyme-free isothermal amplification at room temperature, and a colour change readable in natural light without any instrument. The team is consistently careful about regulatory and clinical positioning - the kit is repeatedly described as a screening flag that prompts follow-up and complements, rather than replaces, eGFR and uACR, and the kit visualisation is explicitly captioned as a research concept, not a validated diagnostic product. What is not present on the wiki is a business model, pricing, manufacturing plan or named regulatory pathway; industry engagement with E-SENSE is framed around clinical credibility and usability requirements rather than commercialisation, and the honest gap they name is the need for real-world paired clinical data before a home device is justified.

**For GEMS:** Two things to steal. First, NUPACK plus a reused iGEM software tool (Wageningen's miRADAR) is a complete, free, high-school-feasible dry lab: HongKong-HS ranked 16 candidate switches on explicit thermodynamic criteria (HMFE vs TMFE, downstream secondary structure blocking the RBS, equilibrium base-pair probability) and predicted the background-leakage failure mode before the gel showed it. Second, their wiki proves that the best data visualisation is mechanism animation plus per-figure provenance - every statistic carries its own population, year and source, and the AI-generated product imagery is labelled as such, which is exactly the standard a research centre's outputs should hold itself to.

### XJTLU-China — dogmaOS — programming translation rhythm for soluble protein expression
Undergrad · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/xjtlu-china/
XJTLU-China asked whether soluble yield of hard-to-express recombinant proteins in E. coli can be improved by deliberately programming *where* translation slows down, rather than by maximising expression. Their dry-lab system catmaOS (Codon-Aware Translation Modeling and Analysis Operating System) chains four models: structural co-translational folding priority (M1), evolutionary conserved slow-codon evidence (M2), a five-layer translation-kinetics and ribosome-traffic engine with constrained Pareto selection (M3-A to M3-E), and host tRNA-pool intervention design (M4). The framework picked a single synonymous G-CSF design (W1-S) out of six candidates and an engineered BL21-AlaPro chassis, both of which went to the bench; Four-Leaf Clover RT-qPCR then measured the actual tRNA knockdown and that number was fed back into M3-A as an updated host context. It won Best Model (Undergraduate) and Best Education (Undergraduate).

**frameworks.** catmaOS is a four-model, five-layer multiscale pipeline and is unusually explicit about what each layer is and is not. M1 is a structural-bioinformatics scoring model: it builds a residue-level evidence table from PDB coordinates (G-CSF, PDB 1RHG chain B, UniProt P09919, RefSeq NM_000759.4), runs DSSP for secondary structure and relative solvent accessibility, solves a self-consistent native-contact occupancy model as chain length grows (Jacobs-Shakhnovich) to detect folding events at a 1 kBT free-energy-drop threshold with a 4 Angstrom contact cutoff, adds Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobic exposure, cysteine-neighbourhood scores, DSSP transition and beta-initiation tracks and an AGGRESCAN-style aggregation propensity, then fuses them with availability-aware weights into a 0-100 priority score and shifts it downstream by a 35-codon ribosome exit-tunnel offset (scanned 30-40 codons for sensitivity). M2 is a comparative-genomics model: MAFFT L-INS-i protein alignment projected back to codons with PAL2NAL, GtRNAdb/tRNAscan-SE high-confidence tRNA gene copy numbers per species, a frozen codon-anticodon wobble-penalty table, a tRNA-adaptation-style effective supply W_s(c) converted to within-species relative 'resistance', a top-25%-resistance slow-codon label, a strict same-amino-acid filter, and Henikoff position-based sequence weighting to produce a weighted slow-codon conservation score with an explicit effective-coverage track. M3 is the kinetic core: M3-A decomposes intrinsic codon dwell into decoding (inverse effective cognate/wobble supply with a near-cognate competition term, K_dec = 0.80, gamma_near = 0.50), peptidyl-transfer (proline/EF-P arrest context), basal translocation and ViennaRNA RNAplfold local-unpaired-probability RNA resistance, with four ablation configurations A0-A3 to attribute mechanism; M3-B feeds that rate vector into TWO independent ribosome-traffic backends — a deterministic Ribosome Flow Model with Extended Objects (RFMEO) steady state and a stochastic Gillespie kinetic Monte Carlo extended-object TASEP (5 replicates, SEM bands, warm-up discarded) — and cross-validates them with Pearson, Spearman, concordance and top-k hotspot overlap plus an alpha-beta boundary-sensitivity grid; M3-C maps traffic-safe dwell envelopes, exit-tunnel availability gates, relative contact-order folding demand, a finite-state productive-pathway propagator p_{L+1} = p_L exp(s Q_L dt_L) run over a 0.5/1/2 scale grid (direction called 'robust' only when the sign holds across scales), and a time-weighted unsatisfied-native-contact exposure proxy E_U = sum_L U(L) tau(L); M3-D closes a first-order steady-state mRNA balance M_ss = k_tx / (k_deg,eff + mu) with a scikit-learn mRNA-decay predictor trained on 5,486 curated E. coli half-life records (Chen 2015, Selinger 2003) split gene-grouped 3,883/765/838; M3-E generates synonymous candidates under reading-frame, GC, motif, restriction-site and homopolymer constraints and selects by constrained Pareto dominance over four frozen objectives (maximise terminal flux J, minimise ribosome load R, maximise productive-pathway C4, minimise exposure C5), with exact enumeration for small spaces and NSGA-II for large ones, scored for precision/recall against exact fronts. M4 extends design to the host: it maps target codons to BL21 tRNA genes, clusters and promoters with a weighted K-12-to-BL21 transfer score (S_map = 0.45 S_signature + 0.20 S_ordered + 0.15 S_count + 0.15 I_80 + 0.05 I_200), proposes copy-number reduction or 1-3 substitutions in a 29-bp promoter core against 15/30/50% weakening tiers, and ranks them with a three-model ML ensemble trained on 112,955 measured core promoters from the published MBRS L4 library (Zhou 2025), held out by -35/-10 motif pairs (67,978/7,680/37,297) achieving r = 0.677, MAE = 0.506 on log2(1+strength).

**datascience.** Two supervised models were trained from public measurement data and one from their own: an mRNA degradation proxy (D2) on 5,486 curated E. coli half-life records with gene/protein/CDS-grouped splits, a 29-bp promoter-strength ensemble on 112,955 measured core promoters held out by -35/-10 motif pairs (a genuinely out-of-distribution split, r = 0.677), and a codon-occupancy regression on 107,627 codon-level Ribo-seq observations across 125 genes with a documented 14-nt P-site offset, first/last 10 codons excluded, and gene-held-out evaluation (22,025 test observations). The team audits its own provenance in public: several dataset source fields are annotated 'unconfirmed', 'remains to be confirmed' or 'not an attributed published dataset size' rather than quietly cited. Model 4's proL promoter screen predicted 0.727 (native) vs 0.386/0.366/0.358 (P1-P3); the built strain BL21-AlaPro was then measured by Four-Leaf Clover RT-qPCR, showing rpoD-normalised mature tRNA falling from 63.98 to 23.42 (alaXW) and 6.828 to 2.254 (proL), and those measured numbers were returned to M3-A as a new effective-supply table for a full A-E rerun. The headline wet-lab readout: TolB-G-CSF model-designed sequence in the engineered host reached a mean soluble/insoluble ratio of 0.140 vs 0.075 for the commercial sequence in WT host (DnaK-normalised, n = 3 biological replicates, ~1.87-fold). Crucially the team also reports the negative result honestly — for PfCHT1 and leptin, insoluble bands weakened but no clear soluble enrichment appeared, and the results figure is literally titled 'Solubility Gains Remain Unclear'.

**dataviz.** Eighteen numbered model figures that read as a single argument. Aligned multi-track profiles put six normalised structural feature tracks (F1-F6) above the availability-aware composite score so a reader can see which feature drove a peak; priority profiles are paired with an evidence-coverage track underneath so a high score with thin evidence cannot be misread as a finding. Figure 8 is a tunnel-length sensitivity heatmap (rows = assumed exit-tunnel length 30-40 codons, columns = codon position, fixed 0-100 teal scale, light-grey cells for genuinely unavailable data rather than zero) so the reader can watch high-priority bands migrate as an assumption changes. Figure 11 is a codon-level audit matrix (18 homolog rows x codons 110-121, green = slow in that species' tRNA context, white = comparable, grey = non-comparable). Figure 14 is a log2(candidate/WT) dwell heatmap restricted to edited positions only, with the x-axis explicitly flagged as non-continuous and the legend explaining that +1 means 2x. Figure 16 is a three-panel dot plot of WT-normalised flux, ribosome load and exposure on matched candidate rows, deliberately NOT collapsed into one score. KMC traces carry +/- SEM bands and separate unblocked residence from blocked waiting. Captions state the direction of preference and whether a quantity is measured or a relative model proxy.

**software.** catmaOS 4.02.06 ships as a downloadable Windows x64 source release with Setup.cmd/Start.cmd, a pinned requirements-lock.txt, a private .venv, a local browser workspace on 127.0.0.1:8767 (sequences never leave the user's machine), a 28-page PDF user manual, and four precomputed read-only interactive demos embedded in the wiki with JSON/CSV export. Every run emits a reproducibility bundle: request.json (typed input, label, source, parameters), result.json on a versioned schema 1.0.0 with input hash, module status and reproducibility record, curves.csv, metrics.csv, exact_candidates.csv, native/evidence-result.json and run.log, all zipped per run_id. The design rule stated on the page — 'missing values stay missing' and 'a completed run confirms the requested task finished; it does not imply every model was executed' — is the discipline most teams lack.

**ihp.** A CARE framework distilled from stakeholder conversations: Create Accessibility, Accountable Storytelling, Real-world Alignment, Ethical Design. It originated in a question from Dr Lanlan Han about who actually benefits and how strong the evidence is. The interview timeline is structured as Problem / Design / Scope, and the team documents how it narrowed its own claim: starting from 'boost heterologous protein expression in E. coli', literature and interviews with Dr Antony Kam and industry expert Dr Xijun Piao (CATUG Biotechnology, Suzhou) pushed them to redefine success as soluble usable protein rather than total expression, and to state explicitly that dogmaOS is 'not positioned as a universal protein-production platform'. Mid-stage consultations with Dr Yongtao Zhu, Dr Chun Chan, Prof Sheng Yang (Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, CAS), Prof Zhiliang Lu, Dr Avinash Pandreka (Oxford Suzhou Centre for Advanced Research), Dr Kozo Hamada and Prof Zhongmei Liu (Jiangnan University) convinced them that translation speed alone could not explain folding outcomes, which is what created Model 3 and Model 4.

**publicEngagement.** Best Education winner (Undergraduate). The team built an explicit education framework rather than a list of events: a four-tier 'Lifelong Learning Pathway' (interest inspiration, knowledge building, interdisciplinary co-creation, professional impact) that replaces age-banding with depth of engagement, crossed with a four-stage activity structure (Reach, Construct, Dialogue, Extension) and Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences as the design lens for choosing an activity format. They reached over 2,000 people through 21 activities — workshops, exhibitions and the Learning Mall Premium online platform — and produced 18 reusable education toolkits, with the Extension stage deliberately designed so each activity leaves behind a game, handbook or toolkit rather than ending at the event.

**realWorld.** Target selection was driven by real demand: G-CSF, leptin, PfCHT1 and FGF2 were chosen with researchers and protein-production companies as proteins that are hard to express in E. coli and have clear research or clinical uses spanning public health, rare disease and basic research. The team maps the project to SDGs 3, 9, 12 and 17. Accessibility is the commercial thesis — rather than selling a service, catmaOS is released as free local software so academic labs and iGEM teams with only basic E. coli facilities can do upstream optimisation instead of paying for repeated trial-and-error. Safety is built in: non-pathogenic strains, BSL-1 practice, autoclaved waste, and FLP-FRT removal of the kanamycin cassette after lambda-Red genome editing.

**For GEMS:** Pair every model score with an explicit evidence-coverage track and run a sensitivity scan over your least-defensible assumption (here, exit-tunnel length), so a figure shows not just the answer but how much of it is real data; and keep competing objectives as separate aligned panels rather than summing them into one invented score. Both are achievable with matplotlib by a motivated 16-year-old and immediately make a model honest.

### Uni-Padua-IT — C.O.S.M.I.C. (Cyanobacterial Oxygen Supply for Martian Inhabitant Complexes)
Undergrad · Italy · https://2026.igem.wiki/uni-padua-it/
Uni-Padua-IT engineered the filamentous cyanobacterium Nostoc sp. PCC 7120 as a Martian life-support organism: it fixes CO2 into breathable oxygen, degrades the perchlorates that poison Martian water (via native NarB and a heterocyst-compartmentalised pcrABD plus chlorite dismutase), and carries pprA from Deinococcus radiodurans for radiation-damage repair, behind a copper-dependent MazF kill switch. Because no free codon optimiser listed their chassis, they forked TIsigner into ReTIsigner, a frequency-weighted codon optimiser that reads any of the 35,799 Kazusa codon usage tables, enforces GC bounds, actively excises RFC restriction sites and reports CAI, GC and translation-initiation opening energy. ReTIsigner was validated in silico over 100 sequences and four hosts, then in vivo: a ReTIsigner-optimised eYFP gave a 2.16-fold common-effect increase in specific fluorescence across DH5-alpha and BL21 (p = 0.002, permutation test stratified by strain). They also built an open-source acoustic (piezo + Arduino) bubble sensor so oxygen production can be followed without opening a sealed culture.

**frameworks.** SvelteKit single-page frontend built from scratch, talking to a Flask backend over a single documented HTTP endpoint (POST /optimise); a worker pool behind Flask shells out to the compiled scientific binaries. The whole stack is shipped as a two-stage Docker image (Node.js 22 build stage; Miniconda runtime pinning Python 3.6.9, ViennaRNA 2.5.1 and Infernal 1.1.5) exposing port 5050.

**datascience.** In silico benchmark over 100 coding sequences optimised for four hosts spanning roughly 31-75% GC, recording GC, CAI, opening energy and failure rate with and without a codon usage table: supplying a table cut the failure rate from 52% to 2% while leaving opening energy essentially unchanged (mean difference +/-0.06 kcal/mol). Wet-lab validation used independent cultures as the unit of replication, three cultures per sample each in technical triplicate, fluorescence compared at matched optical density rather than fixed time, two detection channels, and a permutation test stratified by strain; the team explicitly states the confidence interval (about 1.6-2.8x) and what the data does not license them to claim.

**dataviz.** Results view compares input against each optimised sequence in a results card showing CAI, GC content and opening energy, so sequences no longer have to be analysed one at a time in external tools. A built-in guided tour walks a first-time user through every field of the run configuration. Exports in three reproducible formats (CSV, PDF, FASTA), each recording the full run configuration plus the computed analyses. Validation figures (specific-fluorescence bar charts and ratio plots with 95% CIs) are published as SVG on the wiki, and the system is explained with two architecture diagrams: the POST /optimise request path and one iteration of the annealing loop.

**software.** ReTIsigner is a free, Apache 2.0-licensed codon optimiser for non-model hosts, and it is the clearest example this year of forking an existing scientific tool rather than rebuilding one. The team started from TIsigner (Bhandari, Lim & Gardner), contacted its authors for feedback on their proposal, and then added four things TIsigner lacked: frequency-weighted synonymous codon sampling driven by any Kazusa codon usage table (35,799 organisms) instead of one-amino-acid-one-codon, an optional GC bound enforced as a feasibility filter, active position-targeted removal of restriction sites with a re-check for newly introduced sites, and in-app CAI/GC analysis per output sequence. The restriction-site work is the headline engineering result: optimising perchlorate reductase subunit A for Nostoc under RFC 10 and RFC 1000 constraints was still running after 15 hours under the original random-substitution behaviour, and completed in seconds afterwards, yielding registry part BBa_268WDVEB. Architecturally the optimiser sits behind POST /optimise so it is usable headlessly without the Svelte interface, and the Docker image removes the platform problem that ViennaRNA and Infernal binaries create on Windows ('docker build -t retisigner . && docker run -p 5050:5050 retisigner'). It ships a user guide, a development guide documenting the system and its API calls, a video tutorial (https://video.igem.org/w/rN6WnodTKYxiNitzfSUVZ3) that optimises BBa_E0040 GFP for Clostridium acetobutylicum ATCC 824, and a public repository at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/uni-padua-it/retisigner-svelte (team repo: https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/uni-padua-it). It is self-hosted via Docker rather than offered as a hosted public web service, which is the one gap: there is no URL a stranger can click. They also positioned ReTIsigner honestly against the field, reproducing Table 1 of Demissie et al. (2025) and adding their own row with a tilde rather than a tick in the CAI column, and comparing feature-by-feature against the two previous iGEM codon optimisers (HebrewU 2018, MIT 2023). They published an open call for collaboration on 9 August 2026 offering to optimise any team's sequence for their chassis and received no replies, and they say so on the wiki.

**ihp.** Human practices is written as a sequence of questions with an explicit 'what we changed' and, unusually, a 'what we couldn't fix' for each. Consultations with photosynthesis and cyanobacteria professors (Nicoletta La Rocca, Daniela Billi) cut the cold-tolerance module. iGEM Darmstadt 2025, who had built the same perchlorate constructs in B. subtilis, warned them off pcrABCD's oxygen sensitivity, which led to testing native NarB first and then compartmentalising pcrABD in heterocysts. A presentation to NASA's Open Science Data Repository Analysis Working Group moved the radiation module from survival-at-high-dose to genome integrity over generations, and pushed them toward a terrestrial use case (perchlorate in groundwater near propellant plants) when the Moon turned out to have no perchlorate. ESA flight-operations engineers (Davide Vertuani, Paolo Ferri) made them reason about the journey, not just arrival. Philosopher Telmo Pievani and space-habitat designer Serena Crotti changed how the bioreactor is framed within a crew's daily life. Most relevant to a dry-lab centre: they took their hardware manual and code to an instrumentation professor and an electronics PhD student (Simone Del Favero, Samuele Faccin) before publishing, and as a result weakened their own claim (the sensor detects gas bubbles, it does not measure oxygen), redrew the circuit with no crossing wires, documented timing resolution, and added a table separating proven from untested.

**publicEngagement.** A public survey on space research and biotechnology directly reshaped the team's communication: 76.5% of respondents rated using living organisms for oxygen and water highly while only 28.2% rated colonisation highly, so the team separated the usefulness of the technology from support for settling Mars; 42.2% knew little or nothing about GMOs, so explanations of what they modify and why were rewritten more accessibly; and 94.8% called a genetic safety system fundamental or very important, so the kill switch and confined bioreactor were given more space. Education activities grew out of the same consultations.

**realWorld.** The team identified a terrestrial application independent of any Mars mission: perchlorate contaminates groundwater near propellant and pyrotechnics manufacturing and is regulated, and biological removal is already an active research area. They were unable to secure an ionising radiation source (INFN Legnaro's Van de Graaff accelerator unavailable; IOV Padova's linear accelerator caps at roughly 6 Gy/min against a 6 kGy LD50), and report that the pprA radiation claim is therefore untested rather than glossing over it.

**For GEMS:** Fork and extend an existing, cited scientific tool instead of building a new one, and validate the extension at the bench: ReTIsigner's credibility comes from a 2.16-fold wet-lab expression result, a 52%-to-2% failure-rate benchmark, and a published 'what we are entitled to claim' section that names its own limits. A research centre should also copy their packaging discipline, one Docker command plus a documented HTTP endpoint so the engine is reusable headlessly, and their habit of sending documentation to an outside instrumentation expert before publishing it.

### HBUT-China — IGNITE — oHSV2-Neo-IL-2
Undergrad · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/hbut-china/
HBUT-China targeted microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer, the roughly 80-85 percent of advanced cases that behave as immunologically cold tumours, by arming an attenuated oncolytic herpes simplex virus type 2 with an engineered interleukin-2. Their Best New Basic Part, Neo-IL-2, is an AI-guided interface redesign that weakens binding to IL-2R-alpha (CD25) while keeping signalling through the IL-2R-beta/gamma-c complex, so it activates CD8 T cells and NK cells without driving the regulatory T-cell expansion and dose-limiting toxicity that have crippled wild-type IL-2. The cassette was recombined into an HG52 backbone already deleted for ICP34.5 (neurovirulence) and ICP47 (TAP inhibition, so MHC class I presentation is restored), replacing a CMV-GFP cassette at the gamma-34.5 locus. They won Best New Basic Part in the Undergrad section and Best Oncology Project.

**frameworks.** Two named, reusable frameworks offered as contributions: SHIELD, a six-module full-chain safety paradigm covering safety-by-design, wet-lab operational governance, hardware infrastructure assurance, emergency response, training and education, and public outreach; and HOPES, a closed-loop human-centred methodology for integrated human practices. Plus a documented chassis-comparison exercise weighing HSV-1 against HSV-2 across oncolytic capacity, payload size and other dimensions before committing.

**datascience.** AI-assisted protein interface design followed by multi-tool computational triage: molecular docking, affinity prediction, stability and manufacturability analysis, with PRODIGY used to forecast receptor-binding profiles at 37 degrees C and confirm reduced CD25 affinity alongside retained CD122/CD132 association. The design hypothesis is then tested rather than assumed, with SPR used for direct receptor-binding verification.

**dataviz.** Construction schematics showing the HG52 (ICP34.5-/ICP47-) backbone with TRL/IRL/IRS/TRS repeats and the homologous-recombination replacement of CMV-GFP with CMV-Neo-IL-2-BGH-polyA, three-round plaque-purification panels in bright-field, green and merged channels, flow-cytometry Treg percentage comparisons, qPCR and RTCA traces, tumour growth curves and survival plots, and a watercolour shield diagram linking the six SHIELD dimensions.

**ihp.** Patient, clinician and expert interview transcripts were analysed alongside a public questionnaire on understanding of cold versus hot tumours and a review of previous iGEM human-practices cases, organised through their HOPES closed-loop framework. Safety input came from named virologists, including Qiu Yang, a researcher at the Wuhan Institute of Virology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who works on viral vector safety evaluation and animal model assessment, with multiple rounds of interviews on virology and animal experimentation feeding the risk-assessment design.

**publicEngagement.** Tiered outreach designed per audience rather than one talk repeated: young children (storybooks, five published as PDFs), special-needs children and groups with intellectual disabilities, university students, and elderly communities, including a graded calisthenics set with a basic and an advanced version so seniors of different fitness levels can use it. Formats span hands-on experiments, physical teaching aids and salons.

**realWorld.** There is no venture here and the team does not pretend otherwise, so the instructive material is the part and the safety practice. On reusability, Neo-IL-2 is one of the better-engineered iGEM parts because the characterisation is layered rather than single-assay: SDS-PAGE for expression, qPCR and ELISA for transcript and protein, SPR for direct receptor binding, a Treg selective-activation assay and a T-cell activation assay for the functional claim that actually matters, RTCA for real-time cytotoxicity, and crucially a stability test of Neo-IL-2 expression after high-passage propagation of the recombinant virus, which is the test that tells a downstream user whether the part survives in a working vector. They also state the reuse envelope explicitly and in vector-agnostic terms: the coding sequence is intended for any context needing selective CD8 T-cell and NK activation without Treg expansion, and they name oncolytic viruses, mRNA-LNP and chassis strains as delivery platforms it can move into. Eight new parts were built (six basic, two composite), two existing parts reused, and functional annotations and characterisation descriptions on the Registry entries were deliberately expanded, with a named Part Leader owning the documentation. That combination, a design rationale, a computational prediction, an orthogonal physical measurement of the predicted property, a functional assay of the intended benefit, and a passage-stability result, is what makes a part genuinely inheritable rather than merely registered. On safety, the standout is institutional rather than technical: HBUT initiated and led a five-school joint biosafety manual for anti-tumour synthetic-biology projects with four other university iGEM teams (ZJU-China, BNU-China, JLU-FBH and ZJUT-China), covering oncolytic-virus modification operating standards, GMO leakage hazards and waste-disposal guidance, published as a downloadable PDF and explicitly designed with internally unified but differentiable risk-assessment protocols, since the five teams use different carriers. Their reasoning for doing it is the honest one: an individual iGEM team is limited in research vision, experimental conditions and risk-assessment competence, so cross-team safety communication is how those limits get overcome. Safety is also built into the construct rather than bolted on, with ICP34.5 deleted to cut neurovirulence and improve tumour selectivity and ICP47 deleted to restore antigen presentation, and they state plainly that genetic attenuation cannot eliminate risk entirely because viruses are inherently infectious. Wet-lab practice is documented at BSL-2 with risk assessment, PPE, waste handling and training, photographed down to biosafety-cabinet operation, eyewash stations and fridge labelling. The blunt limitations are theirs: the project is explicitly still in progress, systematic toxicity assessment requires expansion to multiple animal models, and the AI protein-screening system needs further experimental iteration.

**For GEMS:** For any part GEMS wants other groups to reuse, publish the five-layer evidence stack HBUT used for Neo-IL-2: design rationale, computational prediction of the specific property changed, an orthogonal physical measurement of that property (SPR, not just docking), a functional assay of the intended benefit and of the harm avoided, and a stability result after many passages in the working vector. Separately, copy the five-school joint biosafety manual: co-author a shared risk-assessment document with other groups working on the same hazard class, since one lab's risk-assessment competence is narrower than five labs'.

### NFLSHS-CHINA — CroTeen
High School · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/nflshs-china/
NFLSHS-China built a fully heterologous crocetin pathway in E. coli (idi, CrtE, CrtB, CrtI, CrtY, CrtZ upstream to zeaxanthin; CsCCD2 plus Neurospora crassa NcALD downstream to free crocetin), then re-engineered it after wet-lab failure from a two-plasmid system into a single-plasmid, two-T7-cassette construct (pET-Ds-Cro) for strain stability under scale-up. They used AlphaFold3, PrankWeb and CB-Dock2 to guide semi-rational mutagenesis of the rate-limiting CsCCD2 enzyme, with the N366G mutant giving a 1.13-fold yield increase confirmed by HPLC. The commercial side is unusually disciplined for a high-school team: a named B2B beachhead, a filed and accepted patent application on the CsCCD2 mutant, two physical MVPs with full formula tables, and an explicit separation of what is designed from what is still unvalidated. They won Best Entrepreneurship and Best Presentation in the High School section.

**frameworks.** Lean Canvas (problem, solution, UVP, key metrics, customer segments, channels, unfair advantage, cost structure, revenue streams), TAM-SAM-SOM with an explicit refusal to take a percentage of the macro market, SWOT, a risk-assessment matrix, a stage-gated Gantt chart from 2026 to 2032, three named exit options, and Techno-Economic Analysis plus Life Cycle Assessment named as future obligations.

**datascience.** HPLC quantification of crocetin as the core analytical readout; mutant screening comparing predicted variants against measured titre (N366G at 1.13x). No fermentation kinetics model or cost model with numbers.

**dataviz.** Nineteen numbered entrepreneurship figures: pathway maps for the two-plasmid and single-plasmid constructs, the biomanufacturing-to-application three-stage chain, a capability-gap table, a partnership-network map with a disclaimer about which relationships are confirmed, a risk matrix, a SWOT quadrant and an SDG panel. HPLC chromatograms carry the quantitative claims.

**ihp.** Five explicitly staged iHP phases, each written as motivation, action and integration, with dates and named interlocutors. Phase I traced the supply chain to source: an online interview with Iranian saffron grower Ali Norouzi (17 March) produced concrete constraints (15-20 day harvest window, 1-2 g dried saffron per person per day, water shortage, currency volatility), and visits to Daofengtang Rende TCM Clinic and chain pharmacies produced a real price point of 60-90 RMB per gram and the observation that pharmacies barely stock it. Phase II is the strongest: after near-zero crocetin yield on 12 May, Dr Huang Danqiong diagnosed metabolic burden and plasmid instability and told them to collapse to a single plasmid, which they did; Prof Huang Guanqin then reviewed the single-plasmid circuit against scale-up cost on 20 June; Fapon's technical director on 22 July pushed them off blind screening onto AI-guided rational design. Phase III used Associate Professor Li Chenyang twice to kill an unstable aqueous formulation on physicochemical grounds and pick the oil and capsule routes, and a perfumer, Ms Weng, taught the actual blending process. Phase IV took the business plan to Attorney Zhang on 17 September for NMPA/FDA classification, licensing and labelling risk, which changed their claims language across the wiki and social media. This is iHP that visibly rewrote both the construct and the marketing copy.

**publicEngagement.** An online survey plus street interviews run 12-17 March 2026 across mixed demographics found over 60 percent of respondents had never heard of crocetin and routinely confused it with crocin, and that over 40 percent would pay only 5-10 RMB per day for a mood-soothing product. That cognitive gap triggered a dedicated education page and a Xiaohongshu (Rednote) account translating biosynthesis into public infographics. They also presented at the 10th iSCRM and the 1st Grand APiC conference, and built peer resources after hearing that team members elsewhere felt unsure their assigned role mattered.

**realWorld.** This is a real venture attempt, not a canvas exercise. The business model is specifically B2B-first: the beachhead is small-to-medium functional skincare brands and boutique cosmetic R&D labs, chosen because they have shorter decision cycles than multinationals, and the first deliverable is explicitly not a consumer product but standardised samples plus HPLC chromatograms to support a customer's own formulation prototyping. Market evidence is real but qualitative: interviews across the full chain (Iranian grower, TCM clinic and pharmacies, boutique formulators, Fapon, an iGEM-mentor founder, a lawyer), a public survey with reported percentages and a willingness-to-pay band, and a visit to Shenzhen University's fermentation facility. They refuse to multiply the roughly USD 2.0 billion TAM by a made-up share and instead say SOM must be computed from reachable R&D nodes times sample volume per test, which is the correct instinct even though they then do not finish the arithmetic. Hard assets exist: a patent application, Carotenoid Cleavage Dioxygenase 2 Mutant, Preparation Method and Application, filed and accepted, and two physical MVPs with published formula tables down to percentages (essence oil at 0.03 percent crocetin, 0.5 percent vitamin E in cold-pressed olive oil; capsule at 70 percent crocetin-olive oil, 15 percent L-theanine, 13 percent soy lecithin, 2 percent vitamin E). The regulatory path is credible and specific, naming NMPA and FDA classification, production and distribution licensing, and the prohibition on medical claims, with a consequence they actually implemented, standardising functional claims site-wide. The continuation plan is a stage-gated Gantt from 2026 lab validation through 2027 customer testing, 2028 CDMO pilot and 2029 B2B commercialisation to 2030-2032 international registration, where each gate has named prerequisite resources and a numeric-in-principle pass condition, plus three exit routes (trade sale to BASF, Givaudan or DSM-Firmenich; technology licensing with royalties; VC/PE buyout). What is genuinely missing is the money: there are no unit economics, no cost of goods, no price per gram, no funding raised, no registered entity and no incubator place, and the partnership map carries its own honest disclaimer that everything except university support and paid service relationships is a prospective contact rather than a formal agreement. They also list, in their own words, the data still absent before industrialisation, including yield, purity, recovery, batch consistency and pilot-scale mutant validation. Even the downside is faced squarely, including the possibility that fermentation's carbon footprint exceeds agriculture's and that cheap biomanufacturing could destroy saffron growers' livelihoods, for which they propose market segmentation that leaves the high-end plant premium alone.

**For GEMS:** Copy their honesty architecture: a 'Current Validation Status' block that splits completed designs from data still required, and a partnership map annotated to say which relationships are confirmed and which are merely prospective contacts. Pair it with their stage-gate habit, where each phase of the roadmap names its prerequisite resources and the single pass condition that unlocks the next phase, so a project cannot drift forward on enthusiasm.

### CalPolySLO — Accessible Science: Expanding the Synthetic Cell Toolkit for All
Undergrad · United States · https://2026.igem.wiki/calpolyslo/
Cal Poly SLO built a cell-free and synthetic-cell platform aimed at putting synthetic cells into undergraduate hands. The science problem is that PURE-type cell-free reactions run out of energy and that commercial creatine-phosphate regeneration is one of the most expensive parts of the kit, so the team screened a library of polyphosphate kinase 2 (PPK2) enzymes, filtered from roughly 18,000 sequences down to 16 phylogenetically diverse candidates, that regenerate ATP from cheap inorganic polyphosphate. To compare those enzymes they had to build the measurement first: a scalable, interference-corrected luciferase ATP assay with matched standard curves, published protocols, OpenTrons scripts and Excel templates. They also designed a 3D-printed emulsification 'washboard' and a tip-wipe recovery step to make hand-made vesicles reproducible, and wrote the whole thing into CHEM 471, a new undergraduate synthetic-cell lab course.
