**dataviz.** Matplotlib-generated SVG figures throughout: an LCA climate comparison separating enzymatic gross emissions, the residue-substitution credit and the net result across three scenarios; log-axis water and energy comparisons; a 25x25 ipTM heat matrix with the intended diagonal outlined and the two mismatch candidates highlighted in orange; predicted Kd on a logarithmic axis with per-model dots and cluster spans; interactive 3D structure viewers with a pLDDT colour mode; a stakeholder influence-versus-impact map and an SDG interaction map, both downloadable as SVG and PNG; survey charts transcribed from original screenshots with each question's own denominator retained.

**software.** No standalone software tool. Dry-lab outputs are the AF3/HADDOCK/PRODIGY screening archive, the ODE reconstruction (independently re-derived from the report's equations and parameter tables on 20 October 2026, with added parameter stress tests), the LCA and nutrient-accounting workbooks, the downloadable activity-classification CSV, and an AP242 STEP CAD assembly of the Ulva collection ROV exported from Onshape.

**ihp.** Twenty-two HP activities across six activity types are compressed into a register of thirteen numbered decisions (D01-D13), each naming the stakeholder, the quote, the change and the follow-up record - and several of them killed the team's favourite ideas. D02 is the clearest: the team wanted one system in which E. coli produced enzymes and degraded Ulva in a single reaction, but Seawin's Technical Director explained that cells and different enzymes each need their own temperature, pH and nutrient conditions, and Vland's Chief Scientist added that cells themselves generate metabolic acid, so the one-step process was split into separate cell-culture and enzyme-reaction steps and the planned pH-based function switch was abandoned entirely (D03). D04 came from peer pressure plus specialist correction: CCiC judges and teams flagged the expression burden of an extracellular cell-anchored cellulosome, and a Shanxi University doctoral researcher warned against loading too many cohesins onto one scaffoldin because of cleavage risk, so the team moved to a free cellulosome, accepting extraction and purification as explicit tasks, and planned separate expression followed by assembly. D05 is an honest unresolved tension rather than a tidy win: the cellulosome researcher supported adding BglC to hydrolyse accumulating cellobiose while Vland warned that glucose would then inhibit downstream, so the enzyme was retained with the trade-off written into the reaction-condition study. D06 dismantled the CBS-inspired shortcut of feeding hydrolysate straight into culture - Bright Moon pressed on carbon, nitrogen and aeration and Vland demanded composition analysis and experimental validation, so growth and enzyme production became separately measured questions, later yielding the observation that at pH 7 a 40% hydrolysate medium supported growth and target-protein expression with a longer lag phase. D07 is the strongest stakeholder-to-design chain: a beauty-salon manager said she would hesitate to trust Qingdao Ulva as a raw material because of possible pollution, which the team carried into a joint consultation with Professors Ning Wu and Jing Wang at the Institute of Oceanology, CAS, where contamination resolved into two concrete, separately measurable requirements - seaweed's high salt content means inadequate desalting could cause osmotic imbalance on skin, so ultrafiltration desalting and concentration entered the sample-preparation plan, and because E. coli is the production host, endotoxin must be specifically measured and controlled for higher-end or damaged-skin use. Biosafety specialist Prof. Zhihang Chen then converted an end-stage pair of controls (heat treatment plus a kill switch) into process-wide control, separating live cells, nucleic acids and endotoxin, each with its own treatment and assessment target, and prompting work on ClearColi and Rosetta chassis compatibility. D08 had Gather Great Ocean puncture the assumption that a mature brown-seaweed business implies a market for ulvan oligosaccharides - its Ulva powder goes to aquaculture feed, and it told the team to first establish what advantage ulvan oligosaccharides have over other materials - which sent them to the two professors for assay methods they could actually run (moisture uptake by desiccator and balance, in vitro antioxidant assays) and added molecular-weight profiling after the 500 Da skin-penetration literature. D13 reframed feedstock itself: the Yellow Sea Fisheries Research Institute separated ecological abundance, visible shoreline biomass and what a processor can reliably obtain, and added sand removal, dewatering and acquisition cost, so the team retained a reduced-supply scenario instead of assuming continued large blooms. Even packaging was corrected - YUTOECO's engineering manager said the proposal was still too broad, so inner contact packaging is now specified around sealing, barrier and storage needs and only the outer layer explores moulded plant fibre.

**publicEngagement.** Engagement was sequenced on survey evidence rather than instinct: of 259 respondents 228 had at least heard of Ulva (88.03%) but only 34 claimed familiarity, and 142 of 263 knew little or nothing about synthetic biology (53.99%), so the booklet starts with everyday coastal effects and existing post-collection uses before engineered bacteria, surface display or cellulosomes appear at all. A harbour interviewee's remark that online video would reach people better than a poster at the pier redirected the channel strategy to short videos on Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, Douyin and WeChat Channels. A joint activity with OUC-Haide (the 17-C collaboration) was cross-checked before delivery and two content errors - a pH item and an mRNA pairing error - were found and corrected, with simulations, three-level hints and a reset path added. Continued participation runs through the school biology club and repeated lessons rather than one-off events, and the team keeps SDG 4 targets 4.4 and 4.7 separate from its claims about measured learning.

**realWorld.** The real-world case is anchored in the existing Qingdao system rather than in a waste narrative: harbour workers, the Municipal Marine Development Bureau and processors described coordinated pier collection, dewatering and drying, trucking to downstream companies, feed and fertiliser uses and decayed material returned to sea - so the team compares four handling routes on cost, product value and nutrient destination and positions UPKeep as an added high-value step, noting Gather Great Ocean's blunt 'there is no waste material'. SDGs are claimed at target level with the team's own numbers: SDG 12 (12.2, 12.5, 12.6, 12.8) carries the LCA, with the enzymatic scenario at 264 kg CO2e/t gross and about 35 kg CO2e/t net when each kg of remaining dry matter displaces 1 kg of soybean meal at 2.75 kg CO2e/kg, 34 kWh/t against 389 kWh/t for the feed-meal route, and 8,800 L/t water driven chiefly by membrane diafiltration; SDG 14 (14.1, 14.2) carries nitrogen and phosphorus accounting to final destination and marine-ecology consultation; SDG 9 (9.4) the process and enzyme-recovery work; SDG 3 (3.9) storage, odour and coastal handling exposure; SDG 4 (4.4, 4.7) education; and SDG 8 (8.2, 8.8) worker protection and cost responsibility. The SDG dialogue partner was Professor Pierre Failler (Economics, University of Portsmouth), whose advice - 'do the economics first, and don't mix the concepts' and 'doing a single project on its own is very difficult, you need a cluster model' - made the team keep the business plan and the LCA as separate documents. The most concrete real-world act is not a product: after Hongdao interviews about slippery coastal working conditions, on 6 October 2026 the team filed a proposal through Qingdao's 12319 public-service platform requesting anti-slip footwear and gloves for frontline sanitation workers, and received an official reply on 9 October describing purchase and distribution of anti-slip equipment, safety reminders, site inspection and weather-based adjustment of operations; the remotely operated Ulva collection vehicle (a 648 x 462 x 419 mm PVC-framed ROV with a forward nylon-mesh basket, published as an AP242 STEP model) is justified on the same worker-exposure grounds. Entrepreneurship is deliberately modest - the first offer is an oligosaccharide research sample plus production route, assay results and a proposed quality-information sheet to cosmetic ingredient developers, with a cream-base-versus-cream-plus-ingredient demonstrator, revenue only after formulation qualification, and cost priorities named as enzyme production and recovery, purification, drying, batch quality and packaging. Regulatory status is not claimed anywhere; residue destined for fertiliser is explicitly excluded where it contains engineered cells, and no packaging prototype has been made.

**For GEMS:** Keep a numbered decision register like UPKeep's D01-D13, where each row is initial idea / stakeholders / what we heard / what we changed / why it matters, cross-linked to the interview record and to the experiment that tests the change - including rows where two advisers disagreed and the tension was retained rather than resolved. Their second habit is worth copying too: push a vague public worry ('Ulva might be polluted') to experts until it becomes separately measurable specifications (desalting, endotoxin, DNA residue, live-cell viability).

### UMA Malaga — Frida
Undergrad · Spain · https://2026.igem.wiki/uma-malaga/
Frida uses CRISPR/LwCas13a (SHERLOCK-type collateral cleavage read as fluorescence) to screen for the mutations behind rare genetic diseases, with cystic fibrosis as the model disease and a tandem gRNA assembly system (Neith) for multiplexing. Because a single disease can have hundreds of pathogenic variants and each needs its own guide, the team built Diana (diana-grna-designer), a free MIT-licensed web app, command-line tool and F# library that goes from a disease name, OMIM number or MONDO id, through ClinVar's variant list, to ranked and scored guide RNAs, to an order-ready oligo list, to a combinatorial pooling plan and a decoder for the positive wells. The engineering is unusually disciplined for iGEM: 1,164 unit and component tests plus 75 Playwright browser tests, automated axe-core WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility scans of every page state, every dependency pinned and checksum-verified, and exports in GenBank, SBOL 3 and SBOL 2 that are read back by Biopython and pySBOL3 as part of the test suite. Most striking, the wet lab contradicted the software's central heuristic and the team published that: the synthetic-mismatch substitution rule did not discriminate alleles in the placements tried, so the rule became an option to compare rather than a promise.

**frameworks.** A single Blazor Server application (ASP.NET Core 9, C#, Razor components over SignalR, Bootstrap 5) calling an F# library ('gRNA') directly in the same process, with the grna CLI as a second front end over the identical calls so the web page and the terminal always agree. Native science runs as child processes: Bowtie 1.3.1 against a GRCh38 no-ALT index for off-targets, and ViennaRNA via Python 3 for folding. Everything ships in one Docker image (Compose v2) that bakes in the genome index deliberately, because Bowtie memory-maps the index and a volume or bind mount makes alignment more than ten times slower. External calls are limited to NCBI E-utilities, dbSNP Variation Services, ClinVar and the Monarch Initiative. The F# library also builds as a NuGet package (unpublished) referenceable from any .NET project, and the repository carries an agent skill so an AI assistant can install, start, health-check and drive the tool.

**datascience.** Validation is reported as a matrix of what each part of the tool rests on, with three honest categories: automated tests, real sequences and services, and wet lab, where 'Tested' means lab work has started with no results yet and 'Not shown' is recorded as a result rather than a gap. Numbers: 1,164 NUnit/bUnit cases (1,151 pass, 13 self-skip when live services or ViennaRNA are absent), 75 Playwright/Chromium tests against a deterministic pipeline stand-in, pooling invariants proved over many (V, K) pairs (each guide in exactly R wells, no pool over K, every guide with a unique well set, consistent addressing on both plate formats), and decoding tested for single hits, collisions and dropouts. Hand checks rebuilt the rs334 and F508del designs from the NCBI sequences and confirmed the top deletion guides occur only in the deleted sequence, 6-8 letters from any wild-type window. The whole web flow was re-run against the real container on 2026-10-18 (cystic fibrosis disease search returning 1,517 ClinVar records, five designs, adapters, structure, shortlist, pooling and decoding). Performance was timed inside the container: 8-10 s for a transcript-position design, 28-38 s for a chromosome-position design (dominated by the NCBI download of the whole accession), 17 s for the disease search, about 1 s for a 100-guide pooling plan and 97 s for 100,000 guides. Export correctness was checked structurally: the annotated parts tile the sequence with no gap or overlap and equal the oligo DNA across all 64 combinations of repeat, adapters, flanks and T7 promoter, and the files are read back by Biopython and pySBOL3 with no error or warning.

**dataviz.** Ranked guide tables with nine sortable columns (spacer, GC score, GC %, homopolymers, off-targets, folding energy, unpaired share of spacer, mismatches against the other allele, score), filters on score, off-targets, GC range, allele mismatches and sequence fragment, the seed region underlined and the mutation marked in red, and status conveyed by shape and text rather than colour alone. Off-target chips read none/unique/caution/6+ saturated; expanding a row lists every GRCh38 alignment with chromosome, position, strand and mismatches. RNA structure is shown as dot-bracket plus a FORNA force-directed diagram rendered inside the page, so the sequence never leaves the machine unless the user clicks 'Open in FORNA'. Pooling produces a clickable, keyboard-navigable 96- or 384-well plate map where hovering a well lists its guides, and decoded positive wells are marked with a plus sign. Every term carries a plain-language tooltip, held in one file (HelpText.cs). Light and dark themes, a skip link, keyboard-operable tabs, and automated axe-core scans across WCAG 2.0-2.2 A and AA for every page state.

**software.** Diana has three chained but independently usable parts. Disease variants looks a disease up in the Monarch Initiative knowledge graph and lists the ClinVar records NCBI links to its OMIM number, showing ClinVar's own classification and review stars without re-interpreting them, capped at 3,000 records with the list flagged incomplete when it truncates. The Builder takes up to 50 inputs per run as rsIDs (resolved through NCBI Variation Services, keeping only the disease-relevant allele by default so rs334 gives one notation rather than twelve) or strict HGVS including c. positions on NM_/XM_ transcripts, which it converts using the GenBank coding range and says so in a notice; a c. position on a genomic record is refused with advice, because introns would put the guides in the wrong place. It then slides a window (23 nt default, 18-60 allowed) over both the original and mutated sequence on both strands, labels which strand is complementary to the mRNA and puts it first because LwCas13a binds RNA, and scores every candidate on four transparent criteria: GC content against a 40-60% target, homopolymer runs of 4 or more, Bowtie off-target hits in GRCh38 with up to two mismatches, and ViennaRNA minimum free energy of the complete guide under Turner 2004. Candidates sort on the ascending key (off-targets, -energy, -GC score, homopolymers), and the derived 0-1 score is explicitly a relative rank, not a prediction of activity. Two structure checks (is the direct-repeat hairpin intact in the fold, how much of the spacer stays unpaired) and an allele-discrimination count (fewest letters by which the target differs from the other allele, with a 'not discriminating' flag at 0 or 1) inform the choice without changing the ranking. The complete gRNA is built from the 36-nt LwCas13a direct repeat plus the spacer, optionally wrapped in the team's own Frida adapter (BsmBI Type IIS sites plus AAAC and GCTT fusion sites, so the repeat is acquired during Golden Gate assembly instead of being synthesised for every guide) and the BioBricks RFC[10] prefix/suffix adapter, which nest correctly so the junctions complete the standard sequences exactly. Cloning checks scan the DNA that would actually be ordered, on both strands, for ten enzymes (BsaI, BsmBI, SapI, BbsI, EcoRI, XbaI, SpeI, PstI, NotI, EcoRV), excluding sites an adapter carries on purpose, and show RFC[10] and RFC[1000] compatibility badges mirroring the Registry's own Assembly Compatibility rules. Guide Pooling then offers three combinatorial layouts (2D Fragmented, 2D Matrix, 3D) with stated well-count formulas, picks the cheapest automatically, places the result on 96- or 384-well plates and decodes a screen afterwards, distinguishing definite from ambiguous implications rather than hiding the collision case; the classic binary log2 model is deliberately excluded because it requires K = V/2 and breaks the five-guides-per-tandem-array limit. For 100 guides at K = 5 that is 40 wells instead of 100 reactions, a 60% saving. Exports: oligo CSV with optional T7 promoter and top/bottom strands plus a Restriction sites column so the warning travels with the order, FASTA, annotated GenBank, SBOL 3 (RDF/XML, Sequence Ontology roles) and SBOL 2 (added only because a libSBOLj-based tool rejected the SBOL 3 file). CSV fields starting with =, +, - or @ are neutralised so a spreadsheet does not execute them. Deployment is local by design: 'git clone https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/uma-malaga/diana-grna-designer.git && ./start.sh', which checks Docker, disk and Compose, then reports success only once http://localhost:5000/healthz answers; about 10 GB disk and 3 GB RAM. There is no hosted design API, and the wiki says why (the 4 GB index and native tools make a public server costly, and local running keeps patient-adjacent data private) and then demonstrates that a HTTP front end would be thin by writing and running a minimal ASP.NET Core /export endpoint over the same library, while labelling that sketch a test of the idea rather than a shipped service. What is live and clickable is the example gallery at https://diana-grna-designer-7723f5.igem.wiki/, which publishes the unedited grna output for rs334 (48 candidate spacers), F508del (36 candidates) and a 100-guide pooling plan, each recording the date (2026-10-19), the commit (19a8e08), the Docker image sha256, the tool versions (Bowtie 1.3.1, ViennaRNA 2.7.2), the exact commands run, and the note that a second run the same day gave identical designs. Documentation is layered: README.md for usage, architecture, configuration and troubleshooting; docs/ for the runtime contract, library usage, a manual test plan and a validation record; and BIOLOGICAL_REPORT.md, which maps each biological step to the code for a non-programming audience and lists the open scientific questions. The 'Extending Diana' section walks a specific future feature (a wobble-aware allele check) through all six places in the codebase it would touch, with a sketch of the F# function. Licence MIT, with third-party licences listed (Bowtie Artistic 2.0; ViennaRNA free for academic use, commercial use requiring a separate licence), and an explicit statement that parts of the code were written with an AI coding assistant and reviewed by the team, which remains responsible.

**ihp.** The human practices team (named Athena) ran an iterative cycle they call BARI: Bibliographic research, Application, Reflection, Integration, explicitly not a linear pipeline, with each cycle able to send them back to reconsider an earlier assumption. The substantive shift was away from treating Frida as a technology gap: conversations with patients, healthcare professionals, researchers and patient associations revealed territorial inequalities in newborn screening across Spanish autonomous communities, differences in care pathways, and the consequences of diagnostic delay, which moved the question from 'can we build a detector' to 'where in the diagnostic pathway could such a tool actually respond to a need'. The team also records that screening programmes are not definitive diagnostic tools and require confirmatory testing, and that the associated wait can cause irreversible damage in infants. The wet-lab feedback into the software is the clearest integration of all: the lab's failure to discriminate alleles, traced partly to G-U wobble pairs that LwCas13a tolerates, was published, demoted the substitution rule to one option among the ranked candidates, turned the rule's positions and spacer length into user settings so revised placements can be tested without changing code, and set a wobble-aware allele check as the next feature.

**publicEngagement.** A survey of 227 people probed public awareness of rare diseases, and the team reported it with the limits visible: 90.7% recognised the importance of early diagnosis and 87.7% knew newborn screening differs between Spain's autonomous communities, but only 11% identified the cost as a share of family income and only 9.3% the true global prevalence. They also surfaced an awareness-engagement gap, with 63% reporting no rare-disease activity in the past year (144 of 227 chose 'none of the above'). Demographics are published in full (gender, education, age, occupation, contact with a patient) and the wiki states explicitly that the sample is exploratory, that the percentages describe the sample and are not estimates for the general population, and that the reference answers themselves need validating before an overall knowledge score can be claimed.

**realWorld.** Frida targets the rare-disease diagnostic odyssey, where heterogeneous presentation and many candidate mutations can mean years of uncertainty and repeated consultations. The project grew out of the University of Málaga's existing screening and early-detection research, and the PIs' professional network provided the first stakeholder contacts. Diana is deliberately shaped for a clinical-adjacent setting: no account needed, nothing persisted, loopback-only binding, non-root container, and local-only deployment so sequence data never leaves the researcher's machine.

**For GEMS:** Publish a validation matrix that separates what automated tests prove, what a real run against live services proves, and what the bench has actually shown, and record 'not shown' as a result: Diana's wiki states outright that its ranking order, its substitution rule and its pooling layout are untested in the lab, and that the lab contradicted the substitution rule. A research centre should pair that honesty with Diana's two reusable mechanics, a pure scientific core (F#) that the GUI, the CLI and an AI agent skill all sit on as thin front ends, and a published example gallery pinned to a commit, image digest and exact commands so strangers can see real output without installing anything.

### UiOslo-Norway — HePatch
Overgrad · Norway · https://2026.igem.wiki/uioslo-norway/
HePatch engineers the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for thermostability so it could be delivered in a dissolvable microneedle patch without a cold chain, benchmarked against the WHO controlled temperature chain condition of 28 days at 37 C. The dry lab scored 2,260 ESM2/Rosetta substitutions on a 238-residue E. coli construct, retained 989 after a ddG filter, and ranked candidates for the bench. What distinguishes the team is that it put the project in front of ethicists, legal scholars, Norway's national research ethics committees, a medical officer in Kenya's highest-prevalence county and a youth-led organisation in Nairobi's informal settlements - and then published the places where those people broke the project's own premise. Each stakeholder round is closed with a 'What changed?' box naming the previous assumption, the new approach and the updated framing.

**frameworks.** A two-phase candidate-prioritisation pipeline for HBsAg substitutions. Phase 1 scores substitutions on sequence, structure and developability features; Phase 2 prepares checked ProteinMPNN and molecular-dynamics packages. Ethical reflection is structured on Kenneth Pimple's three questions for responsible conduct of research - is it true, is it fair, is it wise - with most of the human-practices work deliberately placed under 'is it wise'.

**datascience.** 2,260 ESM2/Rosetta-scored substitutions filtered to 989 by ddG; an earlier construct-v2 exploration ran AlphaFold2 and ProteinMPNN on six candidates, kept as a separately labelled history rather than merged. Provenance discipline is unusually strict: the pipeline records every input, output and source checksum, and the team states that the selected run reuses preserved ESM2 and Rosetta outputs whose original software versions and seeds were not recorded. Geospatial analysis used WorldPop 2020 constrained counts at 100 m, WorldClim 2.1 BIO1 at 30 arc-seconds, GADM 4.1 boundaries and OpenStreetMap amenity and road tags.

**dataviz.** Original GIS cartography made by the team rather than borrowed from publications: population density, mean annual temperature, road network and hospital locations for Turkana and Nairobi counties, rendered in QGIS at WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), with every data source, resolution and limitation stated in the caption. Plus per-variant structural figures (WT, S54T, T56A, T113S) and the recurring 'What changed?' three-column comparison boxes.

**software.** A reproducible released pipeline containing the reusable code, tests and a synthetic example, with a separate archive preserving the selected run and its full provenance history. The model page carries a blanket disclaimer that none of the in silico output establishes expression yield, solubility, antigenicity, disulfide bonding, particle assembly or biological function.

**ihp.** UiOslo's IHP is the clearest example in this set of engagement that attacks the project rather than endorsing it, and every round ends in a published 'What changed?' box. Professor Kristin Bergtora Sandvik (Criminology and Sociology of Law, University of Oslo, fifteen years on the legal and ethical side of global health including vaccines and cold chains) pointed out that in Norway a vaccination appointment is also when a nurse weighs the child, checks for malnutrition, asks after the mother and notices when a family stops coming - so the team had been thinking about removing the syringe and the fridge without noticing they were also removing the healthcare visit. Professor Kristine Baeroe (Institute of Health and Society) refused to let reduced healthcare involvement count as an automatic benefit, and said of the recipients that children are 'the vulnerable among the vulnerable'. The design consequence is explicit: they moved away from designing for full self-administration towards a trained person being present, began investigating community health workers as administrators, and now describe HePatch as replacing a healthcare visit rather than an injection. Baeroe also told them that studying one country in depth beats a general claim about low-resource settings, which is why the project now writes about Kenya and specifically Turkana County; and she made the communication risk concrete by asking them to imagine a patch arriving in a community with no prior context for it, described as a cure, noting that mistrust in that situation is not irrational and that an intervention can be read as something done to a child rather than for them. Then the team did the thing most teams skip: they designed the Kenyan conversations as a falsification test, stating in advance that the alternative they were genuinely prepared to find - that cold-chain dependence was not a leading barrier in either setting - 'would have undercut the premise of the project as a whole'. Dr Vincent Ebenyo, medical officer at Lodwar County Referral Hospital in Turkana (16.8% hepatitis B prevalence in KENPHIA 2018, the highest county figure in Kenya), partly did undercut it: asked for the single biggest driver of low birth-dose coverage he named unsterilised shared cutting instruments used in ceremonies such as scarification and late health-seeking behaviour first, not the cold chain, which taught the team that transmission prevention and vaccine access are two different problems and a delivery-technology fix only addresses the second. He did confirm the core rationale with a precedent - his hospital had already switched from oxytocin to heat-stable carbetocin because local power instability made cold storage unreliable - but located the cold-chain failure specifically at sub-county and outreach facilities rather than the referral hospital, and noted mothers travelling up to 100 km who arrive a week or a month after birth, far outside the WHO 24-hour window. On self-administration he drew a comparison the team had not considered, that insulin-dependent patients are trusted to self-inject after training, while insisting that training must cover recognising side effects and knowing when to seek care, not just application; and he named the Pharmacy and Poisons Board as the body that would need to run sample trials, which is why the team now treats engagement with Kenyan regulators as part of the project path rather than an afterthought. Edwin Odhiambo, June Alfreds and nurse Steve Donell of Youth and Urbanism in Nairobi's informal settlements went further: Odhiambo said flatly that if HePatch can still only be administered inside a hospital, a mother gains nothing from the fact that it no longer needs a fridge, because she makes the same trip to the same limited set of facilities - a distribution and licensing problem, not a temperature one. Alfreds added barriers the team had not identified at all: teenage mothers unaware of the 24-hour window and stigmatised by providers, Social Health Authority registration requirements that undocumented mothers cannot meet, financial dependency and intimate partner violence determining whether a mother can attend at all, and a day queueing at a hospital being a day of lost income. Donell showed that stigma is locally specific rather than generic - in Nairobi hepatitis B is wrongly linked to sexual behaviour and drug use and mentally associated with HIV, whereas in Turkana the same disease is more often mistranslated as an alcohol-related liver condition - and recommended routing messaging through trusted community health volunteers and faith leaders rather than through specialists or the project itself. The result is a conditional value proposition rather than one universal pitch: transport and storage resilience in remote off-grid Turkana, and expanded distribution to non-hospital providers in Nairobi only if paired with a licensing pathway. The team also publishes two arguments against itself - that solving the cold chain for one vaccine could remove a reason to fund and maintain the shared cold-chain infrastructure every other vaccine depends on, and that since the WHO already permits some vaccines outside 2-8 C under controlled temperature chain rules, protein stability may not be the real bottleneck at all - and names its remaining gap honestly, that the Network for Adolescent and Youth of Africa could not attend, so the adolescent perspective 'remains a genuine gap in what we can currently report'.

**publicEngagement.** Education ran from kindergarten upward - children building model viruses and extracting DNA, sessions at Forskningstorget (the Norwegian public research fair), and presentations to biology students - with photo documentation of each. A separate Dialogues page records the conversations held with ethics and legal experts. The notable choice is a principle adopted from a stakeholder and applied to their own outreach: June Alfreds of Youth and Urbanism told them that raising awareness of a vaccine a family then cannot obtain does not build trust, it destroys it, and the team now treats that as a firm constraint on their own public communication.

**realWorld.** The need is framed at the level of a specific failure point rather than a continent: hepatitis B birth dose must be given within 24 hours, the conventional vaccine is an aqueous aluminium-adjuvant suspension that loses potency irreversibly if frozen as well as if overheated, and the cold chain in Turkana holds at the county referral hospital but not at the generator-dependent sub-county and outreach facilities below it, across a county of about 68,700 square kilometres served by eight hospital-level facilities spaced one to two hundred kilometres apart, with mean annual temperatures above 30 C across most of the inhabited lowlands. SDGs are used as tests, not labels: SDG 3 as primary with named targets 3.3, 3.8 and 3.b and a quantitative benchmark (28 days at 37 C, the WHO controlled temperature chain condition), SDG 9 and SDG 10 as supporting, and an explicit statement that these are intended contributions and not measured outcomes. They decline to claim a fourth, environmental SDG at all, writing that removing refrigeration and sharps could cut some material and energy demand but the polymer patch, sterile packaging and manufacturing have impacts, so a life-cycle assessment would be needed before any environmental claim - a refusal that is rarer and more credible than a claim. A trade-offs table pairs each possible benefit with its risk and with what would have to be measured to settle it (for example, delivery closer to home against work shifting to already stretched community health workers, measured by training time, workload, follow-up and user preference). The regulatory path runs through Kenya's own Pharmacy and Poisons Board rather than an external or parallel route. On equity they commit that a patch must not become a cheaper, less supported option offered only where health systems have fewer resources, and that any future use needs the same safety, dose and protection evidence as other vaccine formats - operationalised as comparing HePatch against the vaccination a child would otherwise receive rather than against no vaccination, because 'measuring our option against nothing makes it look better than it is'. What they claim now is bounded: antigen candidates designed and tested, no complete thermostable vaccine patch, no demonstrated lower emissions, lower cost or improved coverage.

**For GEMS:** Design the stakeholder conversation as a falsification test, stating in advance which answer would undercut the project, then publish it when it partly does - and close every round with a three-column box naming the previous assumption, the new approach and the updated framing, so integration is auditable rather than asserted.

### Vilnius-Lithuania — BMClick: One Shell to Click Them All
Undergrad · Lithuania · https://2026.igem.wiki/vilnius-lithuania/
BMClick rebuilds bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), the proteinaceous shells bacteria use to sequester metabolic reactions, in vitro and makes their surface programmable through click chemistry at an amber-codon-incorporated non-canonical amino acid, turning a natural containment system into a modular platform for working with purified biomolecules. The aim is to recover the organisation a cell provides, protecting therapeutic nucleic acids from nucleases, separating the steps of a reconstructed pathway, and extending the temperature and pH range over which enzymes work, while keeping the precision of in vitro conditions. The project also produced functional macroscopic materials from BMC-T shell proteins, and in vitro encapsulation was demonstrated with a HiBiT-SpyCatcher cargo and confirmed by cryo-EM. The dry-lab deliverable is Ladder Detector, a React + FastAPI web app that segments bands in a gel photograph using GelGenie's released U-Net models and then identifies which commercial ladder was run in the marker lane, a step no existing tool automated.

**frameworks.** React web client plus a Python FastAPI server exposing a REST API documented as OpenAPI 3.1 (Ladder Detector API 0.1.0, Apache 2.0), with five endpoints split into a Segmentation group (GET /segmentation-models, POST /segment-image, POST /extract-band-details) and a Ladder group (GET /markers, POST /detect-ladder). There is deliberately no database layer: the application collects and stores no user data and keeps all configuration in files on the server. Deployment is Docker Compose with three services (frontend on 5173, backend on 8000, interactive API docs at /docs), and the segmentation models are pulled at build time from the GelGenie model registry on Hugging Face, so a HF access token is a prerequisite alongside Git and Docker.

**datascience.** The ladder-identification evaluation is the strongest part of the work. The team contacted Thermo Fisher Scientific for the band patterns of its DNA, RNA and protein ladders, scoped to six ladders their own lab uses, and then built a dataset of 172 marker-lane samples by combining their own gels, figures from published articles, and donated photographs solicited from the Vilnius University Life Sciences Center community and the organisers of the International Biology Olympiad. Because the algorithm is not machine learning but still has tunable parameters, they split 30% for parameter tuning and 70% for evaluation, used K-fold cross-validation within the tuning set, manually grouped samples that came from the same source or the same image so related samples could not leak across the split, and stratified by ladder. Four combinations were then tested on the held-out set: Dynamic Time Warping reached 52.42% (absolute run distance) and 62.90% (relative), while adjusted Needleman-Wunsch reached 89.52% and 91.13%. They published per-class tables, stated the two relevant baselines explicitly (about 17% for guessing one of six, about 26% for always guessing the most common class), and diagnosed their own failure case: Protein_6 was consistently confused with DNA_14 because both ladders have the same number of bands, so the gap penalties that normally separate ladders of different band counts provide no signal and only band positions remain. Relative run distance was chosen over absolute despite similar overall accuracy, because it handled Protein_6 better (61.9% vs 47.62%) and is the simpler of the two. Measured end-to-end annotation time is about one minute or less.

**dataviz.** The core output is the annotated gel image itself: upload a photograph, optionally crop or rotate, mark the marker lanes, and the app detects bands and writes the size labels on. Accepted input is PNG, JPEG, WebP and TIFF; the annotated result comes back as PNG. Where automation is imperfect the user gets real editing tools rather than a take-it-or-leave-it answer: a brush, an eraser and a magic wand for refining band detection, plus the ability to override the identified ladder or edit assigned values directly. A project can be saved and reloaded as a .gelproj file carrying the band segmentation and lane markup, and frontend and backend exchange JSON.

**software.** Ladder Detector solves a real and unglamorous problem: gel annotation is done by hand, is repetitive and inconsistent, and the team found that although several gel-analysis tools exist, none automated the annotation step, even though almost every published gel figure is annotated. The pipeline has two stages. Band segmentation reuses rather than reinvents: GelGenie (Aquilina et al., Nature Communications 2025) showed that a lightweight U-Net and nnU-Net clearly beat classical Watershed and Multi-Otsu approaches, so Ladder Detector runs GelGenie's released models, defaulting to the Universal lightweight U-Net (seconds on an ordinary CPU) with nnU-Net and a sharp-band fine-tune selectable. Ladder identification is the team's own contribution, and the design decision behind it is instructive: their first idea was an image classifier over marker-lane crops, which they dropped after a consultation on two grounds, that they could not gather enough samples to train it reliably and that an image classifier would likely latch onto resolution, lighting or gel provenance instead of the band positions that actually distinguish ladders. They moved to numerical data instead, extracting band centroids from the segmentation mask and deriving absolute run distance (distance from the top of the lane) and relative run distance (normalised by lane height). The absolute approach exploits the empirical near-linearity of migration distance against log10(size): for each ladder in the registry, both sequences are min-max normalised, the log sizes inverted, aligned with an adjusted Needleman-Wunsch, a least-squares line fitted to the matched pairs, and the ladder scored by R-squared minus a penalty per unmatched band. The relative approach compares against per-ladder reference profiles taken from vendor charts and scores 1 - RMSE with the same unmatched-band penalty. The process flow deliberately keeps two human checkpoints, segmentation review and marker-lane selection, and the wiki explains why: segmentation is not always accurate, and when a gel has several marker lanes the app has no reliable way to tell which holds the ladder. The API exists specifically so the tool can become one step in an automated pipeline. It was deployed as a public web client at https://ladder-detector.onrender.com, which is the right instinct, but as of checking the service returns 'This service has been suspended by its owner', so the only working route today is self-hosting: 'git clone https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/vilnius-lithuania/ladder-detector.git', add a Hugging Face token to backend/.env, 'docker compose up --build'. Honest limitations are listed: only six ladders supported because of data availability, segmentation imperfect enough to need manual correction, and the classical identification approach possibly improvable by a trained model given a larger dataset. Licence Apache 2.0; it is described as a prototype.

**ihp.** More than 30 stakeholder meetings over 9 months, structured as open dialogue aimed at constructive criticism rather than presentation, with each insight systematically evaluated afterwards and failing approaches dropped. They named the loop the CLICK cycle (Consider, Listen, Implement, Check, Know your limitations) and published five values including Critical Reflection, which they define as examining their own baseline assumptions and being honest about limitations given that parts of the platform could have therapeutic value. Advice is mapped on an interactive timeline where every meeting records Description, Insights, Integration and Next steps, with three explicit revision points. Concrete redirections: alumni from the 2023 'Exullose' and 2025 'iXPOSE' teams set a realistic nine-month scope; the Kerfeld Laboratory advised on BMC assembly and protein modification; Prof. Rolandas Meškys shaped turning in vitro assembling BMC proteins into a modular platform; Dr. Yali Wang confirmed BMC-T functional material formation was possible after the team's own tests had repeatedly failed; critique from Ieva Lingytė (Biomatter Designs) and Dr. Juozas Nainys (Atrandi Biosciences) expanded a narrow thermostability aim into pH resistance testing and pushed them to find more creative applications, which produced the three-branch toolkit; and a consultation with Augustas Rinkevičius is recorded as 'Rethinking our ladder detection', the meeting that moved the software off an image classifier onto numerical band-distance matching.

**publicEngagement.** Education was rebuilt from scratch after a stakeholder told them their plan was wrong. The team had scouted a venue, contacted student organisations and planned to book a music band for one large science festival; Ieva Lingytė, a past team lead, warned them that a bigger event does not mean a bigger audience and that they should go to people rather than expect people to come to them. They scrapped it. The replacement framework borrows Ray Oldenburg's 'third place' sociology: home is the first place, university and formal events the second, and informal public spaces where people gather by choice (cafés, museums, clubs, shelters) the third, where status matters little and conversation is the main activity. Every event was then placed inside a community that already existed, with the format kept flat and walk-away-able for someone with no biology background who had not planned to meet science that evening: genetics discussed through the animals in the room at a cat shelter, fungi taught as a painting workshop ('Science Paints') at the MO Museum, and slots joined at the 'BŪTENT!' discussion festival and the VU Alumni Festival where the audience already existed. They iterated on format too, shortening and sharpening the questions for the second 'Science Talks' after the first showed people wanted more direct ones, and the discussion festival surfaced recognising fake science marketing as the topic people were most misinformed about. Separate consultations with Uršulė Barkauskaitė and Austėja Klevaitė specifically covered adapting activities for older adults, a group the team had no resources to involve meaningfully before.

**realWorld.** Commercial viability was reviewed with industry rather than assumed: Ieva Lingytė at Biomatter Designs and Dr. Juozas Nainys at Atrandi Biosciences reviewed and reprioritised the three project paths, Dr. Ignas Galminas took a pitch on the platform's commercial potential, Eglė Radzevičienė advised on intellectual property and industry realities, and the Vilnius University Innovation department ran a market analysis in October. Therapeutic plausibility of BMC shells as drug-delivery nanocarriers was checked with Prof. Aurelija Žvirblienė rather than claimed. The team also presented at the Nordic iGEM Conference.

**For GEMS:** Build on the published model rather than training your own, and say why: Ladder Detector takes GelGenie's peer-reviewed U-Net weights for segmentation and spends its own effort on the one step nobody had automated, then rejects an image classifier on the explicit grounds that it would learn lighting and resolution instead of band positions. The transferable practice is their evaluation hygiene, a grouped and stratified split that stops samples from the same gel image leaking between tuning and test, stated random and majority-class baselines, per-class accuracy tables, and a published diagnosis of the one class the method fails on.

### BNDS-China — OrbitColi
High School · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/bnds-china/
BNDS-China built OrbitColi, an engineered E. coli probiotic designed to sense oxidative conditions arising from cosmic radiation and microgravity and respond by producing vitamin B2 and trehalose, replacing fixed-dose supplements that degrade over multi-year missions. The scientific framing is quantitative: ISS crews receive 100-200 mSv per year against a 20 mSv occupational limit, and a three-year Mars round trip may accumulate 300-450 mSv. The team's distinguishing contribution is methodological: they invented and applied a five-step education framework, R.E.A.C.H. (Recognize, Experience, Apply, Communicate, Harvest), to every single outreach activity, with a pre-event diagnostic survey and a matched post-event survey, and they report their own failures against it. Integrated Human Practices used a parallel STAR framework (Scan, Test, Assemble, Reflect) across five cycles.

**frameworks.** Two self-designed frameworks, both documented and reusable: R.E.A.C.H. for education (Recognize the audience's pre-existing attitudes before teaching; Experience through interactive formats; Apply by moving the audience from listeners to designers; Communicate to close the loop by harvesting informed project feedback into Integrated Human Practices; Harvest by quantifying the event's success and planning the next iteration) and STAR for iHP (Scan, Test, Assemble, Reflect) across five cycles: problem validation, end-user and market needs, technical design, biosafety and ethics, and production and final-product development. The REACH structure is published in detailed appendices so other teams can reuse it.

**datascience.** Systematic paired pre/post surveying with reported N and percentages, e.g. kindergarten cohort N = 14 matched responses, 21 student athletes aged 10-13 surveyed before and after, 16 valid responses per question from the elderly session, eight older adults aged 68-82 interviewed at the scoping stage, and two school-wide perception surveys on synthetic biology and on attitudes to engineered-bacteria consumption and space microbial applications, all published as downloadable files.

**dataviz.** Before-and-after bar charts of self-reported technique familiarity and interest; questionnaire-result figures published for each activity (pre and post); a timeline figure of all educational activities; pre-interview and final stakeholder influence/relevance maps for iHP, with the honest caveat printed on the figure that inclusion in the pre-interview map does not mean an interview took place.

**software.** The project includes hardware and software components presented to audiences for feedback; the team learned an AI protein-design workflow from team NBJF (generate structure, fill amino-acid sequence, in-silico screening, wet-lab validation) and explicitly reserved wet-lab capacity because high in-silico scores can lose function in reality.

**ihp.** Five iHP cycles (problem validation, end-user and market needs, technical design, biosafety and ethics, production and final product) were each run through the team's STAR loop. A pre-interview stakeholder map linked each cycle to the expert groups whose input it needed, and a final map recorded each stakeholder's influence on the project and the project's relevance to them. The team documented a hard limit transparently: regulatory restrictions prevented them from interviewing astronauts or national regulatory authorities. Aerospace food and nutrition experts defined the nutritional context; space medicine and clinical experts shaped the health-need and biosafety assessment. Education fed directly back into design, most notably the kindergarten children's biocontainment and mutualism questions. A cross-team exchange with team NBJF on AI protein design taught the team to compartmentalise the workflow and to avoid over-reliance on in-silico prediction, and they adopted NBJF's 'phenomenon-first, jargon-later' principle for explaining their AND logic-gate probiotic to lay audiences.

**publicEngagement.** BNDS-China's practice is distinctive because every activity is written up against the same five-step template, R.E.A.C.H., which forces a pre-event diagnostic, an interactive delivery, a design task, a project-feedback loop and a quantified post-event evaluation - and the team reports honestly where a step was skipped. The highest-value example is a kindergarten programme for pre-literate 5-6 year olds. The Recognize step established through a pre-event survey that children already saw microbes as invisible enemies (hand-washing framing) and that 71.43% preferred interactive games to lectures. The team then rendered BioBrick standard assembly as a colour-coded tactile block system: a blue 'switch' promoter block that must come first, a red 'function' coding-sequence block compared to a light bulb, a yellow 'stop' terminator block compared to a vehicle brake, and a green 'little house' vector and chassis block, with assembly order taught as a chanted mantra ('Flip open the blue switch, let the red function bloom, halt with the yellow brake, and live inside the green room!'). Children worked in pairs and trios called 'syndicates' with visual challenge cards posing local problems (make plants glow to light a path to a playground at night; make a flower that masks the smell of garbage). The cleverest design move: the team deliberately rationed parts, giving one table switches but no coding blocks and the next table the reverse, so children had to discover what they lacked, approach other groups and barter - a lived introduction to the open-source iGEM Registry. A five-act puppet show, 'Microscopic Defense Line', dramatised a grazed arm at cell scale, and deliberately avoided weapons or war imagery: the White Blood Cell puppet hugged the bacterium to represent phagocytosis, two red blood cell actors held hands to bridge a vessel, and platelet actors pressed yellow paper against stretchy cloth to show clotting. Measured results from matched surveys (N = 14): before, 78.57% did not know what it meant to pass a function from one organism to another and 64.29% did not know or only vaguely knew what a gene is; after, 92.86% described synthetic biology as 'building blocks', 92.86% knew the promoter starts expression and 100% knew the coding sequence determines function; 42.86% had thought the body fights invaders like 'little soldiers' and none knew clots form, versus 100% afterwards understanding both white blood cell clearance and platelet repair; 100% enjoyed the activities and 92.86% wanted more science stories. The feedback even changed the project: children asked why immune clearance has to kill ('Can't they just change them? Make them friends?') and worried what happens if the yellow stop block falls off, which the team mapped onto transcriptional runaway, biocontainment and biocontamination and used to question their own antagonistic-clearance therapeutic model. Other formats, each with REACH write-ups: a BioCamp lecture on the whole molecular toolkit (PCR, gel electrophoresis, Southern/Northern/Western blotting, qPCR, rtPCR, FISH, CRISPR-Cas9, gene circuits) where each technique was framed by the question it answers, with the team candidly recording that the Apply and Communicate steps did not happen and that students still found the techniques complicated without hands-on work, and publishing the fix (fewer techniques per session, add pipetting and gel loading, one workflow diagram); a formal debate on 9 March 2026 with the BNDS British Debate Club on whether synthetic biology should modify human traits unrelated to serious disease, supported by a purpose-written Synthetic Bio Debate Information Packet covering definitions, design principles, systems thinking, intervention targets, risks, ethics and governance, with pre- and post-debate questionnaires; a campus art exhibition on environmental protection with a pop-art digital painting and an explanatory signboard, made with a visual-arts student, where the recorded criticism was that the symbols were too abstract; a bilingual comic published in the school newspaper BNDS Review and released as downloadable Chinese and English digital versions; and merchandise-as-conversation-starter at the Hongchuanghui Fair and school carnival, with original E. coli, yeast and budding-yeast cartoon designs on postcards, stickers and acrylic hair clips, where the team explicitly explained which features were biological and which were artistic licence. The inclusivity work is specific about barriers. At Tianyun Rehabilitation Center in Liulihe, Fangshan District, Beijing, working with hearing-impaired children and children with genetic conditions, the team discovered the children had no independent electronic devices and that a conventional questionnaire did not suit their communication needs, so after consulting the centre's teachers they switched to an illustrated storybook, 'Little Chef Mimi and Her Magical Yeast Friends', plus a colouring activity, and relied on the teachers to interpret the children's sign language - concluding that inclusive science education is about making sure every child's voice can be heard, not just making knowledge easier. For children with osteogenesis imperfecta ('porcelain doll' patients), the team first interviewed directors of the Sun and Rain Center rare-disease organisation, who explicitly advised against treating participants as fragile or showing pity; sessions were kept short, and when the team noticed holding pens was physically hard for some children, they abandoned the planned drawing activity mid-session for an open discussion and a 'wishing' segment, then shifted their long-term approach to accessible online workshops and distributing game materials directly to hospitals. For 21 student athletes aged 10-13 with limited access to systematic biology teaching or lab equipment, three experiments (strawberry DNA extraction, saliva pH around exercise, ruler-drop reaction tests) tied biology to their own bodies; afterwards all 21 reported confidence in understanding and completing experiments and all answered the DNA and synthetic-biology questions correctly. A lecture for older adults, built on scoping interviews with eight people aged 68-82 whose concerns were medical safety, side effects and the reliability of health information, used genetically modified food, vaccines and microbial insulin as familiar anchors, taught how to spot misleading health advertising and how AI can help check claims, and included making DNA-themed bracelets and illustrated tote bags carrying health-scam reminders; of 16 post-event responses, 15 (93.75%) rejected a misleading miracle-product claim, all 16 answered the GM food, vaccine, insulin and AI-checking items as intended, 81.25% found explanations easy to understand and 87.5% called the activity very helpful.

**realWorld.** The project targets a documented gap in astronaut health protection: pre-packaged vitamins and antioxidants provide fixed dosing that cannot track real-time biochemical change, and shelf-life degradation makes them unreliable over multi-year missions. Education outputs were deliberately packaged for reuse: an openly available children's book, downloadable comic in Chinese and English, the debate information packet, lecture slide decks, bilingual activity PowerPoints, the strawberry DNA extraction protocol, and detailed REACH appendices so other teams and educators can replicate the structure rather than just the activities.

**For GEMS:** Adopt a single named template for every outreach event - BNDS-China's R.E.A.C.H. (Recognize with a pre-event diagnostic, Experience, Apply, Communicate project feedback back into design, Harvest with a matched post-event survey) - and publish the results including the steps you failed to complete; the paired pre/post numbers and the honest gaps are what turn a scrapbook of events into evidence.

### McGill — LanTurn
Undergrad · Canada · https://2026.igem.wiki/mcgill/
McGill engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae EBY100 to display lanmodulin variants on its surface via the Aga1-Aga2 system for selective rare-earth binding, and to flocculate on command through a blue-light VP16-EL222 / C120 optogenetic circuit driving a truncated 678FLO1 flocculin, so that REE-loaded cells can be separated by gravity settling instead of centrifugation. Light-induced flocculation reached 66-75 percent against 24-25 percent in dark controls, and LanM surface display was confirmed by flow cytometry and confocal microscopy. The commercial case is a full industrial techno-economic analysis rather than a canvas: gate-to-gate CAPEX and OPEX, a unit cost of $11.83-20.58 USD per kg REO, a full-scale NPV case study on the Ashram tailings in Nunavik, Quebec, and seven separate sensitivity analyses. They were nominated for Best Entrepreneurship (Undergrad) and Best Biomanufacturing.

**frameworks.** Technology Readiness Levels (NASA nine-level scale, chosen specifically because Canadian cleantech and mining funding programmes gate on TRL) as the backbone of a four-phase staged development plan, each phase carrying goals, named partners, a funding figure and source, and a risk-and-mitigation table. Plus techno-economic analysis in three parts (gate-to-gate, full-scale case study, sensitivity), competitor tiering into direct, substitute and future, a four-option exit plan, a skill-gap analysis mapped against the advisory board, an IP and freedom-to-operate review, and a one-year incorporation plan with a one-pager.

**datascience.** Genuinely industrial-grade analysis. Mass balances built in Excel at a PLS flowthrough of 1,200,000 cubic metres per year, 1 g/L REE and 80 percent target recovery; unit-cost benchmarking per kg TREO against solvent extraction, column-immobilised lanmodulin and a Caulobacter-based bioadsorbent; NPV of USD 51M over 15 years in the high-uptake case versus USD -0.2M in the low-uptake case, with payback of 2.6-5.9 years. The sensitivity work generates actual engineering targets: breakeven at about 23 mg/g adsorption capacity, rising to about 35 mg/g once a 20-30 percent impurity discount on mixed REO is applied; every 5 percent loss of desorption efficiency costs roughly USD 10M of project value; profitability is governed almost entirely by initial PLS pH rather than the bioadsorbent's operating pH; and the low-uptake case goes negative above a 15 percent discount rate. Separately, the TORCH dry-lab project runs GROMACS molecular dynamics with QM/MM to engineer the LanM binding site, including a real debugging story about periodic boundary conditions inflating RMSD tenfold.

**dataviz.** A tabbed entrepreneurship page with a Sankey flowchart of critical-materials flows, a rare-earth demand-and-project-gap chart, a TEA workflow flowsheet, CAPEX/OPEX tables for both gate-to-gate and full-scale cases, a financial-analysis panel, and seven sensitivity charts (adsorption capacity, desorption efficiency, product purity discount, feedstock grade, yeast dosing concentration, PLS pH, discount rate), plus a tolling-model process diagram and an advisory-board gallery.

**software.** TORCH, a QM/MM and molecular-dynamics pipeline for optimising the lanmodulin binding site, with custom scripts for RMSD, clustering, radial distribution functions and explicit oxygen-distance coordination counting.

**ihp.** Over 100 stakeholders engaged, with a consultation map that traces who informed what and who they were referred to next, explicitly arguing that no consultation stands alone. The consequential ones are documented as reversals. They abandoned ultra-purification of REEs entirely after Dr. Michael Free and others showed the separation factor cannot support the claim and that the economics would hinge on only the last 0.9 percent of purity, repositioning instead on selective pre-solvent-extraction concentration. Feedstock choice came from Dr. Jayme Fehyl-Buska and Dr. Kevin Moran of CVW Sustainable Royalties; Ms. Julia Vilela Carvalho of UNEP steered them to fresh rather than legacy tailings for liability and environmental-regulation reasons; Peter van Alphen, Bastien Fresia and Gilles Roy of Nuvau Minerals Corp. confirmed mines have space and are used to disposing of new materials, which is why the process was designed around equipment mines already run, and recommended the tolling model. Protocol-level consultations repeatedly rescued failing experiments: Dr. Denzel Ignacia raised the flocculation induction OD to 3-5, Mira Loock supplied a surface-display-specific protocol at OD 0.8-1.2 that finally produced positive metal-binding results, Michael Bellucci spotted restriction sites less than 30 bp apart as the reason digests failed. Jan Morrill of Earthworks pushed back on their sustainability framing by insisting re-mining can inflict the same harm as direct mining and taught them a Free, Prior and Informed Consent framework. Dr. Yvette Baninla widened the analysis to the geopolitics of offshore REE processing and Indigenous consultation.

**publicEngagement.** They host their own annual synthetic-biology conference, On the Verge, themed in 2026 as 'On the Verge of Running Out: Building the Bioeconomy', deliberately assembling corporate industry leaders, startup founders, policy experts, researchers and students around resource extraction. They also ran school and summer-camp workshops (microbial painting, acid-base chemistry) and are responding to a teacher's request for more advanced genetic-engineering workshops by exploring chromoproteins for new colours.

**realWorld.** Among the strongest commercialisation cases in iGEM 2026, and the only one in this group with real third-party commitments on paper. The business model is a B2B on-site tolling service: the mine keeps ownership and legal liability for its tailings, LanTurn operates a small modular plant on site and returns a concentrated mixed rare earth oxide, which avoids transport cost and keeps tailings-management liability off LanTurn's books. That model was recommended by Nuvau Minerals Corp. and then re-validated at the REM3 Executive Summit with potential offtakers and feedstock providers. Unit economics are properly built rather than asserted: $11.83-20.58 USD per kg REO gate-to-gate, with about 92 percent of CAPEX in desorption columns and resins and 54-68 percent of OPEX in fermentation, compared against solvent extraction (at worst 12 percent more expensive, at best 370-720 percent cheaper on impure low-grade feedstock), column-immobilised lanmodulin (16-100 percent cheaper) and a lanthanide-binding-tag bioadsorbent. The design choices are individually cost-justified, which is rare: surface display versus purified LanM in agarose resin, flocculation versus continuous centrifugation (though they honestly note this saves only $0.21 per kg TREO and is 'not hugely significant'), and light induction versus copper, ethanol or galactose. The Ashram case study is a real deposit with 51 Mt of flotation tailings at about 0.4 percent TREO, giving a USD 51M NPV over 15 years with a 2.6-year payback in the optimistic case and a marginally negative NPV with a 5.9-year payback in the pessimistic case, and they say so rather than quoting only the good number. The headline $560 billion of locked value in tailings is derived, not borrowed: tailings tonnage times REE concentration times market prices, with a 70 percent discount applied for mixed rather than pure REEs, and they immediately contextualise it against a global REE market of only about USD 4.5 billion. Institutional traction is concrete: entry into the Dobson Lean Startup Accelerator at McGill's Dobson Centre for Entrepreneurship in September 2026, ongoing mentorship from Felicity Meyer, a cleantech investment manager at BoxOne Ventures, guidance from Chris Corkery on McGill's research-commercialisation and tech-transfer route, an eleven-person advisory board spanning hydrometallurgy, mining, VC, biomanufacturing and regulatory affairs, published letters of support from Bastien Fresia of Nuvau Minerals Corp. and Dr. Boyd Davis of Kingston Process Metallurgy, real tailings samples already secured from a large Canadian mining company that plans to continue research with them, and named scale-up facilities (Concordia Bioprocessing Facility at 1000 L, KPM's 10,000 sq ft Kingston pilot plant and its biomining division launching 2027, a Sudbury bioleaching facility). The funding plan is staged and specific: about $28,800 across four quarters for the laboratory phase from university funds and non-dilutive grants (NSERC, NRC IRAP, NFRF), then angel and cleantech VC after incorporation, with later phases pointing at NRCan's CMRDD programme (typically $4M+ for TRL 6-8) and MICA Canada (up to $2.5M for TRL 7-9), benchmarked against actual biomining raises (Allonnia USD 20M Series A, pH7 USD 32M Series B). The IP work is the real thing rather than a slogan: they checked that the foundational yeast surface-display patents US6699658B1 and US7465787B2 have expired, identified live LanM patents (CA3170828A1, CA3223988A1, US20240183787A1) and a pending Princeton application WO2025240129A2 that explicitly claims EL222/C120 optogenetics in S. cerevisiae, and concluded they must differentiate technically, disclose to McGill's Tech Transfer Office before publishing anything patentable, and run a formal freedom-to-operate analysis. Blunt caveats: there is no incorporated company yet, only a one-year incorporation plan; no revenue, no signed tolling contract and no term sheet; and they state outright that many TEA parameters are literature estimates rather than their own measurements, which is exactly why the sensitivity analysis exists as a de-risking to-do list for the wet and dry labs. Their ethical self-assessment is unusually unflattering, admitting LanTurn neither remediates tailings nor meaningfully reduces their volume, that re-mining can reintroduce mining harms to communities that have not seen a project for decades, and that the rare earths will mostly end up in consumer goods and defence rather than the clean-energy story, with a stated commitment not to market it otherwise.

**For GEMS:** Run the techno-economic analysis early and let its sensitivity results set the lab's experimental targets: McGill's TEA produced a hard number (about 35 mg/g adsorption capacity once the mixed-oxide impurity discount is applied) that became the wet lab's de-risking goal, which is how commercialisation work earns its place rather than sitting beside the science. Pair that with their TRL-staged plan, where each phase names its funding figure, funding source and named partner facility, so an institution can see exactly what the next stage costs and who must say yes.

### NBJF — AI-assisted de novo design of a thermostable TdT for enzymatic DNA synthesis
High School · China · https://2026.igem.wiki/nbjf/
NBJF tackled the write step of DNA data storage. Enzymatic DNA synthesis using terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) avoids the toxic chemistry of phosphoramidite synthesis, but wild-type TdT has a melting temperature of roughly 40 C and a catalytic pocket that does not accommodate bulky modified nucleotides. Over seven Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles the team built an AI-assisted de novo protein design pipeline (RFdiffusion backbone generation, ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN inverse folding, ESMFold and AlphaFold refolding checks, TemStaPro and SaProt thermostability scoring), screened a large candidate library down to a shortlist, expressed 85 designs, and obtained a de novo TdT that retains DNA extension activity at elevated temperature and accepts oxyamino-modified nucleotides. A final cycle used 100 ns molecular dynamics at 300/350/400 K to explain why.

**frameworks.** Structure-based generative protein design plus all-atom molecular dynamics, not kinetic modelling. The design loop is: functionally constrained RFdiffusion backbone generation (motif scaffolding, keeping the DNA-binding region and active site as constraints) -> ProteinMPNN/LigandMPNN inverse folding (LigandMPNN used for sequence design in the DNA-containing structural environment) -> ESMFold for structural recovery -> AlphaFold refinement -> TemStaPro (sequence-based) and SaProt (structure-based) thermostability scoring. Cycle 7 is a full biophysics workflow: AlphaFold 3 protein-DNA-dATP-2Mg2+-Na+ complex model, ORCA quantum-chemical geometry optimisation of dATP, RESP charges via Multiwfn, AmberTools parameterisation, ff19SB protein / OL21 DNA / OPC water / GAFF ligand force fields, energy minimisation, NVT heating, NPT density equilibration with gradual restraint release, then 100 ns production runs per system at 300 K, 350 K and 400 K.

**datascience.** Library-scale screening with explicit multi-metric criteria instead of a single score: two independent design batches of 100 backbones each, 1,000 inverse-folded sequences per backbone, scored on both RMSD to the design target and pLDDT, yielding 94 candidates meeting both thresholds. Later cycles add cross-model agreement (ESMFold recovery plus two orthogonal thermostability predictors) and a spatial-placeholder strategy to enlarge the catalytic pocket. Experimental side: 85 de novo sequences expressed under one unified B0034/expression framework, 25 giving detectable SDS-PAGE expression - reported as an application dataset rather than a success claim.

**dataviz.** Quantitative screening plots rather than decoration: RMSD-versus-pLDDT scatter of the whole candidate library showing the trade-off and the small fraction satisfying both criteria, representative predicted-structure overlays showing the failure mode (compact Rossmann-like folds instead of the open catalytic conformation), and MD analysis panels for RMSD, RMSF, DSSP secondary-structure occupancy, hydrogen-bond counts, radius of gyration, SASA, free-energy landscapes and Markov state model populations. The engineering page also carries a reading-guide layout that routes a non-specialist through four entry points.

**software.** No standalone released application, but the team wrote automated scripts chaining backbone generation, sequence design, structural validation, candidate screening and MD analysis, and publish this as a reproducible, scalable de novo protein design workflow explicitly intended to lower the barrier for future iGEM teams. The Software special-award page was not among the project's own pages.

**ihp.** An ASK -> LISTEN -> REFLECT -> INTEGRATE -> EVALUATE framework applied across four milestones, with the team stating up front that they did not want Human Practices to be a photo album. The decisive conversation was with Li Yang, an information-storage professional at Huawei, who pointed out that storage density alone decides nothing and that write/read/reliability/maintenance costs govern adoption - after which the team explicitly abandoned 'build a DNA storage device' and narrowed to the enzymatic-writing bottleneck. Han Minghao (synthetic biology / DNA engineering) then identified TdT thermostability, substrate compatibility and reaction controllability as the specific handles. Later stages cover intellectual property (two lawyers, Zhang and Wu, on who owns an AI-designed protein and on open science versus commercialisation), sustainability (Mr Liao on agricultural production, leading to a stated sustainability position on whether enzymatic synthesis is genuinely greener), and a Responsible AI section. Eight stakeholder categories were mapped.

**publicEngagement.** A seven-stage education programme that is unusually serious about access rather than reach: synthetic biology classes in schools; accessibility work including sign-language science communication and multilingual courses; creative formats (picture books, board games, art activities); community-specific sessions; digital microlearning; an explicit 'Inclusion and Equal Opportunities in STEM' stage; and international/cross-school scientific exchange. The team also co-built an educational website referenced by ZQT-Nanjing.

**realWorld.** The project is positioned as a tool-enzyme improvement inside a named industrial bottleneck rather than a finished product, which is the right call and was itself a Human Practices outcome. Deliverables for reuse: six new coding parts (BBa_263ET0E5 De novo TdT as the primary characterised part, plus five sequence-diverse variants BBa_26DIWVPI, BBa_266N6QG1, BBa_26BMB5EM, BBa_26NOOCP1, BBa_26YHUEKK), new application data added to the existing RBS BBa_B0034 documenting its behaviour across a library of 85 artificially designed coding sequences, and the automated de novo design workflow itself. The IP strand is unusually mature for a high-school team: they asked practising lawyers who owns an AI-generated sequence before assuming they could license it.

**For GEMS:** This is the ceiling, not the benchmark: the generative-design half (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, ESMFold, AlphaFold, TemStaPro) is genuinely reachable by a strong high-school team in one season because the tools are free, documented and runnable on Colab-class GPUs, but Cycle 7 - ORCA quantum chemistry, RESP charge fitting, four-force-field Amber parameterisation and 100 ns MD at three temperatures with Markov state analysis - is not something students assemble unaided. The limiting factors there are mentorship and compute in that order; a Taiwanese programme could reproduce NBJF's screening pipeline with a laptop and a cloud GPU, but would need a university collaborator to attempt the MD.

### SDU-Denmark — Shewanode
Overgrad · Denmark · https://2026.igem.wiki/sdu-denmark/
SDU-Denmark engineered Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 to improve extracellular electron transfer and built the hardware to measure it: first a two-chamber microbial fuel cell as proof of concept, then a single-chamber design with an air-breathing cathode and carbon felt electrode that became the team's primary electrochemical measurement system. The measurement work centres on the outer membrane vesicles that carry the MtrCAB cytochrome complex, asking how to isolate them reproducibly and how to quantify their size, morphology, charge and concentration. Each question is answered with complementary methods, each with stated calibration, controls, replicates and limitations. Along the way the team documented a working anolyte recipe, which the literature generally leaves as 'Shewanella basal medium', and released it for other teams.

**frameworks.** The measurement page is structured by goal rather than by technique: each goal states the question, the method, the calibration, the controls and replicates, the results, a discussion and an explicit limitations section. Complementary quantitative and qualitative methods are paired deliberately (preparative size exclusion chromatography with quantitative BCA; qualitative helium ion and scanning electron microscopy with quantitative DLS and zeta potential), and the team states where a method cannot support a claim.

**datascience.** Vesicle isolation is verified rather than assumed. A BCA assay against a BSA dilution series at 562 nm gives the standard curve, and each size-exclusion fraction is then measured twice, once untreated and once lysed with Triton X-100 for 10 minutes on ice, with an isolation-buffer-plus-Triton control confirming the detergent itself does not shift absorbance. The lysed fractions read 100 to 200 ug/mL against lower unlysed values, which is the argument that intact vesicles are present and only open on lysis; fractions above 2 mg/mL are explicitly flagged as exceeding the assay's upper linear range and excluded from interpretation. Morphology is imaged by helium ion microscopy and SEM and quantified in Fiji (wildtype n = 29 particles, mean Feret diameter 288.3 +/- 97.9 nm, circularity 0.837; mutant n = 18, 300.6 +/- 69.6 nm, circularity 0.767), and the team then states that without a buffer-only blank slide taken through the same fixation and drying the structures cannot be definitively identified as vesicles, and that some sharp-edged objects may be crystallised solvent. Size, concentration and charge come from a Malvern Zetasizer Advance Ultra Red Label with every instrument setting published (material refractive index 1.45, absorption 0.001, 25 C, dispersant RI 1.33, viscosity 0.887, dielectric constant 78.5), three biological replicates from different colonies, and technical replicates where the instrument allowed.
